Preface 

"This is a very active jurisdiction, as to which there are keen differences in thought and conviction, not merely as to the form and manner of the remedy, but the scope of the remedy itself. 

It is, therefore, not to be expected that the practice of today on this subject will have the same measure of permanency as on another dealing with titles to property." 

Thus wrote Mr. Biddle on September 23, 1912, in the preface to the second edition of his New Jersey Divorce Practice, a most remarkable book, as our older practitioners know, for the soundness of its statements, the accuracy of its references and the wisdom of its conclusions.

A period of more than twenty-five years has elapsed since Mr. 

Biddle wrote his preface. During that period, as he wisely foresaw, the practice has undergone important changes. So also our "keen differences in thought and conviction," as he expressed it, have wrought substantial developments in the substantive law. 

Inestimable assistance in the preparation of the chapter on Process and Procedure in Divorce and Nullity Suits and the accompanying forms has been furnished by Norman T. Rogers, Esq., whose experience in this branch of the subject is unique. If the labors of his office may be lightened by a better understanding on the part of practitioners of the principles underlying the acquisition of jurisdiction over defendants in divorce and nullity cases, because of the restatement of those principles under his supervision, he will not be more gratified than the author. 

This foreword would be more than incomplete if I failed to acknowledge gratefully the part performed in the formulation of this work by my colleague and partner, William A. Kaufmann. 

Without his earnest efforts and inspiration, this book could not have been possible. 

Union County Court House, Elizabeth, N. J. 

October 21, 1938.

DOUGAL HERR

Statutes Relating to Divorce, Nullity and Alimony 

1 R. S. (1937) 2:50-1 et. seq.¹ 

CAUSES FOR  

2:50-1 [1]. Decrees of nullity of marriage may be rendered in all cases, when:

Prior Marriage. Either of the parties has another wife or husband living at the time of a second or other marriage; 

Prohibited Degrees. The parties are within the degrees prohibited by law. When any such marriage shall not have been annulled during the lifetime of the parties the validity thereof shall not be inquired into after the death of either party; 

Impotence. The parties, or either of them, were at the time of marriage physically and incurably impotent, provided the party making the application shall have been ignorant of such impotency or incapability at the time of the marriage, or has not subsequently ratified the marriage; 

Incapacity to consent. The parties, or either of them, were at the time of marriage incapable of consenting thereto and the marriage has not been subsequently ratified, provided that where the party capable of consent is the applicant, such party shall have been ignorant of the other's incapacity at the time of the marriage and shall not have confirmed the marriage subsequently to the regaining of capacity by the other party; 

Wife under age. At the suit of the wife, when she was under the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage, unless such marriage be confirmed by her after arriving at such age; 

Husband under age. At the suit of the husband, when he was under the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage, unless such marriage be confirmed by him after arriving at such age. 

No decree of nullity shall be made where a child of the parties has been born, either before or after the marriage, or is likely to be born, unless the court upon an examination of all the facts of 

1. The section number of the Divorce Act of 1907 follows in brackets the section number of the Revised Statutes of 1937. The 1938 laws have also been included. 1

the case shall be of the opinion that such decree will not be against the best interest of the child.

CAUSES FOR Divorce from BOND OF MATRIMONY 2:50-2 [2]. Divorce from the bond of matrimony may be decreed for the following causes:

Adultery. Adultery by either of the parties; 

Desertion. Willful, continued 2 and obstinate desertion for the term of two years;

Extreme cruelty. Extreme cruelty by either of the parties, whether the acts of cruelty have been heretofore or are hereafter committed; provided, that no petition for divorce on the ground of extreme cruelty shall be filed until after six months from the date of the last act of cruelty complained of in the petition, but this proviso shall not be held to apply to any counterclaim. (As amended in 1938).

CAUSES FOR DIVORCE FROM BED AND BOARD 

2:50-3 [3]. Divorce from bed and board may be decreed for the following causes:

Adultery. Adultery by either of the parties; 

Desertion. Willful, continued and obstinate desertion for the term of two years;

Extreme cruelty. Extreme cruelty by either of the parties. 

LIMITED OR PERMANENT SEPARATION-SUSPENSION AND REVOCATION 

2:50-4 [3]. In all cases of divorce from bed and board the court may decree a separation forever thereafter, or for a limited time, as shall seem just and reasonable, with a provision that in case of a reconciliation at any time thereafter the parties may apply for a revocation or suspension of the decree. Upon such application the court shall make such order as may seem just and reasonable.

ADULTERY-COLLUSION, CONSENT AND RECRIMINATION 

2:50-5 [28]. If it appear to the court that the adultery complained of shall have been occasioned by the collusion of the 

2. Effect of imprisonment, see 1 R. S. (1937) 2:50-6 post.

parties, and done with an intention to procure a divorce, or that the petitioner was consenting thereto, or that both parties have been guilty of adultery not condoned, no divorce shall be decreed. 

IMPRISONMENT AS AFFECting DesertION 

2:50-6 [31]. Willful and obstinate desertion shall be construed to be "continued" within the meaning of this chapter, even though after such desertion has begun the deserting party has been imprisoned in this or any other state or any other state or country upon conviction by due process of law for a crime, misdemeanor or offense, not political, committed in this or any other state or country, or for any other reason shall have been under restraint either by due process of law or his voluntary act. 

JURISDICTION OF COURT OF CHANCERY 2:50-7 [4]. The court of chancery shall have jurisdiction in all causes of divorce or nullity and of alimony and maintenance by this chapter directed and allowed. 

JURISDICTION-AFFIDAVIT OF NON-COLLUSION 

2:50-8 [8]. The court of chancery shall not have jurisdiction of any cause for divorce, or nullity of marriage under this chapter, except annulment of marriage brought under the general equity jurisdiction of the court, unless the petitioner or counter claimant shall make his oath or affirmation, which shall be annexed to the petition or counterclaim, that his petition or counterclaim is not made by any collusion between him and the defendant or the petitioner or complainant, as the case may be, but in truth and good faith, for the causes set forth in the petition. 

Every petition or counterclaim for annulment of marriage brought under the general equity jurisdiction of the court, shall have annexed thereto an affidavit made by the petitioner or counterclaimant that his petition or counterclaim is not made by any collusion between him and the defendant or the petitioner or complainant, as the case may be, but in truth and good faith, for the causes set forth in the petition.

RESIDENTIAL REQUIREMENTS IN DIVORCE AND NULLITY SUITS 2:50-9 [5]. NULLITY SUITS. Jurisdiction in suits for nullity of marriage may be acquired:

Personal service. a. By personal service of process upon the defendant within this state when either party is a bona fide resident of this state at the time of the commencement of the suit; 

Publication and Substituted Service. b. When the defendant cannot be served personally within this state, and when at the time of the commencement of the suit the petitioner is a bona fide resident of this state, jurisdiction may be acquired by publication, to be followed, where practicable, by service upon or notice to the defendant without this state or by additional substituted service upon the defendant within this state, as prescribed by law or by rules of court. 

2:50-10 [6]. DIVORCE SUITS. When There is Personal Serv ice. For purposes of divorce, either absolute or from bed and board, jurisdiction may be acquired by personal service of process upon the defendant within this state, under the following conditions: a. When, at the time the cause of action arose, either party was a bona fide resident of this state, and has continued so to be down to the time of the commencement of the suit, except that no suit for absolute divorce shall be commenced for any cause other than adultery, unless one of the parties has been for the two years next preceding the commencement of the suit a bona fide resident of this state; b. When, since the cause of action arose, either party has become, and for at least two years next preceding the commencement of the suit has continued to be, a bona fide resident of this state; provided the cause of action alleged was recognized in the jurisdiction in which such party resided at the time the cause of action arose, as a ground for the same relief asked for in the suit in this state. 

2:50-11 [7]. DIVORCE SUITS. Where Service By Publication. 

When the defendant cannot be served personally with process within this state, and when at the time of the commencement of the suit the petitioner is a bona fide resident of this state, jurisdiction for the purpose of divorce, whether absolute or from bed and board, may be acquired by publication, to be followed, where practicable, by service upon or notice to the defendant without this state, or by additional substituted service upon the defendant within this state, as prescribed by law or rules of court, under the following conditions: a. When at the time the cause of action arose, the petitioner was a bona fide resident of this state, and has continued so to be down to the time of the commencement of the suit, except that

no suit for absolute divorce shall be commenced for any cause other than adultery, unless the petitioner has been for the two years next preceding the commencement of the suit a bona fide resident of this state; b. When, since the cause of action arose, the petitioner has become, and for at least two years next preceding the commencement of the suit has continued to be, a bona fide resident of this state; provided, the cause of action alleged was recognized in the jurisdiction in which the petitioner resided at the time the cause of action arose, as a ground for the same relief asked for in the suit in this state.

PUBLICATION AND SUBSTITUTED SERVICE OF PROCESS IN DIVORCE AND NULLITY SUITS 

2:50-12 [14]. If it shall appear, by affidavit or otherwise, to the satisfaction of the chancellor, that the defendant is out of this state, or cannot upon due inquiry be found therein or conceals. himself within this state, the chancellor may thereupon by order direct the defendant to answer the petition at a certain day named therein not less than two or more than six months from the date of such order. The order or notice thereof shall be published in one of the newspapers published in this state, and designated in such order. The first publication shall be made within twenty days from the date of the order and three publications shall be made thereafter, at least one in each of the three next succeeding calendar weeks, making four publications, one in each of four successive calendar weeks. The order or notice thereof shall be published in such other manner as the particular circumstances of the case may require, if, in the opinion of the chancellor, any further or other publication shall be necessary. 

Service upon the defendant within or without this state of the petition and of such order or notice thereof as service substituted for personal service of process within this state shall also be made within the same time and in such manner as the chancellor may by general rule prescribe.

PUBLICATION EFFECT OF APPEARANCE 

The 1938 legislature has enacted:

In all suits for nullity of marriage or divorce, if a defendant, as to whom an order of publication shall have been made, shall, 3. See Chancery Rule 277.

whether before, during or after publication, appear by the filing of an answer or otherwise, the court shall be deemed to have acquired jurisdiction, notwithstanding that no publication has been made, or, if made, it has not been completed, and the cause may proceed against such defendant in the same manner as if personal service of a citation had been made upon such defendant, but only after service upon such defendant of the petition and such order of publication, or notice thereof, in the manner prescribed by section 2:50-12 of the Revised Statutes, and in such case no publication, or further publication, as the case may be, need be made after such appearance. (L. 1938 c. 191). 

COUNTERCLAIM AND SERVICE THEREOF 4 2:50-13 [L. 1916 c. 57 § 1]. Whenever the court of chancery shall have acquired jurisdiction of any suit under the provisions of this chapter, the defendant therein may, by counterclaim, present to the court any counter suit or cause of action against the petitioner or complainant, which might be brought or charged by the defendant against the petitioner or complainant under the provisions of this chapter.

Upon proof of service of such counterclaim upon the petitioner or complainant, or his solicitor, the court shall have full jurisdiction of such counter suit or cause of action without further service of process.

MINORS AS Parties 

2:50-14 [L. 1915 c. 299 § 1]. A man who has attained the age of eighteen years and a woman who has attained the age of sixteen years may appear and prosecute or defend a suit for divorce or nullity of marriage in his or her proper person or by his or her solicitor. 

2:50-15 [L. 1915 c. 299 § 2]. A parent or guardian shall not be prevented, under the provisions of this chapter from prosecuting or defending any suit respecting the marriage status or relation of such infant.

PARTICEPS CRIMINIS AS PARTY 

2:50-16 [17]. Anyone charged as a particeps criminis shall be made a party, upon his or her due application to the court, subject to such terms and conditions as the court may prescribe. 

4. See Chancery Rule 280.

ASSIGNMENT OF SOLICITOR IN EX PARTE CASES 

2:50-17 [18]. In all uncontested cases where the court may deem it necessary or proper, a disinterested solicitor may be assigned actively to defend the case.

FORMA PAUPERIS 5 

2:50-18 [29]. Whenever any poor person shall have cause of suit under this chapter, and shall make an affidavit that he is not worth one hundred dollars clear estate, the chancellor may, at his discretion, assign to such person a solicitor and counsel learned in the law, to prosecute the cause, who, together with all other officers, shall perform their respective duties therein without fee or reward.

PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE 2:50-19 [9]. PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE GOVERNING. The like process and procedure in suits for divorce or nullity of marriage, including suits for annulment of marriage brought under the general equity jurisdiction of the court, shall be had and pursued as are usually had and pursued in other causes in the court of chancery, except so far as other process and procedure is prescribed by or under the authority of this chapter. 

2:50-20 [19]. AMENDMENTS. Proceedings in any suit com menced under this chapter shall not be set aside, annulled or made void for any defect in matter of form or for any mistake or omission not affecting the real merits of the cause, and the chancellor may permit either party to amend his proceedings in the cause, either in matters of form or substance, and proceed to give judgment according to the merits of the case. 

2:50-21 [32]. RULES BY CHANCELLOR. The chancellor shall, from time to time, make such rules and orders regulating the practice and procedure under this chapter as may, in his judgment, render the proceedings more efficient and simple and prevent unnecessary cost and delay. 

2:50-22 [10]. PETITION IN DIVORCE AND NULLITY SUITS. All suits in the court of chancery for divorce or nullity of marriage, including suits for annulment of marriage brought under the general equity jurisdiction of the court, shall be commenced by the filing of a petition or a counterclaim, when permitted by section 2:50-13 of this title, with the clerk of the court, which shall plainly 

5. See Chancery Rules 287-289.

and fully state the grounds of the application for such divorce or nullity and the relief prayed. 

2:50-23 [11]. CITATION AND CERTIFIED COPY OF PETITION. 

Upon filing a petition the clerk shall make a certified copy thereof to be served on the defendant together with a citation for the defendant to answer.

The citation shall be under the seal of the court, be tested in the name of the chancellor and be substantially in the form contained in section 2:50-24 of this title. 

2:50-24 [L. 1916 c. 64 § 5]. FORM OF CITATION. New Jersey, to wit: The state of New Jersey to greeting: You are hereby cited to answer the petition of a copy of which petition is herewith served upon you, by filing your answer in writing in the office of the clerk of the court of chancery at Trenton, within twenty days after the service, upon you, of this writ and in default of your so doing such order or decree will be made against you as the court shall think equitable and just. 

Witness, his Honor. 

Chancellor of our said state, at 

Trenton, the day of .. 19... .Solicitor. .. Clerk. 

2:50-25 [12, 13]. SERVICE OF CITATION. The sheriff or cor oner, as the case may require, of any county, to whom the citation and certified copy of petition shall be delivered shall serve the same and make return of the citation into the court, and the same shall be filed with the clerk. The citation shall be served by delivering to the defendant personally a copy thereof, together with the certified copy of the petition. 

2:50-26 [15]. ANSWER AND REPLICATION. The defendant shall file an answer to the petition within twenty days after the service, upon him, of the citation, if it be returned "served" or "cited" by the sheriff or coroner, or within the time limited by the order for publication and substituted service, unless in either case the court grants further time for that purpose. The answer shall plainly and fully set forth the defense and shall not be sworn to. 

No replication shall be necessary to put the cause at issue. 

2:50-27 [16; L. 1902 c. 135 § 1]. FAILURE TO ANSWER; TES- TIMONY OF WITNESS IN ANOTHER STATE. If the defendant shall not file an answer within the time limited by this chapter or granted by the court, the court may make an order that the petitioner proceed to take depositions and other evidence and bring on the hearing of the cause ex parte. 

When the defendant has not entered an appearance or made defense to the petition and the cause has been referred to a master, the chancellor may, upon application of the petitioner and on good

cause shown, order such master to take ex parte and without notice the testimony of any witness named in the order in another state or territory, use such deposition and return the same with his report. 

2:50-28 [24]. TRIAL BY JURY. If, in the opinion of the chan cellor, any matter of fact shall render the intervention of a jury necessary in any suit or proceeding for divorce or nullity, the court of chancery may direct an issue for the trial of the same in the supreme court or in one of the circuit courts. 

Decree and APPEALS IN Divorce AND NULLITY SUITS 

2:50-29 [20]. DECREE NISI. If after the hearing of any cause or after a jury trial resulting in a verdict for the petitioner or counterclaimant the court shall be of opinion that the petitioner or counterclaimant is entitled to a decree of nullity of marriage or a decree of annulment of marriage under the general equity jurisdiction of the court or a decree for divorce from the bonds of matrimony, a decree nisi shall be entered. 

2:50-30 [21]. FINAL DECREE. A decree nisi shall become absolute after the expiration of three months from the entry thereof, unless appealed from or proceedings for review are pending, or the court before the expiration of such period for sufficient cause, on its own motion, or upon the application of any party, whether interested or not, otherwise orders; and at the expiration of three months, upon application to the court by the petitioner or counterclaimant, the final and absolute decree shall be entered, unless prior to that time cause be shown to the contrary. 

2:50-31 [21]. APPEAL FROM DECREE NISI. Appeals shall be taken only from the decree nisi and not from the final decree, and shall be taken within three months from the filing of the decree nisi.

ENROLLMENT OF PROCEEDINGS 

2:50-32 [22]. When a cause shall be finally determined, the clerk shall enter or enroll together in order in his book of decrees the proceedings, decretal orders, reports and final decree in such cause. The enollment shall be signed as in other cases. 

NULLITY DECREE-LEGITIMACY OF ISSUE 

2:50-33 [1]. A decree of nullity of marriage shall not render illegitimate the issue of any marriage so dissolved, except where 

6. See Chancery Rules 281, 283. 

7. See Chancery Rules 281, 283.

the marriage, not being a ceremonial one, is dissolved because either party had another wife or husband living at the time of a second or other marriage. Such marriage shall be deemed void ab initio, and the issue thereof shall be illegitimate.

RESUMPTION OF NAME 

2:50-34 [30]. The court, upon or after granting a divorce from the bonds of matrimony to either spouse, may allow the wife to resume any name used by her before the marriage; and may also order the wife to refrain from using the surname of the husband as her name. (As amended in 1938.) 

FOREIGN DECREES OF DIVORCE AND OF NULLITY 

2:50-35 [33]. Full faith and credit shall be given in all courts of this state to a decree of annulment of marriage or divorce by a court of competent jurisdiction in another state of the United States when the jurisdiction of such court was obtained in the manner and in substantial conformity with the conditions prescribed in sections 2:50-9, 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of this title. Nothing herein contained shall be construed to limit the power of any court to give such effect to a decree of annulment or divorce by court of a foreign country as may be justified by the rules of international comity; provided, that if any inhabitant of this state shall go into another state or country, in order to obtain a decree of divorce for a cause which occurred while the parties resided in this state, or for a cause which is not ground for divorce under the laws of this state, a decree so obtained shall be of no force or effect in this state.

ALIMONY AND MAINTENANCE 2:50-36 [L. 1915 c. 299 § 1]. AGE OF PARTIES FOR PROSECU- 

TION AND DEFENSE. A wife who has attained the age of sixteen years may appear and prosecute a suit for maintenance, under any statute of this state, in her proper person or by her solicitor, and a man who has attained the age of eighteen years may defend a suit for maintenance, under any statute of this state, in his proper person or by his solicitor. 

2:50-37 [25]. ALIMONY AND CUSTODY IN DIvorce and Null- 

ITY SUITS. Pending a suit for divorce or nullity, brought in this 

State or elsewhere, or after decree of divorce, whether obtained in this State or elsewhere, the Court of Chancery may make such

order touching the alimony of the wife, and also touching the care, custody, education and maintenance of the children, or any of them, as the circumstances of the parties and the nature of the case shall render fit, reasonable and just, and require reasonable security for the due observance of such orders, and upon neglect or refusal to give such reasonable security, as shall be required, or upon default in complying with the order, may award and issue process for the immediate sequestration of the personal estate, and the rents and profits of the real estate of the party so charged, and appoint a receiver thereof, and cause such personal estate and the rents and profits of such real estate, or so much thereof as shall be necessary, to be applied toward such alimony and maintenance as to the said court shall from time to time seem reasonable and just, or enforce the performance of the said orders by such other lawful ways and means as is usual, and according to the course and practice of the Court of Chancery; orders so made may be revised and altered by the court from time to time as circumstances may require. (As amended in 1938.) 

2:50-38 [25]. ALIMONY. EFFECT OF REMARRIAGE OF WIFE. 

If after the decree of divorce the wife shall remarry, the court of chancery shall not make any order touching the alimony of such wife except that the court of chancery, upon application of the former husband, on notice and upon proof of the marriage of the former wife after the decree of divorce, must modify any order or decree touching the alimony of the former wife by vacating and annulling any and all provisions in any such order or decree, or both, directing the payment of money for the support of the former wife.

DREN. 

2:50-39 [26]. SEPARATE MAINTENANCE FOR WIFE AND CHIL- 

If a husband, without justifiable cause, shall abandon his wife or separate himself from her and refuse or neglect to maintain and provide for her, the court of chancery may decree and order suitable support and maintenance to be paid and provided by the husband for the wife and her children, or any of them, by their marriage, or to be made out of his property and for such time as the nature of the case and circumstances of the parties render suitable and proper in the opinion of the court. The court may compel the defendant to give reasonable security for such maintenance and allowance and may, from time to time, make further orders touching the same as shall be just and equitable and enforce such decree and orders in the same manner mentioned in section 2:50-37 of this title. During the time such maintenance shall be allowed, the husband shall not be chargeable with the debts of the wife.

2:50-40 [26]. SEPARATE MAINTENANCE-SEQUESTRATION. When a husband cannot be found within this state to be served with process, his estate, property and effects within this state and the rents and profits thereof may be sequestered to compel his appearance and performance of any decree or order which may be made in the suit. Such process of sequestration shall be issued only upon special order therefor, to be made upon proof of the claim alleged in the bill and that the defendant cannot be found within the state for the service of process. 

Upon process of sequestration a bond, as provided in cases of ne exeat, may be given in discharge of the writ and the sum in which the party shall give bond, with sufficient surety, shall be endorsed upon the writ in words at length. Where the proceedings are by process of sequestration and the defendant does not appear, the decree shall be enforceable only out of and against the estate sequestered. 

2:50-41 [27]. BOND FOR COSTS. In any suit mentioned in sections 2:50-39 and 2:50-40 of this title the chancellor may, if application is made before answer filed, order a bond to be given in the sum of one hundred dollars by one or more sufficient sureties, with condition to pay such costs as shall or may be awarded by the court to be paid to the defendant. 

In 1938 the legislature enacted:

All suits for alimony and maintenance of a wife or affecting the custody and maintenance of children brought under the provisions of sections 2:50-36, 2:50-37, 2:50-39, 2:50-40 and 2:50-41 of the

Revised Statutes may be instituted in the same manner, and like process and procedure shall be had and pursued, as in other cases in the Court of Chancery, or may be instituted by petition followed by order to show cause or citation in such manner as the Chancellor may by rule prescribe, and the said Chancellor shall have full power and authority to prescribe by rule the method of initiating the proceedings, the process to be had, the method of service, and the procedure to be followed. 

This act shall not be construed to deprive the court of any of the powers conferred upon it by existing legislation. 

This act shall take effect immediately. (L. 1938 c. 234.)

Statutes Relating to Custody and Support of 

Children 1 R. S. (1937) 9:2-1 et. seq.¹ 1 

CHILDREN OF PARENTS DIVORCED IN FOREIGN STATE 

9:2-1 [6]. After a divorce decreed in any other state or country, if minor children of the marriage are inhabitants of this state, the court of chancery, on the petition of either parent, or of a next friend in behalf of the children, such notice being given to parents as the court shall direct, may make such decree concerning their care, custody, education and maintenance as if the divorce had been obtained in this state. If the minor child or minor children have not, at the time of filing of the petition, reached the age of sixteen years, and if it is represented to the court by affidavit or under oath that evidence will be adduced involving the moral turpitude of either parent, or of such minor child or children, or that evidence will be adduced which may reflect upon the good reputation or social standing of the child or children, then the court shall admit to the hearing of such cases only such persons as are directly interested in the matter being then heard. The records of such proceedings, including the petition and accompanying affidavits thereto, shall be withheld from indiscriminate public inspection, but shall be open to inspection by the parents, or their attorneys, and to no other person or persons except by order of the court made for that purpose. 

REMOVAL OF CHILDREN FROM STATE 

9:2-2 [7]. When the court of chancery has jurisdiction over the custody and maintenance of the minor children of parents divorced, separated or living separate, and such children are natives of this state, or have resided five years within its limits, they shall not be removed out of its jurisdiction against their own consent, if of suitable age to signify the same, nor while under that age without the consent of both parents, unless the court, upon cause shown, shall otherwise order. The court, upon application 

1. The section number of the Minors' Act of 1902 follows in brackets the section number of the Revised Statutes of 1937.

13

of any person in behalf of such minors, may require such security and issue such writs and processes as shall be deemed proper to effect the purposes of this section. 

CHILDREN OF PARENTS LIVING SEPARATELY 

9:2-3 [8]. When the parents of minor children live separately, or are about to do so, the court of chancery, upon petition of either parent, shall have the same power to make decrees or orders concerning their care, custody, education and maintenance as concerning children whose parents are divorced. The minor child when in the actual care and custody of the mother in such cases, shall not be taken by the father of such child forcibly or against the will of the mother from her custody, and the court having jurisdiction in the premises shall have authority to make such orders and decrees as will protect the mother in the maintenance of such control and custody until otherwise ordered by the court having jurisdiction. If the minor child or minor children have not, at the time of the filing of the petition, reached the age of sixteen years, and if it is represented to the court by affidavit or under oath that evidence will be adduced involving the moral turpitude of either parent, or of such minor child or children, or that evidence will be adduced which may reflect upon the good reputation or social standing of the child or children, then the court shall admit to the hearing of such case only such persons as are directly interested in the matter then being heard. 

The records of such proceedings, including the petition and accompanying affidavit or affidavits thereto, shall be withheld from indiscriminate public inspection, but shall be open to inspection by the parents, or their attorneys, and to no other person or persons except by order of the court made for that purpose. 

EQUAL RIGHT TO CUSTODY-REVISION OF ORDERS-REMOVAL FROM STATE 

9:2-4 [9, 10]. In making an order or decree relative to the custody of the children pending a controversy between their parents, or in regard to their final possession, the rights of both parents, in the absence of misconduct, shall be held to be equal, and they shall be equally charged with their care, nurture, education and welfare, and the happiness and welfare of the children shall determine the custody or possession.

The court may make the necessary orders and decrees from time to time in relation to such custody or possession, but the father, as

STATUTES RELATING TO MINORS 

15 such, shall not have preference over the mother as to the award of custody of such minor child if the best interests of the child. otherwise may be protected, and in no case shall the court having jurisdiction in this state over the person and custody of any minor permit such child to be removed from this state where the mother or father resides in this state and is the suitable person who should have the custody of such child for its best welfare. 

EFFECT OF DEATH OF PARENT HAVING CUSTODY 

9:2-5 [11]. In case of the death of the parent to whom the care and custody of the minor children shall have been awarded by the court of chancery, or in case of the death of the parent in whose custody the children actually are, when the parents have been living separate and no award as to the custody of such children has been made, the care and custody of such minor children shall not revert to the surviving parent without a decree of the court of chancery to that effect; and the court of chancery shall have the right, upon petition of a next friend on behalf of the children, to appoint such friend or other suitable person, guardian of such minor children, and shall have the right to remove such guardian, and to appoint a new guardian or guardians, and to make such orders, from time to time, as the circumstances of the case and the benefit of the children shall require. 

NON-SUPPORT BY FATHER OF CHILD UNDER 14 YEARS-CUSTODY 9:2-6 [L. 1929 c. 75 § 1]. In any controversy or legal pro ceeding involving the right as between parents to the custody of their child under fourteen years of age, the father who has failed and has been able to support such child for a period of five years or more shall not be entitled to the care, custody or control of such child at or during any time, and the mother having the custody and having supported such child during such period shall be entitled at all times to the care, custody and control thereof. Any order of court at law or in equity made prior to April thirteenth, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-nine, respecting the care, custody or control of such child, upon application to the court by the mother, shall be modified to conform to the provisions of this section, if the father shall have been able and failed to support such child for a period of five years or more. Nothing in this section, however, shall prevent the father from visiting such child while in the mother's custody or under her control upon such terms and conditions as the court may order.

CHILDREN OF PARENT SEPARATED-HABEAS CORPUS-REFERENCE 

9:2-7 [12]. When any husband and wife shall live in a state of separation without being divorced, and shall have any minor child of the marriage, the chancellor, upon such child being brought before him upon habeas corpus, shall award the custody of such child and make such order relating thereto for the access of either parent to such child, at such times and under such circumstances, as he may decree expedient. 

9:2-8 [13]. Whenever a child shall be so brought before the chancellor on habeas corpus the chancellor may refer the writ and all matters and proceedings relating thereto, or involved therein, to a vice chancellor, to advise an order or decree, and who shall have the same powers in relation thereto, as in other causes, matters and proceedings so referred.

PETITION TO Relieve UNFIT OR IMMORAL PERSON OF CUSTODY 

9:2-9 [14]. When the parents of any minor child or the parent or other person having the actual care and custody of any minor child are grossly immoral or unfit to be intrusted with the care and education of such child, or shall neglect to provide the child with proper protection, maintenance and education, or are of such vicious, careless or dissolute habits as to make the child chargeable, or likely to become chargeable, to any township or other municipality, it shall be lawful for any person interested in the welfare of such child to present to the chancellor, or to any justice of the supreme court, or to the judge of the court of common pleas in the county where such minor child is residing, a petition setting forth the facts in the case, duly verified by affidavit and praying that the child may be brought before the chancellor, or such supreme court justice, or judge of the court of common pleas, as the case may be, and for the further relief under this chapter.

Statute Relating to Cancellation of Record of 

Marriage Annulled 

26:8-45. If a marriage has been declared to be null and void by the court of chancery in a suit instituted for that purpose and the chancellor is satisfied by the proof taken before the final decree or by affidavit or otherwise after the final decree that a record of the marriage exists in the bureau of vital statistics, he may order the record to be canceled as hereinafter directed. 

It shall not be necessary to pray for such relief in the petition for an annulment of marriage nor shall the custodian of the record be made a party to the cause for the purpose of such cancellation.

The order shall only recite that it appears to the satisfaction of the chancellor that the record of the ceremony of marriage between parties to the cause (naming them), performed on (date) by (naming the officer), exists in the bureau of vital statistics and that by a final decree bearing date, et cetera, the marriage was declared to be null and void and shall then direct that the said record be canceled pursuant to the direction of this section, citing this section. 

26:8-46. Upon presenting a certified copy of said order to the state registrar, he shall indorse on the return of the marriage the following words: "This marriage declared to be null and void by the court of chancery. See order hereto annexed" and shall annex the certified copy to the return. 

26:8-61. The person procuring the cancellation of a marriage record pursuant to sections 26:8-45 and 26:8-46 of this title shall first pay to the state registrar the sum of one dollar and the state registrar shall pay the same over to the state treasurer. Such fee may be included in the taxable costs in the annulment suit. 18

INQUIRY 

276 [257]. Inquiry. In all suits for divorce or annulment of marriage (except in cases mentioned in paragraph 6 of this rule), before delivering the citation to the sheriff, diligent inquiry as to the defendant shall be made as follows: 

1. By Whom.-It shall be made by the petitioner or his solicitor actually entrusted with the conduct and management of the suit, or by the agent of the solicitor who shall also be a solicitor of this court. 

2. Of Whom. It shall be made of the nearest relatives of the defendant, if known, or, if not known, it shall be made of any person known to be connected with the defendant by marriage or in business, or of any person who the petitioner or his said solicitor or agent making the inquiry, has reason to believe possesses knowledge of the residence or post-office address of the defendant. 

3. In What Manner.-It may be be made in person or by letter, and shall state that suit for divorce has been, or is about to be, commenced (according to the fact) against the defendant, and that the object of the inquiry is to give him notice of such suit that he may appear and defend it; and when made by letter, shall enclose a proper postage stamp for the return of an answer. 

4. Proof of Inquiry.-After making such inquiry the petitioner or his said solicitor or such agent shall file an affidavit setting out the nature of the inquiry and its results, and in cases mentioned in paragraph 7 of this rule, shall annex thereto a copy of the description of the defendant mentioned in that paragraph. 

The affidavit shall fully specify the inquiry made, of what persons and in what manner, so that by the facts stated therein it may appear that the inquiry has been made in good faith and for the purpose of effecting actual notice to the defendant; if the affidavit shall disclose that the inquiry has elicited information of the residence or post-office address of the defendant, it shall be accompanied by an affidavit of the person furnishing such information, disclosing the affiant's knowledge of such residence or post-office address, if such affidavit can be obtained. 

In case it is disclosed that the defendant resides out of the State,

yet if process shall be returned served upon him, an affidavit must be filed satisfactorily identifying the person served, and stating the circumstances under which he was served in this State. 

5. Certificate of Solicitor.-In all cases in which it does not appear that the defendant had actual notice of the suit and when the inquiry has not been made by the solicitor of record for the petitioner, the affidavit of the person making the inquiry shall be accompanied by the certificate of such solicitor that he verily believes the inquiry has been made in good faith and for the purpose of effecting actual notice to the defendant, but without success; and the court may require the affidavit of the petitioner also in any case. 

6. When Inquiry Unnecessary.-The inquiry mentioned in this rule need not be made if the petitioner, or his solicitor, personally knows the present age, residence and occupation of the defendant; in which case he shall file an affidavit particularly stating his knowledge and the grounds of the same. 

7. Description of Defendant.—If the defendant resides or may be found in this State, the petitioner or his solicitor shall deliver to the sheriff, with the citation, a written description of the age, residence and occupation of the defendant, as known, or ascertained by such inquiry; but the requirements of this paragraph may be dispensed with by order. (Jan. 1, 1917.)

NOTE.-Rules 276 and 277 embody the provisions contained in Rules 53, 

59 and 60 of the Revision of the Rules made in 1910, in so far as those provisions related to divorce cases.

§ 1. Kinds of Matrimonial Suits. In England until the year 

1857 matrimonial litigation was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical courts. Those courts entertained suits for nullity, termed suits for divorce a vinculo matrimonii, in which the marriage, whether void or voidable, was adjudged void for causes antedating the marriage. Marriage was not subject to dissolution in the spiritual tribunals for causes postdating the marriage. Instead, these courts granted divorces from bed and board. 

For complete dissolution for causes postdating the marriage application was made, usually by the wealthy only, to Parliament and ordinarily after the ecclesiastical court had decreed a separation. 

In addition, the ecclesiastical courts afforded remedies in actions known as suits for restitution of conjugal rights, and suits for jactitation of marriage.2 The writ of supplicavit was a remedy in Chancery sometimes invoked by the wife against the husband." 

In New Jersey none of the jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical courts in matrimonial causes devolved upon the Court of Chancery. 

Prior to 1794 the legislature granted divorces and until 1844 there was concurrent jurisdiction in the legislature and in the Court of Chancery. Now triable in the Court of Chancery under the statute or under the general equity jurisdiction of the court is the suit for nullity for causes antedating the marriage. Next is the suit for divorce from the bond of matrimony which has for its object the complete dissolution of the marriage for postnuptial causes. 

1. Infra § 4. 

2. Infra § 3. 

3. Infra $5. 

4. Chapter 6 et seq infra. 29 29

§2 

5 This suit is to be distinguished from the suit for divorce from bed and board, which suit in turn is often confused with the suit for separate maintenance under the statute. Until the year 1902 the Divorce Act, in enumerating causes for dissolution of the marriage, failed adequately to distinguish between nullity of marriage and divorce from the bond of matrimony." Other matrimonial matters cognizable in the Court of Chancery include the award of alimony either as an incident to a suit for divorce or in an independent proceeding for separate maintenance, or after a final decree of absolute divorce granted in a foreign jurisdiction; the specific performance of maintenance agreements; 10 the custody and support of children either in conjunction with a suit for divorce or for separate maintenance, or independently. The protection of the marriage status in various situations is another instance of matrimonial litigation.12 From this enumeration it should not be inferred that the court may not have inherent jurisdiction in other matrimonial matters which may arise. 11 

§ 2. Effect of Ecclesiastical Law. With the vesting of juris diction over matrimonial causes in our Court of Chancery many of the principles and rules of the ecclesiastical law were adopted. 

The defenses of condonation,18 recrimination 14 and connivance 15 are a few instances wherein the ecclesiastical law has been followed. The triennial cohabitation rule in impotence cases is a more recent example.10 That the ecclesiastical law in matrimonial causes is a part of our common law,17 dormant until matrimonial jurisdiction was vested in the Court of Chancery, is ably urged by 5. Infra §§ 126, 162. The Act of 1891 was declared unconstitutional, Middleton v. Middleton, 54 N. J. Eq. 692, 35 Atl. 1065, 37 Atl. 1106 (E. & A. 1896).

INTRODUCTION 

Dr. Bishop,18 but it is probable that in New Jersey the law of the spiritual courts in matrimonial causes is not a part of our common law.19. Our court has been guided and well served by the judicial precedents of the church tribunals, but has "adopted" the rule of the ecclesiastical courts in a given case rather than following it as a binding precedent.20 In some instances the ecclesiastical rule has been flatly rejected in favor of equitable considerations.21 At any rate, the court is not governed by the ecclesiastical rules in regard to process and procedure. These matters are expressly regulated by the statute relating to divorce, and where such statute is silent, by the statute regulating Chancery procedure and by the Chancery Rules.22 

§ 3. Jactitation of Marriage. This proceeding lay in the ecclesiastical courts and was akin to a criminal suit. In a suit by the man the libel alleged that he "is in no way married to or united with this lady; that she has falsely and maliciously boasted and reported that she is married to him, whereas, in fact, no marriage has taken place; and that on her being desired to desist from such conduct she paid no attention, but continued, falsely and maliciously, to boast and report such fact to the no small prejudice and injury of the complainant; that the court will pronounce that she has been in no manner married to the complainant; that it will restrain her from such conduct and condemn her in the costs of the suit." The defenses were three in number, (1) to deny the boasting, (2) to plead a marriage, (3) to plead that the boasting was authorized. When the second defense was interposed, the suit assumed the nature of a nullity suit.23

§ 4  

In New Jersey there is no proceeding known as jactitation of marriage. The void marriages which may be annulled under the statute or under the court's general equity jurisdiction are marriages performed in fact, but void in law. However, if there has been no marriage in fact or in law, but a mere boasting—a marriage in masquerade—as where a woman holds herself out as a man's wife without the benefit of a ceremony or without such cohabitation as would evidence a common law marriage, it would seem that the Court of Chancery possesses the jurisdiction in a direct proceeding to declare the man's status as single, at least if he be domiciled within the state. 24 In addition, injunctive relief commanding the defendant to desist from boasting might be decreed.25 

§ 4. Restitution of Conjugal Rights. In the ecclesiastical courts the desertion of a spouse was not cause for a decree a mensa et thoro. In lieu thereof, a party might apply for the restitution of conjugal rights. The decree in this suit compelled the parties to live together provided that the libelant was not guilty of a matrimonial offense.26 The words of the decree in suits brought by the wife were that the husband "take the wife home and treat her with conjugal affection." 27 While the church tribunals enforced a resumption of cohabitation, they wisely refrained from attempting to enforce matrimonial intercourse.28

With us the Court of Chancery as a tribunal has not succeeded to the ecclesiastical jurisdiction to entertain suits for the restitution of conjugal rights. Nor did the English Court of Chancery enforce a resumption of cohabitation. Our Divorce Act of 1794 20 conferred jurisdiction upon the Court of Chancery to hear suits for divorce and nullity of marriage, but to no tribunal has the legislature ever given any power to compel cohabitation of a husband and wife. While it is the duty of the parties to live together

§ 5. 

Writ of Supplicavit. In England this writ issued out of the Court of King's Bench or Chancery to protect the complaining party from personal violence and abuse. There have been instances in the English Court of Chancery in which a wife resorted to this writ to compel her husband to find sureties to keep the peace. Although formerly resorted to in a few American jurisdictions the writ seems now to be obsolete. No instance of the issuance of this writ by our Court of Chancery has been observed. 

§ 6. 

Cohabitation Pending Suit. During the pendency of a suit for divorce from bed and board or from the bond of matrimony it is ordinarily improper for the parties to live under the same roof. It matters not whether the pending suit was instituted in the court of this state or of some other state. In either event the separation of the parties during such pendency is proper and justifiable, and is the basis for the allowance of alimony pendente lite to the wife, as well as for the rule that the time during which a suit is pending bona fide cannot ordinarily be computed as a part of a desertion period. A pending suit for nullity of marriage is also justification for the cessation of cohabitation. Any other rule would subject the complaining spouse in divorce cases

It is not, however, a contract within the constitutional restriction against the impairment of the obligation of a contract. Marriage is something more than a contract. True it is that the consent of the parties is essential, but when the contract to marry is executed

§ 10. Situs of Marriage Status. The marriage status re sulting from a contract of marriage between competent parties is intangible. It exists only as a legal conception and can have no actual situs. But for the purpose of acquiring jurisdiction in suits for divorce and nullity of marriage, and in suits to protect the marriage status, the courts have accorded it a situs, resembling the situs of land, as an incident to the domicile of either of the parties. 

§ 11. -Protection of Marriage Status. The marriage status or res will be protected by the court in proper cases at the instance of an interested party either as an incident to a suit for divorce or independently thereof. Where the situs of the marital res is in New Jersey, the Court of Chancery has not hesitated to entertain a direct proceeding to decree a foreign fraudulent divorce to be null and void, or to decree injunctive relief against a party prosecuting a fraudulent suit for divorce in a foreign jurisdiction.10 But situations may arise in which a party may wish to have his or her marital status declared by a decree of the court in rem so as to settle the validity of the marriage for all time.

$ 12. Law Governing Marriage. While the dissolution of marriage is regulated by the lex domicilii,12 as a general rule, with some exceptions to be noted, the validity of a marriage is tested by the law of the place where the marriage was performed-the lex loci contractus. If a marriage celebrated in another state or country is valid according to the laws of such state or country, it is valid in New Jersey. 13 This is a well established principle of the unwritten international law of marriage-a principle established to avoid the infinite mischief and confusion which would ensue if the law of the parties' domicile or nationality were to govern. 

The unwritten international law of marriage is, unless and until overridden by constitutional or statutory changes, a part of the law of New Jersey. Sir Edward Simpson observed: 

"From the doctrine laid down in our books-the practice of nations and the mischief and confusion that would arise to the subjects of every country, from a contrary doctrine, I may infer that it is the consent of all nations that it is the jus gentium, that the solemnities of the different nations with respect to marriages should be observed, and that contracts of this kind are to be determined by the laws of the country where they are made. If that principle is not to govern such cases, what is to be the rule, where one party is domiciled, and the other not? The jus gentium is the law of every country, and is obligatory on the subjects of every country. 

Every country takes notice of it; and this Court observing that law, in determining upon this case, cannot be said to determine English rights by the laws of France, but by the law of England, of which the jus gentium is part." 14

If a common law marriage is valid where performed, it is valid in this state.15 Unless a foreign marriage contravenes the law of nations or some express and positive statute, it will be recognized as valid in New Jersey, albeit the parties intentionally went into another state for the purpose of evading the law of their domicile.16 However, the Uniform Marriage Evasion Act,17 which has been adopted in some states, 18 modifies the rule that a marriage valid where performed is valid everywhere. Suppose the marriage is valid where performed, but is void under the Marriage Evasion Act in a second state which is the present domicile of the parties. 

Should New Jersey refer the validity of the marriage to the lex loci contractus or to the lex domicilii? In a Minnesota case a marriage of first cousins, valid in Kentucky where performed, was held invalid in Minnesota in view of the rule in Illinois under the Marriage Evasion Act where the parties were domiciled.¹º 

But with us it would seem that, unless the marriage offends against the accepted opinions of Christendom, the law of the place where the marriage was performed should govern as that is the law of nations which, until superseded by a local statute or constitutional provision, is the law of New Jersey.

The celebration of a marriage on board a vessel may occur on the high seas or within the territorial waters of a country. Where a marriage is performed on the high seas, it has been held that there is no law on the high seas and consequently the law of the parties' domicile governs the validity of the marriage.27 The better authority, however, holds that the laws which follow a ship upon the high seas are the laws of the state or nation in which the owner is domiciled and not the law of the state within which the ship is registered, and, if the marriage is valid in the state wherein the owner resides and is not in contravention of the principles of Christendom, it is valid everywhere under the ius gentium.28 According to the only reported case in New Jersey, a marriage ceremony performed upon a ship, whether upon the high seas or within the territorial waters of a foreign nation, is governed by the laws of the nation where the owner of the vessel resides, whether the ship be a government vessel or a merchantman.29 The Restatement provides riage is performed in country in which U. § 13. -Polygamous, Consanguineous, etc., Marriage. Bear ing in mind that the unwritten international law of marriage governs the validity of a foreign marriage and that such law is a part of the law of New Jersey until superseded by a local constitutional or statutory mandate, it should be noted that an exception has been engrafted upon the general rule of the international law of marriage that the validity of a foreign marriage is to be referred to the lex loci contractus. If a foreign marriage is odious by the common consent of nations, by the unwritten international law of marriage which is a part of our law, New Jersey may refuse to recognize it as valid. Polygamous marriages and marriages of very close consanguinity constitute the exception. 

The practice of polygamy and polyandry is repugnant to the policy of the monogamous countries of Christendom. Consequently, by the ius gentium a foreign polygamous or polyandrous marriage is void, notwithstanding its validity by the lex loci contractus.2 Section 2:50-33 of the Revision providing that polygamous marriages shall be void from the beginning is a regulation governing domestic marriages. While the statute coincides with the existing law of nations it adds nothing thereto. Under the law of nations it would appear to be immaterial that the parties were domiciled in the jurisdiction in which the polygamous marriage was performed and recognized. If the domicile of one of the parties in New Jersey were essential, we would be extending to foreigners the right to practice polygamy while denying it to our own citizens. Plural marriages sanctioned under the Indian tribal custom have, however, been recognized as valid in a number of states. Intermarriage between blacks and whites is not

However, if the marriage is void in the state where it was performed because of local prohibitions, by the ius gentium the marriage would also be void in New Jersey. 8 -Consanguinity. It will be observed that a marriage celebrated in New Jersey between parties within the degrees prohibited by our statute is totally void. However, it by no means follows that a foreign marriage between parties within the degrees prohibited by our statute is in all instances void in New Jersey, although the parties are domiciled in this state and have left the state in order to contract such marriage in evasion of our laws. The Uniform Marriage Act embraces this very situation, but such act has not been adopted in New Jersey. While our legislature has the authority to enact a statute rendering foreign marriages between our citizens void if not performed in compliance with our statute regulating domestic marriages, our statute is silent as to the recognition of foreign marriages.¹

-Prohibitions Against Remarriage After Divorce. In 

New Jersey the parties may remarry without restriction after the entry of a final decree of absolute divorce or of nullity. Provisions against remarriage after a final decree of divorce do exist, however, in some states.14 Such a prohibition is to be distinguished from the interlocutory, provisional or nisi decree which exists in our practice and in the practice of some other jurisdictions. A foreign decree of divorce from bed and board is also to be distinguished from the prohibition under consideration.15 

On the other hand, the prohibition against remarriage existing in the various states ordinarily does not continue the marriage state, but merely forbids for a limited period of time, or for the lifetime of the parties, the remarriage of either or both of the spouses divorced.

In New Jersey the question, which is one solely of conflict of laws, has seldom arisen. In Marculies v. Marculies, a petitioner for divorce remarried in New Jersey prior to the expiration of the period of time allotted under a Virginia decree of divorce.16 

The contention that the marriage performed in New Jersey was void in view of the inhibition contained in the Virginia decree was brushed aside by the court. Remarriage in New Jersey in violation of a restriction contained in a foreign statute or in a foreign decree of divorce is not opposed to the public policy of our state. The Marculies case left untouched several questions which may arise as a result of a prohibition of remarriage contained in a foreign decree of divorce. A remarriage may occur in the state where the divorce was decreed or in a state other than New Jersey. 

If the remarriage is performed in the state where the decree of divorce was granted and is valid in such state,17 the remarriage is valid in New Jersey. If the remarriage is void in such state, 13. 1 Bishop, Marr. Div. & Sep. (1891) § 862. See also Restatement, Confl.

§ 15. 

Void or Voidable Marriage; Collateral Attack. Prior to its dissolution by death or by a final decree of divorce or of nullity, a marriage may be valid, voidable or void. Until 1857, the ecclesiastical courts in England possessed jurisdiction to annul a marriage for such canonical defects as were prescribed by the Church. The creation by the Church of unreasonable impediments to marriage occasioned the passage of 32 Hen. 8, C. 38, which gave to the temporal courts the power to restrain by prohibition the impeachment of a marriage without the Levitical degrees, but not marriages within those degrees. The temporal courts restrained by prohibition the dissolution of a marriage by the ecclesiastical courts after the death of one of the parties. But the common law judges were presumed incompetent to apply the canon law, so that whenever a marriage was attacked collaterally in a temporal court for a canonical disability the marriage was held to be valid. On the other hand, the common law courts took cognizance of the civil disabilities which rendered the marriage absolutely void. Out of the conflict in jurisdiction between the spiritual and temporal courts grew the distinction between void and voidable marriages, and this distinction, firmly embedded in the English common law, was transplanted to this country as a part of the unwritten law.21 As was observed by Sir John 

Nichol: 22 "The difference between void and voidable is so clear that no person who ever looked into any elementary book on the subject is ignorant of it. The canonical disabilities, such as consanguinity, affinity, and certain corporal infirmities, only make the marriage voidable, and not ipso facto void, until

"Civil disabilities, such as a prior marriage, want of age, ideotcy, and the like, make the contract void ab initio, not merely voidable: these do not dissolve a contract already made; but they render the parties incapable of contracting at all: they do not put asunder those who are joined together, but they previously hinder the junction; and if any persons under these legal incapacities come together, it is a meretricious and not a matrimonial union; and, therefore, no sentence of avoidance is necessary." Whether a particular marriage at the present time is void or voidable depends upon the rules of the common law as transplanted from England to this state except as the common law has been supplanted by statutory regulation.24 The institution of marriage being subject to the control of the state, the legislature may alter the common law by rendering a void marriage voidable or vice versa, but until the legislature speaks unequivocally the common law prevails. As to whether a marriage is void or voidable by reason of specific impediments such as want of, and incapacity to, consent,25 fraud, duress and mistake, 20 prior marriage,27 prohibited degrees,28 impotence 29 and nonage¹ has been left for consideration in subsequent sections.

MARRIAGE § 20. Age of Parties; Consent of Parents.¹ At common law the age of consent for marriage was twelve years for females and fourteen years for males. A marriage between parties under seven years of age was entirely void at common law. If either of the parties was over seven years but under the age of consent, the marriage was inchoate and imperfect, but unless and until confirmed upon reaching the age of consent it was voidable at the instance of such spouse without judicial sentence.2 The failure or refusal of the parents or guardian to consent to the marriage of a minor who has attained the common law age of marriage does not invalidate the marriage. The effect of the Divorce Act of 1907 relating to the annulment of a marriage where the wife is under sixteen, or the husband is under eighteen years of age,* is to advance the common law age of consent.5 

Where the parties were each over seven years of age but under the common law age of consent, the impediment was not canonical. Nevertheless, a marriage between such parties is not void under the nullity statute, but at the suit of the party under the statutory age of consent is, until affirmed or annulled, merely voidable. The consent of the parents to the marriage of a minor does not render the marriage any the less voidable. In the interest of society and possible offspring the law has wisely rendered these marriages valid although voidable. While the nullity statute had for its purpose the discouragement of marriages of persons of immature years, it places in the hands of youth the opportunity for trial marriage. By an act in 1933 the legislature nullity of marriage for impotence a marriage performed in 1899 was treated as voidable.

§ 21. Miscegenation. 

At common law there is no inhibition against the intermarriage of persons of different races or color. 

While the legislature undoubtedly possesses the authority to forbid marriages between persons of different races,10 in the legislative history of the state there is no trace of any such prohibition. 

However, if such a marriage is void in another state where performed, it is void also in New Jersey.11 No criminal liability attaches by reason of a marriage in this state between persons of diverse races. 

§ 22. 

Consent of Parties. In order to constitute a valid marriage it is indispensable that competent parties mutually consent to become man and wife.12 The consent must be mutual,¹³ and the parties must intend to assume a present matrimonial status as distinguished from a mere engagement to marry in futuro.¹ª

The consent must be genuine. While words and forms may denote a matrimonial consent, they are not conclusive that the parties actually intended to enter the marital relation.15 Mutual con- § 23. -Want of, and Incapacity to, Consent. sent of competent parties to assume a present matrimonial status being essential to a marriage, at common law a marriage, ceremonial or otherwise, lacking at its inception the contractual element of mutual consent is totally void 18 and not merely voidable.

333 if subsequently mental capacity should exist.18 The decision in a recent case declaring that the nullity statute has altered the common law rule by rendering the marriage voidable has been criticized.19 In that case a decedent was married on his death-bed in a hospital at a time when he lacked sufficient mental capacity to contract a marriage. The marriage was collaterally attacked after his death by decedent's sister. Acknowledging that at common law the marriage was void, the court concluded that the allowance of the remedy of nullity coupled with the statutory legitimation of issue rendered the marriage voidable instead of void ab initio. The fact that the legislature has provided the remedy of annulment where a party was incapable of consenting does not render the marriage any the less void. Undoubtedly, the legislature may change the common law rule, but until it does so unequivocally, the common law rule persists. Void marriages, although subject to collateral attack during and after the life of the parties 20 should, nevertheless, on the ground of public policy be annulled in a direct proceeding in rem. Bigamous marriages are void at common law and yet the statute provides a direct proceeding for their annulment.21 Nor may statutory legitimation of issue under the nullity statute be regarded as rendering the marriage voidable. There is nothing to prevent the legislature from conferring the status of legitimacy on issue although the marriage is totally void.22

A marriage may be void for want of genuine consent of a mentally competent person or for lack of consent occasioned by the mental deficiency of one of the parties. The former case is illustrated by a marriage of mentally competent parties in jest.23 The second situation is exemplified by the marriage of a person while intoxicated, 24 or while afflicted with a mental disease or weakness at the time of the marriage to such an extent that he could not have comprehended the nature of the act.25

Whether a person of alleged mental incapacity is actually incompetent is a question to be determined by the particular circumstances. No inflexible rule should be attempted, but, generally

MARRIAGE § 27. License; Common Law Marriage. Never accepted as a part of the common law in some, and abolished after a period of trial in other states of the Union, 16 the common law marriage continues to be recognized in New Jersey.17 Our statutory provisions relating to the requirement of a license and to the formal solemnization of marriages and subjecting the official performing the ceremony to criminal punishment for the omission of prescribed requirements are directory merely and do not abridge the validity of common law marriages in this state. 18 However, there has been agitation for the abolition of the common law marriage in New Jersey.19

The two essentials of a common law marriage are capacity and mutual consent presently to become man and wife.20 Cohabitation with matrimonial habit and repute is evidence of marriage, but it should not constitute indispensable proof.21 The common. law requires nothing more of the parties who are under no legal disability than proof of a contract of marriage made in words of the present tense.22 The rule is expressed in Jackson v. Jackson: "Where there is no ceremonial marriage there must be an agreement entered into between the man and woman, in words of the present tense, to live together as husband and wife. There are probably but few instances of mutual consent, by which each party in precise or unambiguous terms takes the other as spouse; but no particular words are necessary to declare an intention to enter into a contract of marriage. If from what was said by the parties, aided by the circumstances surrounding their entering upon their relationship, it can be gathered that they proposed to enter into a contract thenceforth to live as husband and wife, it will be sufficient." The consent must be unconditional and of a matrimonial character. Consent of competent parties to concubinage does not constitute marriage.24 A marriage per verba de futuro cum copula has not been given express sanction by our courts. Such a marriage, recognized in some jurisdictions, is based on a promise to marry followed by sexual intercourse. Cohabitation with matrimonial habit and repute is not an essential element. For such marriages it is presumed that at the time of the act of coition the parties, in reliance upon the promise to marry, mutually consented to become man and wife.25 § 28. -Habit and Repute. A common law marriage can have no existence as such unless competent parties have manifested a present mutual consent to become man and wife. Witnesses to such marriages are unusual. There being frequently no other evidence of such a marriage, some other mode of proof is necessary in order to show that the parties at some time presently intended to take each other as man and wife. The doctrine of habit and repute, derived from the Scotch law,28 supplies the proof to establish such type of marriage.27 Whether the conduct of competent parties evinces a matrimonial intent or manifests an illicit relation depends of course on manifold circumstances. Each case must hinge on the particular facts. The general rule is put in Costill v. Hill: "The general rule, under proofs of the kind considered, is that where a man and woman constantly live together, ostensibly as man and wife, claiming to be such, and so demeaning themselves towards each other, and are received into society and are treated by their friends and relations as having and being entitled to that status, the law, in favor of morality and decency, will presume that they have been legally married. Such cohabitation and repute are said to be matrimonial, in distinction from that occasional, hidden and

Habit consists of the parties' cohabiting ostensibly as man and wife. Repute is the general reputation established as a result of the visible cohabitation of the parties. The repute must be of a general nature, extending to the relatives and friends of each of the parties with whom they spend their daily lives.20 In order to establish a presumption of a common law marriage by habit and repute, not only cohabitation, but reputation as husband and wife must be shown.¹ The resumption of cohabitation between parties to a divorce coupled with matrimonial habit and repute may constitute a common law marriage.2 Habit and repute standing alone do not constitute a common law marriage. Such proof amounts to no more than evidence of a matrimonial intent, which may be rebutted by other testimony.* -Necessity of Habit and Repute. 

Habit and repute, especially when coupled with an express agreement to become man and wife, have been sufficient evidence of the existence of a common law marriage. So where the parties are married by a supposed justice of the peace, cohabitation with matrimonial habit and repute may sustain a common law marriage." May a private agreement in the present tense operate as a common law marriage in the absence of proof of matrimonial habit and repute? On this question the authorities are not in harmony. The answer must depend on the precise circumstances.

Atlantic City Railroad Co. v. Goodin, 62 N. J. Law 394, did not go that far."

§ 32. Presumptions Relating to Marriage. The law favors matrimony, and disfavors divorce and separation.25 Every presumption is in favor of marriage.26 The universal maxim of the law is semper praesumitur pro matrimonio. Once the fact of marriage, whether ceremonial or otherwise, is demonstrated, the law clothes the marriage with every reasonable presumption in favor of its validity. One who seeks to impeach a marriage has the burden of proving its invalidity by evidence so strong and persuasive as to leave no room for reasonable doubt.27 This presumption extends to a foreign marriage.28 The presumption is one of the strongest known to the law. § 33. 

-Second Marriage. Ordinarily, the presumption of the validity of a marriage is transferred from the first to a second marriage, necessitating clear and convincing proof of the validity and existence of the former marriage.¹ The presumption has no application where it is proved that the parties to the former marriage are alive and the marriage is subsisting.2 

In aid of the validity of a second marriage, assailed on the ground that one of the parties had a husband or wife living at the time of the ceremony, the law may presume before the lapse of seven years that the spouse by the former marriage is dead. 

When a person disappears he is presumed to be alive for the period of seven years in the absence of contradictory proof. But when this presumption conflicts with the presumption in favor of the validity of a second marriage, it is not absolute. It loses vitality as time passes and, although seven years have not elapsed, it may be so weakened by the passage of time that it succumbs to the presumption of innocence attaching to the parties to the second marriage and yields to the presumption of legitimacy if issue have been born of a ceremonial marriage. One who attempts to impeach the second marriage must prove not only the first marriage, but that its existence continued up to the time of the second marriage. The presumption in favor of the validity of the second marriage is not overcome by proof merely that the spouse was living at a time less than seven years before the time of the second marriage. The presumption of the continuance of life fades gradually with the expiration of time until at the end of seven years of absence of a party the presumption of death arises. If a second marriage is contracted after a spouse has been absent for seven years the marriage is considered as valid if there is no rebutting proof of the continued life of the absentee. A decree of nullity of the second marriage will be refused in such circumstances. § 35. General Principles. It is not intended to treat in extenso of the law pertaining to domicile, but rather to give a few of the principles which are apt to be useful in matrimonial litigation. The reader may consult, when necessary, several treatises in which the subject is more exhaustively discussed.¹ Postponed for future discussion herein are questions pertaining to the necessity of domicile in matrimonial litigation, to wit: in suits for divorce and nullity, in suits for separate maintenance, and in suits to enjoin the prosecution of a foreign suit for divorce or to declare a foreign decree of divorce null and void; likewise the question of a child's domicile as it pertains to an award of custody." 3 "Domicile," frequently spelled "domicil," is that place in which a person has voluntarily fixed his habitation, not for a mere temporary or special purpose, but with the present intention of making it his home, unless or until something which is uncertain or unexpected shall happen to induce him to adopt some other permanent home. The domicile of origin is the domicile received by a person at birth by operation of law." Domicile must be distinguished from residence, although frequently the word

A person retains his domicile of origin until he acquires a new one by choice.10 To effect a change of domicile a person must effect a voluntary and actual change of residence to the place chosen for the new domicile with the present intention of making it his home, unless and until something which is uncertain or unexpected shall happen to induce him to adopt some other permanent home.¹¹ The party who alleges a change of domicile has the burden of proving such change.
