§ 37. Separate Domicile. The rule that the domicile of the wife follows that of the husband has certain exceptions. Perhaps the principal exception, noted elsewhere, is that for the purpose of divorce the wife may acquire a separate domicile if she is the petitioner. But aside from the wife's suit for divorce, it has been recognized that the wife may acquire an independent domicile in certain cases.18 Our cases abound in dicta as to when, aside from divorce, the wife is entitled to establish a separate domicile. In general it has been stated that the wife's domicile as that of her husband terminates with the reason upon which it rests and, when the union between the two ceases and an attitude of hostility arises, they each may have different domiciles.19 The husband's actual consent to the wife's living apart will enable her to acquire an independent domicile.20 The husband's misconduct, sometimes referred to as an implied consent, will give the wife the capacity to maintain an independent domicile, but what constitutes misconduct has not been very clearly adjudicated.21 

The expressions in the cases may be observed. Thus it has been stated that the wife may acquire a separate domicile "for such misconduct on his part, inimical to the union, as justified her in selecting another," 22 "by abandonment, or by such conduct, inimical to cohabitation, as would secure to the wife a decree of divorce a vinculo or mensa et thoro," 28 "only by his consent, acquiescence or abandonment or by conduct on his part amounting to a matrimonial offense,' ,"24 "such cause only as would entitle her to a decree of divorce or a judicial separation from him under the statute,' ," 25 "where he abandons her or conducts himself in such a manner as would constitute in law a matrimonial offense and

DOMICILE 

rule that the domicile of the legitimate, unemancipated minor, whether male or female, is the domicile of the father, if he is living, has been accepted as part of our law. Such minor takes the domicile of his father by operation of law and, if the father changes his domicile, the domicile of such minor child follows.

The minor may change his physical residence, but he is presumed incapable of forming an intention to effect a change of domicile." 

The general rule applies although the child may have been born and may have lived in a country other than that of the father's residence.10 The reason usually assigned for fixing the child's domicile as that of his living father as a matter of law is that the father is the natural guardian, is entitled to the child's custody and services and is responsible in some degree for the care and discipline of the child. The legislature has not encroached upon this general rule in direct terms as it has done in defining the domicile of married women. Instances in which the law has accorded a minor the capacity to acquire a domicile of his own choice have resulted from judicial sanction rather than from legislative fiat.

The child's domicile may cease to be that of his father where the father abandons him,11 although in such a case the child may take the domicile of the mother if she is alive and has the child's custody. The child's domicile may be that of the mother if she is awarded custody by a court of competent jurisdiction. If the husband is guilty of a matrimonial offense justifying the wife in living separate and apart from him and she takes the minor child with her, the domicile of the child is that of the mother.12 But the mother may not change the domicile of the child if she leaves, or remains away from, the father without justification or without his consent.13 And whether the father's consent that the mother

CHAPTER The Marriage in Divorce and Nullity Suits SECTION 43. NECESSITY OF EXISTING MARRIAGE

EFFECT OF DEATH PLEADING THE MARRIAGE 46. PROOF AND CORROBORATION 

§ 43. Necessity of Existing Marriage. The general principles relating to the subject of marriage have gone before.¹ The remedy of divorce is available only to persons who are validly married. To divorce parties who are not husband and wife is mere nullity. A common law marriage between the parties is sufficient. Likewise, a voidable marriage is sufficient because such marriage is valid until annulled at the instance of the party at whose option it is voidable. But the court may not decree a divorce if the marriage is void by reason of a prior subsisting marriage of either of the parties. Nor may a decree of divorce be granted if the parties are already validly divorced. A divorce may not be granted where the marriage has been dissolved by the decree of a court in a foreign jurisdiction if the foreign decree is entitled to recognition in New Jersey.º

The remedy of nullity of marriage presupposes the existence of a marriage between the parties, ceremonial or otherwise, but the marriage must have been void or voidable at its inception.10 The void marriage creates no marital status and consequently no decree of the court in a direct proceeding is essential, but it is the

Proof and Corroboration. In suits for divorce the marriage of the parties, ceremonial or otherwise, is an essential element to be proved, whether or not the defendant admits it. 

Similarly, in suits for nullity of marriage, including those instituted under the general equity jurisdiction of the court, proof of marriage is essential.19 Proof of a marriage for the purpose of dissolving it, especially where the marriage is not denied, may be much less strict than the proof required to prove residence or the cause of action.20 Yet, if the suit is by the wife for divorce with the incident of alimony involved, strict proof will be required if the husband denies the marriage. Primary proof of the marriage may be supplied by the testimony of the petitioner.21 

The rule requiring corroboration in divorce and nullity suits 22 extends to the fact of marriage.23 The defendant's admission of the marriage is not sufficient, 24 yet, where the defendant admits the marriage, particularly where such admission operates to his prejudice,25 very little corroborative proof is required. As to whether a finding of the fact of marriage in a prior separate maintenance action is res judicata of such fact in an action for divorce without corroborative proof.26 In the case of a ceremonial marriage a certified copy of the marriage record is sufficient, although not necessary." In suits for divorce the necessary corroboration of a ceremonial marriage may be supplied by the production of the original certificate of the marriage issued to the parties by the officer performing the ceremony, properly identified by the petitioner. Corroborative proof of a ceremonial marriage may be furnished by the testimony of a party who attended the ceremony, or even by habit and repute, which is almost always incidentally supplied by the corroborating witnesses.28 If the marriage is de-

§ 47.

Jurisdiction of Chancery. 

In suits for nullity of marriage the Court of Chancery exercises a jurisdiction conferred upon it by statute and, as well, an inherent and fundamental jurisdiction in certain cases which will be observed farther on.¹ These two jurisdictions are separate and distinct.2 At the time the colonies were settled and until 1857 the jurisdiction of all matrimonial causes in England was vested in the ecclesiastical courts. Such courts were never transplanted to New Jersey and the Court of Chancery has not succeeded to their matrimonial jurisdiction. 

For the first time statutory jurisdiction over matrimonial causes was conferred upon the Court of Chancery by the Divorce Act of 1794. That act and subsequent acts down to the year 1902 classified nullity of marriage as divorce. The Constitution of 1844 stripped the legislature of its authority to grant divorces, and in view of the inclusion of nullity in the word "divorce" in the

The statutory jurisdiction of the court is presently derived from section 2:50-7 of the Revision. The causes for which the statute permits a suit for nullity of marriage are enumerated in an ensuing section. With respect to suits for nullity of marriage reference should be made to the general chapter on divorce where a number of matters are discussed which may apply as well to the nullity suit." 

§ 48. 

Nature of Proceeding. The suit for nullity of marriage is regarded as equitable in its nature and, generally speaking, subject to the rules, maxims and equitable defenses existing in courts of equity.10 However, caution should be exercised in the importation of equitable principles and maxims into the proceeding for nullity of marriage, for the suit is sui generis, involving the state as well as the immediate parties.¹¹ Principles well adapted to ordinary equitable proceedings should not be applied if they tend to contravene the public policy as to nullity of marriage. Too frequently, perhaps, we are apt to seize upon some equitable principle, or some principle of general application, which is ill-adapted to the triangular nullity suit.12 -Proceeding as In Rem. In suits for nullity of marriage, as well as in suits for divorce,13 the proceeding is in rem or at least quasi in rem. Although the marriage is absolutely void,14 and no marital status has come into existence, the status of the parties, as married or unmarried, is the res or matter upon which the declaratory decree may operate. However, it seems that the views on this matter have not been in accord.15

$ 49. Marriage. The subject of marriage generally, and as it pertains to suits for nullity of marriage, has gone before.16 

§ 50. Residence. The residence within the state of one of the parties is a prerequisite to the acquisition of jurisdiction by the court of a suit for nullity of marriage. Section 2:50-9 of the Re vision prescribes the necessary requirements when the suit for nullity of marriage is instituted for one of the causes enumerated in section 2:50-1.17 Section 2:50-9, as well as sections 2:50-10 

and 2:50-11,18 was derived from the Uniform Divorce Act pro posed by the National Congress on Uniform Divorce Laws. Sec tion 2:50-9 of the Revision provides: 

2:50-9. Jurisdiction in suits for nullity of marriage may be acquired: 

Personal service. a. By personal service of process upon the defendant within this state 19 when either party is a bona fide resident of this state at the time of the commencement of the suit;

Publication and Substituted Service. b. When the defendant cannot be served personally within this state, and when at the time of the commencement of the suit the petitioner is a bona fide resident of this state, jurisdiction may be acquired by publication, to be followed, where practicable, by service upon or notice to the defendant without this state or by additional substituted service upon the defendant within this state, as prescribed by law or by rules of court." 20 As in the case of suits for divorce under sections 2:50-10 and 

2:50-11 of the Revision,21 "bona fide resident" within the meaning of section 2:50-9 is equivalent to "domiciled." 22 Where a suit for nullity of marriage is instituted for a statutory cause, either of the parties, or the petitioner in the case of service of process by publication and substituted service, must be domiciled within the state at the time of the commencement of the suit. quiry, then, is as to whether the wife has the right to establish a domicile separate from that of her husband for the purpose of instituting a suit for the annulment of her voidable marriage. 

Our decisions seem somewhat in conflict on this question. In 

Avakian v. Avakian the court conceded that a wife who left the matrimonial domicile in another state had the right to establish an independent domicile in this state for the purpose of instituting suit to annul a marriage voidable because of duress. But in two later cases the court refused to exercise jurisdiction of petitions to annul marriages voidable because of the nonage of the wife where she left the matrimonial domicile in a foreign state without her husband's consent and without "such cause only as would entitle her to a decree of divorce or a judicial separation from him under the statute." To require that a wife who has cause for nullity of marriage must also have cause for divorce before she may obtain a separate domicile within this state for the purpose of invoking our jurisdiction seems to carry the fiction of the unity of domicile to a reductio ad absurdum. It seems that a wife who has cause for the annulment of a voidable marriage under our law should be accorded the right to obtain a separate domicile, irrespective of the situs of the matrimonial domicile and regardless of whether she may have cause for divorce or a judicial separation under our statute." 

§ 52. Separate Domicile of Wife as Defendant. Section 2:50-9 of the Revision requires merely that in the case of personal service of process upon the defendant within the state either of the parties shall be domiciled within the state at the time of the commencement of the suit.

$ 54. -Proof and Corroboration of Residence. As a part of the petitioner's case it is essential that the residential requirements necessary to sustain jurisdiction be proved. The petitioner's testimony is usually sufficient as primary evidence of the residence of one of the parties at the time of the commencement of the suit. In addition, corroborative proof as to residence is essential as well as corroboration as to the marriage and as to the cause of action, and this rule obtains whether the suit for nullity is instituted under the statute or under the general equity jurisdiction of the court.10 For further details respecting corroboration of residence, reference should be made to the section dealing with the corroboration as to residence in suits for divorce.11

§ 56. Law Governing Nullity. The statute requires that at least one of the parties to a suit for nullity of marriage shall be domiciled within the state at the time of the commencement of the suit. This is a residential requirement prerequisite to the acquisition of jurisdiction by the court.15 As to what law controls the determination of the court after jurisdiction has been acquired over the subject matter of the suit and over the parties, is another and different question on which the authorities are not altogether in harmony. As has already been observed, the law of the place where a marriage is performed, the lex loci contractus, ordinarily governs in testing the validity of the marriage, 16 and it is this law to which some courts refer the dissolution of the marriage by a decree of nullity, some going so far as to require that the suit be brought in the jurisdiction in which the marriage was performed.¹7 18 With us a suit for nullity of marriage is maintainable by a spouse domiciled within the state at the date of the institution of the suit, and the law by which the validity of the marriage is adjudged is the law of New Jersey, notwithstanding that the marriage may have been performed in another state or country. Illustrative of this rule is the annulment of a marriage for nonage and for fraud.19 It is possible, then, that a marriage may be void or voidable under the law of the place where performed and hence void or voidable in New Jersey by the ius gentium,20 and yet not subject to annulment under our law. Causes for Nullity. The causes for which a marriage may be annulled are antenuptial. The causes must have existed, if at all, at the time of the marriage.22

The causes for nullity of marriage are those enumerated by the statute and those which are cognizable under the general equity jurisdiction of the court. Want of affection between the parties at the time of the ceremony is not a cause for nullity of marriage.23 

The statutory causes as enumerated by section 2:50-1 of the Re vision are as follows: 

2:50-1. Decrees of nullity of marriage may be rendered in all cases, when:

Prior Marriage. Either of the parties has another wife or husband living at the time of a second or other marriage; 

Prohibited Degrees. The parties are within the degrees prohibited by law. When any such marriage shall not have been annulled during the lifetime of the parties the validity thereof shall not be inquired into after the death of either party;

Impotence. The parties, or either of them, were at the time of marriage physically and incurably impotent, provided the party making the application shall have been ignorant of such impotency or incapability at the time of the marriage, or has not subsequently ratified the marriage; 

Incapacity to consent. The parties, or either of them, were at the time of marriage incapable of consenting thereto and the marriage has not been subsequently ratified, provided that where the party capable of consent is the applicant, such party shall have been ignorant of the other's incapacity at the time of the marriage and shall not have confirmed the marriage subsequently to the regaining of capacity by the other party; 

Wife under age. At the suit of the wife, when she was under the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage, unless such marriage be confirmed by her after arriving at such age;

Husband under age. At the suit of the husband, when he was under the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage, unless such marriage be confirmed by him after arriving at such age. No decree of nullity shall be made where a child of the parties has been born, either before or after the marriage, or is likely to be born, unless the court upon an examination of all the facts of the case shall be of the opinion that such decree will not be against the best interests of the child.24

These statutory causes and the causes embraced within the general equity jurisdiction of the court will be considered individually in ensuing chapters.25 

§ 58. 

27 Ratification. In suits to annul a voidable, as distinguished from a void marriage,26 relief will be denied where the petitioner has ratified or confirmed the marriage. Ratification or confirmation presupposes knowledge of the thing ratified. The ratification of a voidable marriage relates back to the date of the marriage rendering the voidable marriage valid ab initio and thus destroying the cause of action. The ratification may occur during the pendency of a suit to annul the marriage.28 

Where the marriage is absolutely void, there cannot be a ratification; 29 nevertheless subsequent conduct of the parties after the removal of the impediment may create a marriage valid for the first time. For instance, there may have been a ceremonial marriage after the bar has been removed.¹ A decree of nullity of a void marriage may be refused where the subsequent cohabitation of the parties spells out a common law marriage.2 An examination of the statutory causes for nullity of marriage will reveal that the principle of ratification has been incorporated into several of the causes.³ 24. 1 R. Condonation. The doctrine of condonation, invoked in suits for divorce, has no application in suits for nullity of marriage, at least where the marriage is void ab initio.5 Yet the defense of ratification in nullity suits is not far remote." 

§ 60. 

Collusion. Collusion between the parties is as effective a bar to the suit for nullity of marriage as it is to the suit for divorce. The law with respect to collusion has been developed primarily in suits for divorce and for that reason the subject in its entirety will be treated farther on in a chapter on divorce." 

An affidavit of non-collusion and merits must be annexed to a petition or counterclaim for nullity of marriage as well as to a petition or counterclaim for divorce.8 

§ 61. Effect of Decree of Nullity. A decree of nullity of marriage, the decree a vinculo matrimonii in the ecclesiastical law, rendered for causes antedating the marriage, differs in its consequences from a decree of divorce from the bond of matrimony, which is based on causes supervening the marriage. Where the marriage is void ab initio, as where the cause alleged is a prior existing marriage," the decree is merely declaratory that no marriage in law has ever existed. The declaration of the status is considered a matter of sound public policy. The decree of nullity, being in rem, binds the whole world and settles for all time, so far as the marriage status is concerned, the rights of third persons as well as the rights of the immediate parties.10 Where the marriage is voidable, as distinguished from void,¹¹ the decree of nullity relates back to the time of the marriage and renders the marriage void ab initio.12

§ 62. Legitimacy of Issue. The effect of a decree of nullity of marriage is now controlled by section 2:50-33 of the Revision. 

Section 2:50-33 provides: 

2:50-33. A decree of nullity of marriage shall not render illegitimate the issue of any marriage so dissolved, except where the marriage, not being a ceremonial one, is dissolved because either party had another wife or husband living at the time of a second or other marriage. Such marriage shall be deemed void ab initio, and the issue thereof shall be illegitimate.18

Strictly, this provision probably applies only to decrees of nullity rendered in pursuance of the statutory jurisdiction of the court and not to decrees of nullity entered in pursuance of the general equity jurisdiction of the court.14 However, another statutory provision relative to the legitimation of children born of a ceremonial marriage, although the marriage be annulled, would seem to be all-inclusive.15 § 63.

The Cause in General. In connection with this chapter reference should be made as well to what has been already discussed pertaining to suits for nullity of marriage. It has been deemed advisable to treat in a previous chapter several matters of general application in suits for nullity of marriage.¹ 

A prior subsisting marriage as a cause for nullity of marriage is a statutory cause. It was a cause for nullity of marriage under the first Divorce Act.2 Section 2:50-1 of the Revision, so far as is pertinent, provides: 

2:50-1. Either of the parties has another wife or husband living at the time of a second or other marriage.³

At common law and under our statutes a prior subsisting marriage renders a marriage utterly void. While no judicial sentence of nullity is necessary, it is desirable that the marriage be annulled in a direct proceeding. In order to annul a marriage, the former marriage of either of the parties must have been undissolved at the time of the marriage.5 Consequently, a decree of nullity will be refused where prior to the marriage the former relation was dissolved by death or by an absolute divorce. 

A prior marriage subsisting at the time of the marriage will not in all cases warrant relief. For instance, a petition for nullity will be dismissed if it appears that following the void marriage

INSPECTION -TRIENNIAL COHABITATION RULE  88. ALIMONY AND  § 78. 

The Cause in General. In connection with suits for nullity of marriage for impotence, reference should be made to what has gone before pertaining to suits for nullity. A number of matters are of general application in suits for nullity of marriage and have accordingly been so treated.¹

Impotence was a canonical impediment which, except for a brief period of time in New Jersey, renders the marriage voidable only. For the cause of impotence the Court of Chancery did not succeed to the jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical court to nullify a marriage. In 1873 Chancellor Runyon so held. In response to the suggestion of Chancellor Runyon the legislature in the succeeding year included impotence as a cause for nullity of marriage. The statute now provides: 

2:50-1. The parties, or either of them, were at the time of marriage physically and incurably impotent, provided the party making the application shall have been ignorant of such impotency or incapability at the time of the marriage, or has not subsequently ratified the marriage.5 

1. Chapter 6 supra. 

2. Supra § 19. 

3. Anonymous, 24 N. J. Eq. 19 (1873). 

4. Rev. Mar. 27, 1874 § 4 set out in Steerman v. Snow, 94 N. J. Eq. 9, 11, 118 Atl. 696 (1922). 5. 1 R. S. (1937) 2:50-1d. 100

§ 101 

IMPOTENCE 

The present statute requires that the impotence complained of shall have existed at the time of the marriage. The cause is antenuptial. And so it was in the ecclesiastical law. Impotence originating after the marriage is not within the statute, nor does incurable impotence constitute a willful desertion as a cause for divorce. The impotence existing at the time of the marriage must be permanent and incapable of being satisfactorily remedied. Impotence within the statute is the want of power of copulation." 

Mere sterility is not impotence.10 Barrenness consequent upon the removal of the ovaries before marriage does not constitute impotence,¹¹ but the fraudulent concealment of sterility may constitute an independent ground for nullity of marriage under the general equity jurisdiction of the court.12 Impotence may result from a physical condition of the husband or wife which permanently precludes sexual relations.13 Or a spouse may be impotent quoad hanc as regards the other only. Impotence quoad hanc is sufficient. Universal impotence is not essential.¹4 

Total incapacity of either of the parties may be the fact. Or coitus with a woman may be possible, but by reason of irremediable vaginal obstructions it may be imperfect, abnormal, unnatural and incomplete intercourse. In such circumstances Dr. 

Lushington, in annulling a marriage where complete sexual intercourse was permanently impossible observed: "Sexual intercourse, in the proper meaning of the term, is ordinary and complete intercourse; it does not mean partial and imperfect intercourse: yet, I cannot go the length of saying that every degree of imperfection would deprive it of its essential character. There must be degrees difficult to deal with; but if so imperfect as scarcely to be natural, I should

25

Technically there cannot be a ratification of a void marriage, so that the decisions rendered prior to 1902 wherein relief was denied were based on the applicant's delay and insincerity. Of these we have two reported cases. In the first, decided in 1877, the husband's application was dismissed for want of sincerity,26 as was evidenced by continued cohabitation, delay in instituting the suit after the statute allowed this cause, and the apparent reasons for the institution of the suit.27 In the second case, the husband's delay was explained satisfactorily.28 

Under the Divorce Acts of 1902, 1907 and their subsequent reenactments, ratification has been successfully urged, but this bar has not always been unmixed with the element of insincerity. 

What constitutes ratification of a marriage voidable by reason of impotence must depend to a large extent on the facts of each case. In view of the nature of the impediment continued cohabitation of the parties does not alone ratify the marriage. But cohabitation coupled with a long delay in applying for relief and the acceptance of the benefits of the marriage, including support, may show a distinct affirmance of the marriage by the wife, particularly where the application is made in a counter suit.29 In one suit instituted by the wife in which there was no proof to indicate insincerity, an unexplained delay of eleven years during which the wife reaped the benefits of the marriage was held to constitute a ratification.¹ A delay of nine years was held fatal to the husband although cohabitation lasted but four months, a case placed upon the ground of ratification and lack of sincerity."

§ 89. 

In suits for nullity of marriage on the ground of incapacity to consent, a number of matters of general application may arise. These matters have been discussed in a prior chapter to which the reader should refer.¹ Incapacity to consent is a cause for nullity of marriage under the statute and, as well, under the general equity jurisdiction of the court. The cause is antenuptial. In this chapter the statutory cause will be discussed, leaving the general equity jurisdiction of the court for subsequent consideration.2

Incapacity to consent was not listed as a statutory cause for nullity of marriage until the passage of the Divorce Act of 1902.³ 

The cause was carried into the Divorce Act of 1907 and into its subsequent re-enactments. At present section 2:50-1 of the Re vision governs: 

2:50-1. The parties, or either of them, were at the time of marriage incapable of consenting thereto and the marriage has not been subsequently ratified, provided that where the party capable of consent is the applicant, such party shall have been ignorant of the other's incapacity at the time of the marriage and shall not have confirmed the marriage subsequently to the regaining of capacity by the other party.*

§ 95. Proof and Corroboration. Together with proof of the marriage,25 and of the residential requirements, the petitioner has the burden of proving, if the defendant is the alleged incompetent, that at the time of the marriage the defendant was incapable of consenting to the marriage, and that the petitioner was ignorant of the defendant's incapacity at such time, and that he has not thereafter confirmed the marriage, whether or not the defendant has regained capacity subsequent to the marriage.27 

The evidence must show the defendant's incapacity to consent as of the time of the marriage, 28 and for this purpose proof of incapacity prior and subsequent to the time of the marriage, if not too remote, is admissible. The point to be established in each case is whether the spouse was so deficient in capacity at the time of the marriage as to be incapable of entering into the marital relation with understanding and reason. No greater mental capacity is required than is essential to the execution of ordinary contracts or testamentary dispositions. Proof of mere weakness of intellect which does not preclude a party from understanding the nature and significance of the marriage contract falls short of incapacity to consent.29 If the defendant was mentally capable of understanding the nature of the marriage at the time it was performed, the fact that subsequent to the marriage circumstances arising out of the relation induced a recurrence of a mental disease which had existed prior to the marriage does not justify a decree of nullity under the statute.¹ 

Proof of defendant's insanity at the time of the marriage is proof of his incapacity to consent.² 2 The proof of incapacity of the defendant to consent as of the time of the marriage may ordinarily be supplied by the testimony of the petitioner or by the testimony of others. Section.

Medical testimony is resorted to, as well, in the ordinary case. Vice Chancellor Green observed: "The abstract opinions of medical experts as to a person's mental condition may be entirely satisfactory in the consideration of the subject from a medical standpoint, but in the solution of questions involved in judicial investigation, they must be tested and qualified with reference to the facts on which such opinions are based. A man may be mentally unsound in a medical point of view, from certain conditions which exist, which would not, in a legal sense, relieve him from responsibility. He may be subject to mania, and, medically, of unsound mind, yet if the peculiar phase of mania had no influence upon the act brought in question, such act is not, in the law, invalidated; he may be an imbecile and, medically, of unsound mind, but if he has sufficient mind to reasonably understand the act which is brought in question, he is legally competent. To judicially determine if the person is, in a legal sense, of unsound mind, we must therefore have the facts on which medical gentlemen have proceeded in forming their opinion." 4

In addition, the evidence produced in support of a spouse's incapacity to consent at the time of the marriage may consist of the record of an adjudication of mental incompetency. An adjudication is competent evidence as prima facie proof of the finding therein contained, but it is not conclusive." The probative force of an adjudication after the marriage must depend to a large extent upon the time which has elapsed between the performance of the marriage and the inquisition.  107. ALIMONY AND  § 98. 

The Cause in General.¹ A number of matters of general application in suits for nullity of marriage have been treated in a prior chapter to which reference should be made. These rules are usually as applicable to the suit for nullity of marriage for nonage as to suits for nullity on other grounds.2 

At common law the marriage of a female under twelve and a male under fourteen years of age was voidable only, unless the parties were below the age of seven years. Nonage of the wife or of the husband as a cause for nullity of marriage first appeared in the Divorce Act of 1907. This act was not retrospective in its operation and did not affect marriages of minors performed prior to its enactment. The statute is operative although the parents consent to the marriage, and although at the time of the marriage the petitioner intended to disaffirm the marriage when he reached the legal age. Yet a decree of nullity may be refused where the defendant married the petitioner in reliance upon his fraudulent representation that he was of legal age and the marriage has been consummated. The purpose of the act is to discourage, but not to prohibit, marriages

2:50-1. Wife under age. At the suit of the wife, when she was under the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage, unless such marriage be confirmed by her after arriving at such age. 

Husband under age. At the suit of the husband, when he was under the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage, unless such marriage be confirmed by him after arriving at such age. No decree of nullity shall be made where a child of the parties has been born, either before or after the marriage, or is likely to be born, unless the court upon an examination of all the facts of the case shall be of the opinion that such decree will not be against the best interests of the child.11

It will be observed that in the present statute a wide discretion is apparently intended to be given to the court in cases where a child has been born or is likely to be born of the union. 

This limitation on the right to a decree of nullity is annexed only to the provision allowing suits by the husband, but from the viewpoint of the best interests of the child it would seem to be immaterial at whose instance the suit is brought. No decision has yet appeared in our reports in which this restriction has been discussed, but in some states similar statutory provisions allowing the court a discretion in divorce suits have been construed.¹ 12 § 99. Who May Sue. The suit for nullity of marriage for nonage is available only to the spouse who was under age at the time of the marriage and who has reached the age of eighteen years (formerly sixteen years for females) at the time of the institution of the suit.15 That the defendant is under the age of eighteen years at the time of the institution of the suit would seem to be immaterial, except that in such case it is necessary that he or she be represented by a guardian if under the age of eighteen or sixteen years respectively.16 The parents, as such, may not sue to annul a marriage of their child voidable because of nonage.¹7 Inasmuch as the husband or wife must now be at least eighteen years of age in order to institute suit for this cause of nullity,18 the suit may be brought in his or her own name without the intervention of a next friend.19 $ 102. As a result, no suit for nullity of marriage will lie until the party alleging nonage has reached the age of eighteen years.22 

It is not necessary that the suit be instituted immediately upon petitioner's arrival at the statutory age, but delay may, in certain cases, be an element denoting ratification.23

The Jurisdiction in General. 

§ 108. 

In addition to the jurisdiction to annul marriages conferred upon the Court of Chancery by statute,¹ the court possesses and exercises a general and fundamental jurisdiction in certain cases. This jurisdiction is separate and distinct from the statutory jurisdiction," although under each jurisdiction the cause must be antenuptial. The Court of 

Chancery already had jurisdiction to avoid ordinary contracts for want of consent, fraud, etc., and marriage being a contract as well as a status, it was but a step to apply to the marriage contract its general jurisdiction over ordinary contracts. This it did in 1870. This jurisdiction to avoid marriage contracts is not derived from the ecclesiastical courts.5 A number of matters of general application in suits for nullity of marriage, whether for statutory causes or for causes under the general equity jur-

12 Want of, or Incapacity to, Consent.¹¹ At common law a marriage devoid of genuine mutual consent is a sham and utterly void.¹² Being void the Court of Chancery under its general equity jurisdiction may adjudge and declare it so. If the want of consent results from an incapacity to consent the suit may be instituted under the statute,13 but the statute should not be construed as depriving the court of its general equity jurisdiction to annul marriages void because of "incapacity to consent." Where the parties are each mentally competent at the time of the ceremony but do not intend a contract of marriage, the suit must be instituted under the general equity jurisdiction of the court.

-Jest. Fraud as a cause for nullity of marriage is another instance where the Court of Chancery has declared marriages void without the aid of statute. This it originally did in 

1873 in the leading case of Carris v. Carris.27 In England the doctrine of the Carris case has been expressly disapproved, for in that country if there is consent to the marriage no fraud inducing the consent will justify a decree of nullity.28 

The fraud may consist of an affirmative false representation or the withholding of the truth when it should be spoken.29 Fraud cannot be said to have existed unless the party possesses knowledge of his existing impediment at the time of the marriage. An innocent misrepresentation or suppression is not enough.¹ Nor can a spouse claim to have been defrauded if he or she knew of the defect of the other spouse before the marriage.2

A marriage induced by fraud has been regarded as voidable only, and, if ratified, the petitioner is barred of relief. A voluntary second marriage, performed ceremonially between the parties during the pending of the suit for nullity, and subsequent cohabitation, amount to a ratification.¹

§ 120. Tuberculosis. § 121. 

-Concealment of Mental Disease. 

Insanity existing at the time of the marriage usually cannot constitute a fraud, for, as was stated by Chancellor Walker, "as defendant was incapable of consenting to the marriage, he probably was incapable of making the representations in such a way as to be responsible for them." Such insanity is, however, within the scope of the statutory cause "incapacity to consent." 5 As to the concealment of a hereditary mental disease some doubt was expressed in one case, in which the proofs were inadequate, that such concealment would be sufficient fraud to vitiate a consummated marriage," but later the Court of Chancery annulled a consummated marriage where the husband misrepresented that he was in good health when in fact he was suffering from epilepsy." Duress as defined by our courts is that degree of constraint or danger, either actually inflicted or threatened and impending, which is sufficient in severity or in apprehension to overcome the mind of a person of ordinary firmness. The duress must have existed at the time of the ceremony so as to disable the party from acting as a free agent and must be directly the inducing cause of his or her entering into the marriage. Duress in inducing a marriage does not exist if the petitioner had an opportunity for deliberate reflection after the alleged duress and prior to the time of the marriage. It would seem to be immaterial whether the coercion comes from the defendant or from a third person.

§ 125. 

Mistake. Under the general equity jurisdiction of the 

Court of Chancery a marriage may be annulled for want of genuine matrimonial intention or purpose where one of the parties is mistaken, through the other's fraud perhaps, as to the legal effect of the ceremony, as where a party believes a ceremony to be a mere betrothal instead of a marriage.20 A marriage devoid of matrimonial intention or purpose by reason of mistake as to the identity of person, the canonical error personae,21 probably would entitle a party to a declaration that the marriage was void.22 This field of general equity jurisdiction has been for the most part untouched by reported decisions. Future adjudications must deal eventually with the effect of mutual mistake of the parties when such mistake goes to an essential of the marriage. 

The distinction between consummated and unconsummated marriages in fraud cases 28 undoubtedly will be imported into this field.

 165. ALIMONY AND  § 126. Kinds of Divorces. The ecclesiastical courts recog nized two kinds of divorces (1) divorce a mensa et thoro (2) 134

§

DIVORCE 

divorce a vinculo matrimonii. The divorce a mensa was a judicial separation, while the divorce a vinculo was the annulment of marriage for antenuptial causes.¹ With us divorces are of two kinds, the divorce from the bond of matrimony and the divorce from bed and board. The divorce from the bond of matrimony, while frequently described as divorce a vinculo, is for causes postdating the marriage and should not be confused with nullity of marriage for antenuptial causes.³. The divorce from bed and board is a judicial separation and corresponds to the ecclesiastical divorce a mensa et thoro. In the case of a wife whose sole object is to obtain support from her husband in the Court of Chancery, the suit for separate maintenance should be preferred to the suit for divorce from bed and board for reasons explained farther on." 

§ 127. 

Jurisdiction of Chancery. 

In England jurisdiction of matrimonial causes was vested in the ecclesiastical courts until 1857. At that time the Court for Divorce was established and to this court was delegated the exclusive right to hear and dispose of causes matrimonial.Ⓡ 

In the exercise of its matrimonial jurisdiction the ecclesiastical courts were restricted to granting decrees of nullity, divorce a vinculo matrimonii, and decrees of divorce from bed and board. 

Within the church courts marriage was indissoluble except for causes antedating the marriage. Parliament, however, had the power to sever the bond of matrimony for postnuptial causes and this it did usually after the parties had been divorced from bed and board by the decree of the ecclesiastical court. On the other hand, the High Court of Chancery of England was without inherent jurisdiction over matrimonial causes."

The New Jersey Court of Chancery inherited no fundamental or inherent jurisdiction from the English Court of Chancery because its English prototype possessed no such jurisdiction. The court is in no wise an ecclesiastical tribunal and therefore has not succeeded to the power of the ecclesiastical courts to decree divorces from bed and board or to decree nullity of marriage. The state fosters and promotes the relation by allowing competent persons to enter into it at their own volition. But once the relation is created it may not be altered or terminated by consent of the parties. The marital status is indissoluble except for causes allowed by the state, proved in the manner specified by the state acting through its courts. In every suit for divorce, there are at least three parties, the husband and wife and the state. The suit is a triangular suit, sui generis. Usually the state does not appear by counsel or plead, but at all times it is represented by the "conscience of the court." A peculiar responsibility rests upon the court, particularly in ex parte cases.19 But it may appear by counsel under the statute.20

Because of the deep concern of the state in maintaining the integrity and permanence of the marital relation it is stated as a general rule that the law disfavors divorce and nullity of marriage and will do nothing to facilitate them.21 This general proposition pervades the entire field of law, being recognized in courts of law 22 as well as in equity whether or not the particular proceeding is one for the dissolution of a marriage.23 Further, it has been stated that proceedings for the dissolution of marriage must be strictly adverse, that the statute must be strictly construed, and that the courts will dissolve the relation only when the complaining party is strictly entitled to a decree.25 Yet several portions of the statute have been held to be remedial and as such to be construed liberally.26 It seems that the statute 24

§ 129. Proceeding In Rem.28 

In suits for divorce the court is concerned with the marital status 29 of the parties to the suit. 

This status or res, as it is commonly designated, is, of course, intangible and exists only as a legal conception. The proceeding for divorce is directly against the marriage status. Consequently, the suit is regarded essentially as a proceeding in rem or at least quasi in rem. The decree of divorce is self-executing. 

It actually operates upon the marital status without any further proceeding.¹ Other instances of proceedings in rem in matrimonial litigation which may be mentioned are the suit for nullity of marriage, injunctive relief against the prosecution of a suit for divorce in a foreign state, and a declaratory decree in equity adjudging a foreign decree of divorce to be null and void in this state. Decrees for alimony may be quasi in rem.5 In some states a suit for divorce from bed and board is a proceeding in personam, but with us no such distinction between a proceeding for divorce from bed and board and from the bond of matrimony has been drawn.

§ 132. Residence. 2:50-11. When the defendant cannot be served personally with process within this state, and when at the time of the commencement of the suit the petitioner is a bona fide resident of this state, jurisdiction for the purpose of divorce, whether absolute or from bed and board, may be acquired by publication, to be followed, where practicable, by service upon or notice to the defendant without this state, or by additional substituted service upon the defendant within this state, as prescribed by law or rules of court, under the following conditions: (a). When at the time the cause of action arose, the petitioner was a bona fide resident of this state, and has continued so to be down to the time of the commencement of the suit, except that no suit for absolute divorce shall be commenced for any cause other than adultery, unless the petitioner has been for the two years next preceding the commencement of the suit a bona fide resident of this state; (b). When, since the cause of action arose, the petitioner has become, and for at least two years next preceding the commencement of the suit has continued to be, a bona fide resident of this state; provided, the cause of action alleged was recognized in the jurisdiction in which the petitioner resided at the time the cause of action arose, as a ground for the same relief asked for in the suit in this state.¹7

§ 133. -Residence as Meaning Domicile. 25 The status of marriage 26 exists only as a legal conception. Because a decree of divorce alters or dissolves the marriage status, it becomes important to ascertain the situs of the status. A court in a particular state cannot exercise authority over a marriage status which is not within its territorial limits any more than it can by its decree affect land outside of its prescribed jurisdictional boundaries. The domicile of the parties was seized upon by the courts as determinant of the situs of the marital status or res. This thought is neatly expressed by one writer: . . The res here is not a tangible res that court and counsel can see and touch. It is intangible, and some device had to be manufactured whereby the situs of the res could be determined, since the situs was going to determine jurisdiction in rem. 'Domicil' was hit upon by the courts of 

England and of the United States as being evidence of the situs of the res, . . . and it came to be regarded not only

With us the notion that the domicile of the parties or either of them controls the situs of the marriage status has been recognized from an early date. As concisely stated by Chancellor 

Zabriskie: 

"Proceedings with regard to the validity, or dissolution of marriage, are, as was held in the celebrated case of the Duchess of Kingston, proceedings in rem. They actually operate upon the matter; they affirm, constitute, or dissolve the marriage relation. By the well settled principles of the jus gentium, or rules acknowledged by the codes of all civilized nations, and given effect by comity of law, when not controlled by positive enactments, the positive and relative status of every person is regulated by the law of domicil." 28 

The requirement in the earlier Divorce Acts that the parties be inhabitants or residents of the state was uniformly construed to mean that they must be domiciled within the state.29 The requirement of sections 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision that either party, or in the case of service of process by publication, the petitioner, must be a "bona fide resident" of this state means that they, or either of them, must actually be domiciled, in the sense already observed,¹ within the state. In order that a petitioner may comply with the jurisdictional requisite of domicile within this state it is not indispensable that he shall select a fixed habitation in a distinct locality so long as he dwells within the territorial boundaries of the state with the explicit intention of abiding in this state. However, the mere domicile of the parties within the state is not, of itself, sufficient. The domicile of the parties when the cause of action arose, the continuance of such domicile down to the time of the commencement of the action, and the two year period of domicile in certain cases are, as well, prerequisites to the acquisition of jurisdiction under the present statute. 3

§ 134. -Necessity and Sufficiency of Actual Residence. 

party may not acquire a domicile in this state in the first instance without actually residing here. The term "bona fide resident" which is used throughout sections 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision is equivalent to domicile. The statute does not require that the parties, or either of them, be actually residing in this state at or for the particular period of time therein specified. 

Consequently, it is possible that a party, continuously domiciled in this state, may fulfill the domiciliary requirements of the act although he was not actually residing in the state at the time the cause of action arose or at any time before the commencement of the action." A technical domicile would seem to be sufficient. An absence from the state may, however, indicate a change of domicile.

If neither of the parties is domiciled in this state at and for the particular period of time prescribed by the act, the actual residence of one or both of the parties in this state is insufficient on which to base jurisdiction in suits for divorce. A party who did not reside in this state prior to his imprisonment in the state prison has been held not to be domiciled in the state for the purpose of jurisdiction in a suit for divorce."

If the petitioner arrive in this state with the avowed object of dwelling here in order to procure a standing upon which to found a divorce suit, a violent presumption arises that the residence in this state is not animo manendi.12 The petitioner may show, however, either that his purpose in coming into this state was not for a divorce or, if he had such an intention, that he also had the further aim of abiding permanently in this state irrespective of his success in the divorce action.13 In connection with non-residents coming into this state for a divorce, it is also essential to consider under subdivision b of sections 2:50-10 and

§ 139. Continuity of Domicile. According to the obiter in one case, a petitioner, domiciled in the state when the cause of action under the statute arose, upon returning to this state after having in the interim transferred her domicile to another jurisdiction, may sue for divorce under subdivision b of sections 

2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision for a cause which had accrued prior to her departure from this state. The objection urged at one time that the use of subdivision b would defeat every case of continued residence under subdivision a does not seem to be of importance. The continuity of domicile to the time of the commencement of the action under subdivision a, or for that matter under subdivision b, is exacted in order that the marital status or res, widely recognized as the foundation of jurisdiction in suits for divorce, will have its situs in this state so that the court may take jurisdiction at the commencement of the action. 

If the petitioner returns to this state, as she did in the Adler case, and continues to be domiciled here for two years next preceding the commencement of the action, the marital res is within the reach of the court at the time the suit is commenced.

 § 140. Change of Domicile Pendente Lite. There is nothing in sections 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision which requires in any case that the domicile of the party upon which jurisdiction is based shall continue in this state after the suit has been commenced. The party upon whose domicile jurisdiction has attached may in fact change his domicile to another state or country at any time after the suit is commenced without affecting the jurisdiction of the court to deal with the marital status. Perhaps the statutory requirement, or want of it, may be explained on the theory that the parties may not withdraw the status from the court's jurisdiction under the general rule that jurisdiction depends upon the state of things at the time the suit is commenced and that, after jurisdiction vests, it cannot be ousted by subsequent events.10 

§ 141. Proviso of Subdivision b. Under the proviso of subdivision b of sections 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision, "provided the cause of action alleged was recognized in the jurisdiction in which such (or the petitioner) party resided at the time the cause of action arose, as a ground for the same relief asked for in the suit in this state," 11 it would seem sufficient if the cause for divorce is recognized definitely in the foreign jurisdiction either by statute or by usage. "Such party" in the proviso of subdivision b of section 2:50-10 refers to either of the parties who since the cause of action arose has become domiciled in New Jersey for at least two years next preceding the commencement of the suit, and upon whose domicile jurisdiction is to be based. For instance, if the petitioner alone becomes domiciled in this state since the cause of action arose and the cause of action arose while the petitioner was domiciled in a state not then recognizing the cause alleged as a ground for divorce, jurisdiction will be declined although the defendant was domiciled in another jurisdiction at the time the cause of action arose which did then recognize the cause as a ground for divorce. If, however, the defendant alone, or as well as the petitioner, should become domiciled in this state since the cause of action arose, the jurisdiction may well be supported on the defendant's domicile under section 2:50-10 if he has fulfilled the two year residential requirement and the cause was recognized in the defendant's former domicile at the time it arose. § 142. -Counterclaim by Non-resident. 

If the court acquires jurisdiction of a suit for divorce by reason of the petitioner's domicile within the state at or since the time the cause of action arose and for the requisite period of time, it may grant a decree of divorce to the defendant counter-claimant domiciled in another state who has been brought in by publication and substituted service of process. The dismissal of the original petition does not operate to oust the court of jurisdiction to decree a divorce on the counterclaim.18 The statute relating to the filing of a counterclaim 19 is quite sweeping, but it must, it seems, be construed with sections 2:50-9, 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision.20

If the petitioner cannot fulfill the necessary domiciliary requirements on which to base a decree of divorce, the counterclaim of the non-resident defendant cannot be supported.

§ 146. 

Proof and Corroboration Generally. As a general rule in every suit for divorce three essential elements must be proved and the proof may not rest solely upon the uncorroborated testimony of the petitioner. These elements are: the marriage,² the residence, and the cause of action. The admissions of the defendant in his answer will not supply sufficient proof of these essential requisites, or any of them," nor will the absence of testimony on the part of the defendant, although he files an answer." It is a firmly established rule of evidence that a divorce will not be granted upon the petitioner's testimony unless corroborated as to the elements in the proofs necessary to sustain the decree." 

The rule obtains although the court may believe the petitioner's testimony without corroboration. The requirement of corroboration is not a statutory requisite, but has been evolved by the courts as a rule of evidence to insure the state's interest in the preservation of the marital status against collusive and otherwise fraudulent divorces."

Where it is evident to the court that there is no collusion, less corroboration may be required, and conversely where the court scents collusion, it is likely that it will require a greater amount of corroboration before it will be induced to believe the petitioner's story. Corroboration as to Handwriting and Contents. 

Formerly it was the rule that the petitioner's testimony that a document, such as a letter, was in the handwriting of or was signed by the defendant required corroboration by the testimony of other witnesses, 25 but this holding has been overruled. The rule now is that the petitioner's testimony as to the defendant's handwriting or signature must be corroborated, but agreeably to the rule existing in other situations,26 such corroboration may be furnished by the surrounding facts and circumstances adequately established if such is the best corroborative proof available." DIVORCE § 148. 

Defenses in General; Equitable. The state is a party to every suit for divorce and nullity of marriage and it is the policy of the law that all proper defenses be made or compelled.¹ In furtherance of this policy the legislature has authorized the court in ex parte cases to appoint a solicitor actively to defend.2 After jurisdiction of matrimonial causes was conferred upon the Court of Chancery by the Divorce Act of 1794, the proceedings for divorce and nullity of marriage came to be regarded as equitable in their nature, and as such the maxims and equitable defenses prevailing in ordinary suits in equity have been held to be, to some extent at least, applicable. In some instances particular equitable maxims and defenses have been successfully urged, as, for example, the doctrine of unclean hands, and of laches. Although the court has not inherited the ecclesiastical jurisdiction, it has adopted some of the defenses recognized in the ecclesiastical law, as for instance, in divorce, the defenses of condonation, and recrimination. Yet when an equitable maxim intervened, the court has refused in some instances to adhere to a rule which had existed in the church courts.10 In importing equitable defenses and ordinary defenses into the triangular matrimonial suit the public policy should not be overlooked.11 § 149. Unclean Hands. The maxim "He who comes into equity must come with clean hands" is of general application in courts of equity and as an equitable defense 12 has been to some extent imported into matrimonial litigation. whether collusion exists. But the judicial mind is ever careful to distinguish between collusion and the indicia of collusion. Unlike connivance, collusion cannot exist without an agreement or understanding between the parties to the suit.10 It is not collusion for the parties to be desirous of being divorced.11 In a suit by the wife for divorce her failure to ask for alimony or for custody of the children when such relief might be obtained is not collusion, although her omission to pray for such relief may be prompted by the hope that her husband will not defend. Such circumstance is suspicious and may induce the court to interrogate the witnesses more at length in order to discover whether an agreement or understanding between the parties exists, or it may cause the court to require better corroborative proof, but it is not collusion per se.12 Without more, it is not collusion for defendant, upon being called by the petitioner, 18 to admit the cause of action.14 But the willingness or reluctance of the defendant to admit may suggest or dispel the notion of collusion.15 

An agreement or understanding between the parties may amount to collusion if its essence is to impose a case upon the court by the suppression of evidence or by the manufacture thereof, or if the agreement, express or implied, is designed to suppress a defense to the suit. The mere fact that a defense is withheld is not enough. The suppression of the defense must result from an agreement or understanding between the parties. But, if the agreement is that no defense shall be made, this is, in itself, collusion and, upon ascertaining such fact, the court will not inquire as to whether or not the defense, if interposed, would have constituted a valid and effective defense, but the court may, barring imposition by the manufacture or suppression of evidence, dismiss the petition without prejudice 16 to the institution of a suit which shall not be collusive.17

Usually the proof of an agreement between the parties to suppress a defense is circumstantial, but occasionally it is direct." 

From what circumstances will the court infer the existence of such an agreement? The failure of the defendant husband to renew in defense a charge of adultery, which he had made in a previous suit instituted by him and which never came to hearing, was deemed insufficient in a case where the petitioner testified that there was no arrangement or understanding between the parties that the defense should be suppressed.19 The court has declined to draw the inference from the fact that a non-resident defendant wife came into the state to be served with process and then failed to offer a defense. The suspicion of the court was aroused, but it was satisfied that the defendant's voluntary appearance within the state may have been prompted by the fact that the state in which she resided did not recognize foreign decrees of divorce based upon publication and substituted service.20 But the circumstantial proof of collusion was held to be sufficient in a case in which the defendant husband came into another county to be served and during the pendency of the suit the petitioner succeeded in procuring the deposit of money by the defendant husband to be paid to her when the divorce should be obtained; 21 and likewise in the Sheehan case, where the court inferred an agreement not to defend from the fact that the husband had, before the suit was commenced, advanced money to the wife's solicitor for the purpose of bringing the suit.22 

An agreement between the parties in anticipation of the suit, or during its pendency, relating to alimony or property does not necessarily constitute collusion. But if the agreement tends to promote or facilitate, or is conditioned upon, a divorce, the agreement, as such, is unenforceable,23 and will bar relief in the suit for divorce.24 So where the defendant husband appeals to his wife to institute suit and agrees that if she will do so he will give her a lump sum or a periodic allowance in settlement provided she obtains a decree, it is inferable that there is an agreement not to

Condonation. Irrespective of the particular cause alleged, the doctrine of condonation applies in suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony and from bed and board, but the doctrine has no application in suits for nullity of marriage.2 Because it is of general application in suits for divorce, it will be discussed herein in toto rather than reserved for each particular cause for divorce hereinafter treated. This bar is essentially of the unwritten law, although in adultery cases the doctrine has been recognized by the legislature in section 2:50-5 of the Revision."

It has come to us by adoption from the ecclesiastical courts. Ordinarily, condonation presupposes the existence of a completed cause of action for divorce. This is clear in adultery cases.5 

In desertion cases the continuity of the two years' period of desertion may be interrupted by sexual relations, but until a cause of action accrues by reason of a willful, continued and obstinate desertion for the term of two years,' a condonation, technically speaking, cannot exist. In extreme cruelty cases the nicety of the distinction seldom has been observed. Acts of extreme cruelty

§ 155. 

-Revival of Offense. To every condonation is annexed a condition that the condonee shall treat the other spouse in the future with conjugal kindness,16 and especially refrain from a repetition of the offense condoned.17 While condonation is usually based on the repentance of the offender so that it constitutes no defense where the subsequent conduct of the condonee negatives the idea of repentence, 18 nevertheless the condition attached to condonation may be breached by subsequent conjugal unkindness notwithstanding that it is evident that there had been a bona fide repentance at the time of the condonation.19 But the condition should not be affixed to the condonation indefinitely. If revival is to be based essentially on repentance for the offense condoned, the condition should exist only so long as the subsequent conjugal unkindness is reasonably referable to a want of repentance of the particular offense condoned.20

Any condoned matrimonial offense may be revived whether the offense is adultery, extreme cruelty or desertion. At one time a matured cause of action for desertion which had been condoned could not be revived, 21 but because it is now settled definitely that a desertion which has accrued prior to the time of the filing of the petition need not continue as willful and obstinate down to the commencement of the suit,22 the offense may be revived after a condonation subsequent to the two years' period.28 And

The effect of a breach of the condition of a condonation is to permit the complaining party to rely upon the original cause of action which has been condoned,25 although if the act or acts breaching the condition also constitute a matured matrimonial offense the aggrieved spouse may and should 26 set up the original and subsequent offenses as causes for divorce.27 In extreme cruelty cases, except perhaps where the act constitutes extreme cruelty per se,28 it is unusual to treat a condonation as of a completed cause of action for divorce. In the many cases involving a course of misconduct there are sometimes frequent condonations and frequent revivals by subsequent misconduct until there is a cessation of normal cohabitation. Usually the court considers the entire series of acts in order to determine whether the defendant has been guilty of extreme cruelty. -Nature of Reviving Offense. The condition of a condonation may of course be breached by the commission of the same offense. For instance, adultery revives adultery whether the subsequent act of adultery is committed with the same person or another.20 Where parties between whom an adulterous relation has once been established are found living together under circumstances which would induce an unprejudiced mind to conclude that their inclinations had not changed, the fair presumption is that the illicit intercourse has continued.¹ A condoned offense may be revived also by the commission of a different offense cognizable as cause for divorce. Thus the offense of adultery may be revived by subsequent acts of extreme cruelty.2

Hence any act which amounts to conjugal unkindness is sufficient to revive a condoned offense whether the original offense was adultery, desertion or extreme cruelty. What acts are tantamount to conjugal unkindness must be left, and rightly so, for each particular case. 

In cases based upon adultery, conjugal unkindness sufficient to avoid the condonation has been held to include the carrying on of a secret correspondence with the adulteress, giving her money and presents, visiting her without the wife's knowledge, meeting the co-respondent in the late hours of the night, inviting the corespondent to the home in the husband's absence and openly professing a lack of affection for the husband,' continued association with persons of the other sex, coupled with cruel treatment, inadequate support and repeated desertions. In desertion cases a subsequent and immediate resumption of a willful and obstinate desertion will avoid a condonation although the later desertion has not run for the statutory period.⁹ In extreme cruelty cases the offense may be revived by subsequent unprovoked acts of cruelty although such acts may not, standing alone, be sufficient to constitute extreme cruelty.10

6 written law. With us the doctrine is statutory insofar as adultery is in bar of adultery, but as will be presently noticed the statute is not exclusive so as to override the unwritten law. The doctrine has been subjected to severe criticism, and in some few states has been supplanted by the doctrine of "comparative rectitude." But in New Jersey the doctrine is firmly embedded as a part of our statutory and unwritten law and the tendency is to apply the doctrine irrespective of the particular recriminatory offense urged. 

The recriminatory charge must, however, amount to the commission of a matrimonial offense. It may be added that the matrimonial offense must be cognizable under our statute and it is immaterial that the parties were domiciled in a state which did not recognize the offense as cause for divorce at the time it accrued. "8 -Adultery to Adultery. In the first act conferring jurisdiction upon the Court of Chancery section five provided among other things that if it appeared to the court "that both parties have been guilty of adultery, then no divorce shall be decreed." Adultery voluntarily committed by the petitioner, if properly pleaded, or, if shown by the petitioner's own case, is a bar to a suit for divorce for defendant's adultery under this statute and its subsequent reenactments. Without the aid of the statute the same conclusion would be reached.10 Adultery committed by the petitioner during the pendency of the suit is a bar.¹¹ -Desertion to Adultery. § 157 

13 is now settled that, if the petitioner has been guilty of a willful, continued and obstinate desertion for the statutory period, which desertion has accrued as a cause of action 18 prior to the time when the act of adultery was committed by the defendant, the defendant may set up such accrued cause of action for desertion in bar.¹4

In order that the desertion be a recriminatory bar to a charge of adultery, it must have been a willful, continued and obstinate desertion for the statutory period.15 If during the statutory period the defendant has consented to the separation or the separation is by mutual consent, there cannot exist a desertion which may be pleaded in recrimination.16 Furthermore, the cause of action for desertion in favor of the defendant must have accrued at a time which antedated the commission of the act of adultery by the defendant. The petitioner's desertion may have been willful, continued and obstinate originally, but if before the expiration of two years of such desertion the defendant commits an act of adultery, the desertion of the petitioner, whether simple or constructive, ceases. To hold that the desertion of the petitioner continues in the face of an accrued cause of action for adultery in his favor would be to make condonation of the adultery by the petitioner compulsory at the risk of desertion. Nevertheless, in some decisions the court has permitted a desertion incomplete at the time of the commission of the defendant's act of adultery to be set up in bar where at the time of the filing of the petition the two years have elapsed." This conclusion cannot be reconciled with underlying principles. -Miscellaneous Offenses. Considering some other particular situations not embraced by section 2:50-5 of the Revision one finds that extreme cruelty is a bar to a charge of adultery,26 and undoubtedly the converse is equally true.27

-Effect of Condonation and Connivance. The mandatory part of section 2:50-5 of the Revision, whether the bar urged is collusion, consent or recrimination, is that "no divorce shall be decreed." ³ Hence a defendant who has been guilty of uncondoned adultery is not entitled to a decree of divorce by way of counterclaim because of the petitioner's adultery by proving that the petitioner consented to or connived at his act of adultery.

Connivance. The doctrine of connivance in suits for divorce is an application of the general maxim volenti non fit injuria which has found expression in the various branches of law.20 

The doctrine was applied in suits for divorce a mensa et thoro in the ecclesiastical courts, and without the intervention of statute would be a part of our unwritten law 21 in suits for divorce.22 

Section 2:50-5 of the Revision provides among other things that "if it appear to the court that the adultery complained of ....,23 or that the complainant was consenting thereto, then no divorce shall be decreed.

" 24 

The doctrine of connivance as a bar to suits for divorce is invoked principally in suits in which adultery is complained of. 

This is the scope of section 2:50-5 of the Revision but it is not to be understood that the doctrine may not be applicable in suits for divorce brought for other causes. In desertion cases, of course, consent by the petitioner negatives the existence of any cause of action.25 The doctrine of connivance may find application occasionally in suits for divorce for extreme cruelty,20 but in extreme cruelty cases the petitioner's consent is implied usually from his provocation which completely negatives the very existence of a cause of action.27 In extreme cruelty cases wherein adultery within

Connivance differs from collusion, although the two terms are frequently used interchangeably. Connivance is unilateral on the part of the petitioner, while collusion cannot exist without an agreement or understanding between the parties.20 

In cases where adultery is complained of, section 2:50-5 is mandatory that no divorce shall be decreed if it appears that the complainant was consenting to the adultery complained of. The statute embraces cases of express consent or such consent as may be imputed to the petitioner. The word "consenting" is broader than connivance and embraces it. The statute merely affirms the unwritten law, insofar as it concerns an act of adultery complained of, and should be given the same effect as the rule of the unwritten law.¹

The consent or connivance must be as to the adultery "complained of." However, a husband who consents to or attempts to procure the commission of adultery by his wife with certain persons may be deemed to have consented to subsequent acts of adultery complained of, although committed with other persons, in the absence of proof that in the interim he has persuaded his wife to lead a virtuous life.2 Condonation of repeated acts of adultery may afford an inference of consent to future acts. But under the statute the consent must precede the act. A husband who has not registered a prior consent to the act of adultery complained of might possibly ratify his wife's conduct and not be barred of relief on the ground of consent or connivance. So consent to subsequent acts of adultery not complained of is not a bar to relief for a prior act of adultery committed by the wife in the absence of the husband's consent or connivance.¹

The consent of the petitioner need not be, and rarely is, express, but it may be inferred from his affirmative conduct or even his passiveness when circumstances are such as to impose upon him a duty to act. The conduct of the petitioner must be such as to cause or to have a tendency to cause the commission of the adultery complained of. The refusal of marital intercourse, although without justification, is not a consent to the commission of adultery, unless accompanied by words or conduct from which a consent may reasonably be inferred. The consent of the petitioner may be active or passive. Those cases need no discussion in which the petitioner's affirmative conduct is obviously intended to induce the defendant to commit adultery. For example, a husband's consent will readily be inferred where he employs a third person to commit adultery with his wife. And so where the wife is the petitioner and has caused her husband to be lured into adultery.10 A husband may be guilty of causing his wife's entrapment where the persons he employs to watch his wife intentionally, and without the husband's knowledge or express consent, induce the wife to commit adultery. 

Qui facit per alium, facit per se.11 The husband's consent may be inferred where after introducing his wife in her bedroom to the co-respondent as a prostitute he gives her liquor and leaves her with the adulterer 12 or where he invites the co-respondent to sleep in the same bed with him and his wife and then abandons her to the adulterer.18

The husband may remain passive and be consenting. Imputed consent of the husband in desertion cases where he fails to make just advances will be noticed farther on.¹ In adultery cases the law imposes upon the husband the duty to protect his wife and, if he sees acts or conduct on her part which a reasonable man could not see without being convinced that his wife's honor is being placed in jeopardy, he is called upon to exercise peculiar vigilance
