§ 162. 

Effect of Decree of Divorce. A final decree of divorce from bed and board alters the marital relation partially, to the extent that the parties are each forbidden by the order of the court to cohabit for the time specified in the decree or until the decree is vacated or suspended. But in most other respects the marital status remains undisturbed. The parties are still husband and wife so that each is unable to marry without subjecting himself or herself to a charge of bigamy.⁹ 

In suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony the first decree is the decree nisi as will be observed farther on.10 By the final decree the marital relation is dissolved in all respects, save that in a suit by the wife she may be entitled to the incident of support under an order for alimony. Each of the parties is permitted to re-marry on the entry of the final decree.11 The final decree of divorce does not, as does the final decree of nullity,12 avoid the marriage from its inception. The operation of the decree of divorce is prospective rather than retrospective.

quently, all property rights dependent upon coverture are left undisturbed by the decree.18

A final decree of divorce from the bond of matrimony, if valid, severs and dissolves the marital status with the result that property rights of husband and wife based upon the existence, of a marriage may be affected. The wife's inchoate right of dower in lands of her husband situated in this state 14 is extinguished by a final decree of divorce from the bond of matrimony whether the decree is obtained at the suit of the husband 15 or of the wife.16 

Likewise, the decree bars the husband's right of curtesy in lands of the wife situated here.17 If the lands are situated in another state or country, the effect of a New Jersey decree of absolute divorce on dower and curtesy must be determined by the lex rei sitae.18

Vested interests are not, as a general rule, disturbed by a decree of divorce unless the instrument under which the vesting occurred provides therefor expressly or by implication.19 The effect of divorce upon an agreement between husband and wife for maintenance may be observed farther on.20 However, a decree of divorce may change the nature of the vested interest if the particular estate is dependent upon coverture. For instance, an estate by the entirety, being dependent upon the existence of a marriage, is converted into a tenancy in common upon the dissolution of the marriage by the entry of a final decree of absolute divorce at the suit of either of the parties.21

§ 166.

The Cause in General. With respect to suits for divorce for adultery reference should be made to a previous chapter where, for convenience, a number of matters of general application in divorce litigation have been discussed. In the ecclesiastical courts adultery was cause for divorce a mensa et thoro. With us the cause was allowed in the first Divorce Act and at present 

1. Chapter 13 supra. 

2. Act of Dec. 2, 1794 (Pat. Laws 143). 2 185

§ 167 

adultery by either of the parties is cause for divorce from bed and board or from the bond of matrimony.3 Adultery is the voluntary sexual intercourse of a married person with one not the husband or wife of that person.* The husband may be guilty of adultery although his act also amounts to rape." 

But if the wife is ravished, this is not her adultery in the criminal law or in the law of divorce. A married man may be guilty of adultery although the woman is unmarried, and in this respect the courts follow the ecclesiastical rule rather than the rule prevailing in the criminal law.8 Antenuptial incontinence is not adultery. A void foreign decree of divorce 10 is no protection against a charge of adultery although the intercourse may have taken place elsewhere.11 Sodomy, bestiality, and the like have not in our state been held to amount to adultery. In some states such offenses against the law of nature constitute distinct grounds for divorce. Coming to the knowledge of the other spouse, such offenses may, however, constitute extreme cruelty. The cause of action for adultery arises when the offense is committed.12 Aside from divorce, it may be observed that adultery may constitute a bar to dower.13

§ 172.

Recrimination. Although the proofs show that defendant has been guilty of adultery, relief will be denied if it is proved satisfactorily by defendant that the petitioner has been guilty of uncondoned adultery, desertion or extreme cruelty. The rules pertaining to recrimination, including pleading and proof, have already been noticed in connection with suits for divorce for desertion and for extreme cruelty as well as for adultery." § 173. Connivance. If it is proved that the petitioner connived at the commission of the act of adultery complained of, he or she is barred of relief. The bar of connivance is invoked principally in suits for divorce for adultery, but occasionally application of the bar may be found in suits for divorce for other causes. 

It has been deemed practical to treat of this defense elsewhere. 

§ 174. Insanity. 

Insanity. In suits for divorce for adultery insanity of the defendant is a defense if he or she was generally insane at the time of the commission of the act complained of. Insanity of the defendant occurring subsequently to the commission of the act is not a defense although the defendant is committed to an institution.10 However, such subsequent insanity and adjudication may be considered in determining the mental condition of the party at the time the offense was committed. The mental incapacity sufficient to excuse the commission of an act of adultery must be more than mere mental weakness 11 or extreme nervousness.12 As expressed in one case nothing short of insanity so pronounced that the defendant is unable to apprehend the nature of her conduct will excuse the offense of adultery.18 However, if a wife is mentally deranged, but not totally incompetent, a duty may in some circumstances devolve upon the husband to surround her with greater protection, if he is aware of her condition, lest the law infer his consent to the adultery charged.¹¹ § 175. On April 1, 1870, what is now Chancery Rule 278 was promulgated as Rule 158.21 Later it became Rule 259 and provided: 

In suits for divorce on account of adultery the petition shall state the name of the person with whom the adultery was committed, if known, and, if not known, shall set forth the description of the person or such designation of the time, place and circumstances under which the act or series of acts were committed as will enable the defendant and the court to distinguish and individuate the particular offense or offenses intended to be charged; and no reference 22 shall be ordered in a suit in which the offense is not so designated; and if the name of the person is stated to be unknown, it must be shown on the reference that it was not known at the commencement of the suit.

Under Rule 259 it was required that the name of the particeps criminis be alleged in the petition, if known, and, if not known, that the petition set forth the description of the person or such designation of the time, etc. The requirement as to the allegation of the name of the particeps criminis, and his description, if not known, was in the alternative with the designation of time, place and circumstances. If the petitioner named the co-respondent, or, if unknown, described him, he complied literally with Rule 259 without pleading the time, place and circumstances.

§ 176. 

Proof of Adultery. In addition to proof of the marriage, and of the residential requirements,¹º the burden of proof is on the petitioner to prove the alleged adultery. The proof may consist of direct or circumstantial evidence, or both combined may lead to a conviction of guilt.11 Almost invariably adultery is clandestine and seldom are the participants surprised in flagrante delicto. Hence the testimony of an eye-witness is not often available—"not one case in a hundred in which that proof would be attainable" observed Sir William Scott in the ecclesiastical court 12 and later Chancellor McGill.18 The court may disbelieve the direct testimony of an alleged eye-witness.14 The extent to which the court will believe the testimony of an eye-witness depends largely upon the character of the witness, the possibility of his story, and the conduct of the petitioner, especially after the time of the alleged adultery. Direct testimony is not to be rejected because it is improbable. The direct testimony must be impossible.15 The direct testimony of a witness is discredited when from the position he states he occupied it is proved that it would have been a physical impossibility to have seen the commission of the act.16

§ 177. -Proof of Defendant's Identity. Whether the proof be direct or circumstantial, or both, the identity of the defendant must be proved satisfactorily.17 Evidence of the commission of the offense, especially where the testimony of the witness is uncorroborated and the adultery is denied by the defendant and by the alleged particeps criminis, will not support a decree where the witness did not see the defendant's face or recognize him,18 or where the witness had never previously seen the defendant,19 or had seen him but once before and some years previously.20 Attempts to prove the defendant's identity by testimony of a witness that he had heard the voice of the defendant at a particular place have proved unsuccessful in some of the reported cases.21 

§ 178. Credibility of Witness. In determining the credi bility to be given to the testimony of a particular witness in a suit for divorce for adultery the character of the witness is important. The intelligence, age, etc., of the witness, his motive in testifying, the probable influence exerted upon him by one of the parties, and the like, are factors to be considered.22 The testimony of a servant of the petitioner is apt to be colored by reason of his or her employment.23 Similarly, the testimony of the mother of the petitioner who opposed the marriage.24 In sections following the testimony of particular witnesses, such as detectives, the particeps criminis, etc., will be considered.

§ 181. -Testimony of Procurers, etc. The testimony of pimps, procurers, etc., may be direct evidence of the offense, or circumstantial. Such testimony is admitted in adultery cases, but such witnesses are to be relied upon only so far as their testimony is intrinsically probable or is corroborated by circumstances.26 

Alone or as confirmatory of the testimony of the paramour it is usually insufficient on which to ground a decree, but when corroborated by other witnesses a decree has been granted even as against the defendant's alibi,27 or the denial of the defendant and the paramour.28 Likewise, a decree may be founded on the testimony of witnesses who are keepers of brothels wherein the adultery was committed, if such testimony appears credible from other circumstances.29 

§ 182. -Testimony of Detectives. The testimony of hired detectives employed to discover evidence of adultery may be direct or circumstantial evidence as to the commission of the act. In either case it is likely to be influenced by the monetary reward consequent upon success and, while such testimony is generally admitted, the court subjects it to close scrutiny.¹ The reliability of the detective agency employed is to be considered. In the ecclesiastical courts confessions of the parties as evidence was regulated by the 105th canon passed in 1603. This canon provided that "Forasmuch as matrimonial causes have been always reckoned and reputed among the weightiest, and therefore require the greatest caution when they come to be handled in judgment, especially in causes wherein matrimony, having been in the Church duly solemnized, is required, upon any suggestion or protest whatsoever, to be dissolved or annulled: we do strictly charge and enjoin, that in all proceedings to divorce and nullities of matrimony, good circumspection and advice be used, and that the truth may (as far as possible) be sifted out by the depositions of witnesses, and other lawful proofs and evictions, and that credit be not given to the sole confession of the parties themselves, however taken on oath either within or without court." 8 With us, as in the spiritual courts, the admissions and confessions of the parties as to the cause for divorce have been allowed

The subject of corroboration has been discussed generally in another place. In determining whether the circumstances are sufficient to convict one of guilt we are guided by the ecclesiastical rule,22 applied in Day v. Day,23 and fully expounded by Chancellor Green in the 

Berckmans case. "To establish the existence of adultery, the circumstance must be such as would lead the guarded discretion of a reasonable and just man to that conclusion. It must not be a rash and intemperate judgment, moving upon appearances that are equally capable of two interpretations. .... ....

The facts proven must be such as cannot be reconciled with probability and the innocence of the parties. 

Where the conduct of a party admits of two interpretations, equally consistent with probability, the one involving guilt and the other consistent with innocence, the rule of evidence as well as the dictates of justice, require that the interpretation should be favorable to innocence." 24 This rule has been repeatedly recognized and further citation is hardly necessary.2 25 § 187. Opportunity. -Opportunity. As already observed, the opportunity of the defendant and paramour to commit the act of adultery must concur with the criminal desire before guilt will be inferred from circumstantial proof. As to whether there is a sufficient opportunity to move the judicial mind to a conclusion of guilt, the criminal desire being adequately proved, depends of course on the particular facts. No attempt will be made to detail the many cases involving this element of circumstantial proof, but enough may be given to show how the mind of the court has reacted to particular situations. In general, "the proof of opportunities, complementary to evil intentions, necessary to circumstantially establish a charge of adultery, must put the parties in some place

Such proof is circumstantial and the case is to be disposed of in accordance with the accepted canon, already noted,19 that if the proof relied upon is reasonably capable of two or more interpretations, any one of which is consistent with the defendant's innocence, a decree is not warranted.20 An important circumstance is the length of time after marriage when the disease becomes manifest as excluding the inference that the disease was contracted as a result of sexual intercourse prior to the marriage. If it is proved or admitted that one spouse became afflicted with a venereal disease at a time sufficiently long after the marriage that no inference is possible except that the disease was contracted after the marriage and the other spouse is free from the infection, such fact presents a prima facie case of adultery, leaving to the defendant, if he wishes, the burden of counteracting this presumption by showing that his condition was not in consequence of the commission of adultery. As illustrative, proof that the disease had manifested itself in one of the spouses twelve years after the marriage was deemed sufficient prima facie evidence of adultery; likewise four years after the marriage; 22 but proof that a husband within six months after the marriage was infected was deemed insufficient to raise a presumption of adultery.28 And when sufficient time has elapsed since the time of the ceremony to warrant a presumption of adultery, the explicit denial by the defendant on the stand may be sufficient, depending upon the particular case, to overcome the presumption of guilt.25 21 When sufficient time has elapsed since the time of the marriage to raise a presumption of adultery from the presence of a venereal disease and the defendant attempts to avoid the presumption by charging that the petitioner communicated the disease to him, he shoulders the burden of proving his charge and, failing, a decree against him is warranted.20 Where it is proved or admitted that

§ 190. -Denial of Adultery. The denial by the defendant and the co-respondent on the stand of the commission of the act of adultery is to be expected from the nature of things. Such evidence is to be regarded as weak and will not defeat a clear case based upon direct or circumstantial evidence or both. Yet as weak as the evidence is, it may aid in tilting the scales in favor of innocence in a doubtful case." 

§ 191. 

-Failure to Deny Adultery. The state being a party to all divorce suits,10 the defendant's failure to answer or to produce evidence or to take the stand does not entitle the petitioner to a decree no matter on what ground the suit is brought.¹¹ In adultery cases, however, the defendant's failure to take the stand and deny the crime charged is of significance 12-"a most suspicious incident." 13 The court in its discretion may allow the proofs to be opened to hear the defendant's denial, but it is reluctant to grant such privilege unless good reasons exist for the omission.¹

 § 193. -Res Judicata of Fact of Adultery. There is little objection to the use of the doctrine of res judicata to preclude the granting of a decree of divorce for adultery, but when the prior adjudication of the fact of adultery is urged to support a decree of divorce the objection raised in a recent desertion case should be noticed.20 An adjudication in a prior proceeding for divorce against the co-respondent that the defendant was guilty of adultery is not res judicata in the absence of intervention 27 by the defendant in the prior suit.28

The record of the criminal conviction of the defendant for adultery is not res judicata of the fact of adultery in a subsequent suit for divorce,29 but the admissibility of such evidence under the label of admissions and confessions should be noticed.¹ § 194.

 The process and procedure in suits for divorce for adultery do not differ essentially from the process and procedure in suits for divorce for other causes and in suits for nullity of marriage. Consequently, the entire subject has been reserved for consideration farther on.2

 § 196. 

The Cause in General.¹ In connection with suits for divorce for desertion the reader should refer, as well, to a previous chapter where, for convenience, a number of matters of general application in divorce suits have been treated.2 In the ecclesiastical courts desertion of one of the spouses was not cause for divorce a mensa. Instead, the aggrieved party could sue for the restitution of conjugal rights. With us, willful, continued and obstinate desertion as cause for divorce was incorporated in the first Divorce Act conferring jurisdiction on the Court of Chancery to decree divorce. Then the term was for seven years. The term was reduced to five and then to three years, and presently the statute provides that divorces from the bond of matrimony and from bed and board may be decreed for "willful, continued and obstinate desertion for the term of two years.' "6 To come within the scope of the statute every desertion must contain four elements: (1) cessation of cohabitation, which, however, may be satisfied by a refusal of sexual relations (2) willfulness, an intention on the part of the deserting party to desert (3) obstinacy, a state of mind on the part of the deserted party in opposition to the separation (4) the continuity of the three preceding elements without interruption for the term of two years.10 

To constitute a statutory desertion as cause for divorce these four elements must exist whether the desertion complained of is a simple or a constructive desertion. § 197. Marriage. The subject of marriage generally, and as it relates to suits for divorce, has been discussed in previous chapters.¹¹

DESERTION § 198. Residence. A number of matters of general applica tion respecting residence (domicile) in suits for divorce have gone before, 12 but here the requirements in suits for divorce for desertion, as they are set out in sections 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision, 13 may be summarized. 

-Absolute Divorce. 

1. Where the defendant is served personally with process in

New Jersey as outlined hereinafter,14 the Court of Chancery acquires jurisdiction to decree a divorce from the bond of matrimony for desertion: a. When either of the parties was domiciled 15 in New Jersey at the time the cause of action arose 16 and has continued to be so domiciled for at least two years next preceding the commencement of the suit, or b. When, since the cause of action arose, either of the parties has become domiciled in New Jersey and has continued to be so domiciled for at least two years next preceding the commencement of the suit, provided that the cause of action alleged (desertion) was recognized in the jurisdiction in which such party was domiciled at the time the cause of action arose as a ground for the same relief (absolute divorce) asked for in the suit in this state.¹7 The wife is entitled to maintain a separate domicile for the purpose of instituting suit for divorce for desertion, and for the purpose of fulfilling the two years' domiciliary requirement the period may begin to run when the original desertion commences. She need not await the expiration of two years of desertion before she is entitled to establish a separate domicile.18

§ 199. 

-Accrual of Cause of Action. A cause of action for divorce for desertion is not the original act of desertion. Whether the desertion is a simple or a constructive one, a cause of action does not arise prior to the expiration of two years of a continuously willful and obstinate desertion.27 But once two years of a willful, continued and obstinate desertion has elapsed the cause of action for divorce for desertion vests or accrues in favor of the deserted party 28 at which time the desertion becomes established permanently unless thereafter the aggrieved spouse condones 29 the offense.¹

As respects the accrual of a cause of action for divorce for desertion in its relation to the residential requirements specified by sections 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision, the early decisions are definitely to the effect: (1) that the cause of action arises not at the commencement, but at the termination of two years of a willful, continued and obstinate desertion, so that, if either of the parties becomes domiciled in New Jersey at any time prior to the expiration of the two years' period of desertion and fulfills the two years' residential requirement next preceding the commencement of the suit, the court may acquire jurisdiction

Motive of Deserting Party. If the defendant actually deserts the petitioner and such desertion is continuously willful on his part and persists against the will of the petitioner for the term of two years, it is usually immaterial to inquire as to the motives for the desertion,¹¹ so long as the desertion was not justified by the commission of a matrimonial offense by the petitioner,12 or the motivating factor is not of such a nature that the consent of the petitioner to the separation may properly be inferred. The desertion of the defendant is not excused although caused by the petitioner's refusal to go through a religious ceremony following a civil marriage.18 The petitioner need not show

§ 201. Agreement of Separation.16 If the parties separate by mutual consent, whether the separation is in pursuance of an oral agreement or under articles of separation, ordinarily a statutory desertion cannot exist unless and until one of the spouses properly requests a resumption of the marital relation.17 However, articles of separation executed during the statutory period relied on are at the most evidentiary only. They reflect the intention of the parties to live separately with the consent of each other. The circumstances attending the execution of the articles may nevertheless demonstrate that the separation was against the will of the petitioner and willful on the part of the defendant. 

In order to obtain support from the husband a wife may submit to the necessities of the case and join in executing articles although she may steadfastly oppose the separation.18 

§ 202. 

Commencement of Desertion. Not until there is a cessation of cohabitation coupled with an intent of the deserter to desert against the will of the deserted party can it be said that a simple desertion has commenced. A simple desertion may begin at the time of the separation of the parties, but it is not indispensable that the defendant's intent to desert coincide with the act of separation.19 If the original separation is by mutual consent for an indefinite period of time, a desertion cannot commence until one of the spouses demands the resumption of marital re-

lations.20 In the case of a wife who leaves the home without her husband's consent, her desertion usually does not originate until the husband has made just advances to secure her return and she has refused to comply.21 But this is not necessarily so where the wife complains of the husband's desertion.22 A desertion commenced subsequent to the time of the separation of the parties is a simple rather than a constructive desertion.28 In constructive desertion cases the desertion must commence, if at all, at the time the aggrieved spouse leaves the other in consequence of his or her extreme cruelty.24 § 203.

Cohabitation and Sexual Relations. The mere fact that during the statutory period the parties have lived under the same roof on several occasions does not arrest an otherwise willful, continued and obstinate desertion, if it is clear from the proofs that in fact no sexual relations occurred between them.25 

Furthermore, where the desertion is predicated on the refusal of sexual relations, a separation of the parties to the extent that they occupy different homes is not essential.26 

A desertion by the wife may be arrested if during the two years' period the parties resume marital relations.27 However, a desertion by the husband, otherwise willful, continued and obstinate for the term of two years, is not necessarily interrupted by sexual relations for a brief period of time during the two years' period if the wife was induced fraudulently to submit to his sexual embraces on promises of continued cohabitation. If upon satisfying his passion he again leaves, the continuity of the desertion is not broken. The resumption of sexual relations during the two years' period does not, strictly speaking, amount to condonation, although akin to it. Condonation of a desertion usually presupposes that the two years' period has elapsed, resulting in a vested right in favor of the deserted party.28 The

§ 204. Tacking Periods of Interrupted Desertion. The question here assumes that the desertion has been interrupted before the expiration of two years and that sufficient time has elapsed since the cessation of the arresting factor to comprise a period of two years if the periods prior and subsequent to the interruption may be tacked. It is not to be confused with the question of the revival of a completed cause of action for divorce for desertion after condonation. The effect of the confinement or imprisonment section of the statute is also excluded.* In the reported cases the question under consideration has arisen in two situations. Where the continuity of the two years' period of desertion has been arrested by the resumption of marital relations, a tacking of the two ends has been considered as contrary to the statutory requirement. Tracey v. Tracey, in the 

Court of Chancery, has been followed by the Court of Errors and Appeals in Hyer v. Hyer.' But where the two years' period has been arrested by the pendency in good faith of a prior matrimonial suit, tacking has been allowed. First raised, but undecided, in Johnson v. Johnson, and later suggested in Barbour v. Barbour,10 the point was finally decided in Hartpence v. 

Hartpence, in Chancery, after the decision in Hyer v. Hyer, 29. Supra § 155.

No matter what intervenes to arrest the desertion, the desertion stops and to permit the tacking of the two ends so as to constitute a two years' period of desertion is to stretch the statutory requirement that the desertion must be willful and obstinate continuously for the term of two years. § 205.

Effect of Pendency of Former Proceedings. When a spouse institutes a suit for divorce or for nullity of marriage it is deemed not only improper that the parties should cohabit,¹2 but, furthermore, it is presumed that the petitioner consents to the separation. Such consent is inconsistent with the existence of the element of obstinacy in a subsequent suit by the same petitioner for divorce for desertion. Consequently, as a general rule, none of the time occupied by the pendency 18 of a former suit for divorce or for nullity of marriage instituted by the same petitioner may be computed as a part of the period of desertion.14 

The circumstance that the former proceeding was dismissed without prejudice 15 ordinarily cannot operate to include the time consumed by the pendency of the former suit.16 Nor will the former suit be dismissed nunc pro tunc so as to avoid the effect of its pendency on a period of desertion, for it is the rule that a petition will not be dismissed nunc pro tunc if such dismissal disturbs a status or impairs a right.17 However, the presumption of consent to the separation attending the prosecution of a suit for divorce or for nullity of marriage is merely a convenient rule of

§ 206. Effect of Decree A Mensa. The decree a mensa et thoro is the decree of divorce from bed and board which enjoins cohabitation without dissolving the marriage status.¹ It should not be confused with a decree for support and maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision in which the husband's obligation to support his wife is enforced without directing a limited or perpetual separation. 

Although a desertion, simple or constructive, is willful and obstinate at its inception, the continuity of its willfulness and obstinacy for the term of two years may be arrested by a decree of divorce from bed and board, whether the decree was obtained by the petitioner or by the defendant. So long as a decree a mensa forbids cohabitation, the separation ordinarily cannot be deemed to be a willful and obstinate desertion.15 A foreign decree of separation may prevent or arrest the running of a desertion period, if by reason of the decree the parties are absolutely enjoined from cohabiting until the decree is annulled by an order of the court in the foreign jurisdiction. Willful and obstinate desertion shall be construed to be "continued" within the meaning of this chapter, even though after such desertion has begun the deserting party has been imprisoned in this or any other state or country upon conviction by due process of law for a crime, misdemeanor or offense, not political, committed in this or any other state or country, or for any other reason shall have been under restraint either by due process of law or his voluntary act.5 The forerunner of section 31 was enacted in 1887 as a result of the decision in Wolf v. and 1900. Where applicable, section 2:50-6 continues as such a willful and obstinate desertion, already begun, during the time the deserter is imprisoned or under restraint within the meaning of the section.12 The original desertion may have been a constructive or a simple desertion.18 Where the section is applicable, the intent of the deserting party to desert during the period of confinement or restraint is imputed, as well as the absence of consent to, or acquiescence in, the separation by the deserted party. Where it is proved that the defendant has been imprisoned, the effect of section 2:50-6 necessarily is to exclude proof on the issues of willfulness or obstinacy during the term of imprisonment or restraint. them. While usually the doctrine is invoked by the wife, it is equally available to the husband.10 Section 2:50-2 of the Revision which permits a suit for divorce from the bond of matrimony for extreme cruelty does not abolish suits for divorce for constructive desertion. The causes of action are substantially different, notwithstanding that extreme cruelty is the basis on which the law constructs an intent to desert.

In constructive desertion cases the law imputes to the deserter an intent willfully to desert. But nothing short of the commission of the offense of extreme cruelty will give rise to this imputed intent on the part of the wrong-doer. The extreme cruelty must be of such a degree as would entitle the aggrieved spouse to a divorce on the ground of extreme cruelty. Cruelty of a lesser degree the law does not recognize as a basis on which to construct an intent to desert.11 The commission of an act of adultery by the husband may justify the wife in leaving without risking a charge of desertion, but in a suit at her instance for constructive desertion the adultery must have been committed under such circumstances as amount to extreme cruelty.12 

Before the intent to desert will be imputed the aggrieved spouse must have been forced to leave the wrong-doer in consequence of the other's extreme cruelty.18 Hence if the acts of extreme cruelty are committed while the parties are separated no intent to desert ordinarily can be constructed.14 The aggrieved spouse's departure from the home is the usual mode of separating from the culpable party, but it happens occasionally that they continue to occupy the same house, without cohabitation, and the circumstances may justify the arrangement. A wife to whom the husband has been extremely cruel undoubtedly must take some affirmative step to sever relations, but circumstances may forbid an immediate departure from the home. Barricading herself in a room temporarily until she can leave the home may be as effec-

In one case where the time at which the desertion commenced was of importance, the swearing out of a warrant for the husband's arrest and the cessation of marital relations was deemed a sufficient separation for the purpose of beginning a period of constructive desertion.15

While in some of the earlier cases it is intimated that the husband's cruelty must be "practiced for the purpose of driving his wife from his abode," 16 at present it is not an essential ingredient that the husband should consciously entertain, in connection with his acts of extreme cruelty, any settled purpose to drive his wife away. If he is extremely cruel to his wife in consequence of which she is obliged to leave him to protect her life or health, the law imputes to the husband the intent to desert irrespective of his actual intent.17

The distinction between a case of simple (actual) desertion and constructive desertion has not always been observed clearly in the reported cases. In the doctrine of constructive desertion the law takes no cognizance of the deserter's actual intent. If he commits the matrimonial offense of extreme cruelty necessitating the separation of the other spouse, the law constructs his intent to desert and precludes him from asserting what was his actual intent. The doctrine of constructive desertion should not be applied where it is unnecessary to impute or construct an intent to desert on the part of the deserter. In the ordinary case where the wife leaves her husband in consequence of his extreme cruelty, whether she departs from the home or not, it is often quite impossible from the proofs to spell out an actual intent on the husband's part to get rid of his wife by committing the acts of extreme cruelty. Consequently, his intent to desert his wife is implied or constructed without regard to his actual intent.18 This is the case ordinarily, but a simple desertion may well exist if it can be shown that the husband committed the acts of extreme cruelty for the conscious purpose of ridding himself of his wife. 

Here an actual intent may be present. If, on the other hand, 15. Csanyi v. Csanyi, 93 N. J. Eq. 11, 14, 115 Atl. 76 (1921).

the spouse who has been guilty of extreme cruelty actually and voluntarily leaves the aggrieved spouse, this is a case of simple desertion.10 It is unnecessary to "construct" an intent to desert on the part of the spouse guilty of the offense of extreme cruelty when an actual intent manifested by an actual voluntary departure or separation can be shown. But if, as in one case, a wife is extremely cruel to her husband and in consequence thereof he compels her to leave, this is a constructive desertion on the part of the wife because an actual intent on her part cannot be inferred when her departure was involuntary.20

The proofs may show that the husband has been cruel to his wife, but not in the degree recognized as extreme cruelty. The wife may leave him but without legal justification. Subsequent events may demonstrate an actual intent on the part of the husband to desert, a subsequent simple desertion by him.21 Where a husband without justification forcibly ejects his wife, or tells her to get out, or locks the door against her, or misconducts himself for the conscious purpose of forcing his wife out, an actual intent on the husband's part to desert his wife is discoverable, although the wife is the one physically to leave the home. In these situations we have a simple desertion, and notwithstanding that in cases where the husband misconducts himself with the conscious intent to get rid of his wife, such misconduct may amount to extreme cruelty. But some of the cases have unnecessarily constructed an intent to desert and classified the husband's desertion as constructive.22

Similarly, in suits by the wife for separate maintenance an abandonment by the husband can be justified only if the wife has been guilty of a matrimonial offense.24 In this respect the rule of the ecclesiastical courts in suits for the restitution of conjugal rights is followed.25 In such suits nothing amounted to a bar except such facts as would entitle the defendant to a divorce a mensa.26 Justification for the separation partakes of the nature of recrimination,27 except that a matrimonial offense is urged in recrimination when admittedly the defendant is also guilty of a matrimonial offense. § 216. 

Refusal of Sexual Relations; Impotence. Formerly it was thought that the mere unjustified refusal of a spouse to engage in sexual intercourse with the other was not desertion so long as the parties dwelt within the same house and there was not a total repudiation of marital duties and responsibilities.Ⓡ 

But beginning with Raymond v. Raymond, a suit by the wife, the refusal of sexual intercourse persisted in willfully, continuously and obstinately for the term of two years has been held to constitute desertion. While in many of the cases there has existed, as well, a total repudiation of all duties and responsibilities,10 nevertheless, it is definitely settled that the separation of the parties and the cessation of other marital duties is not indispensable. The unjustified refusal of sexual intercourse persisted in willfully, continuously and obstinately for the term of two years is desertion, whether the unjustified refusal is by the wife ¹¹ or by the husband.12 A wife may be guilty of desertion if she persistently and without justifiable cause refuses to indulge in normal sexual intercourse by permitting penetration.18 If the husband has been guilty of adultery, the wife may justify her withdrawal from the sexual relation without being guilty of desertion.14 The refusal must continue as willful and obstinate for the term of two years.15 The mere fact that the parties have not indulged in sexual relations for two years is not desertion.

§ 217. -Corroboration as to Refusal of Sexual Relations. 

Because of the difficulty encountered in corroborating the testimony of the petitioner in a desertion case based upon the refusal of sexual relations, the subject will be treated specially here rather than in a later section dealing more generally with corroboration in desertion cases, but the general section as to corroboration in desertion cases¹ and the foregoing section relating to corroboration in divorce and nullity suits generally 2 should be consulted.

Because the parties are reluctant to publicize the fact that they have ceased to engage in the sexual act, it has been stated that slight evidence is necessary to corroborate a desertion premised upon the refusal of sexual relations. The extent to which the corroborative proof should go cannot be prescribed except generally. Enough proof should be produced to satisfy the court that

When the husband complains, corroborative proof as to his bona fide efforts should be introduced, particularly where he has induced, although not justified, the separation. An outstanding case involving corroboration of the petitioner's testimony in desertion cases based upon the refusal of sexual relations is Haskell v. Haskell in the Court of Errors and Appeals. 

In an ex parte suit by the husband based upon the refusal of sexual relations since the time of the marriage the testimony offered in corroboration was supplied by two friends and a physician. One witness testified as to the petitioner's physical and mental condition before and after the marriage and also was permitted to testify as to conversations had with the petitioner as to the wife's refusal. The second witness testified substantially as the first. The physician was permitted to relate conversations had with the petitioner and, in addition, testified that the petitioner was physically capable. If the wife is so infected, it would seem to be immaterial whether the husband contracted the disease before or after the marriage. If a husband, knowing that he is in such a state of health that by having sexual relations with his wife he will run the risk of communicating a venereal disease to her, recklessly has connection with her and thereby communicates the disease to her, he is guilty of extreme cruelty and the presumption is that he knew his own state of health and the probable result of the connection.³ -Necessity of Communication. In one state the court declared that the mere presence of a venereal disease is not extreme cruelty. In New Jersey the wife may not be without a remedy if the mere presence of a venereal disease is not to be denominated extreme cruelty. § 219. Abuse of Marital Rights; Perversion.

1 -Other Charges. Whether a particular unfounded accusation may constitute extreme cruelty will depend upon the severity of the charge, whether it was made falsely and maliciously, privately or publicly, and whether the complaining party suffered substantially in health in consequence of the unfounded accusation. The rules just considered with reference to accusations of adultery and incest may provide a safe guide in determining the question. 

In certain cases a false and malicious charge of murder, 24 or attempt at murder,25 may constitute extreme cruelty. A false and malicious charge of insanity may amount to extreme cruelty.20 

Likewise, a husband who imputes to his wife physical malformation and consequent incapacity for the sexual relation may be guilty of extreme cruelty.27 An accusation that a wife is a drunkard has been held insufficient.28 

§ 221. 

Vile and Offensive Language. The use of vile, abusive and offensive language without more is ordinarily not such extreme cruelty as will support a suit for divorce for extreme cruelty, or for constructive desertion, or as will justify a party in abandoning the matrimonial home without subjecting himself or herself to the risk of a charge of desertion at the end of the statutory period. Certainly, the use of such language is not extreme cruelty per se and a search has failed to reveal a single reported case in which vile and offensive language alone, not amounting to charges of infidelity,20 was deemed to have caused the complaining party to suffer in health to the extent that the court. would grant a divorce or separation. The cases have consistently been the other way whether the offending party has been the husband or wife.¹ Vile language coupled with drunkenness, although habitual, ordinarily does not constitute extreme cruelty. § 255 

DESERTION § 224. Just Advances; Separation by Mutual Consent. 

Where the parties separate by mutual consent, either orally or under articles of separation, with the exception already noted,20 there cannot exist a willful and obstinate desertion. The consent of the spouses to live separately being express, there is no need to search for the element of contribution or inducement from which to imply a consent. The separation being by mutual consent, the husband cannot successfully urge that his wife has deserted him unless and until he has properly requested a resumption of the connubial relation.21 The separation of husband and wife is disfavored and, barring the commission of a matrimonial offense, the law accords to each of the parties the right to terminate a separation existing by mutual consent.22 If the husband is in a position to make, and does make, a bona fide request for the resumption of marital relations, his consent to live separately is thereby withdrawn. If the wife refuses to resume cohabitation, she thereupon becomes a deserter, and if the desertion continues as willful and obstinate for the succeeding two years a cause of action for divorce for desertion will accrue in favor of the husband.28

The separation of the parties by mutual consent also bars the wife from contending successfully that her husband has deserted her, unless and until she requests her husband to resume cohabitation or until the agreement to live separately expires by its own limitations. The husband not being a deserter originally, a duty devolves upon the wife to conclude the separation. Until she makes a bona fide effort to terminate the separation, her consent, as well as her husband's consent, to live separately will ordinarily be deemed to continue.24 However, if the wife in good faith

In this case it definitely appears that by his conduct the husband had induced the separation. Chancellor Zabriskie concluded that because the husband had contributed to the separation his consent thereto must be implied unless and until he had made "the advances or concessions which a just man ought to have made, to put an end to this desertion." 29 Where the husband has induced, although not justified,¹ the separation, the cases have consistently followed the Cornish case in imposing upon the husband the duty to make the advances and concessions of a just man at the risk of being deemed a consenting party to the desertion. Until the husband makes the advances and concessions of a just man it cannot be said that the desertion of the wife has commenced to run. Moreover, where the wife leaves without her husband's express or tacit consent, or without a consent which may be said to flow from the husband's contribution to the desertion, his assent to the continuance of the desertion is inferred until he makes the advances of a just man or until such advances are excused. This rule is so stated in many of the cases, but the facts therein frequently show contribution on the part of the husband or repulsion by him of his wife's overtures. § 226. -Simple Desertion; Sufficiency of Husband's Ad- 

Where the husband is the petitioner and is under a duty to tender overtures to conclude the desertion of the wife,¹ the formulation of an inflexible rule should not be attempted as to the extent to which the husband must go. It has properly been observed that every case must be judged by its own peculiar circumstances.15 Here again, the element of the husband's contribution or inducement to the wife's desertion is an important factor. Where the husband is free from fault for the original separation, the circumstances attending the original separation should be proved fully so that the court may be satisfied with the efforts made by the husband to conclude the separation. Less should be expected of the husband who is blameless for the desertion of his wife.16

Just advances are not a matter of mechanics. The law does not prescribe that a man whose wife has left him should write so many letters, see her so often, and tender fragrant bouquets on week-ends for the two years' period. In every case the court probes the apparent intent of the husband in order to ascertain whether his wife's desertion was against his will. The court must, of course, explore the husband's mind by observing the outward manifestations thereof, by his words and conduct. 

Nevertheless, a man may perform numerous formal gestures towards reconciliation and yet other proof might indicate that his attitude toward his wife has been such as to cause the continuance of the separation.

If, in view of the circumstances attending the separation it appears that the husband has made just advances, and that the wife has persistently repulsed such overtures, consistent efforts for the duration of the two years' period are not required if from the proofs it is evident that further efforts would prove futile.¹7

The number of efforts to be made before the court will adjudge that further attempts are useless cannot be prescribed with precision. Each case must rest upon its particular facts and circumstances.1 18 Where the wife is wholly at fault, a single letter, 14. Supra § 225.

So long as the wife does not consent to the separation, or its continuance, and refrains from actively causing the original desertion or its permanence, the law will infer that the desertion is against her will. The desertion may be obstinate without active efforts on her part.13 Even the wife's express acquiescence in the desertion will not in every case preclude her from obtaining a decree. 

The proofs may show affirmatively that within the statutory period the wife was unwilling to live with her husband, but nevertheless the desertion may be against her will if the continued desertion of the husband cannot be said to have resulted from the wife's attitude. Where the wife's acquiescence arises from a reasonable belief that in case her husband should return he would, notwithstanding her efforts to effect his reformation, resume a course of conduct grossly violative of his duty and causing her constant physical or mental suffering, her acquiescence in such circumstances is not voluntary and will not bar relief. The husband's past misconduct inducing the wife's belief need not amount to extreme cruelty in that degree which is necessary to sustain at the wife's instance a suit for divorce for extreme cruelty or for constructive desertion.14

desertion a cause of action vests in favor of the deserted spouse.20 

At the end of such time it is too late for the offending party to repent whether such party be the husband 21 or the wife.22 Furthermore, the deserting party is precluded from tendering overtures to conclude the desertion if he or she has been guilty of adultery. The deserted spouse is not compelled to condone a vested cause of action for adultery at the risk of becoming a deserter.23

When a spouse, whether husband or wife, is guilty of such extreme cruelty as would entitle the other to a divorce for extreme cruelty and the offended spouse leaves in consequence of the other's extreme cruelty, it seems that the offended spouse may claim a desertion after the lapse of two years from his or her departure and that the guilty party may not during the two years' period tender any advances which the innocent party is obliged to accept. The offense of extreme cruelty when committed becomes vested in favor of the party offended to the same extent as does adultery and, although the suit is based upon desertion rather than upon extreme cruelty, the law will not compel the innocent spouse to condone the offense of extreme cruelty at the risk of becoming a deserter. The desertion will run despite repentances and advances on the part of the offender. 

This point has not, perhaps, been expressly determined, but it seems to be a logical result of the decision in a recent case.24 

Yet there are dicta in prior cases involving suits for divorce for desertion from which it might be inferred that a spouse guilty of extreme cruelty may repent and that the offended party must accept bona fide advances tendered during the two years' period.

§ 229. 

Collusion. Collusion between the parties will result in a dismissal of a suit for divorce for desertion as well as a suit for divorce for other causes and a suit for nullity of marriage. 

The bar not being peculiar to desertion as a cause, the whole subject has been discussed elsewhere.¹ To every petition for divorce an affidavit of non-collusion and merits must be annexed." 

§ 230. 

Condonation. 

Condonation by the petitioner is a bar to the suit for divorce for desertion unless, as in other cases, the condition of the condonation is breached by subsequent conjugal unkindness. This particular bar, including the pleading and proof, has been treated in connection with the suit for divorce for adultery and for extreme cruelty. In addition, it should be observed that in desertion cases the notion of conjugal unkindness and revival has crept into cases where the husband has fraudulently induced his wife to submit to sexual relations prior to the expiration of the two years' period and has then abandoned her.' 8 

§ 231. Recrimination. The commission of a matrimonial of fense by the petitioner is a bar to the suit for divorce for desertion. 

The subject of recrimination as it relates to suits for divorce for any cause has already been noticed. In addition, extreme cruelty, or adultery committed within the home, will justify the departure of the injured spouse and preclude the assertion of a cause of action against him for divorce for desertion." § 232. § 233. 

Proof and Corroboration. 

In addition to proof of the marriage,22 and of the residential requirements,23 the burden is on the petitioner to prove a two years' period of willful, continued and obstinate desertion. All uncertainties of fact are resolved against the petitioner.24 That the defendant intended to desert the petitioner must be proved. Proof that the parties have been separated for the term of two years is not sufficient. The intent to desert cannot be inferred from the mere unexplained fact that the parties have been separated. Mere separation or absence continued for the term of two years is not willful, continued and obstinate desertion.25 The circumstances and the manner of the desertion must be proved in order that the court may determine whether the desertion possesses the elements of willfulness and obstinacy continuously for the term of two years.2 

It is important that the facts and circumstances attending the original separation should be proved, although a simple desertion is alleged, particularly where the desertion commenced at a time subsequent to the separation of the parties in another state.27 

Letters, etc., between the parties written about the time of the separation are particularly important because they usually reflect the minds of the parties far better than oral evidence.28 

The petitioner should prove the date of the commencement 29 of the desertion in accordance with the allegation, but proof of the date of the commencement of a simple desertion is usually

The general rule that a divorce will not be decreed upon the uncorroborated testimony of the petitioner 14 applies in a suit for divorce for desertion. It is necessary that the testimony of the petitioner be corroborated as to the marriage,¹5 as to the residential requirements,16 and as to the cause of action.¹7 19 The corroborative proof must show that the defendant willfully deserted the petitioner against the will of the petitioner and that such desertion persisted without interruption for the term of two years. Categorical corroboration is not essential, 18 but the petitioner must produce sufficient corroborating evidence to convince the court that his or her testimony showing a willful, continued and obstinate desertion for the term of two years is true.¹ 

The extent to which the corroborative proof should go cannot be prescribed definitely. To some degree the court may be guided by the nature of the desertion alleged, the availability of proof, and the probability of collusion. For instance, where the desertion is based upon the refusal of marital relations, less corroborative proof is usually available than in other cases.20 The defendant's failure or refusal to deny the desertion, although he is at the hearing, does not alone, sufficiently corroborate the charge.21 The petitioner may call the defendant,22 but his admission of the charge is not sufficient corroboration, although the conduct of the defendant on the stand, especially his reluctance to admit, may furnish the necessary corroborative proof in some cases.28

§ 234. -Res Judicata of Fact of Desertion. It is now set tled that an adjudication of abandonment in a separate maintenance decree entered by consent is not res judicata of the fact of desertion in a subsequent suit by the wife for divorce for desertion. And it would seem to be in harmony with the public policy as to divorce 20 that the decree for separate maintenance should not be conclusive as to the fact of abandonment although the bill for maintenance has been tried on the merits. § 237. The Cause in General. In connection with suits for divorce for extreme cruelty it is well to refer to what has already been discussed pertaining to suits for divorce. A number of matters are of general application and consequently have been so treated.¹ 3 In the ecclesiastical courts in England extreme cruelty was cause for divorce a mensa et thoro. Furthermore, the English Court of Chancery issued the writ of supplicavit to restrain the husband from injuring his wife." With us the first act conferring jurisdiction on the Court of Chancery went no farther than to include extreme cruelty as cause for divorce from bed and board. Not until the year 1923 was extreme cruelty made a cause for divorce from the bond of matrimony as well as from bed and board. The 

1923 enactment, commonly referred to as the Blackwell Act, is now section 2:50-2c of the Revision and, as amended in 1938, provides: 

2:50-2c. Extreme cruelty by either of the parties, whether the acts of cruelty have been heretofore or are hereafter com-

The 1923 act merely provided a new remedy for the cause of extreme cruelty.5 The act was held to be remedial and as such to be liberally construed." It was retroactive as to acts of cruelty committed prior to its passage. While suits for divorce for extreme cruelty are usually instituted by wives, the husbands have not been wholly unsuccessful in this suit.º

The question as to when a cause of action for divorce for extreme cruelty arises has been discussed in a recent case. There it is stated that a cause of action for divorce for extreme cruelty, whether the relief sought is a divorce from bed and board or from the bond of matrimony, arises or vests at that moment of time when the offense is committed, that is to say, at a time when an act or acts have been perpetrated which would be sufficient then to induce the court to believe that there is reasonable apprehension of injury to the health or life of the complaining spouse.23 The question has received practically no consideration in the reported cases as it may pertain to the domicile of the parties under the jurisdictional sections 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of the Revision. It would seem that if the petitioner relies upon a single act of extreme cruelty, 24 such as the communication of a venereal disease, 25 or the commission of adultery within the home,26 the cause of action may readily be said to vest at the time of the communication of the disease or at the time the adultery was committed, so that, if the parties were

What Constitutes Extreme Cruelty. 

1923 extreme cruelty was not cause for divorce from the bond of matrimony. But this cause has been ground for divorce from bed and board ever since the Court of Chancery was given jurisdiction in matrimonial causes. Before the year 1923 the offense of extreme cruelty had long constituted the basis for constructive desertion in suits for absolute divorce 29 and the foundation for a constructive abandonment in suits by the wife for separate maintenance.¹ Moreover, the offense of extreme cruelty has been recognized as an affirmative defense in recrimination to adultery,2 as 

27. Infra § 241. 

28. Supra § 199. 

29. Supra § 212. 

1. Infra § 393. 

2. Supra § 157.

§ 283

justification for the separation in suits for divorce for desertion,³ and as "justifiable cause" for the husband's abandonment in suits by the wife for separate maintenance. In these various situations the definition and conception of extreme cruelty has been so developed in this state that it may be stated that the offense of extreme cruelty is the same irrespective of the manner in which it comes into issue in matrimonial litigation." The courts have recognized the risk of inaccuracy involved in attempting to define extreme cruelty. It has been said to be tantamount to the word saevitia in the civil law which had a well recognized meaning in the ecclesiastical courts. The general rule has been stated that to justify a divorce from bed and board for extreme cruelty of the husband such conduct by the husband must be shown as will justify the court in believing that if he is allowed to retain his power over his wife and she is compelled to remain subject to him, her life or her health will be endangered, or that he will render her life one of such extreme discomfort and wretchedness as to incapacitate her to discharge the duties of a wife. The remedy essentially is quia timet. The courts interfere mainly to prevent future harm, rather than to punish the offender for what has already been done." This is the general rule which has found expression in the books, but, admittedly, no rigid rule can be laid down to define the extent of injury, actual or apprehended, which will move the court to decree a divorce. Much depends upon the particular circumstances, and heretofore in the chapter on Desertion a number of particular acts of extreme cruelty have been considered, for convenience, in connection with the suit for divorce for desertion. The inquiry to be made in each case in order to ascertain whether there has been extreme cruelty seems to be three-fold: (1) what were the acts and conduct of the defendant (2) what purpose, actual or imputed, motivated the defendant (3) what effect did the acts have, or will they have if continued, upon the health and life of the petitioner? In treating of extreme cruelty the conduct of the defendant may be classified into one of three groups. The conduct may amount to extreme cruelty per se. In such cases the law will presume from the nature of the defendant's conduct that it is malignant and intended to force a separation and that its effect upon the petitioner is such as to imperil his or her life or health, or to render his or her life one of extreme discomfort and wretchedness. In cases of extreme cruelty per se it is necessary to prove only the commission of the act of extreme cruelty complained of. The defendant's intent and the effect upon the petitioner's health is irrebuttably presumed. For instance, a husband who harbors a paramour in the home commits extreme cruelty per se,14 as well as a spouse who communicates a venereal disease to the other.15 The second group comprises acts and conduct which might render the life of the petitioner one of extreme discomfort and wretchedness, but which under any circumstances cannot be said to constitute extreme cruelty. In the third group are cases which may or may not amount to extreme cruelty depending upon the motive of the defendant, actual or imputed, the severity of the misconduct, and its resulting effect upon the petitioner's life or health,10 Except where the defendant's conduct amounts to extreme cruelty per se, proof of the commission of a certain act or acts does not alone make out a case of extreme cruelty. In each case the court must look not only to the acts committed to see if they are wrongful, but the court must, as well, inquire as to the effect of the misconduct of the defendant upon the health, mental and physical, of the complaining spouse. Acts which would imperil the health of a refined and delicate wife might be endured with

While in the earlier cases the courts were reluctant to grant relief unless there was some physical violence proved, no longer is physical violence necessary. Physical violence may be less damaging to a wife than a course of abusive treatment which gradually undermines her health. 18 Aside from cases of extreme cruelty per se, the test of extreme cruelty is not to be found so much in the means employed, but rather in the effect produced upon the complaining spouse and, principally, whether the acts and conduct of the defendant have been of such a nature that it may be said that the defendant's set purpose, conscious or imputed, is to get rid of the petitioner. In other words, judging from the wrongful acts already committed, is it the defendant's intention to ill-treat the petitioner in the event cohabitation is resumed in such wise that her life or health will be, if they have not already been, endangered? In the final analysis the motive and character of the defendant is a determining factor, for the court may more surely determine therefrom whether it is reasonable to apprehend that the life or health of the complaining spouse will suffer if cohabitation is resumed. Thus it may be ventured, although in direct language the cases have not gone so far, that essentially the offense of extreme cruelty is a desertion, a condition of the minds of the parties, without the two years' requirement. Even prior to the enactment of the statute in the year 1923 allowing extreme cruelty as cause for absolute divorce, extreme cruelty was made the basis upon which an intent to desert was constructed in suits for absolute divorce for constructive desertion.19

In considering the effect of the defendant's misconduct upon the complaining spouse the court will have due regard for her appearance on the stand, her age, 20 the condition of her health, her delicacy and sensitivity,21 including whether she was pregnant at the time of the commission of the alleged acts of extreme cruelty.22

The application by the wife of croton oil to the clothes of her husband in order to keep him at home is an unusual instance of extreme cruelty." § 242. -Single Act. If the single act is extreme cruelty per se, such as the communication of a venereal disease to the other spouse, the commission of the act is extreme cruelty, for it is irrebuttably presumed that the defendant intended to force a separation and that the result of the act is to affect detrimentally the health of the complaining spouse. Aside from an act amounting to extreme cruelty per se, a single act may or may not constitute extreme cruelty depending upon the nature of the act, the attending circumstances, the provocation, and the motive of the defendant, actual or imputed, from which the court may determine whether it is reasonable to apprehend that the life or health of the complaining spouse is endangered. A husband who attempts to kill his wife will be adjudged guilty of extreme cruelty if it is reasonable to suppose that he will complete the act if given an opportunity. A single blow given in a fit of passion and repented of, or in a drunken condition when reason was dethroned, ordinarily does not constitute extreme cruelty. It is the apprehended danger which the actual violence committed reasonably forecasts which will move the court.10

§ 243. Provocation. In suits for divorce for extreme cruelty the element of provocation is an important consideration. 

A wife may not ordinarily complain if her husband's misconduct is caused by her own provocation. There is an implied consent to the treatment given to her by the husband. The remedy of the wife in such cases is within her own power.¹ 

11 Provocation is an element in suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony for extreme cruelty or for constructive desertion as well as in suits for divorce from bed and board.12 Depending upon the particular case, a wife may be denied a decree of divorce where she provoked her husband by unfounded accusations of adultery or incest,13 or by her refusal properly to care for her husband's children by a former marriage.14 If, however, it should appear that the misconduct is excessive and out of proportion to the provocation, it might be the province of the court to interfere.15

But the inference afforded by the cohabitation of the parties under the same roof is not conclusive on the question of condonation,19 or on the extremity of the cruelty. A wife may continue to reside under the same roof with her husband because of necessity or in the hope that he will reform.20 

In suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony for extreme cruelty under section 2:50-2 of the Revision the petitioner need not await the expiration of six months from the date of separation in order to institute suit.21 Indeed, the petition may now include allegations of acts of extreme cruelty committed during the six months' period preceding the commencement of the suit.22 

That a wife solicits a re-union does not necessarily militate against her nor weaken the proof of her husband's cruelty.23 § 245. Insanity and Intoxication. In suits for divorce for extreme cruelty the insanity of the defendant arising after the cause of action has accrued is not a defense, at least where the misconduct is of such a nature as to amount to extreme cruelty per se.24

Nor is the defendant absolved because the acts of extreme cruelty arise from insane delusions. This is as true in suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony 25 as in suits for

Pleading. In addition to the allegation of marriage 20 and of residence,¹ etc., in drafting the petition as discussed below,² the pleader must set forth the alleged act or acts of extreme cruelty with sufficient particularity as to time and place to enable the defendant fairly to meet the charge or charges. It has been the practice to plead the acts particularly although it has been urged that such pleading amounts to pleading the evidence. The act or acts should be characterized as extreme cruelty. A general charge that the defendant has been guilty of extreme cruelty is ordinarily insufficient to allow proof of specific acts. Proof of gross abuse of marital rights is not available under an allegation that the defendant used abusive and filthy language. Customarily, the acts of extreme cruelty are alleged in chronological order. The same manner of pleading should be followed in alleging extreme cruelty in an answer." Forms 11, 102 should be consulted. They may be varied to meet the particular case. When the suit is for divorce from the bond of matrimony under section 2:50-2 of the Revision, the date of the last act of extreme cruelty preceding the commencement of the six months' proscribed period should be alleged, but it is now permissible to include in the petition all acts of extreme cruelty which have been committed down to the filing of the petition. § 247. Proof and Corroboration. Besides the proof of the marriage,¹¹ and of the domiciliary requirements,12 the petitioner has the burden of proving the cause of action.13 In proving the cause of action the definition and conception of the offense of extreme cruelty should always be kept in mind.¹4 -Corroboration. When the testimony of other witnesses is offered in corroboration, categorical corroboration is not necessary. Their testimony need not go to each act of extreme cruelty testified to by the petitioner, especially where the testimony of the petitioner is uncontradicted, 22 so long as they bear witness to enough to satisfy the court that the petitioner's testimony as a whole is credible and worthy of belief.23 As it was put in one case, "If he beat her once it is fair to assume, in the circumstances, that he did it again. If he beat her at the times as to which her testimony is corroborated, her story is acceptable as true that he assaulted her on the occasions as to which corroboration is lacking." 24

§ 248. -Res Judicata of Fact of Extreme Cruelty. Where in a suit by the wife for divorce for extreme cruelty it is sought to establish the offense by the production of a decree for separate maintenance adjudicating that the husband has been guilty of extreme cruelty, a recent decision in a desertion case and the observations noted in another section should be consulted.27 Where the proofs have failed to show acts of sufficient gravity to warrant a decree for the wife, it has been the practice to dismiss the petition without prejudice to pleading the same acts in a subsequent suit should the husband continue his abuse. However, it would seem that if the facts are not disproved, but merely insufficient to establish a case, the same acts in conjuction with subsequent acts may be alleged and proved although the decree of dismissal contained no saving clause.28 § 249.

Collusion. Collusion between the parties is a bar to suits for divorce for other causes and to suits for nullity of marriage as well as to suits for divorce for extreme cruelty. Accordingly, the subject has received consideration in a prior chapter.20 § 250.

Condonation. Condonation by the petitioner of the alleged extreme cruelty is a bar unless the cause is revived by breach of the condition of the condonation. This defense is general in the law of divorce. It has been discussed heretofore in its entirety, including the pleading and proof.¹ § 251. Recrimination. Although the defendant may have been guilty of extreme cruelty, a divorce will be denied if it is proved that the petitioner has been guilty of an uncondoned matrimonial offense. The doctrine of recrimination extends as well to suits for divorce for causes other than extreme cruelty, so that it has been found convenient and practicable to treat of this defense, including the pleading and proof, in a general chapter.2 How-
