This chapter is devoted essentially to the procedure peculiar to suits for divorce and nullity, including suits for nullity instituted under the general equity jurisdiction of the court. The general chancery practice is referred to when deemed consistent with the scope of the book; for further particulars relative thereto, reference should be made to the several textbooks on the subject.¹ A brief treatment of the procedure in suits for separate maintenance ² and in independent proceedings for custody and maintenance of children will be found elsewhere.³ 

The general table of contents in the beginning of this work, and the index farther on should also be consulted. 2 

§ 255. Interviewing the Client and Witnesses. For the benefit of solicitors who lack experience in matrimonial litigation, it may not be out of place to offer a few practical suggestions with respect to the relationship of solicitor and client in this class of cases.

In no other sort of litigation is the solicitor so often called upon to represent persons of whom he knows little or nothing, most of whom have had no previous occasion to consult a lawyer and probably never will again. In no other sort of litigation is emotion so stirred or evidence so apt to be unreliable. So far as the solicitor's duty to the court is concerned, especial care should be exercised to ascertain the real facts of each case and to decline retainers in all cases found to be collusive or unfounded in fact. 

It is wise also to be particularly careful to avoid all misunderstandings with the client. The crucial time is the occasion of the first interview. Take pains to ascertain from your client at the first interview not only whether there is a cause of action within 

1. As, for example, Dickinson, Chan. Prec. (1894); Tyree, Chan. Pr. in 

N. J. (1933); Kocher & Trier, N. J. Chan. Pr. & Prec. (1924). 

2. Infra § 401. 

3. Infra §§ 446, 447, 460, 461.

§ 297 

the jurisdiction of the court, but whether sufficient corroborative proof will be available. Have his statements of fact reduced to writing, go over it carefully with him and get him to verify it under oath. File the original in your safe, using a copy for your open file. Not infrequently it happens that a client will change his story later on; hence the reason for the suggested precaution is obvious.

If a case seems doubtful, explain carefully to your client before undertaking it what in your judgment are the chances of success or failure. In this connection, do not seek the advice of an 

Advisory Master as to what your chances of success may be in a doubtful case; the matter may later be referred to him and even it if is not, if the outcome were such as to seem out of accord with his advice he might be embarrassed.*

Have your understanding respecting compensation and payment of costs written out and signed by both yourself and your client, and give one signed copy to your client. The amount of compensation and the terms of payment should be reasonable. 

If your client is a woman, include a provision that in the event the court should award counsel fees and costs against the husband the same will be credited when received on account of her obligation to you. The fairest form of such an agreement will fix compensation for your services at separate stages of the proposed suit, in order that if there be a substitution of solicitor at any stage of the proceedings the amount of your compensation will not be left subject to dispute.

Arrange at the first interview to meet those witnesses whose corroborative testimony you determine to be requisite, interview them at the earliest opportunity and, where possible, get their statements in writing sworn to, or at least signed by them. It is wise to secure all such statements before filing the petition. 

Where your client is a defendant, even though a counterclaim is not to be filed, most of the above suggestions are pertinent. 

Be particularly careful to qualify predictions of success. The outcome of a matrimonial suit is often uncertain because issues of fact rather than of law are usually involved. 

Frequently a petitioner is anxious to secure the decree as expeditiously as possible. Be careful to raise no false hopes on this score. It is better to err on the conservative side in your predictions, so as to avoid a frequent source of disappointment and misunderstanding. Having accepted the retainer, prosecute the suit without unnecessary delays. Your client will be very appre- 

4. See In re Judges in Chancery, 101 N. J. Eq. 9, 137 Atl. 151 (1927).

§ 256 

ciative if the decree is secured earlier than the time you have predicted. Usually there is no need for more than two or three interviews with your client before the time comes to prepare for hearing. Avoid unnecessary interviews, as wasting your client's time as well as your own. The petition with its verification and the affidavit under Rule 274 should be prepared and ready for execution at the second interview.

Do not place yourself, or anyone in your office, in the position of a witness in the case. If any investigation is required in aid of the proofs let it be done by others. It is improper for a solicitor or any person associated with him to testify on behalf of his client, if it can be avoided."

In preparation for the hearing have all of the witnesses attend with your client at your office, if possible, in order that each may be prepared more intelligently by hearing the statements of the others. Rehearse the whole case, question and answer. Eliminate the immaterial and redundant by pointing out to each witness what facts within his knowledge are important to the case and what facts are of no consequence. See that their answers to your questions state the facts clearly and tersely, in order that no time will be wasted at the hearing. If affidavits have been executed and used on a preliminary application, have affiants read over copies of them carefully, in preparation for cross-examination. 

Bear in mind always that in matrimonial cases the solicitor is more apt to incur the unjust criticism of his client than in any other sort of litigation. The way to avoid it is to give no possible occasion for misunderstanding.

Schedule of Fees. Under section 22:2-17 of the Re vision the fee payable to the Clerk on the filing of the original petition or bill is $25.00. This includes all charges of the Clerk's office in the case up to and including final decree, together with execution fees.

If extra certified copies of the petition or of other pleading or order are required, they are charged for at the rate of $2.00 minimum, plus ten cents per folio in excess of 20 folios.

The reference fees are $50.00 in uncontested suits and $60.00 in contested suits. If final hearing in a contested suit extends

Election of Remedies. Where the choice offered is between two remedies not inconsistent with each other, the selection of one does not preclude the subsequent prosecution of the other. Hence, if a party secured a decree for divorce from bed and board, he or she may afterwards have a decree for divorce from the bond of matrimony upon the same cause of action." 

The doctrine of election of remedies will not preclude a subsequent suit for absolute divorce for a cause which has accrued since the filing of the bill or petition in the former suit, or the counterclaim in the former suit in case the defendant in that suit brings the subsequent suit. But if such cause of action accrued prior thereto, so that it could have been included as a cause of action in the prior suit, it will be barred under the doctrine of res judi-

§ 259. Inquiry Under Rule 276. Rule 276 provides: 

Inquiry. In all suits for divorce or annulment of marriage (except in cases mentioned in paragraph 6 of this rule), before delivering the citation to the sheriff, diligent inquiry as to the defendant shall be made as follows: 

1. By Whom.-It shall be made by the petitioner or his solicitor actually entrusted with the conduct and management of the suit, or by the agent of the solicitor who shall also be a solicitor of this court. 

2. Of Whom.-It shall be made of the nearest relatives of the defendant, if known, or, if not known, it shall be made of any person known to be connected with the defendant by marriage or in business, or of any person who the petitioner or his said solicitor or agent making the inquiry, has reason to believe possesses knowledge of the residence or post-office address of the defendant.

4. Proof of Inquiry.-After making such inquiry the petitioner or his said solicitor or such agent shall file an affidavit setting out the nature of the inquiry and its results, and in cases mentioned in paragraph 7 of this rule, shall annex thereto a copy of the description of the defendant mentioned in that paragraph. The affidavit shall fully specify the inquiry made, of what persons and in what manner, so that by the facts stated therein it may appear that the inquiry has been made in good faith and for the purpose of effecting actual notice to the defendant; if the affidavit shall disclose that the inquiry has elicited information of the residence or post-office address of the defendant, it shall be accompanied by an affidavit of the person furnishing such information, disclosing the affiant's knowledge of such residence or postoffice address, if such affidavit can be obtained. 

In case it is disclosed that the defendant resides out of the State, yet if process shall be returned served upon him, an affidavit must be filed satisfactorily identifying the person served, and stating the circumstances under which he was served in this State. 

5. Certificate of Solicitor.-In all cases in which it does not appear that the defendant had actual notice of the suit and when the inquiry has not been made by the solicitor of record for the petitioner, the affidavit of the person making the inquiry shall be accompanied by the certificate of such solicitor that he verily believes the inquiry has been made in good faith and for the purpose of effecting actual notice to the defendant, but without success; and the court may require the affidavit of the petitioner also in any case. 

6. When Inquiry Unnecessary. The inquiry mentioned in this rule need not be made if the petitioner, or his solicitor, personally knows the present age, residence and occupation of the defendant; in which case he shall file an affidavit particularly stating his knowledge and the grounds of the same. -General Comments. The inquiry required under the Rule is a preliminary step to the acquisition of jurisdiction of the person of the defendant in suits for divorce and nullity of marriage. 

The Rule applies to all suits for divorce, absolute and limited, and

§ 303 

to all suits for nullity of marriage, including those instituted under the general equity jurisdiction of the court. 

It is essential that jurisdiction be secured over the defendant in divorce or nullity proceedings in strict accordance with the statute and rules of court. The method of acquiring such jurisdiction is therefore the most important procedural phase of such suits. Because of the far-reaching social and personal significance of such decrees, the steps by which jurisdiction over the defendant's person is to be secured must be taken with the greatest care. 

Sound public policy requires that the court be ever vigilant in supervising these procedural steps, in order to insure against the entry of invalid decrees. Indeed, its caution in this respect must be exercised as diligently as its scrutiny of the proofs on the merits. 

Jurisdiction over the cause of action is, of course, essential to the validity of a decree for divorce or nullity, but under our statute it is no less essential that the court secure jurisdiction over the person of the defendant. The statute requires that in all cases of divorce and nullity the defendant must be brought into court adversely.

In furtherance of the public policy expressed in the statutory provisions for securing jurisdiction over the defendant, the court has prescribed certain rules with respect to the method of perfecting personal service of process upon the defendant in the state and of notifying absent defendants. These rules are reasonable and necessary and their strict observance is as essential to securing jurisdiction over the defendant as is the observance of the statutory requirements.

Where the defendant is served personally with process within the state, the rules properly and necessarily require procedure making for the greatest certainty that such personal service is actually made upon the defendant himself. More is required than the "served" return of the serving official, who in practice usually follows instructions received from the solicitor of the petitioner. 

He does not know the defendant personally or where he may be found to be served. Hence the importance of Rule 276. This requirement affords an effective means for the identification of the person to be served and lends to the "served" return to the writ real assurance that proper personal service has been effected. 

This Rule applies as well, and properly so, in all cases of absent defendants. The statute requires actual notice of the suit to be given to an absent defendant, where practicable, in addition to the publication. Hence it is just as important that the information required by the Rule for the identification of the defendant be ascertained and proved as it is in cases where the

§ 259 

defendant is personally served in the state. The court is enabled thereby to determine that jurisdiction has been acquired by actual notice to the defendant, and where notice is impracticable following publication, to find that all-important fact. 

Serious responsibility for complying with this Rule rests squarely upon the petitioner's solicitor. It is probably correct to state that in more than one-third of the divorce and nullity suits instituted in this state some defect appears in the proofs under this Rule, necessitating further labor on the part of the solicitor. 

A reasonable understanding on the part of solicitors of the fundamentals underlying the Rule will convince them of its wisdom and necessity, and their careful and painstaking adherence thereto, in all its requirements, will be found to save time and trouble, not only on the part of the solicitor, but of the court. -When to be Made. The inquiry, when necessary, must be made before delivering the citation to the sheriff for service. 

Hence it may be made after filing the petition and obtaining the certified copy and citation, but in practice it is better to make the inquiry before drawing the petition in order that the residence of the defendant may be alleged in the petition in compliance with Rule 275. 

-By Whom Made. 

Obviously, paragraph 1 of Rule 276 was inserted to enable the court to retain absolute control over the inquiry through the litigant and through the litigant's solicitor as an officer of the court. It is in furtherance of the sound policy of placing upon petitioner's solicitor the burden of conducting a sincere and diligent inquiry. See paragraph 5 of Rule. 

-Of Whom Made. Under paragraph 2 of Rule 276, the in quiry must be made primarily of the nearest known relatives. 

If successful, no further inquiry need be undertaken. If unsuccessful, or no relatives are known, the inquiry must be extended to persons in the other three classes stated and in the order prescribed in the Rule.21 The further inquiry need not be carried beyond the class from which the facts are successfully ascertained, but otherwise it must be inclusive of all such persons known in each of the classes. It is to be noted that inquiry is required without regard to where the person inquired of may reside. The test of inquiry is diligence and good faith, not convenience nor saving of time. No less a standard could be laid down consistent 

21. See Barker v. Barker, 63 N. J. Eq. 593, 595, 53 Atl. 4 (1902).

§ 305 

with the jurisdictional requirements of our statute as to personal service of process within the state, or actual notice to absent defendants, if practicable, in addition to publication. The practicability of substituted service upon an absent defendant can be determined only upon proof of a complete inquiry within the full scope of this Rule. Such an inquiry, when necessary, must extend to all persons known (wherever they reside) within each of the classes set forth in this paragraph of the Rule; and the proofs must clearly reveal all such persons in each of the classes as defined in the Rule, and that due inquiry has been made of each of them. -In What Manner. Paragraph 3 of Rule 276 is so clear and specific that comment is unnecessary.22 -Proof of Inquiry. The proof of inquiry must scrupulously comply with paragraph 4 of Rule 276 [Form 156 et. seq.]. A perfect inquiry improperly proved can be of no avail. In proving an inquiry by mail the results should include the original of any reply received, not a copy. If no reply was received, the proof should show whether the solicitor's return address was upon the face of the envelope of the letter of inquiry, pursuant to postal regulations governing the return to sender of undelivered mail, and whether the letter was returned undelivered for any reason. 

The envelope of a returned letter of inquiry should be identified and annexed to the proofs to establish the postal markings upon it. 

The affidavit of inquiry should be filed with the Clerk after delivery of the citation to the sheriff, or upon the return of the writ "non est." -Certificate of Solicitor. Paragraph 5 of Rule 276 places the responsibility for the quality of the inquiry upon the shoulders of the solicitor of the petitioner and authorizes the court in any case to require an affidavit from the petitioner of the facts showing the impossibility of furnishing notice of the suit directly to the defendant, and disclosing the names of all persons available for inquiry. [See Forms 159-161A]. -When Inquiry Unnecessary. Inquiry is not dispensed with under paragraph 6 of Rule 276 unless one of two persons has personal knowledge of the present age, residence and occupation of the defendant. The personal knowledge of a third person is

not enough. If the solicitor of record possesses such personal knowledge, then he may execute and file his affidavit to such effect. 

If the petitioner is the one having the personal knowledge, then he or she executes the affidavit, to which there should be annexed the certificate of the solicitor under paragraph 5 of the Rule [Forms 151, 152] in all cases in which it does not appear that actual notice of the suit has been given to the defendant. The affidavit of personal knowledge of the present age, residence and occupation of the defendant, whether executed by the petitioner or by the solicitor of record, should state particularly and circumstantially such knowledge and the grounds of the same. Such affidavit should be sufficient in particulars and circumstances to show actual knowledge of the facts and to justify the court in believing that the present residence of the defendant is as stated therein. If the petitioner or the solicitor knows that at a certain date in the past the defendant lived at a certain place and the affidavit so states, that is not sufficient. Inquiry then must be made to determine the residence of the defendant as well as his age and occupation at the time the affidavit is made. § 260. Drafting the Petition. § 263. Joinder of Non-matrimonial Cause. 

vides: 

Rule 20 pro In a suit for divorce or annulment of marriage no nonmatrimonial cause of action shall be joined without leave of court.

Since the severance of matrimonial causes from other litigation in Chancery and their reference to Advisory Masters, this Rule has been difficult of application. The practice is to allow such joinder where the non-matrimonial cause is merely incidental to the matrimonial cause and independently unimportant; otherwise, to decline to order such joinder. The distinction is not always easy to make. It lies largely in the discretion of the Advisory 

Master to whom application is made. Leave will not usually be granted unless the issues can be tried together more conveniently than separately, or where parties other than husband and wife must be brought in upon the non-matrimonial issue, unless such third parties have no personal interest.¹¹ 

Leave should first be obtained, but in practice the court has construed the Rule liberally in proper cases, so that, if such joinder is made without leave of the court, leave may be granted afterwards nunc pro tunc on application. A non-matrimonial cause may be set up in the counterclaim, but should not be set up singly or in conjunction with a matrimonial cause without leave of court.1 12

§ 264. Filing of Petition; Securing Citation. After the petition for divorce or nullity has been drawn, and the original and at least two copies typed, and the original and at least one copy signed by the solicitor and counsel, and after the affidavit of non-collusion and merits has been executed by the petitioner and annexed to the original and to at least one copy, the next step is to file the petition and obtain a citation. The petition must be filed within the time provided for by Rule 279. The Rule specifies that: 

If it shall appear by the jurat to the oath or affirmation, annexed to the petition for divorce or other matrimonial proceeding that such oath or affirmation was taken more than eight days before the filing of the petition or bill, if the same was taken within this State, or more than fourteen days, if the same was taken in any other State or Territory of the United States or in the Dominion of Canada, or more than thirty days if taken elsewhere, the cause shall not be proceeded with until the Chancellor shall be satisfied that the petition or bill was filed with such diligence as the circumstances of the case permitted.

At the time Rule 279 was originally promulgated the word "divorce" in the statutes comprehended "nullity" as well, and Rule 279 should be so construed.18 Petitions for nullity of marriage under the general equity jurisdiction of the court must also be filed within the time fixed by Rule 279. In practice Rule 279 is not strictly applied unless circumstances should appear indicating some ulterior motive for withholding the filing of the petition or some undue delay beyond the respective lengths of time provided by the Rule. But it is advisable to adhere to the Rule whenever possible. 14 Within the time just noticed the original ¹¹ petition is delivered or sent, together with one copy, addressed to "Clerk in Chancery, State House Annex, Trenton, N. Service of Process. The requirements for service of process in divorce and nullity suits are sui generis. The statutory methods prescribed should be strictly adhered to. There are but two modes of service provided in suits for divorce and nullity: (1) personal service of process upon the defendant within this State, 25 (2) when personal service within the State cannot be obtained, then by publication to be followed, if practicable, by the substituted service prescribed by Rule 277.26 These two methods will be considered in ensuing sections. The latter provisions of paragraph 4 Rule 276 are frequently overlooked. They constitute a requirement additional to that of inquiry where personal service of process is made within the state upon a non-resident.defendant. After filing with the Clerk the citation, with its "non est" return,2 24 the sheriff's affidavit and the other affidavits as above noted, application is made for an order for publication, or as it is sometimes called, an order to answer.

Probably this order may be taken as of course without filing affidavits showing compliance with the requirements of Rule 276. 

But if so taken, it would be at the solicitor's peril. In practice the proofs of compliance with Rule 276 are filed upon the application for the order for publication in order that the petitioner may be protected by an adjudication as to the requisite form required to accomplish substituted service in the circumstances of the case, pursuant to the requirements of Rule 277, within the statutory period of twenty days from the date of the order for publication.

For example, in a case in which the defendant was a member of the Byrd Antarctic Expedition, in addition to notifying him by registered mail under paragraph 3 of Rule 277, service upon the sponsor of the expedition was prescribed under a six months' order.

After full and complete inquiry under Rule 276, satisfactorily proved, if the defendant cannot be located, one of two courses is open to the petitioner: (1) he may have a provision in the order for publication for special substituted service under paragraph 4 of Rule 277 if the circumstances reasonably warrant the belief that such special substituted service will be likely to afford defendant actual notice of the suit; or (2) he may take on order dispensing with special substituted service pursuant to the first alternative of paragraph 5, Rule 277. This order is distinct from the order for publication, but may be entered at the same time or subsequently to the entry of the order for publication in the usual form [Forms 166-176], but not later than twenty days after the entry of the order for publication.

Where the proofs of compliance with Rule 276 establish a complete but unsuccessful inquiry and are dated immediately prior to the application for the order for publication, the order dispensing with special substituted service may be had at the same time as the order for publication, but where some time has passed since the date of the affidavits application for the order dispensing with special substituted service must be accompanied by petitioner's supplemental affidavit under Rule 276 stating shortly, what, if anything, has been learned concerning defendant's whereabouts since the date of the affidavit of inquiry, and whether the names and addresses of any persons in each of the classes set forth in paragraph 2, Rule 276 have been ascertained. If the status appears to be the same as shown in the affidavits of inquiry, then the order dispensing may be entered if applied for within the prescribed time.

Occasionally it happens that, following the entry of an order for publication in the usual form directing substituted service to be made in the manner prescribed by the rules of court (Rule 277), the substituted service cannot be effected in accordance with paragraph 1, 2, or 3 of the Rule, due to the defendant's evasion

The alternative procedure under paragraph 5, Rule 277, where substituted service following order for publication is impracticable and where it clearly appears that no special substituted service could have been directed had it been applied for under paragraph 4 of Rule 277 is, upon the application for the order of reference, to file affidavits of the solicitor and the petitioner showing in substance a continuance of the inquiry within the full scope of the Rule for defendant's whereabouts since the date of the affidavits of inquiry filed upon the order for publication and that defendant's whereabouts could not be ascertained, and that the circumstances admitted of no special substituted service being devised.

Rule should be obeyed and the order itself should not be published.

The form of the notice [Form 177] as prescribed by Rule 36 must be used. Any substantial departure will be fatal to jurisdiction, as, for example, the omission of the solicitor's post-office address.25

The requirement of Rule 36 that the notice shall "state briefly, in general terms, the object of the suit" is complied with by describing the relief sought: in divorce, a dissolution of the marriage; in nullity, an annulment of the marriage. The ground need not be stated, but, if stated, it must be a ground constituting a cause of action under the statute. If the ground stated in the notice is not that pleaded, the notice is fatally defective.20

§ 269. 

-Substituted Service. In addition to obtaining the order for publication and publishing the notice thereof in the manner described in the previous section and within twenty days after the date of the order for publication (the same period of time required for the first publication of the notice of the order), the solicitor must comply with the requirements of section 2:50-12 of the Revision as to substituted service to be made upon the defendant within or without this state of the petition and of the order for publication or notice of such order "in such manner as the Chancellor may by general rules prescribe." The general rule prescribed by the Chancellor for substituted service in divorce and nullity suits is Rule 277 which is as follows: 

Substituted Service. How Made.-Service upon the de fendant of a certified copy of the petition and of the order to answer (or notice of that order) as service substituted for personal service of process in this State may be made— (NOTE.-As to the "Notice of that Order," see Rules 33, 34, 35, 36 and 39.) 

27. Stone v. Stone, 28 N. J. Eq. 409 (1877). 

28. L. 1938 c. 191.

§ 327 

1. By personal service upon the defendant, either within or without this State, to be proved by affidavit stating the age, residence and occupation of the affiant, the source of his knowledge of the identity of the person served, and the place and time of the service; or, if such service cannot be made, then either 2. By leaving the said papers at the residence, or usual place of abode, or usual place of business of the defendant within or without this State, to be proved by affidavit of affiant's knowledge that the place where the papers were left was the residence, or usual place of abode, or the usual place of business of the defendant; or 

3. By mailing the said papers to the post-office address of the defendant by registered letter with request for a return receipt (unless the registry is dispensed with by special order in the cause), to be proved by the affidavit of the solicitor of the petitioner stating the time of the deposit of the papers in the post-office, with postage prepaid, a particular statement of the address, and the result of such mailing; this proof to be accompanied by an affidavit of the person furnishing information of the post-office address, disclosing the affiant's knowledge of such post-office address, if such affidavit can be obtained; or 

4. By such service as the court may direct upon application for special substituted service in the cause, to be made within twenty days from the date of the order to answer. 

5. When Service Impracticable. No adjudication pur suant to the statute shall be made that publication could not be followed practicably by service upon or notice to the defendant, without this State, or by additional substituted service upon the defendant within this State, unless so made upon an application for special substituted service under paragraph 4, or upon application for the order of reference; and in the latter case, unless it is made clearly to appear that no special substituted service could have been directed if application had been made therefor within the time allowed by paragraph 4. 

6. No order of reference shall be made in any case falling under this rule (277) until its requirements and the requirements of the preceding rule (276) shall have been satisfied. -General Comments. The publication and substituted service are mandatory jurisdictional prerequisities. Service must be made of certified copies of the petition and of the order for publi-

§ 269 

cation. In lieu of such a copy of the order, notice of the order may be served. In practice it is the rule to serve with the petition a copy of the notice as published. The 1938 amendment expressly provides for service of the petition and order for publication, or notice thereof, although publication or further publication is rendered unnecessary by reason of defendant's appearance.28

Substituted service within twenty days from the date of the order for publication is prescribed, if it can be made practicably. 

The presumption is always in favor of the service being practicable. The petitioner has the burden to show that it was impracticable. This question is adjudged by the court upon the affidavits filed under Rule 276 and supplemental affidavits. Rule 

277 simply designates the methods of making the prescribed service. The statute virtually makes the Rule a part of it by direct reference and, accordingly, the Rule must be strictly followed. 

It can be relaxed only as the statute prescribes. There is no relief in the statute from the necessity for substituted service of the requisite papers except in instances where the court adjudges that it cannot practicably be made.

It should be noted that this Rule prescribes in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 specific methods for making substituted service. In most cases such service can be made in one of these ways and the order for publication accordingly prescribes the method of service by reference to the Rule rather than by setting out the method at length in the order. The arrangement has proved quite practicable. The designation by the Rule of the methods for service and their incidents is instructive to the Bar and makes for greater dispatch of service and uniformity of proofs that would be so were the order in every case to specify the method of service. 

-Personal Service. Under the provisions of paragraph 1 of 

Rule 277, substituted service must be made upon the defendant personally whenever practicable. It is considered that such service is effected when made by registered mail which results in the receipt of a personally signed return card, the signature on which is proved to be the defendant's. But recourse to registered mail service is not to be had, as authorized by paragraph 3, Rule 277, simply to serve petitioner's convenience. It should be limited to cases where the circumstances proved show that personal service pursuant to paragraph 1, or the service under paragraph 2 of the Rule, cannot be made practicably because of the considerable 

28a. L. 1938 c. 191.

$ 329 

expense involved, or that timely arrangements could not be made, or for a like compelling reason.

The proof of personal service must accord with the provisions of this paragraph of the Rule. The affidavit [Form 179] should carefully identify the person making the service, definitely specify the papers served, when and where they were served, and that they were handed to the defendant personally, and should disclose the means used by affiant for identification of the person served as the defendant. The solicitor should use great care in selecting a qualified and reliable person for making the service, and should give explicit instructions to such person to the end that proper service of the requisite papers be made upon the defendant. In practice it is advisable, where the affidavit of service is to be executed outside the state, to furnish a form of the affidavit and to give instructions that a proper certificate be annexed to prove the authority of the official before whom it is subscribed and sworn to. -Leaving Papers at Residence. The above suggestions respecting paragraph 1 of Rule 277 apply equally to paragraph 2. 

This method should be resorted to only where the primary service under paragraph I cannot be effected and the affidavit [Form 180] should show the reasons for personal service not being made. -Mailing the Papers. Recourse to service by registered mail under paragraph 3 of Rule 277 may be had only where the methods of service prescribed by the preceding paragraphs were unavailable practically, because of the considerable expense involved, or because of defendant's location being such that available means of communication rendered timely service impossible, or because of some similar compelling reason.

The registry provision of this paragraph was specified in order that with the receipt of the registered article containing the requisite papers there would be definite assurance that defendant had actual notice of the suit. Registered mail service, without exception throughout the world, is maintained upon a very high standard and its rules and regulations as to accuracy of delivery warrant its acceptance as a reliable medium for transmission of notice of important matters to the person addressed. After this 

Rule was first promulgated the postal regulations were changed. 

Originally a signed registry return card was an incident of the registration of any mail and without special request for it, or extra charge. Some years back the postal regulations were amended so as to require a request for a return receipt card and

§ 269 

an additional fee. The signed return card is so essential to the proof of a successful service by this method that it must be requested in all cases where substituted service is resorted to under this paragraph and the Rule has now been amended so as to require it. When a return card has been lost, a duplicate original may be obtained through the sending post office.

The service under this paragraph must be proved by the solicitor's affidavit [Form 181]. This provision implies that the actual mailing should be attended to by the solicitor himself and that indubitably is the better practice. The spirit of the Rule should be obeyed. If the mailing is not made by the solicitor himself, he should give special instructions in regard to it and entrust it only to a reliable agent. The proof should then be by affidavit of the solicitor establishing the service in detail in accordance with this paragraph, supported by his agent's affidavit showing the actual mailing and the service in detail. The proof of results of the service must include the original registry return card, the signature on which must be proved. If it be that of the defendant the quality of the service is unimpeachable and on a parity with actual personal service pursuant to paragraph 1 of this Rule as heretofore referred to under that paragraph. If the signature is that of an agent for defendant, the connection of that person with the defendant, as actually known, or as ascertained upon inquiry made of the agent, should be established by affidavit. In such case a proved written admission of defendant, or a proved oral admission of actual receipt of the requisite papers by registered mail, is acceptable as showing a successful personal service. 

This paragraph provides for dispensing with the registry provision, but sets no standard to warrant such omission. In practice such dispensation may be provided for in the order for publication wherever the proofs of inquiry may warrant, as, for example, it appearing that defendant is not reasonably available for substituted service under paragraph 1 or 2 of Rule 277, that his residence is definitely ascertained, but that he is shown from experience to be hostile to the receipt of any communication from petitioner, or petitioner's solicitor. Under postal regulations, he cannot refuse to accept first class mail, unregistered, so that the registry provision of paragraph 3 may be dispensed with and substituted service may be ordered by unregistered mail under that paragraph. The provision has been dispensed with by order entered nunc pro tunc as of the date of the order for publication where a successful substituted service was proved to have been made by unregistered mail, the registry provision inadvertently not having been followed [Forms 181A, 181B].

§ 331 

The provision of the Rule requiring that proof of the actual residence of the defendant be made by means of the affidavit of the person who furnished evidence of the facts for the purpose of the substituted service must be complied with in all cases of inquiry made under Rule 276 if it is possible to secure such affidavit [Form 182]. In case it cannot be obtained, the proofs under this paragraph should affirmatively show why it cannot be obtained. In cases where no inquiry is necessary under Rule 276, this affidavit is not required, but in lieu thereof proof of the age, residence and occupation of the defendant must have been furnished pursuant to paragraph 6 of Rule 276. The affidavit of the person furnishing evidence of the defendant's residence, except as aforesaid, is required to be furnished where it can be procured in order to make more certain that the prescribed substituted service has actually been effected upon the defendant. -Special Substituted Service. A consideration of the first three paragraphs of Rule 277, in conjunction with section 2:50-12 of the Revision, discloses that the fundamental purpose of these requirements is to effect actual notice of the suit upon the defendant. Where the proofs of a complete inquiry under Rule 276 establish that defendant is not available for substituted service under the order pursuant to paragraphs 1, 2, or 3, Rule 277, the service required may be made as the court may by order specially direct, but such service must be effected within the prescribed time, namely, twenty days. The proofs sometimes show that defendant, although not available for service as prescribed by the preceding paragraphs of the Rule, can be served by some other method. In such case an order may be taken authorizing the special service. The more usual instances of the application of this paragraph are where the defendant cannot definitely be located at all and where the proofs under Rule 276 disclose the existence and identity of a person, or persons, either near relatives or business or social connections of defendant, of whom due inquiry has been made, under circumstances which give reason to believe that actual notice of the suit may be effected successfully upon the defendant by directing service to be made upon such person or persons. In practice, the motion is made at the time of the application for the order for publication and in such case that order will embody the terms of the special substituted service, instead of the usual provision for substituted service. Occasionally, application is made after the entry of the order for publication (but within twenty days thereafter, for the service to be prescribed must be made within that time) and upon supplemental proofs

§ 269 

under Rule 276. Usually these proofs show the impracticability of the prescribed substituted service upon defendant as ascertained subsequent to the entry of the order for publication and the necessity for the proposed special substituted service. It must be borne in mind that proof of impracticability of substituted service is not alone sufficient to warrant the conclusion that jurisdiction can be obtained upon publication alone. A further prerequisite is that special substituted service has been applied for and obtained, or that the alternative procedure has been resorted to as prescribed by the next paragraph of this Rule. In any event it must be understood that an application under the paragraph now being considered cannot be maintained except upon proofs under Rule 276 which establish that a complete inquiry has been made within the full scope of that Rule. As has heretofore been stated, nothing less than proof of an inquiry extended to all persons in each of the classes designated in paragraph 2, Rule 276, will be accepted as proof of such complete inquiry, and as warrant for prescribing a special substituted service upon someone in lieu of the defendant. This type of service is at least secondary to actual service upon defendant and is not countenanced for mere convenience. 

It is a last resort, so to speak, and justifiable only where the foundation for it is adequately established by the proof under 

Rule 276. 

Paragraph 5 of -When Substituted Service Impracticable. 

Rule 277 relates to the ultimate aspect of the prescribed substituted service under section 2:50-12 of the Revision. As already emphasized, such service together with publication (except where defendant appears) is a jurisdictional prerequisite in absent defendant cases. Though the service is mandatory, it is limited to cases of practicability. Jurisdiction is acquired by publication alone where the prescribed service is impracticable. This paragraph lays down the practice in such cases. It is alternative. 

Upon application under paragraph 4 of Rule 277, within twenty days from the entry of the order for publication, an order may be entered dispensing with special substituted service. The proofs under Rule 276 must support the judgment residing in the order, or the application will be denied. The order is not to be had for the asking. Unless the proofs under Rule 276 show a complete and unsuccessful inquiry and sufficiently disclose the fact that no special substituted service can be directed, the order cannot be entered. If these proofs alone are to be relied upon they must have been executed contemporaneously with the application for the order for publication. If they antedate that order for any

§ 333 

substantial period, at least petitioner's further affidavit must be submitted on the application for order dispensing with special substituted service bringing the inquiry to date, to show what, if any, change in the status has occurred since the filing of the original proofs. And this is a reasonable precaution, since the prescribed substituted, or special substituted, service is to be made within the twenty-day period after the order for publication and since, through a complete and timely inquiry under Rule 276, the defendant's whereabouts, or significant information connected therewith, may possibly be secured within the twenty-day period, sufficient to effect service under the order for publication by one of the methods set forth in paragraphs 1, 2, 3 or 4 of Rule 277.

If such information is disclosed by the subsequent inquiry, then obviously the prescribed provisions for substituted, or special substituted, service will be ineffective to confer jurisdiction, despite the proof of inquiry originally filed.

When application is made under paragraph 5 of Rule 277 it is the established practice to take the order for publication in the usual form and a separate order dispensing with special substituted service.

The latter (alternative) procedure in paragraph 5 of Rule 277 is that most often resorted to and seems preferable. The inquiry for practicable purposes is carried down to the order of reference, or through the entire period of the order for publication, as contrasted with the period of inquiry under the preceding alternative procedure which, of necessity, continues only down to the twentieth day following the date of the order for publication. The more extensive period of inquiry usually indicates a more diligent and more sincere effort to give defendant actual notice of the suit which must reflect the more favorably upon the quality of the decree obtained. The showing of impracticability of substituted service and that clearly no special substituted service could have been directed had timely application been made for it under paragraph 4 of Rule 277 is made primarily from the proofs of inquiry under Rule 276 as filed on the entry of the order for publication, but is supported by the proofs submitted on the application for order of reference supplementing the proofs of inquiry and bringing them down to date with no change in the information reported upon the original inquiry.

The utmost caution should be observed in all causes brought within the provisions of paragraph 5 of Rule 277. It should be resorted to only after the most diligent and exhaustive inquiry possible has been made within the existing circumstances of the par-

§ 270 

ticular case. The jurisdiction is the weakest that can exist and for that reason the decree obtained is the most vulnerable to attack. Of course, there are proper cases in which decrees for divorce or nullity, resting upon the jurisdiction in rem, or quasi in rem, may be entered, although no actual notice has been given to defendants, but the careful practitioner will limit such cases to those where the circumstances necessarily admit of no actual notice to defendants. Nothing short of the actual impracticability of such notice by substituted service will satisfy the standard set by our statute for jurisdiction over such causes. A full realization of the significance of this mandate of our statute will convince the practitioner of the necessity for strict and full compliance with the standards expressed in the requirements of Rule 276 and its cognate, Rule 277. They are simply the means, provided of necessity, to give expression to the legislative objectives laid down by the statute and are the sine qua non to every valid decree for divorce or for nullity of marriage.

 § 271. Entitling Causes for Nullity. The statute and Rule respecting the assertion of a cause of action by way of counterclaim are not compulsory. As respects suits in which the defendant may assert a counterclaim for divorce or nullity, the only requirement of the statute is that the court shall have acquired jurisdiction "of any suit under the provisions of this chapter."  § 274. Replication. An amended petition relates back to the date of the filing of the original petition. Hence, if a petitioner seeking a divorce. relies upon desertion as the cause of action, it must have accrued 2 at the time the petition was filed rather than at the time of the filing of an amended petition.³ -Leave of Court. Leave of the court must always be obtained for the amendment of a petition for nullity or for divorce.* [Forms 17-20]. Since process is issued by the Clerk forthwith upon the filing of the petition, pursuant to the statute, there is in such case no interval of time between the filing of the petition and the issuing of process, as there is in all other suits in Chancery. In the practice under the general equity jurisdiction the solicitor himself issues the process, and Rule 80 providing for amendments as of course before process is issued has therefore no application to divorce and nullity cases. But upon the filing of a bill for separate maintenance, the general practice prevails. 

Under Rule 80 an amendment may be taken as of course before process is issued. And it would seem that a counterclaim, whatever relief be prayed therein, may be amended as of course at any time before service of copy, inasmuch as no process issues thereon.

When leave to amend a petition or bill is applied for prior to final hearing in contested suits, or at any time in uncontested suits, notice of the application will be required if the defendant has been brought into court. An order to show cause may issue on verified petition, or the matter may be brought on on notice and affidavits. -Notice of Amendment. After the petition for divorce or nullity or the bill for maintenance is filed, or after the copy of the counterclaim is served, amendments may be made to either, by leave of the court and on such terms as may be ordered. Generally speaking, such terms are designed to afford reasonable notice of the amendment to the opposing party, with suitable opportunity to meet the newly presented issues or facts. In an early case where the original petition for divorce failed to allege the jurisdictional fact of petitioner's residence in New Jersey and the case went to hearing ex parte with no notice to defendant of an amendment supplying the jurisdictional allegations, the petitioner was permitted after the hearing before the Master to take an order to show cause why a decree should not be entered on the Master's report, or (in the alternative) to issue a new citation."

In a later case, under the Divorce Act of 1907, where the petition alleged simple desertion and the case was referred ex parte, the petitioner proved a cause of action for constructive desertion and was permitted to amend and to take an order to show cause upon the defendant why a decree should not be entered upon the report and proofs.'

If the defendant appears and the amendment is ordered the only terms usually made are that a copy of the amendment be served and that the defendant have a certain time, usually ten days, in which to meet it. If the defendant is not yet in court, the order will make suitable provision for service of the amended petition or notice of it with the citation. If the defendant is in court but does not appear to oppose the motion, the provision for notice will vary with the circumstances of the case. 

The order usually provides that the copy to be served on the defendant may be certified as true by petitioner's solicitor, unless the defendant is not yet in court, in which case it must be certified by the Clerk [See Forms 21-24]. 

-When Amended Petition or Counterclaim Re-engrossed. 

When leave of court has been secured for the amendment of a petition or counterclaim, the better practice in all cases is to reengross the same in its amended form, and it is imperative to do so when the amendment relates to a petition or counterclaim for divorce or nullity, except where the amendment is of some immaterial non-jurisdictional matter, because it is essential that a new affidavit of non-collusion and merits [Form 1] be annexed.Ⓡ

A form of supplemental petition is included hereinafter which may be varied to meet the particular case [Form 27]. § 277. Objections to Pleadings. On a motion in limine to dismiss a petition for divorce the court can consider only the allegations of the petition, all of which, for the purpose of the motion, when well pleaded, must be regarded as true.29 The same rule applies to a counterclaim, which is essentially an affirmative pleading. Such an objection cannot be made on the ground that the pleading is sham, that is, that it sets up facts which are untrue, for motions to strike out pleadings as sham are entertained only against defensive pleadings. Nor can an objection to a defensive pleading be made on any ground whatsoever in divorce or nullity suits, for in such cases it is held that Rule 69 (formerly Rule 67) does not apply." A motion in one case to dismiss a petition for divorce on the ground that "there is no basis in fact for the petition, and in all truth and honesty the petition does not exhibit the true state of facts, and the latter will preclude all possibility of success" was held over until final hearing."

The policy of our law favors defenses in divorce and nullity suits, so that any attack upon them, pending suit, is discouraged. 

Therefore such an attack can never be justified if its purpose. is to procure the dismissal of a defensive pleading. 

An affirmative pleading in divorce and nullity cases, however, may be objected to on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action. The attack is by motion before answer, and is the equivalent of a general demurrer under the old practice. But

A suit for divorce is not pending, at least not pending bona fide, until after the petition has been filed and the defendant has been personally served within the state with the citation or by publication and substituted service.14 If relief is granted, the cause is pending until a final decree of divorce.15 If an appeal is perfected from the decree nisi in cases of absolute divorce and nullity within the time allowed, the suit would be pending during the appeal. But, if a petition for divorce or nullity is dismissed, it may be queried whether the suit is pending until the time for appeal has elapsed.16

The filing of an amended petition is not the beginning of a new suit, but merely a continuation of the original litigation." The death of either of the parties abates the action without a right of revivor in anyone.18 [See Form 297]. Furthermore, condonation by the petitioner after a suit for divorce has been commenced will destroy the cause of action, so that the suit is no longer pending, although not dismissed of record.¹º

The court may appoint a solicitor with instructions to defend, although the defendant may not desire to put in a defense. Thus in a suit for divorce for desertion it appeared that in prior litigation the husband's petition for divorce had been dismissed and the wife had been granted a decree for separate maintenance upon consent by the husband, although upon the proofs she was not entitled to the decree. In the subsequent suit by the wife for divorce for desertion the husband defaulted, the case was referred ex parte, and the court appointed a solicitor to defend. An an- swer was filed denying the allegation of desertion and by agreement the defense was presented by stipulating into the case the evidence taken on defendant's behalf in the prior proceeding.10 

The power conferred upon the court by section 2:50-17 of the 

Revision to appoint a solicitor actively to defend carries with it an implication of power to compel compensation by the husband of the solicitor assigned. Were this implied power in doubt, it is beyond question that section 2:29-131 of the Revision (formerly section 91 of the Chancery Act) gives the court the authority to award counsel fees to the solicitor assigned as against the husband.20 The order assigning the solicitor [Form 287] usually provides that the defendant wife may apply for alimony and suit moneys, including counsel fee. § 286. § 355 

hearing.21 The proceeding does not differ essentially from other hearings in the Court of Chancery. Rule 115 et seq. govern the manner in which the hearing is to be conducted. In the ordinary case it is not necessary to submit trial briefs. But, if unsettled legal questions are involved, or if there is a question about which the court is apt to be unfamiliar, it is the duty of solicitors to aid the court by furnishing trial briefs. 

We must await an adjudication as to whether a matrimonial suit may be heard in camera in cases where there is a child under 16 years of age and petitioner includes as a second cause of action allegations under section 9:2-3 of the Revision and files the necessary affidavit.22 Is any inference to be drawn from the legislative failure to abide by recommendations of our Divorce Congress

Commissioners in 1907 that all ex parte hearings be in open court and public?

The conduct of the hearing, including the order of proof, is within the discretion of the court as in other cases in Chancery. 

In the ordinary ex parte case there is no need to supply purely cumulative evidence unless the court requires it. Ordinarily, the petitioner should be the first witness in order that the evidence may be adduced in connected form. Nevertheless, if there be some corroborating witness whose time is particularly valuable, such as a physician, leave may be obtained from the court to put him on as the first witness.

In examining the petitioner, whether the cause is contested or uncontested, bear in mind clearly the three essential elements requiring proof: the marriage,28 the residential requirements,24 and the cause of action.25 If the solicitor will rehearse the questions and answers carefully with his client and witnesses before the hearing, the facts may be adduced without unnecessary prolixity.

with her, but when I told him of my suspicions he denied emphatically that they were justified. However, his coldness toward me became more pronounced. He got to sleeping in the guest room and repulsed me when I tried to get him to return to my bed. He became increasingly angry when I tried to reason with him, accusing me of nagging him. 

Q. Did his attitude and conduct toward you, as you have described it, change for the better or for the worse as time went on?

A. It became increasingly worse until finally there was scarcely any communication between us. He got so he took no meals at home and tried to avoid seeing me. 

Q. What finally happened on or about January first, 1932?

A. The situation became so unbearable to me that on that day 

I faced him, determined to make a last effort to win him back. He tried his best to avoid talking to me, as usual, but I insisted. I told him I was sure he must be going around with some other woman, that I could not go on with him under such conditions. I pleaded with him to give her up and come back to me. I reminded him of how happy our marriage had been at first and promised that it would be just as happy again if he would only be himself again. He became very angry and cursed me. He said, "Yes, of course it's true that I'm going around with another woman. Anybody but a damn fool would have known that long ago and left me. I'm through with you and I'm getting out for good. You can go to the devil." I kept pleading with him but it was no use. He packed two bags with his clothing and left. 

Q. How soon thereafter did you see him again?

A. Three days later, after I had returned to my parents' home, my father and I went to his parents' home at No.

Street, Newark, and talked with him there in an effort to get him to return. 

Q. What was the conversation?

A. Both my father and I pleaded with him to return. He said, "No I'm tired of you and I'm through," and that was all he would say, no matter how much we pleaded with him. 

When we saw it was useless, we left, and I have never seen him to speak to since that time. 

Q. Did he ever communicate with you, directly or indirectly, after that? 

A. No.

§ 287. Jury Trial. 

vides: 

Section 2:50-28 of the Revision pro- 

2:50-28. If, in the opinion of the chancellor, any matter of fact shall render the intervention of a jury necessary in any suit or proceeding for divorce or nullity, the court of chancery may direct an issue for the trial of the same in the supreme court or in one of the circuit courts. This provision is not important. The parties have no absolute right to a jury trial in a matrimonial cause. In the reports there is no case wherein a jury trial was had, and in practice no instance is to be recalled in which a jury trial has been requested. The verdict of the jury would not be binding on the Chancellor as can be gleaned from section 2:50-29 of the Revision. § 288.

Dismissal. The rules governing dismissals in equity practice have received consideration by several text-writers and there is no need to consider the subject except so far as it is peculiar to divorce litigation [Forms 89-96]. A suit for divorce or nullity of marriage which has been suffered to lie without substantial prosecution for one year may be considered as abandoned and the petition may be dismissed, on notice; the court may nevertheless order the cause to be proceeded with, but before the making of any such order the court shall be informed by affidavit of the reason for the delay, what relations the parties have sustained to each other since the commencement of the suit, and whether any, and if so, what understanding or agreement exists, or has existed between them; and if the cause shall be permitted to proceed, an order to answer shall be taken and served on the defendant, either within or without this State, if service be practicable.

In ex parte causes the affidavit [Form 269] contemplated by Rule 286 should be presented or forwarded to the Advisory Master at Trenton, together with draft of order for leave to proceed and to answer [Form 270 et. seq.]. If the delay occurred before defendant was brought into court, the order to answer clause is unnecessary because, leave to proceed having been granted, the defendant will be noticed to answer by the next step in the cause -service of process, or proceeding under an order for publication. 

If the order to answer is taken, service must be made unless it be shown on the application by affidavits establishing a complete inquiry following substantially Forms 170 and 171 that such service is impracticable. In such case the order for leave to proceed may include a provision dispensing with service of an order to answer as impracticable. The court acts under this Rule in an ex parte case of its own motion to stay a reference or further proceeding in the cause until the Rule has been satisfied. This is logical. 

With the unreasonable delay, there should be a satisfactory explanation of the reason and a re-affirmance of the substance of the statutory affidavit of non-collusion before the cause should be proceeded with.

In practice, the Rule in contested cases is left to the parties to avail themselves of, if they so desire, and the court seldom intervenes of its own motion. On a motion by the defendant for dismissal under the Rule the burden is upon petitioner to satisfy the court of the reasonableness of the delay, etc., or a dismissal will result. Sound public policy calls for such litigation to be vigorously prosecuted and speedily concluded, if due regard is to be had for defendant's rights and the best interests of society. In a proper case, the court may fix a short day before which the necessary steps for final hearing shall be undertaken, or a dismissal suffered. After order of reference has been made, such applications should be brought before the Advisory Master to whom the case has been referred.

§ 291. -Entry Nunc Pro Tunc.21 A decree dismissing a petition for divorce nunc pro tunc has been allowed where the defendant was entitled to the decree and through inadvertence it was not entered." But it will not be allowed so as to disturb a status or to impair vested rights. Thus, a decree of dismissal nunc pro tunc has been refused where a petitioner in a pending suit, usually for divorce for desertion, seeks to get rid of the effect of the pendency of a prior suit.23 § 292. 

-Effect as Res Judicata; Without Prejudice. The dismissal of a suit in equity for failure of proof after a hearing on the merits is ordinarily a bar to the institution of a new suit for the same cause of action so long as the decree of dismissal stands unreversed.24 There may be some question as to whether the decree of dismissal is res judicata until the time for appeal has expired. To avoid the bar, the court, in divorce as well as in other litigation in equity, may, in certain cases, dismiss the petition without prejudice [Form 89]. A dismissal without prejudice is tantamount, to a non-suit at law in that the same facts may be alleged

Some instances in which the court has dismissed a petition for divorce without prejudice may be observed. In adultery cases the petition has been dismissed with a saving clause where the petition alleged adultery with persons unknown and the proofs showed the commission of adultery with a particular person.27 In extreme cruelty cases where the proofs have failed to show sufficient acts to make out a case for the wife, the dismissal of her petition without prejudice to alleging the same acts in the event that the husband continues his abuse may be noted.28 Yet, if the facts are not disproved, but merely are held to be insufficient to establish a cause of action for extreme cruelty, it may be urged that a dismissal without a saving clause does not exclude proof of the same acts of cruelty in conjunction with later acts in a subsequent petition for divorce. A decree of dismissal in a prior suit would adjudicate only that the acts of cruelty then complained of did not make out a case, not that the prior acts plus possible subsequent acts might not, taken together, show extreme cruelty. In a constructive desertion case where the proofs fell short of showing extreme cruelty as justification for leaving, the court dismissed without prejudice.29 And where the petitioner has mistaken his remedy and sued for divorce for desertion instead of for nullity, a dismissal without prejudice to filing a petition for nullity has been entered.¹ Because of collusion 2 or for want of sufficient corroboration, the court may dismiss without prejudice.³

Decree Nisi. If the petitioner succeeds on the hearing of a petition for divorce from the bond of matrimony or for nullity, the first decree is the decree nisi. Section 2:50-29 of the Revision provides: 

2:50-29. If after the hearing of any cause or after a jury trial resulting in a verdict for the petitioner or counterclaimant the court shall be of opinion that the petitioner or counterclaimant is entitled to a decree of nullity of marriage or a decree of annulment of marriage under the general equity jurisdiction of the court or a decree for divorce from the bonds of matrimony, a decree nisi shall be entered. In uncontested cases prepare in duplicate the decree nisi [Forms 52-80; 128-143] before the final hearing so that at the end of the hearing it may be signed at once by the Advisory Master if the decree be for the petitioner. This is the better practice but it is permissible to prepare the decree afterwards and mail it in duplicate to the Advisory Master. The decree nisi should not be dated. 

All decrees nisi are forwarded in duplicate by the Advisory Master to the Clerk who thereupon dates and enters the same and certifies and returns the copy to the solicitor. A stamped, selfaddressed envelope should be provided for the Clerk's return of the certified copy. The decree nisi should be filed as soon as possible, for until the dating and filing of the decree nisi by the Clerk the time for showing cause or for an appeal does not begin to run.

The decree nisi does not terminate the marriage relation and the solicitor should so inform his client lest misunderstanding should occasion a premature re-marriage.17 And, furthermore, the solicitor should caution the client that, until the final decree is signed and entered at the expiration of the three months' period, the marriage still subsists. -Entry Nunc Pro Tunc. Although the parties to a suit for divorce or nullity are still living, it has been held that the decree nisi may not be entered nunc pro tunc, for the reason that such an entry would abridge or abolish the time within which an appeal could be taken, or an objection urged to making it absolute.20

The same has been held as to a nunc pro tunc entry of a decree nisi upon the reversal of a decree of dismissal.21 However, it has been suggested, although not determined, that the decree nisi may be entered nunc pro tunc with a provision that the three months be allowed for showing cause or for an appeal and, if within such three months no steps are taken, that a final decree be entered thereupon nunc pro tunc. Perhaps this method is not authorized by the statute, yet in certain cases involving re-marriage and legitimacy of children, it might be urged.

-Practice on Showing Cause. The practice on showing cause is regulated by Rule 283:

When any person intervenes to show cause why a decree nisi in a suit for divorce or for annulment of marriage should not be made absolute, he shall give notice thereof in writing stating the ground or grounds, to the party holding the decree, or to his solicitor, and shall serve the same, together with affidavits showing cause; and the party holding the decree, in turn, shall serve affidavits in reply upon the intervener, or his solicitor, within ten days after service of the intervener's affidavits; and no affidavits in reply to those of the party holding the decree shall be permitted without express leave of the court. After all affidavits are served the matter shall be brought on for hearing before the Advisory Master who advised the decree, on a regular motion day, upon five days' notice by either party to the other. 

The appropriate forms will be found hereinafter [Forms 81-85].

§ 296. Opening Decree Nisi to Permit Defense. Opening a decree nisi before the time has elapsed for the entry of the final decree in order to allow the defendant to answer is to be distinguished from "showing cause" by the defendant or others why the decree nisi should not be made absolute. Instances in which application has been made to vacate the decree nisi to allow a defense may be noted. Thus in a suit for divorce for adultery against the wife the decree nisi was vacated to permit her to deny the commission of the offense where a solicitor had declined to undertake her defense for lack of money and she was unaware that her husband could be compelled to provide for her defense. The decree nisi was vacated notwithstanding that on the ex parte hearing her adultery was quite abundantly proved. The Vice Chancellor was of the opinion that "a defendant who comes forward and says he desires to defend a case for divorce should be given an opportunity to do so at any moment before the Chancellor's signature is actually affixed to the final decree. The only limitation I can think of would be an apparent lack of good faith on the part of the applicant, which would be the case if it clearly appeared he did not intend to answer even after obtaining the right to do so his attempt being merely for delay prompted by ulterior motive." This may be contrasted with a case where, in a suit for divorce for desertion against the husband, the court refused to vacate the decree nisi to let in a defense.10 -Practice. The application by defendant to open the decree nisi to permit a defense is made to the Advisory Master who advised the decree, by petition in the cause with accompanying affidavits and order to show cause [Forms 81-85]. The court may open a decree nisi taken ex parte, although, since application was made, the three months' period at the end of which the petitioner is ordinarily entitled to a final decree has terminated. The court may vacate the decree nisi only for the purpose of allowing the defendant to answer and, if the defendant is defeated on the merits, then the order vacating the decree nisi may be vacated, leaving

§ 299. 

A collateral attack upon a final decree of divorce is usually made in property suits after the death of one of the spouses for the reason that a direct attack in the cause will not lie. The lack of jurisdiction of the court, rendering the decree void, is the usual ground on which the attack is premised. This want of jurisdiction is usually not unmixed with fraud committed by the spouse obtaining the decree.24 It is doubtful that a spouse who has been guilty of collusion 25 in obtaining a decree of divorce may attack the decree collaterally on that ground in a property suit even after the death of the other spouse, 20 but perhaps this disability should not extend to innocent third persons who will be divested of property rights by the decree, 27 § 300. § 300 

When newly discovered evidence is the ground alleged, the new matter must be of such a character that, if it had been heard, it would probably have altered the decree.20 The court will not open the final decree and allow a re-hearing merely to enable the defendant to impeach the credibility of witnesses who testified in the hearing.21

It is of importance that application to open a final decree of divorce be made immediately upon the discovery of the facts. 

Delay in making application may bar the applicant from obtaining relief under the doctrine of laches. Whether or not the applicant is in laches depends upon the particular circumstances, including the length of time after discovery of the facts, the reasons for the delay, and the detriment suffered by the adverse party, or innocent third persons.22 Ordinarily, delay is not fatal where no new rights have intervened.23 The re-marriage of a party, and particularly the birth of children, may move the court to refuse to open a decree, especially where the applicant has failed to move promptly upon the discovery of the facts," but re-marriage does not necessarily bar an opening of the decree,25 especially when the party re-marries after having received notice that the decree was under attack.26

Where the final decree is entered during the lifetime of the parties, it may not be questioned by any proceeding in the cause after the death of one of the parties, but where property rights are involved, a collateral attack has been recognized as the proper method if sufficient grounds exist for contesting the validity of the divorce decree. Yet, where a final decree of divorce was inadvertently entered after the death of the petitioner, the decree was vacated on petition in the cause.28

§ 301. 

Amendment of Decree. A discussion of the amendment of decrees in Chancery in non-matrimonial cases may be found elsewhere.2 In divorce litigation the amendment of decrees may be observed, as where the court has allowed an amendment of a decree of divorce to insert a provision for permanent alimony inadvertently omitted. However, no longer is an amendment of the decree necessary to provide for permanent alimony. 

Under the present statute the jurisdiction of the court continues so that alimony may be fixed even after final decree on petition in the cause.*

A decree of dismissal may be amended by the striking of a recital. The right of the solicitor to make application for himself to amend the decree as respects counsel fee has been upheld. The application to amend the decree is by petition and notice and under Rule 135 should be made to the Advisory Master who advised the decree.

§ 379 

 § 304. Appeal. Appeals from orders and decrees in matri monial proceedings differ but little from appeals from other causes heard in the Court of Chancery. Consequently, no attempt will be made to embrace the entire appellate practice. For a detailed treatment of the practice on appeal the reader should refer to several excellent textbooks devoted exclusively to the practice in the Court of Chancery.27 Appropriate forms for appeals in divorce litigation will be found hereinafter [Forms 455-468]. 

In matrimonial proceedings, contested and uncontested, the time within which an appeal must be taken is regulated by the practice in other causes in Chancery except where the statute relating to divorce otherwise prescribes.28 When a petitioner or counterclaimant is successful in a suit for divorce or nullity of marriage, the first decree is the decree nisi. Section 2:50-31 of the Revision expressly provides that an appeal should be taken from the decree nisi and not from the final decree, and shall be taken within three months from the filing of the decree nisi.29 An appeal after such time is too late, at least where the decree nisi has been made absolute.¹ It would seem that for the purpose of appeal the court may suspend the running of the decree nisi period pending the determination of an application to show cause against making the decree nisi absolute. Formerly the time within which to appeal from a decree nisi in suits for divorce or nullity under the statute was six months, and until the enactment of the Revision there had been a six months' provision in suits for nullity instituted under the general equity jurisdiction of the court for fraud, etc.³ 2 The statute relating to divorce makes no other provisions relative to the time of appeal and hence the statute regulating appeals from Chancery governs in other situations.* From an interlocutory order an appeal must now be taken within thirty days from the filing of the order. From a decree dismissing a petition for divorce, for nullity or for separate maintenance the appeal
