must now be taken within three months. An appeal from an order contained in the decree nisi, as an order for permanent alimony, or for the custody of children, must now also be taken within three months. Upon the expiration of the time for appeal the rights of the successful party become vested. The Chancery Act at one time provided that, in appeals from final decrees, the Chancellor might in his discretion, by order made not more than six months after the time hereinbefore limited for taking an appeal, extend the time for appeal for a period not exceeding six months from the expiration of the time so limited. So far as this provision applied retroactively so as to revive the right of appeal, it was declared unconstitutional. Furthermore, the provision was construed to require the making of the order before the time for appeal had expired. The amendment to the Chancery Act as found in section 2:29-119 of the Revision, provides that "in all cases where final decree has been or may be filed, after June second, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-seven, the chancellor may, in his discretion, by order made not more than thirty days after the time herein above limited for taking an appeal, extend the time of the appellant for taking his appeal for a period not exceeding thirty days from the expiration of the time so limited." 

While this provision may apply to final decrees of dismissal in divorce litigation, it would seem to be inapplicable to decrees nisi so far as respects the dissolution of the marriage. The statute relating to divorce would seem to be exclusive in regulating the time of appeal. However, section 2:29-119 may apply to orders contained in, but not a part of, the decree nisi, as orders for permanent alimony and for custody of children.

As in other cases on appeal from the Court of Chancery, the duty of the Court of Errors and Appeals on appeal from a decree in a matrimonial proceeding is to inquire whether there is any error in the decree appealed from and not whether the reasons given for the conclusions reached below are tenable. Great weight is given to the finding on a question of fact.10 The question of credibility of the witnesses pre-eminently is one for the

Advisory Master to decide. Nevertheless, the appellate court is not foreclosed by conclusions reached below respecting the credibility of the witnesses.12 The judgment of the Advisory 

Master on fact questions is to be reviewed by the same standards as the verdict of a jury. The question before the appellate court is not whether that court would have arrived at the same conclusion upon the evidence, but whether the judgment of the Advisory Master is sustainable on any reasonable basis. 

On appeal from a decree dismissing a petition for divorce, the appellate court on motion will not dismiss the appeal on the ground that after the entry of the decree of dismissal the parties became reconciled, for, if the decree of dismissal is affirmed, the matter is disposed of in favor of the respondent and, if reversed, the respondent may obtain relief in the Court of Chancery.13 

§ 305. Maiden Name. 

amended in 1938, provides:

Section 2:50-34 of the Revision, as 

2:50-34. The court, upon or after granting a divorce from the bonds of matrimony to either spouse, may allow the wife to resume any name used by her before the marriage; and may also order the wife to refrain from using the surname of the husband as her name.

The Divorce Act of 1907 authorized the court upon or after granting a divorce from the bond of matrimony to allow the wife to resume her maiden name or the name of a former deceased husband.14 However in the Revision, before the 1938 amendment, the court upon or after granting a wife a divorce from the bond of matrimony could allow her to resume her maiden name or the name of a former deceased husband.¹ But under the 1938 amendment the court, upon or after granting an absolute divorce to either spouse, may allow the wife to resume any name used before the marriage, and furthermore may order the wife to refrain from using the husband's surname. 15 This matter is discretionary with the court. If the petitioning wife desires to resume her maiden name, or former name, it is

customary to include in her petition for divorce a paragraph setting out her maiden name, or her former name, and to pray that she may be allowed to resume her maiden or former name [Form 15]. If the court grants permission to the wife to resume such name, there must be incorporated in the decree nisi a provision reserving the privilege as is shown in Form 73. The inclusion of this reservation in the decree nisi leads automatically to the inclusion in the final decree prepared by the Clerk of a provision that the petitioner is free to resume the use of her maiden or former name 

[Form 88]. 

If there are infant children of the marriage in the wife's custody, her application for leave to resume her former name will not ordinarily be granted unless good reasons should appear. But where there are no children, her application is granted as a matter of course.

The statute now permits the court to make an order in favor of the petitioning husband that from and after the entry of the final decree the wife shall desist from the use of his surname. 

Similarly, on application by the defendant wife the court may permit her to use her former name.¹ In either case there should be a reservation in the decree nisi [Form 74]. 16 If the decree nisi contains no provision reserving the privilege of the petitioning wife to resume her maiden or former name, she must file a petition in the cause requesting that she be permitted to resume such name and the reasons why she desires to resume her former name [Form 97]. This petition may be filed before or after final decree and should be filed with the Advisory Master who heard the case. If permission is granted, an order is entered [Form 98]. 

Under the 1938 statute the petitioning husband may also make application after the entry of the decree nisi or final decree that the wife be ordered to resume her maiden name [Forms 99-101].

Likewise, the court has the authority to entertain the application of the defendant wife after decree nisi or final decree.17 

§ 306. Office of Designated Advisory Master in Trenton. 

A few observations respecting the office of the Advisory Master in Trenton seem appropriate in treating of the practice in divorce and nullity suits. The present encumbent is Advisory Master 

16. Under the Divorce Act of 1907 this was also permitted, see McCarter v. McCarter, Dk 105-381. 

17. This was permitted also under the Divorce Act of 1907, McCarter v. 

McCarter, Dk 105-381.

§ 383 

Norman T. Rogers whose office presently is Room 349 in the

State House Annex. 

The Advisory Master acts somewhat in the role of the English Master of the Rolls in certain matters, including matrimonial causes. In 1933 he was designated by the Chancellor to attend to particular matters in the Trenton office quite aside and distinct from his designation under Rule 131 (now Rule 129).

In matrimonial causes he has been designated to advise the Chancellor in matters coming under present Rules 117, 128e and the various rules relating to divorce litigation. In matrimonial causes he determines: (1) whether the petition or bill sets out a cause of action and, in form, complies with the rules. In divorce and nullity suits he inspects the petition and counterclaim in order to ascertain whether or not Rules 274 and 280, respecting the affidavit of non-collusion, have been complied with, and Rule 275, respecting the addresses of the litigants in the petition; (2) whether the statute and Rules (276, 277) respecting service of process have been met; (3) to which of the Advisory Masters the case is to be referred when it is ready for reference. 

The Clerk, rather than the designated Trenton Advisory Master, attends to the filing and certification of papers, issuance of citations, the collecting of fees and drafting of final decrees. On application the Clerk's office will draft orders of reference and decrees nisi, but it is the better practice for the solicitor to do so.

 -Master Taking Testimony Out of State In Ex Parte Case. 

Section 2:50-27 of the Revision provides in part: 

2:50-27. When the defendant has not entered an appearance or made defense to the petition and the cause has been referred to a master, the chancellor may, upon application of the petitioner and on good cause shown, order such master to take ex parte and without notice the testimony of any witness named in the order in another state or territory, use such deposition and return the same with his report. 

This provision was enacted in the year 1902.22 The practice has become obsolete since matrimonial causes have come to be heard before Advisory Masters. 

-Testimony of Witnesses In State De Bene Esse. The stat utes relative to the taking of testimony of witnesses within the state are of general application in suits and actions of a civil nature, and are not peculiar to matrimonial causes. They are here noted for the convenience of the practitioner. The forms are included hereinafter [Forms 307-312].

WHEN AUTHORIZED; OFFICER Before Whom TAKEN 

2:100-10. If any material witness in an action or suit of a civil nature, or any material witness for any defendant in any indictment pending in any of the courts of this state, be in this state, but is aged, very infirm, or sick, or is about to go out of this state, the deposition of such witness may, at the option of either party, in such civil suit, or at the option of the defendant in such indictment, be taken de bene esse before any justice of the supreme court, or judge of the court of common pleas, or supreme court commissioner, or master in chancery.

NOTICE TO ADVERSE PARTY 

2:100-11. The officer before whom a deposition is to be taken under authority of section 2:100-10 of this title shall cause notice to be given to the adverse party immediately, or at such short day as the case in the opinion of such officer may require, to attend and be present at the taking thereof, and to put questions and cross-examine, if he shall think fit. 

22. L. 1902 p. 447; C. S. 1910 p. 2236.

When plaintiff, complainant or petitioner has become entitled to proceed ex parte, the notice required by this section need not be given.

COMPELLING ATTENDANCE; COMPENSATION 

2:100-12. Any material witness described in section 

2:100-10 of this title, being in this state, may be compelled to appear and be examined before any of the officers mentioned in said section 2:100-10, in the same manner and under the same penalties as if subpoenaed to appear and testify in the court wherein the action or indictment is pending. Any such witness shall be allowed compensation for his time and attendance at the same rate as if he had personally appeared and given testimony in the cause before the court in which it is pending.

SWEARING OF DEPONENT AND SUBSCRIPTION TO TESTIMONY 

2:100-13. Every person deposing as provided by section 

2:100-10 of this title shall be sworn to testify the whole truth and shall subscribe the testimony given by him, after the same shall be reduced to writing, which shall be done only by the officer taking the deposition, or by the deponent in his presence.

TRANSMISSION OF DEPOSITION TO COURT 

2:100-14. A deposition taken under authority of this article shall, when so taken, be retained by the officer taking the same until he shall deliver it, together with a certificate of the reasons of its being taken, and of the notice, if any was given, to the adverse party, with his own hand to a judge or the clerk of the court for which it is taken, or any such deposition may, by the officer taking it, be sealed up, directed and transmitted, either by mail or private messenger, to such judge or clerk, who shall open and immediately file the same, in the office of such clerk, there to remain as of record.

OATH OF MESSENGER DELIVERING DEPOSITION

-Testimony of Non-Resident Witnesses by Commission. 

The statutes regulating the taking of testimony of witnesses residing out of the state are of general application in any action or proceeding of a civil nature, or in any criminal proceeding where the defendant under indictment seeks the testimony of such witnesses. The statutes are reproduced here for convenience. The forms will be found included hereinafter [Forms 313-318]. 

WHEN COMMISSION AUTHORIZED 

2:100-16. If a material witness in any action or proceeding of a civil nature, or a material witness for any defendant in any indictment pending in any of the courts of this state reside out of this state, the court in which such action or proceeding or indictment is pending, or any judge thereof, in term or vacation, on affidavit or proof thereof to the satisfaction of such court or judge, and on such terms as the court or judge may direct, may award and issue, under the seal of the court, a commission to such person or persons, as the court or judge may think fit, authorizing such person or persons, or any two or more of such persons, to examine de bene esse such witness on oath.

NOTICE OF APPLICATION, ETC. 

2:100-17. A party intending to apply for a commission to examine any witness pursuant to section 2:100-16 of this title shall give eight days' notice of such application, and of the names of the witnesses to be examined, and of the place of their residence, and also of the name or names of the person or persons whom the party applying intends to nominate as commissioner or commissioners, and shall serve therewith a copy of the interrogatories intended to be annexed to such commission, in order that the adverse party may examine the same and submit cross-interrogatories if he think proper. The notice required by this section shall be served on the attorney or solicitor, when the party appears by attorney or solicitor. If, however, the defendant or respondent has defaulted in pleading, and the plaintiff, complainant or

§ 307  

petitioner has become entitled to proceed ex parte, the notice required by this section need not be given. 

2:100-18. The issuing of the commission may be ordered and the interrogatories may be approved upon shorter notice than is directed by section 2:100-17 of this title, by consent of parties, or upon matter being made to appear to the said court or judge to excuse the want of full notice, and that shorter notice is necessary to prevent delay. 

NAMES OF WITNESSES IN COMMISSION; 

INTERROGATORIES AND APPROVAL OF 

2:100-19. 

The name of every witness to be, examined by virtue of a commission issued pursuant to section 2:100-16 of this title shall be inserted in such commission. The interrogatories for the examination of such witness shall be drawn and signed by the parties or their attorneys or counsel in the cause in which the testimony is to be used, or such of them as shall request such commission, and be approved of by the court or one of the judges thereof, and shall be annexed to the commission. Each party shall be at liberty, with the approbation of the court or judge, to insert in the interrogatories such questions as he may think proper or necessary.

COMMISSIONERS' OATH 

2:100-20. The commissioner or commissioners appointed under this article, or under the general power or authority of the court of chancery, or such of them as shall act, shall, before they enter upon their duties, take an oath faithfully, fairly and impartially to execute the commission, which oath may be taken before any person lawfully authorized to administer an oath in the state or country, where such commissioner or commissioners reside or may be at the time.

-Testimony of Non-Resident Witness De Bene Esse. 

statutes regulating the taking of testimony de bene esse of nonresident witnesses are reproduced for convenience. [Form 319.] 

BEFORE WHOM TAKEN 

2:100-26. Any party in a civil cause or any defendant in any indictment desiring the testimony of any witness who resides out of this state may, instead of taking his testimony by commission, take the testimony of such witness de bene esse before any judge of any supreme, circuit or district court, or court of common pleas, of the state or country where such witness is, or before any commissioner of deeds appointed by the governor of this state, resident in the state or country where such witness is, or before a commissioner specially appointed for that purpose by the court in which such action is pending, or any judge thereof, or before a master in chancery of this state.

§ 391 

 NOTICE TO ADVERSE PARTY 

2:100-27. Notice in writing of the time and place of an examination pursuant to section 2:100-26 of this title and of the names of the witnesses to be examined shall be given to the adverse party, his attorney or solicitor, that he may be present and put interrogatories if he shall see fit, which notice shall be served, allowing time for attendance after service not less than at the rate of one day, exclusive of Sundays, for every fifty miles of travel. In all cases at least ten days' notice, exclusive of Sundays, shall be given; and in cases where such testimony is desired to be taken of witnesses residing in any foreign country, or in any state of the United States, situate west of the Mississippi river, so many days' notice shall be given as shall be directed by the court in which the cause shall be pending, or any judge thereof, at chambers.

OATH OF OFFICER AND WITNESS; SUBSCRIPTION BY WITNESS 

2:100-28. The officer taking testimony under authority of section 2:100-26 of this title shall first take an oath fairly and impartially to take the same, before some person authorized to administer an oath in the place where he shall reside. 

The testimony of such witness shall be taken on oath, administered according to the law of this state, upon interrogatories to be then and there put by the parties, or any of them, or any person authorized in their behalf, and such interrogatories and the answers thereto shall be reduced to writing by the officer taking such testimony, and shall be subscribed in his presence by the deponent. 

TRANSMISSION OF TESTIMONY 

2:100-29. The testimony, when taken, reduced to writing and subscribed as provided by section 2:100-28 of this title, shall thereupon be certified, sealed up, indorsed, directed and forwarded, as is required in case of depositions taken under section 2:100-16 of this title, or if the testimony of such witness be taken before a master in chancery, such testimony may be certified and delivered by the master taking the same to the clerk of the court in which such action is pending, or to any judge thereof.

§ 307 

 TESTIMONY MAY BE TAKEN STENOGRAPHICALLY; 

OATH OF STENOGRAPHER 

2:100-30. In all cases where the testimony of a witness de bene esse is taken upon notice, pursuant to the provisions of this article, such testimony may be taken stenographically by or in the presence of the judge, commissioner or other officer named in the notice. Before the taking of the testimony the stenographer, if other than the judge, commissioner or other officer named in the notice, shall be sworn by the judge, commissioner or other officer designated in the notice to carefully, faithfully and impartially take the evidence and to make a true and correct transcript thereof, which oath shall be in writing, and shall be attached to and be a part of the return of the judge, commissioner or other officer named in the notice. 

-Taking of Testimony of Witnesses by Consent. The stat ute provides for the taking of testimony of witnesses de bene esee by consent in any civil action.

STIPULATION TO TAKE 

2:100-31. The attorneys or solicitors of record in any civil action may stipulate in writing to take de bene esse, without order of the court in which such action is pending, the testimony of any witness in such action, whether such witness reside or be within or without this state. 

MATTERS TO BE STATED IN STIPULATION 

2:100-32. The stipulation mentioned in section 2:100-31 of this title shall state the name and residence of the witness whose testimony is to be so taken, the time when and the place where and the officer before whom such testimony is to be taken, and whether such testimony may be taken stenographically. The stipulation may designate as the officer before whom such testimony shall be taken, any officer whom it would have been lawful for the court to designate for the purpose in a commission duly issued by the court on application therefor made as provided by this chapter to take de bene esse the testimony of such witness. 

If it is stipulated to take such testimony stenographically, the name of the stenographer may be designated in the stipu-

§ 393 

lation, or, if not so designated, he shall be designated by the officer before whom the deposition is to be taken. 

The stipulation shall be filed with the clerk of the court in which the action is pending before the testimony is taken. 

TRANSCRIPTS TO EACH PARTY; FILING 

2:100-33. The stenographer designated pursuant to section 

2:100-32 of this title shall make two transcripts of the testimony which shall be subscribed and sworn to before the officer designated to take the testimony. One transcript so subscribed and sworn to shall be delivered to each party.

Either party may file the transcript with the clerk of the court in which the action is pending.

UPON FILING, TESTIMONY MAY BE USED AS EVIDENCE 

2:100-34. When the deposition of a witness has been taken and the transcript filed as provided by this article, either party may use the testimony so taken on the trial of the action in the same manner, and with the same force and effect as if such testimony had been taken under a commission duly issued by the court on application therefor made as provided by this chapter to take de bene esse the testimony of such witness. -Letters Rogatory. This subject is not confined to matrimonial litigation. The general text-books should also be consulted.23 24 A commission to take the depositions of non-resident witnesses de bene esse under the statute is a substitute for letters rogatory.2 

Letters rogatory are seldom used today except where it is impossible to execute a commission in the foreign jurisdiction as is the case in Germany at present, or where the commission is inadequate. If it becomes necessary to resort to the letters rogatory, the reader may obtain information concerning their execution in a particular country by referring to the law digest of the country in Martindale-Hubbell Law Directory under the heading of "Depositions." Inquiry of the consular office in New York City of the particular country for rules and regulations is also recommended.

Constitutional and Statutory Provisions. 

The recognition of foreign decrees of divorce and of nullity of marriage is now governed essentially by statute. Prior to the enactment of section 33 of the Divorce Act of 1907, New Jersey, in common with other civilized jurisdictions, extended recognition to decrees of divorce and of nullity of marriage of other states and countries under the rules of interstate and international comity, except, in the case of decrees of sister states, where extraterritorial recognition was obligatory under the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution. Except as to decrees rendered by a court of a foreign country, the rules of comity were superseded in 1907 394

§ 395 

by the provisions of section 33,¹ although thereafter the cases are not without applications of the former rules of comity. Section 

33 of the Divorce Act of 1907 became section 2:50-35 in the 

Revision and provides: 

2:50-35. Full faith and credit shall be given in all courts of this state to a decree of annulment of marriage or divorce by a court of competent jurisdiction in another state of the United States when the jurisdiction of such court was obtained in the manner and in substantial conformity with the conditions prescribed in sections 2:50-9, 2:50-10 and 2:50-11 of this title. Nothing herein contained shall be construed to limit the power of any court to give such effect to a decree of annulment or divorce by a court of a foreign country as may be justified by the rules of international comity; provided, that if any inhabitant of this state shall go into another state or country, in order to obtain a decree of divorce for a cause which occurred while the parties resided in this state, or for a cause which is not ground for divorce under the laws of this state, a decree so obtained shall be of no force or effect in this state.2

The Revision makes no substantial change in section 33 of the 

Divorce Act of 1907. The words "territory" and "possession" have been dropped, but these terms are now embraced within the word "state" by reason of the Revision, section 1:1-2. Section 33 

of the Divorce Act of 1907 was derived from the Uniform Divorce Act which was recommended to the various states for adoption by the National Congress on Uniform Divorce Laws. 

adopted by the States of Delaware and Wisconsin as well as by New Jersey. The section is probably inapplicable to foreign decrees of divorce and of nullity of marriage rendered prior to January 1, 1908. It is substantially a copy of a prior Massachusetts statute, which was declared constitutional by the United States Supreme Court in a case in which an inhabitant of Massachusetts, while retaining his domicile in that state, left the jurisdiction in order to obtain a foreign decree of divorce."

Section 2:50-35 is of course subordinate to, and will yield to the 

Federal Constitution when the two conflict. However, this section compels recognition of decrees of divorce of sister states to a greater extent than does the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution, so that instances will rarely arise in which the federal mandate will compel recognition and the local statute will not. But the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution and a few of the effects of the clause may be noticed. 

The Federal Constitution provides: 

Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State. And the Congress may by general Laws prescribe the 

Manner in which such Acts, Records and Proceedings shall be proved, and the Effect thereof." 

Pursuant to this provision Congress enacted:

That the acts of the legislature of the several States shall be authenticated by having the seal of their respective States affixed thereto; that the records and judicial proceedings of the courts of any State shall be proved or admitted in any court within the United States by the attestation of the clerk, and the seal of the court annexed, if there be a seal, together with a certificate of the judge, chief justice, or presiding magistrate, as the case may be, that the said attestation is in due form. And the said records and judicial proceedings authenticated as aforesaid shall have such faith and credit given to them in every court within the United States, as they have by law or usage in the courts of the State from whence the said records are or shall be taken.Ⓡ 

When the federal full faith and credit clause becomes operative, the effect is to compel New Jersey to give to a decree of divorce or of nullity of a sister state the same force and effect in New Jersey as it has in the state where rendered. If the parties are no longer man and wife by virtue of a decree of divorce or of nullity of a sister state, and the decree has been obtained in such manner as to be entitled to full faith and credit in New Jersey, this state may not regard the parties as divorced in the sister

On the other hand, inasmuch as each state has the right to regulate the dissolution of the marriage contract so far as such contract affects its own citizens,10 a decree of divorce or of nullity of marriage may be valid in New Jersey notwithstanding that in other states it is not entitled to recognition under the federal full faith and credit clause.¹¹ This rule is contrary to that existing in actions strictly in personam.12 The full faith and credit clause of the Federal 

Constitution does not extend to decrees of divorce and of nullity of foreign countries which are not subject to the jurisdiction of the United States.13

Law Governing Recognition of Foreign Decrees.¹4 

Let us assume that a spouse obtains a foreign decree of divorce at a time when neither of the parties was domiciled in New Jersey. Such a decree may be attacked in this state collaterally at least, and in such case the question arises, by what law shall the validity of the decree be tested. Suppose, for instance, a decree, which is not embraced within the constitutional mandate of the Federal Constitution, is entitled to recognition in the state of the domicile of the defendant in the foreign suit but does not command full faith and credit under the New Jersey statute.

defendant's first husband had obtained a Nevada divorce rendered against his wife on publication while she was domiciled in another state. Nevada was not the matrimonial domicile of the parties and because the divorce was decreed without personal jurisdiction it would have been invalid in New York had the defendant been domiciled in New York. Neither the defendant nor her first husband ever had been domiciled in New York. The Court of Appeals held that the law of the defendant's domicile governed. The court observed: "Whether it (the second marriage) is invalid depends upon the status of the defendant when it occurred. If the state of which she was then a citizen recognizes such a decree as that obtained in Nevada, and gives it full force and effect, then it is not for us to say that it is void as to her. It is for that state to determine what its policy requires. It is the final judge as to how far, as to its own citizens, the principles of comity shall be applied. If the defendant is freed of all the obligations of the Missouri marriage in the state of her domicil, she is freed everywhere."15

In New Jersey the question under consideration does not appear to have been expressly adjudicated in any reported case. In the few cases in which it appeared that neither of the parties was domiciled in New Jersey at the time of the entry of the foreign decree, the foreign decree was invalid in the state of the defendant's domicile as well as in New Jersey, but it is apparent from the cases that the court has applied the New Jersey law and the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution.16 It may be questioned whether the comprehensive language of the first part of the section 2:50-35 of the Revision is not a direction that the law of New Jersey is to govern although the domicile of the parties and the matrimonial domicile was elsewhere at the time of the entry of the foreign decree. Domiciliary Requirements.27 In order to attack a foreign decree of divorce collaterally in the Court of Chancery it is not essential that New Jersey was the domicile at the time of the separation of the parties, or at the time of the entry of the foreign decree, or that either of the parties was domiciled in New Jersey at the time of the entry of the foreign decree although it is sought to impeach the decree for fraud of the complainant in inducing the foreign court to find the jurisdictional fact of domicile. § 313. Estoppel and Laches. The authorities in the va rious states are not, perhaps, wholly in accord as to whether party who obtains a foreign decree of divorce, or who consents to the entry of the decree, may contest its validity. In many states the party is estopped to impeach the foreign decree, although it is absolutely void for lack of jurisdiction of the court rendering the decree. In a recent case in Rhode Island a wife in her suit for divorce from bed and board was estopped to set up a Nevada decree, apparently void, procured by her on a counterclaim to the husband's suit for divorce." The decision of a state court that a party is estopped to contest the validity of a decree of divorce is a matter of local law and presents no federal question.Ⓡ With us it has not been altogether uncommon for the courts to import into the sui generis divorce and nullity suits maxims and rules commonly applied in equity suits. In domestic suits for divorce and nullity of marriage the courts in several instances have had recourse to rules generally applicable to suits in equity. 

Equitable defenses to some extent at least have been applied.º 

In some cases the doctrines of laches 10 and unclean hands have been applied to bar relief.¹¹

With respect to foreign decrees of divorce it may be well to review our cases briefly. In Kirrigan v. Kirrigan, to an applica-

§ 314. 

The courts of this state are not obligated under the rules of comity or under the statute to recognize a foreign decree of divorce or of nullity in cases where the court of the foreign state or country was without jurisdiction. Before our courts are compelled to give full faith and credit to such decrees the court of the foreign state must have had the authority, as a court, to divorce the parties; 1º it must have had control of the marital status, the subject matter

The full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution does not prevent the courts of this state from questioning the jurisdiction of a court of a sister state in granting a decree of divorce or of nullity. The provisions of that clause preclude the reexamination of the cause on the merits, but they do not affect the jurisdiction of the court rendering the decree or of the court in which the decree is offered.22 

§ 315. Presumption of Jurisdiction of Foreign Court. 

When a foreign decree of divorce is assailed, the presumption is that the foreign tribunal had jurisdiction of the subject matter and of the parties unless jurisdictional defects appear on the face of the record. The presumption is of course rebuttable. If the foreign decree is attacked upon the ground of fraud in the jurisdiction, 23 the fraud will not be presumed, but must be established by clear and convincing evidence.24 § 316. 

-Res Judicata of Jurisdictional Fact.25 Suppose that a decree of divorce rendered by the court of a sister state is attacked in a second state for want of jurisdiction of the subject matter or of the person and by a court of competent jurisdiction in the second state is adjudged valid in a proceeding of which the court has jurisdiction. The rule of res judicata in such circumstances would scarcely harmonize with the public policy of the state as expressed by the legislature in the statute.27 

§ 317. 

-Domicile in Foreign Jurisdiction. Prior to the passage of section 33 of the Divorce Act of 1907 the judicially declared policy of the State of New Jersey was to recognize foreign decrees of divorce on the ground of comity where the complainant had been domiciled in the foreign state or country in which the divorce was decreed, notwithstanding that the defendant had not resided in such foreign state or country and had not been served with process therein, provided that a substituted service had been made in accordance with the statutory provisions of such foreign state or country and that actual notice of the pendency of the suit had been given to the defendant and a reasonable opportunity afforded to defend, and that the ground upon which the foreign decree rested was one which the public policy of this

Fairchild that an adjudication by a foreign tribunal that the complainant had been domiciled in the foreign jurisdiction was final unless it is made to appear that such tribunal was induced to find the jurisdictional fact of domicile by fraud practiced upon it by the complainant.29 On the other hand, decrees of foreign states and countries were refused full faith and credit under the rules of comity where the court of the foreign state or country was without jurisdiction of the marital status. In instances where decrees of divorce and of nullity of foreign states and countries were refused recognition the element of fraud of the complainant in inducing the foreign tribunal to find the jurisdictional fact of domicile was stressed,¹ but certainly the foreign decree was void although the foreign court was in full possession of all the facts and had not been misled on the jurisdictional inquiry of domicile.2

At the present time full faith and credit is extended to foreign decrees of divorce under the statute. Under the statute the courts of this state are not obligated to extend recognition to foreign decrees of divorce in cases where neither of the parties was domiciled in the foreign state or country, although the defendant was served personally with process within the foreign jurisdiction or appeared in the suit. As before the passage of section 33 of the 

Divorce Act of 1907 the courts, in refusing to recognize foreign decrees of divorce, have consistently stressed the element of fraud, consisting in the circumstance that the complainant fraudulently induced the foreign court to find the jurisdictional fact by simulating a domicile in the foreign jurisdiction." -Decrees A Mensa. A decree of divorce from bed and board, the ecclesiastical decree a mensa et thoro, does not dissolve the marital status, but affects merely the obligation of the parties to live together.¹¹ In England at the present time a suit for divorce from bed and board may be maintained if the parties are living there. Domicile is not necessary.12 14 With us the domicile of the parties is a residential requirement under the statute in domestic suits for divorce from bed and board.18 Consequently under the statute relating to foreign decrees a decree of separation of a sister state is not entitled to recognition where neither of the parties had been domiciled in the state in which the decree was granted.15 Nor under the rules of international comity, which govern the recognition of decrees of foreign countries, is it likely that a decree a mensa of a foreign country will merit recognition where neither of the parties had been domiciled in the foreign jurisdiction.

A decree of separation of a sister state rendered against an absent defendant upon constructive service of process does not command obligatory recognition under the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution where it has not been decreed at the matrimonial domicile 16 of the parties.17 Indeed, in some states a decree of separation rendered upon constructive service of process against an absent defendant in a state which is not the matrimonial domicile will not be recognized as a matter of comity.18 It remains to be decided by the United States Supreme 

Court whether a decree of divorce from bed and board of a sister state rendered upon personal jurisdiction of the defendant by a court of a state in which neither of the parties had been domiciled is entitled to obligatory recognition under the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution. It is not improbable that the court will regard a suit for divorce from bed and board as one affecting to some extent the marital status and that a decree of a state based on mere residence coupled with personal

In view of the rule requiring the domicile of the party in domestic suits for nullity of marriage for statutory causes 19 a decree of nullity of marriage of a sister state, territory or possession of the United States does not command recognition under section 2:50-35 where neither of the parties had been domiciled in the foreign jurisdiction at the time of the commencement of the suit. While it may be that the substantial conformity provision of section 2:50-35 of the Revision is inapplicable to foreign decrees of nullity based upon fraud or duress because that section relates to section 2:50-9 of the Revision which does not comprehend suits for nullity under the general equity jurisdiction for fraud and duress, nevertheless our Court of Chancery has required that the domicile of at least one of the parties be in this state as a jurisdictional prerequisite in such suits.20 It is therefore probable that, although section 2:50-35 of the Revision may be inoperative, our courts will decline under the rules of comity to recognize decrees of nullity granted by the courts of sister states, territories and possessions for fraud or duress where neither of the parties had been domiciled in the foreign jurisdiction at the time of the commencement of the suit.

In some states and countries the courts will render a decree of nullity of marriage if the marriage was performed there.21 Such a decree would not be recognized by our courts under section 2:50-35 or under the rules of international comity unless the place of marriage coincided with the domicile of at least one of the parties at the time of the commencement of the suit. 

The question as to when a state court has such jurisdiction of a suit for nullity as to entitle its decree to obligatory recognition under the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution has not yet confronted the United States Supreme Court. It would seem, however, that the court will require nothing short of the petitioner's domicile and personal service of process on the defendant within the state or his appearance, or, where the defendant is absent and is served constructively, that the decree must have been rendered at the matrimonial domicile of the parties.22

-Matrimonial Domicile. The matrimonial domicile, in the sense here used, is the place where the parties last lived together as husband and wife. The importance of matrimonial domicile lies in the federal cases and there are some states, notably New York,23 in which the courts will go no further than they are obliged to go under the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution in recognizing decrees of sister states rendered upon publication and substituted service of process. In Atherton v. 

Atherton the wife abandoned her husband in Kentucky, which was the matrimonial domicile and the domicile of the husband.

While so domiciled, the husband obtained a decree of absolute divorce in Kentucky based on constructive service of process upon the wife living in New York. The Supreme Court held that the 

Kentucky decree was entitled to obligatory recognition in New York.24 In Haddock v. Haddock the husband abandoned his wife in New York, which was the matrimonial domicile and which remained by reason of the husband's desertion the domicile of the wife, and acquired a domicile in Connecticut. A decree of absolute divorce rendered by a Connecticut court on constructive service of process upon the wife was held not entitled to obligatory recognition under the full faith and credit clause of the 

Federal Constitution.25

Suppose the wife obtains a decree of divorce at the matrimonial domicile based upon constructive service of process upon a nonresident husband.26 Or let us assume a wife unjustifiably refuses to accompany her husband to a new domicile. Is a decree of divorce obtained by the husband upon constructive service of process in the new domicile entitled to obligatory recognition under the Federal Constitution? With us the situs of the matrimonial domicile is unimportant as the basis for jurisdiction of our court in suits for divorce and nullity of marriage.28 As respects recognition of foreign decrees of divorce and of nullity of marriage, the situs of the matrimonial domicile was quite immaterial under the rules of interstate and international comity governing the recognition of such decrees prior to the enactment of section 33 of the Divorce Act of 1907, although the defendant was served by publication and substituted service of process. The domicile of the petitioner in the foreign jurisdiction was sufficient so long as proper notice of the pendency of the suit was served upon the absent defendant. With respect to the situs of the matrimonial domicile, section 33 of the Divorce Act made no change in the law existing prior to 1907. Under section 33 the courts of this state extended recognition to decrees of divorce and of nullity of sister states, territories and possessions rendered upon service by publication and substituted service of process without regard to the situs of the matrimonial domicile of the parties so long as jurisdiction had been acquired in the manner and in substantial conformity with the conditions prescribed in sections 5, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 14 of the Divorce Act and with the conditions prescribed in Chancery Rules 257, 258.  § 319. —Residence in Foreign State for Divorce. Prior to the passage of section 33 of the Divorce Act of 1907 a foreign decree of divorce was not invalid merely because the petitioner's residence in the foreign jurisdiction had been acquired for the purpose of obtaining a divorce. Such purpose affected merely the character of the petitioner's residence in the foreign jurisdiction. Presumably such residence was temporary and lacked the animus manendi¹ essential to effect a change of domicile." 

The proviso of section 2:50-35 of the Revision expressly pro vides for the case of an inhabitant of New Jersey who goes into another state, territory or country in order to obtain a decree of divorce for a cause which occurred while the parties resided here or for a cause which is not ground for divorce in this state. This proviso will receive consideration in the next section. The proviso does not apply to an inhabitant of another state who went into a second state and there obtained a decree of divorce. Such decrees come before our courts occasionally and it may be inquired whether the law of New Jersey applies. In order for our courts to ascertain whether the petitioner became domiciled in the foreign state or country his purpose in going into the foreign jurisdiction is material. In one case the presumption that the petitioner had not acquired a bona fide residence (domicile) in the foreign jurisdiction was held to govern on a motion to strike where it appeared from the bill for maintenance that an inhabitant of New York left that state for the purpose of obtaining a Mexican decree of divorce. Later he became domiciled in New 

Jersey and the suit for separate maintenance was instituted." 

In another case on a motion to strike out a petition for divorce and to set aside the service of the citation it appeared that the husband left the state of New York, the matrimonial domicile, and procured a Nevada decree of divorce. Almost immediately thereafter he removed to New Jersey. The petitioner admitted on the motion that he went to Nevada in order to procure a divorce, but contended that this court had no jurisdiction to declare the Nevada decree invalid. His application to strike out the petition and to set aside the service of the citation was denied."

-Inhabitant Leaving State for Divorce. Section 33 

of the Divorce Act of 1907 contained a proviso which in effect declared that a foreign decree of divorce shall be of no effect in this state if obtained by an inhabitant of this state who goes into another state, territory or country in order to obtain a decree of divorce for a cause which occurred while the parties resided in New Jersey or for a cause which is not a ground for divorce in New Jersey. Section 33 is substantially a copy of a prior Massachusetts statute. It may be noted that the proviso omits reference to possessions of the United States, but expressly includes decrees of foreign countries. The Revision does not alter this proviso except that the word "territory" has been dropped, but "state" includes "territory." 10 The proviso, when otherwise applicable, embraces foreign decrees of divorce from bed and board as well as divorces from the bond of matrimony, but it is not applicable to foreign decrees of nullity of marriage. The Uniform Divorce Congress omitted foreign decrees of nullity from the operation of the proviso for the probable reason that there never had existed an efflux of emigrants to other states and countries for the purpose of obtaining decrees of nullity of marriage. 

The word "inhabitant" contained in the proviso, as well as the words "bona fide resident" in sections 2:50-9, 2:50-10, 2:50-11 of the Revision, 12 certainly can connote nothing less than "domicile" in this state.18 Consequently, if a person is merely residing temporarily in this state, a residence without the animus manendi, the proviso is inapplicable. The proviso has no application to a foreign decree of divorce obtained by an inhabitant of another state who leaves such state to go into a third state in order to obtain a divorce.14

-Cause for Divorce. If the cause for divorce arose while the parties were domiciled in New Jersey or in some other state, the proviso is applicable to a foreign decree of divorce obtained by an inhabitant of this state who left the state in order to obtain the decree where the ground alleged in the foreign suit is not recognized as cause for divorce in New Jersey. In the proviso the words "parties resided" appear. The framers evidently did not contemplate the possibility that a cause for divorce may arise. while the parties have separate domiciles,15 one of which is in this state. If the parties have separate domiciles, the domicile of the petitioner in the foreign suit at the time the cause arose would seem to be intended.

If the cause arose while the parties were domiciled in another state, the proviso would be inapplicable if the inhabitant should see fit to sue for divorce in a foreign jurisdiction on a ground recognized in this state. Desertion under our statute must be for two years, and a foreign decree of divorce granted to an inhabitant of this state in the circumstances mentioned in the proviso will not be recognized by our courts.16 17 -Intent to Obtain Divorce. § 321. Separate Domicile of Wife. The rule that a wife may acquire an independent domicile for the purpose of instituting suit for divorce 25 is recognized in extending full faith and credit to decrees of divorce of foreign states and countries.26 However, it is a question of fact to be passed upon by our courts as to whether the wife had sufficient justification for leaving her husband so as to be able to acquire a separate domicile. Notwithstanding that the foreign court has decreed that the wife had sufficient cause for leaving her husband and for such cause has granted a divorce, our courts may re-examine the facts insofar as it is essential to ascertain whether jurisdiction based on the wife's domicile existed.27

Where the fraud does not go to the jurisdiction of the subject matter or of the person, but goes to the cause of action, as perjury and the like, may our courts refuse to accord the foreign decree full faith and credit? The inquiry pertains, as well, to foreign decrees and judgments other than decrees of divorce and of nullity, and as to this the authorities, it seems, are not wholly in accord. As respects the recognition of foreign decrees of divorce and of nullity where there has been fraud other than in the jurisdiction, it was possible prior to the adoption of section 33 of the Divorce Act of 1907 to challenge such decrees, collaterally at least, on the ground that the cause of action stated had been fabricated. But it would seem that the courts are now governed exclusively by section 2:50-35 of the Revision (formerly section 33 of the Divorce Act), and under that section, if the foreign court had acquired jurisdiction in conformity with the conditions prescribed in section 2:50-35, the decrees of sister states, territories and possessions must be recognized irrespective of fraud which reaches to intrinsic matters not affecting jurisdiction. The rules existing prior to 1907 may, however, apply to decrees of foreign countries inasmuch as recognition may be extended by the rules of international comity. § 324. Under

§ 326. Enjoining Foreign Suits for Divorce. Of recent years two proceedings have been utilized to protect the status of marriage from migratory divorces. The first is the injunction to restrain the prosecution of suits for divorce in another jurisdiction and the second is a proceeding to declare a foreign decree of divorce null and void in New Jersey. The first will be here considered, leaving the latter for discussion farther on in this chapter.21

In ordinary cases it is settled that the Court of Chancery has jurisdiction to enjoin the prosecution of a suit in a foreign jurisdiction.22 Under certain conditions this jurisdiction may be exercised where the purpose of the injunction is to restrain the defendant from prosecuting a suit for divorce in a foreign jurisdiction.28 An injunction to restrain the prosecution of a suit for divorce in a sister state is not in contravention of the full faith and credit clause, or the equal privileges and immunities clause, of the Federal Constitution.24

§ 327. -Domicile and Service of Process.28 What are the domiciliary requirements and under what circumstances may the restraining order be served upon the defendant outside of the state? In our leading case of Kempson v. Kempson it appeared that the matrimonial domicile, the place where the parties last cohabited as man and wife, was in New Jersey and that the complaining wife, if not the husband, was domiciled within the state at the time of the filing of the bill for injunctive relief. The injunction order was served personally upon the defendant in New York." He violated the injunction and was attached in this state for contempt. On appeal from the order adjudging him in contempt the Court of Errors and Appeals held that service of the restraint upon him outside of the state conferred jurisdiction on the court inasmuch as New Jersey was the matrimonial domicile and the domicile of the complainant. Direct Attack. In the Court of Chancery a foreign decree of divorce may be attacked collaterally, as in a suit for divorce or for separate maintenance, and directly. The direct attack is not ancillary to any other proceeding. It is an independent suit to declare the marital status. 

The declaratory judgment or decree is not peculiar to matrimonial litigation. It has been utilized to determine the personal status of a person other than his marital status." It is now settled that the Court of Chancery under certain conditions has jurisdiction to declare that in New Jersey a foreign decree of divorce is null and void. This is an instance in which the court protects the marital status or res. The suit in the ecclesiastical courts known as "jactitation of marriage" also resulted in a declaratory decree, but in a decree which declared that no marriage existed,' a decree quite similar to our decree of nullity of marriage on account of a prior subsisting marriage.Ⓡ

In declaring a foreign divorce null and void the Court of Chancery exercises an inherent jurisdiction. Thus far the basis of the decree has been fraud in the jurisdiction of the foreign court in that the defendant obtained the foreign decree of divorce upon the false assertion that he was domiciled within the foreign state when in fact he was domiciled in New Jersey. In declaring the foreign divorce invalid the court has relied upon section 33 of the Divorce Act of 1907, now section 2:50-35 of the Revision."

 § 331. -Domicile and Service of Process.10 A declaratory decree may be granted in cases where at the time of the rendition of the foreign decree the complainant and defendant were each domiciled in New Jersey and this state was the matrimonial domicile in the sense that the parties last cohabited here as man and wife, and where at the time of the filing of the bill to annul the foreign decree the complainant is domiciled in this state.¹¹ 

Where the matrimonial domicile was in another state and neither of the parties was domiciled in New Jersey at the time the bill was filed, jurisdiction was declined in Floyd v. Floyd. The domicile of the defendant wife for the purpose of the bill is the domicile of her husband elsewhere, although she may actually be resi- Ident in this state when the bill is filed.12 The court will not take cognizance of a bill where it appears that neither of the parties was domiciled in New Jersey at the time of the commencement of the suit.13 It may be wondered whether the court will assume jurisdiction of a bill to declare a foreign decree of divorce invalid where the matrimonial domicile was in another state, but subsequently the complainant or defendant became domiciled in New Jersey. In one case the wife obtained a decree of separation in 

New York. Thereafter, the husband obtained a Mexican decree and thereupon became domiciled in New Jersey. In a suit by the wife for separate maintenance it was suggested on motion to strike out the bill that a direct attack would not have been proper. 

The situation differed from that in Floyd v. Floyd in that the husband was domiciled in New Jersey when the bill was filed.¹¹ 

It is likely that the court will assume jurisdiction if the complainant is domiciled in the state at the time of the filing of the bill, although the matrimonial domicile and the domicile of each of the parties were in some other state when the fraudulent decree was obtained. In such cases there has been no fraud perpetrated upon the courts of this state, but the domicile of the complainant places the marital res within the state. § 336.

Common Law Obligation to Support. From the status of marriage¹ there arise sundry obligations, and of these perhaps the common law duty of the husband to support his wife is the most familiar. There are, of course, other incidents which the common and statutory law have attached to the marital relation. At common law the wife is not liable for the support of the husband, but under the Poor Act there exists some responsibility. Before a husband is obligated at common law to support his wife a valid marriage must exist. A voidable marriage until annulled in a direct proceeding, or a common law marriage, is sufficient to give rise to this common law obligation. Under a void marriage there arises no obligation to support, but as to third persons the husband may be estopped to deny the marriage where he has held out a woman to be his wife. 

Several explanations have been offered for the origin of the common law duty of the husband to support his wife. One writer urges that it results from the husband's ownership of the wife's labor at common law, while it has also been suggested that the reason partly is that the common law gave the wife's fortune to

the husband. It is clear that the obligation to support arises out of and is an incident to the status of marriage. So long as the parties are husband and wife the husband may not by agreement be released from the obligation to support his wife. The wife's consent to such release can no more destroy this duty imposed by law than can the spouses dissolve the marital status by mutual consent. The obligation is a fixed and absolute one imposed by law upon the husband.' The duty to support may be liquidated as to amount by an agreement for maintenance, but such an agreement does not create the obligation or necessarily get rid of it.9 The husband's common law obligation to support his wife exists notwithstanding the independent means possessed by the wife,10 or the want of means on the part of the husband,¹¹ or the lack of affection between the parties.12 In many respects the 

Married Women's Act 18 has given to the wife rights which were not hers at common law, but these privileges do not strip her of her common law right to support from her husband.¹¹ Even the wife's right to her separate earnings 15 does not absolve the husband of the obligation.

§ 338. -Duration and Termination of Obligation. The common law duty of the husband to support his wife is a continuing obligation. It endures throughout the continuance of the marital relationship, including the time during which a suit. for divorce or for separate maintenance between the parties is pending. This obligation of the husband, coupled with the impropriety of cohabitation pending a matrimonial suit,10 is the basis for the allowance of alimony pendente lite.¹¹ The obligation to support survives despite the commission of adultery by the wife unless and until the husband procures a divorce,12 although the Court of Chancery has declined to enforce this existing duty under section 2:50-39 of the Revision (formerly section 

26 of the Divorce Act of 1907) on the ground that such adultery is "justifiable cause" for an abandonment by the husband if not for his refusal or neglect to support.18 "Consummated marriage,' observed Chancellor McGill, "carries with it rights and duties which, so far as a faithful wife is concerned, can morally end only with the life of one of the parties. Her right to support and maintenance continues so long as it is just that she shall retain it." 14 The obligation terminates upon the death of one of the parties, 15 but as alimony it survives a final decree of divorce, although absolute, (but not a decree of nullity) obtained at the instance of the wife.1

§ 339. Alimony; Alimony as Support. Alimony [L. alimonia, alimonium, nourishment, sustenance, fr. alere, to nourish]¹7 "in its origin, was the method by which the spiritual courts of England enforced the duty of support owed by the husband to the wife, during such time as they were legally separated pending the marriage relation." 18 In the ecclesiastical courts the marriage was indissoluble except for causes antedating the marriage.

With us alimony was allowed as an incident to suits for divorce from the time of the passage of the first Divorce Act in 1794 conferring jurisdiction on the Court of Chancery. At the present time alimony as an incident to a suit for divorce or for nullity of marriage is regulated by sections 2:50-37 and 2:50-38 of the

Revision. Prior to the enactment of the Revision these two sec tions comprised section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907 as amended. 

These two sections provide as follows: 

2:50-37. Pending a suit for divorce or nullity, brought in this State or elsewhere, or after decree of divorce, whether obtained in this State or elsewhere, the Court of Chancery may make such order touching the alimony of the wife, and also touching the care, custody, education and maintenance of the children, or any of them, as the circumstances of the parties and the nature of the case shall render fit, reasonable and just, and require reasonable security for the due observance of such orders, and upon neglect or refusal to give such reasonable security, as shall be required, or upon default in complying with the order, may award and issue process for the immediate sequestration of the personal estate, and the rents and profits of the real estate of the party so charged, and appoint a receiver thereof, and cause such personal estate and the rents and profits of such real estate, or so much thereof as shall be necessary, to be applied toward such alimony and maintenance as to the said court shall from time to time seem reasonable and just, or enforce the performance of the said orders by such other lawful ways and means as is usual, and according to the course and practice of the Court of Chancery; orders so made may be revised and altered by the court from time to time as circumstances may require. (As amended, L. 1938 c. 235). 

2:50-38. If after the decree of divorce the wife shall remarry, the court of chancery shall not make any order touching the alimony of such wife except that the court of chan-

Section 2:50-37 provides for an award of alimony to the wife and maintenance to the children pending 19 a suit for divorce or for nullity of marriage and upon or after 20 decree of divorce whether the decree of divorce be one from bed and board or from the bond of matrimony. Sometimes, the award made in suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony is classified as statutory alimony to distinguish it from the award allowed in suits for divorce from bed and board. But section 2:50-37 makes no such distinction.21

In the ecclesiastical courts in England the award of alimony incidental to a decree a mensa et thoro truly enforced the common law duty of support because the decree enjoined cohabitation of the parties without dissolving the marital status. And so with us where the decree is for a divorce from bed and board. 

But a divorce from the bond of matrimony terminates the marriage and ordinarily the incidents dependent upon the marital status cease. However, the common law obligation of the husband to support his wife as an incident to the marriage 22 is saved by section 2:50-37 from terminating upon the dissolution of the marriage at the suit of the wife. "The subject-matter of divorce having been, by statute, committed to the court of chancery," observed Justice Pitney, "and causes for absolute divorce having been allowed other than such as rendered the marriage void ab initio, there followed, as a logical consequence, the allowance of permanent alimony in cases of absolute divorce, as a means of enforcing the continuing duty of support which the husband owed to the wife, and of which he was not permitted to absolve himself by his own misconduct, although that misconduct resulted in a dissolution of the marriage." 28 The allowance is not a part of

§340. Alimony as Contract or Debt. The award of ali mony is the liquidation, as of a particular time, of the husband's common law obligation to support his wife. This obligation flows from the marriage and is not dependent upon the agreement of the parties." Nor is the award of alimony a simple contract. This phase of the nature of alimony was discussed in a case involving the constitutionality of the amendment to section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907 (now section 2:50-38 of the 

Revision) providing for the termination of alimony upon the wife's re-marriage. "As to the fact that the act is unconstitutional because it impairs the obligation of a contract, it is sufficient to say that an order of the Court of Chancery to pay alimony is not a contract. Such an order may always be modified or vacated by the court which made it. It has none of the essentials of a simple contract and such contracts, and not the so-called 'contracts of record', such as judgments of a court were, in my opinion, the contracts referred to in the constitution. Therefore, in my opinion, the law in question is constitutional." The entry of the order or decree by consent does not make the award contractual.

Such consent is as to the liquidation of the obligation, but it does not create it.? -Alimony as a Debt. The award of alimony is not a debt within the constitutional prohibition against imprisonment. The

In 1903 the section of the Bankruptcy Act relative to debts released by a discharge was amended to provide that a discharge in bankruptcy shall release a bankrupt from all of his provable debts, except "for alimony due or to become due, or for maintenance or support of wife or child," etc. While this amendment carried the implied recognition that arrears of alimony were a debt, nevertheless ip a case decided after the passage of the amendment, but which dealt with the law as it existed prior to the amendment, the court declared that the amendment was merely declaratory of the existing rule that alimony was not a provable debt.18 At any rate, whether alimony is or is not a provable debt, the bankrupt husband is not released by his discharge in bankruptcy under the 1903 amendment.

§ 342. -Assignability of Alimony. A claim of the wife to alimony, not yet liquidated as to amount by an order or decree of the court, is not assignable by the wife. "A wife's claim for an allowance of alimony is a purely personal right, and not, in any sense, a property right. It is, in its nature, not susceptible of assignment by the wife to another, nor capable of enjoyment by her in anticipation." 15 The claim or right of the wife to alimony, temporary or permanent, is of such a personal character that it will not survive in favor of the representative of a deceased wife.16

Accruals of permanent alimony are vested 17 and may be assigned as fast as they accrue.18 But accruals under an order pendente lite are not vested, at least prior to final decree in suits for separate maintenance,19 so that, if such accruals are assignable, the assignee takes the risk that such accruals may be wiped out by the court retroactively upon a showing of sufficient cause.20 

§ 343. Liability for Debts of Wife. On a motion for summary judgment our Supreme Court has held that arrearages of alimony due under a New York decree which had accrued at the time of the filing of the petition in bankruptcy by the wife passed to the trustee, but on appeal the point was reserved.22 

Subsequently, the Court of Chancery has recognized that alimony accrued up to the filing of the wife's petition in bankruptcy should pass to the trustee.28 It is but equitable that creditors who may have relied on the order for alimony should have recourse to the accruals for payment of debts contracted by the wife after the entry of the decree. But the courts have declined to appropriate the alimony of the wife, although accrued, for payment of debts contracted prior to the entry of the decree.24

§ 344. -Public Policy; Consent Decrees.2 To every di vorce suit the state is a party. This triangular suit leading to the alteration or dissolution of the marriage is one which is not favored by the law. Consequently, so far as concerns the alteration or termination of the marital status, the statute relating to divorce should be, although it has not always been, strictly construed.26 But as respects alimony in the suit for divorce, the same strict construction should not be given to section 2:50-37 of the Revision. In all its phases, jurisdictional or otherwise, section 2:50-37 should be construed quite liberally so as to permit the liquidation and enforcement of the husband's existing common law duty to support his wife.27 While a divorce may not be obtained by mutual consent, the entry of an order or decree for alimony by consent is not contrary to public policy.28 

§ 345. Necessity of Personal Jurisdiction. A personal decree or order for alimony, pendente lite or permanent, may not be entered against a husband unless the court has acquired jurisdiction of the person of the husband by service within the state. 

An order or decree in personam rendered against a husband who has not been personally served within the state and who has not appeared is of no validity in this state or elsewhere, 29 although the main suit is for divorce from bed and board.¹ These are familiar principles relating to jurisdiction in suits in personam and are not confined to proceedings for alimony.2

If the husband is a non-resident, but owns property within the state, such property may be sequestered and the proceeding for alimony in the divorce suit may proceed quasi in rem. § 347.

Jurisdiction of Chancery. In connection with the award of alimony pendente lite, reference should as well be made to a preceding chapter where a number of matters have, for convenience, been discussed.¹ The obligation of the husband to support his wife persists pending matrimonial litigation, but because it is usually improper, or impossible, for the parties to cohabit pending the suit, the wife may receive support as alimony in proper cases while she is living separate from her husband. 

Thus is the husband's obligation to support his wife pending the suit liquidated.* An allowance may be made for the support and maintenance of a widow and children under the statute pending a will contest, but this allowance is not alimony."

§ 348 

Concededly, the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery to make a permanent allowance is statutory, but there has been some difference of opinion as to its jurisdiction to make a temporary award. Section 2:50-39 of the Revision (section 26 of the Divorce 

Act of 1907) has never in express terms conferred authority upon the court to make a temporary allowance in suits by the wife for separate maintenance. Recently it has been declared, that the jurisdiction exercised in awarding maintenance pendente lite in a suit under section 2:50-39 is inherent in the sense that it arises ex necessitate when jurisdiction is conferred by statute to make a permanent award. The jurisdiction is not inherent in the sense that jurisdiction was inherited from the English Court of Chancery. As respects the award of alimony pendente lite under section 2:50-37 of the Revision (section 25 of the Divorce Act of 

1907) in suits for divorce and nullity of marriage, the statute has expressly authorized the award since the year 1902 by the inclusion of the clause, "Pending a suit for divorce or nullity." 

But long prior to the addition of this clause in the Divorce Act of 1902 temporary support had been decreed to the wife in proper cases, so that it would appear that the statute merely confirms the fundamental jurisdiction, is declaratory of it, but does not abrogate it. This view permits the allowance of temporary alimony in matrimonial suits in which there exists no statute, as, for instance, an award in a suit in Chancery to collect arrears due under a foreign decree a mensa, or in a suit for nullity of marriage brought against the wife under the general equity jurisdiction of the court for fraud, etc.10 Nevertheless, it has been held that the jurisdiction of the court to award alimony pendente lite in suits for divorce is statutory only.¹¹ § 348. 11 Discretion of Court. -Independent Means of Wife. Before the enactment of the 

Married Women's Act in 1852 the wife could not possess separate property and there was much more reason to award alimony pending matrimonial litigation than at the present time.¹ But now whether the wife complains or is complained against the court in exercising its discretion may decline to award the wife alimony or maintenance pendente lite if it appears that she is possessed of independent means adequate for her support.15 Thus in a suit for separate maintenance an award was denied where the income of the wife trebled that of her husband.16 If her means are inadequate, however, the court may fix an award, taking into consideration the amount which the wife may realize from her separate property.17 The nature of the wife's property and whether it can and should be disposed of for her support pendente lite are matters to be considered.18

§ 350. Effect of Order in Other Court. There are several courts, other than the Court of Chancery, which may order the husband to support his wife and children. Under various statutes jurisdiction is exercised by police magistrates, the Court of Common Pleas, the Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court, and the Family Court (Newark).28 Orders are usually made in pursuance of the Disorderly Persons' Act,24 the Poor Act,25 or the 

Crimes Act.26

In suits by the wife for separate maintenance in the Court of Chancery a prior order made by a police magistrate in pursuance of the Disorderly Persons' Act for the support of the wife and child has been held to be a bar to an application for maintenance pendente lite while such order is in effect and is being obeyed by the husband. The wife has been barred on the ground that while the order is being obeyed the husband does not neglect or refuse suitably to support his wife, a jurisdictional requisite to relief under the separate maintenance statute,27 and on the grounds of election of remedies and res judicata, although the proceeding before the magistrate was instituted by the overseer of the poor.28 

Whether or not a prior adjudication is res judicata in bar would seem largely to depend upon the particular statute under which the order was made. The cause of action under the separate maintenance section of the Divorce Act (section 2:50-39 of the 

Revision) may differ from the cause of action sued upon in the prior proceeding. The cause of action under the Poor Act apparently has been regarded as different from that for separate maintenance under the Divorce Act, although the cause of action. under the Disorderly Persons' Act has been considered as the same as that under the Divorce Act.29 At any rate, where the husband has failed to comply with an order for support made under the

However, the obligation of a husband to support his wife pending a divorce suit is legal as well as moral. And as respects his insanity, he is, nevertheless, liable to third persons for necessaries furnished during the period of insanity. Alimony pendente lite has been awarded in a suit by the wife for divorce from bed and board for extreme cruelty where the extreme cruelty resulted from an insane delusion.⁹

 § 352. 

Vested Right. With respect to alimony and maintenance pendente lite to accrue in futuro, the wife has no vested right. The orders are subject to modification prospectively upon proof of a change of circumstances.10 11 While arrearages of permanent alimony and maintenance become vested, in the absence of fraud, as they accrue," arrears of maintenance pendente lite accruing under an order entered in a suit for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision are not vested, at least prior to final decree.12 However, the accrued alimony pendente lite under an order entered in a suit for divorce has been held to be vested.18 Nevertheless, if the accruals are not reserved in a final decree dismissing the wife's petition for divorce, they may be lost.¹4 14 § 353. Good Faith and Laches. These two equitable concepts, the good faith of the wife and her laches, if any, as well as the consideration of the probability of the wife's success on the merits, as disclosed by the affidavits, are always weighed upon her application. Delay in the application for alimony may tend to show want of good faith on the part of the wife, or even condonation of the offense charged, although condonation is not so readily inferred by the wife's delay as it is upon the part of the husband. This has been already observed.15

On the basis of lack of good faith on the part of the wife, temporary support has been refused in several reported cases. In one case in which the wife sued for divorce for adultery, alimony pendente lite was denied where it appeared that the suit had not been instituted by the wife in good faith for the purpose of obtaining a divorce, but merely for the purpose of compelling support. The husband had already obtained a foreign decree of absolute divorce.16 In another case the want of good faith of the wife in instituting a suit for divorce a mensa was a factor in denying the application.17 As to whether the application of the wife must be in good faith when she is complained against, the court supposed in one case that the wife's denial under oath of the
