The mere delay of the wife in instituting the suit or in seeking support should never of itself absolve the husband of his obligation to support his wife pending matrimonial litigation. But no broad or general rule should be attempted. Delay is always a circumstance which may be indicative of some other factor relevant upon the consideration of the wife's application. Delay may evidence insincerity, or throw doubt upon the wife's probable success at final hearing. It may be urged that the delay, particularly for a long period of time, in the absence of explanation, demonstrates that the wife is not in need 20 of temporary support. But if the wife makes out a prima facie case or, as defendant, denies under oath the commission of the offense charged, and is in need, delay alone will not preclude an ad interim allowance for her support.

An examination of the reported cases in which temporary support has been denied reveals that the element of delay is usually coupled with some other circumstance. No useful purpose would be served by summarizing most of the cases. In each case the particular facts must be observed: whether the wife is complaining or defending, the ground alleged and the defense invoked, the lapse of time, etc. In some cases it is apparent that the wife was possessed of independent means, or failed to present a prima facie case or defense in view of the husband's denial under oath, or, having cause for separate maintenance, failed to seek support at an earlier date.21

§ 354. Quantum of Proof; Where Wife Complains. In suits by the wife for divorce and for separate maintenance her affidavits in support of the application for alimony pendente lite must make out a prima facie case, that is, taking her affidavits as true, the affidavits must present a case which, in the absence of any defense, would justify a decree in her favor.22 If the wife's suit is for divorce, corroboration is necessary at final hearing, 28 so that on the application pendente lite corroborating affidavits are required to make out a prima facie case.24 But in suits for separate maintenance where corroboration is not essential at final hearing,25 a prima facie case may be made out without support from corroborating affidavits; yet it is the safer practice to substantiate the charge by the affidavits of others, particularly where in her bill she alleges a constructive abandonment.

In suits for separate maintenance the court may look into the nature of the case made by the bill and answer as well as to the affidavits of the parties 26 and in this respect suits for divorce from bed and board have been similarly treated.27 If the bill for separate maintenance fails to charge that the defendant has without justifiable cause abandoned or separated himself from the complainant and has refused or neglected suitably to maintain her, maintenance pendente lite will be denied."

But no award should be made if the husband denies the charge under oath and produces affidavits which make it doubtful that the wife will succeed at final hearing.¹ Particularly in a suit for separate maintenance does the court exercise caution where it appears that the complaining wife has left the home and seeks to justify her departure.2 "The rule seems to be," observed Chancellor Walker, "that as well in cases for divorce a mensa et thoro as in those for alimony pure and simple (separate maintenance), where the wife has in fact left the husband on account of his alleged derelict conduct,³ her application for alimony and counsel fee pendente lite will be scrutinized and decided upon the weight of the testimony then presented and the rules of law applicable thereto, just as other litigated motions are decided, even though she be a favored suitor. 

Where his sworn denial is abundantly corroborated, and the case made by the pleadings and affidavits on the preliminary motion is with him by the application of the usual rule concerning the burden of proof, he should not be visited with any interlocutory order for allowances where it appears that the wife has left him either because of his alleged extreme cruelty or adultery; because a wife who leaves her husband does so at her peril, and assumes the burden of making the desertion constructively his by establishing his guilt by clear and satisfactory proof." 4 § 355.

When the wife is in need she is entitled to alimony pendente lite if in good faith she denies under oath the commission of the matrimonial offense charged against her. Corroborating affidavits in support of her denial ordinarily are not necessary, but, if supporting affidavits may be obtained, it is best to use them. If the wife denies under oath the commission of the offense charged, the court will be reluctant to permit the husband to defeat the application by granting a voluntary dismissal of his petition for divorce. Where the wife denies under oath the commission of the offense, the court, in the exercise of its discretion, makes the allowance very much as a matter of course, particularly where the husband charges adultery.10 Until final hearing the wife should be presumed innocent of the charge of adultery if she denies its commission under oath.11 Even in desertion cases where the defendant wife admits that she left her husband and sets up under oath as justification 12 the commission of adultery or extreme cruelty by the husband the court may allow alimony pendente lite,13 and notwithstanding the denial by the husband under oath of the commission of the offense charged in justification.¹ If the court declines to allow alimony, it may, nevertheless, award suit moneys 15 and, in addition, may make an allowance for the children of the marriage in her custody.

On the one hand, the court is ready in proper cases to compel a husband to support his wife pending matrimonial litigation. On the other hand, it is cautious lest it force a man to support a woman who is not his wife and to whom he owes no obligation of support. 

In suits by the wife for divorce or for separate maintenance the husband may urge that there was in fact no marriage between him and the petitioner, or else, having admitted the fact of marriage, may contend that it is invalid and that its invalidity has never been cured, or, being valid, that it has already been dissolved. If in a suit by the wife for separate maintenance or for divorce the husband under oath denies the fact of marriage, an order for alimony pendente lite cannot be made upon the mere allegation or ex parte affidavit of the wife. In such circumstances the wife must establish by evidence, other than by her own affidavit, facts so corroborating her claim as to make a reasonably plain case of the existence of the marriage relation.17 The wife carries the burden of proving the marriage on the preliminary application and, if it appears doubtful that the wife will on final hearing establish the marriage, temporary alimony will be denied.18 If the husband admits the fact of marriage and continuous cohabitation as husband and wife, but it is also admitted by the petitioner that at the time of the ceremony a suit for divorce was pending against her first husband, the burden is upon the wife to prove, in accordance with the rules already considered,10 that subsequent to the rendition of the final decree of divorce dissolving her first marriage the illicit relation was changed into a matrimonial union. If there is doubt that the parties became man and wife after the removal of the impediment, alimony will be denied.20 

If the husband admits the marriage but alleges that it has been dissolved by a foreign decree of absolute divorce, the wife's burden is to establish that the decree is invalid. If the result of that issue appears to be in substantial doubt, no allowance will be made.21 -Nullity Suits. tice of taking an order to show cause on the petition for alimony pendente lite has of late years largely superseded the practice of applying on notice. If there is no good reason for proceeding by order to show cause, the notice is as efficacious and tends to reduce the bulk of papers necessary to be filed in the case. The reason for the practice by order to show cause rather than by notice is that originally, in cases where for any reason five days' notice could not be given, the order to show cause might be made returnable in less than five days. Under the present practice, however, and under Rule 168, if there is reason for giving shorter notice than five days, it may be done by notice after first securing the permission of the court and so stating in the notice. Hereinafter included are forms of petition for allowances pendente lite, order to show cause, notice and order for payment. [Forms 198202.] 

In support of the application for allowances pendente lite affidavits are used, although the court may require oral testimony if it sees fit. The affidavits should conform to the provisions of Rule 

89, and should adhere to the rules of evidence. Solicitors should use great care to assure themselves that the affidavits which they prepare express the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Since the court does not have the benefit of cross-examination, it is the solicitor's duty to cross examine his own witnesses before drafting the affidavits. There should be no evasion or equivocation permitted, so far as the solicitor can prevent it. His first duty is to the court. The affidavits must not be hearsay, or otherwise present evidence which, if orally offered in open court, would be incompetent.20 The affidavits should not be taken by the solicitors of the respective parties.¹ In order that a complaining wife may obtain alimony pendente lite her proof must make out a prima facie case, that is, proof which, if true, would warrant granting the decree ultimately prayed for. If her petition is for divorce, corroborating affidavits are essential to make a prima facie case." 

The financial condition of the wife and the extent of her needs pendente lite must be disclosed. The petition and affidavit should set out precisely the property and income of the wife or, if none, should state that fact positively and circumstantially, rather than the conclusion that she is destitute. It is the function of the court to decide from the facts alleged whether or not she is destitute.

§ 358. -Hearing of Application on Return Day. Upon the return day of the order to show cause, or notice, the solicitor of the wife moves the matter. If the defendant wishes to oppose the application, his solicitor must serve copies of all answering affidavits upon the wife's solicitor before the matter is moved. It is better practice to serve the answering affidavits before the return day in order to avoid an adjournment to permit the solicitor of the applicant to study them and to reply to any new matter set up therein.

The proceedings are quite informal. The court seeks to do

§ 359 

equity as well as may be without hearing the main case and may allow new affidavits to be filed by either of the parties, may refer the whole matter to a master for preliminary hearing of witnesses, or may, itself, hear oral testimony in order to adjudge the preliminary application as equitably as may be. 

The solicitor for the wife states in a few words that the application is for ad interim relief to the wife and children and gives to the court the following information: 

1. The nature of the relief prayed for in the main suit (divorce, nullity or maintenance). 

2. Which party brings the suit. 

3. Concisely the facts set out in the affidavits. It is improper to state anything as a fact which is not set out in the affidavits. If applicant is the petitioner and the suit is for divorce, the extent to which the facts are corroborated should be stated. The affidavits are not to be read at length, but only such portions as the court may direct. The needs of the wife (and children) and, as far as the affidavits go, the faculties of the husband should be stated.

Respondent's solicitor then states his client's case in the same manner. If his affidavits disclose new matter, proper to be met by rebuttal affidavits, applicant will be granted an opportunity to meet them. For this purpose an adjournment may be required, but, if the wife appears to be destitute and the delay is caused by the husband's avoidable (or perhaps unavoidable) delay in serving his reply affidavits, the adjournment may be upon terms which will provide some immediate relief to the wife. 

After the court has ruled, the solicitor of the applicant (or, if the application be denied in toto, the solicitor of the respondent) prepares the order embodying the court's ruling. This should be submitted to the opposing solicitor for his consent as to its form before being handed to the court. All the affidavits used on the application, on both sides, must be handed to the court for filing before the order is advised.

§ 360. Termination of Award. A decree dismissing the wife's petition for divorce terminates prospectively an order for temporary alimony and in the absence of a saving clause in the decree of dismissal the wife loses whatever rights she may have had to accrued installments.21 And so with the dismissal of the wife's bill for separate maintenance.22 If a defendant wife has been awarded alimony pendente lite in a suit by the husband for divorce or for nullity of marriage, a decree dismissing the husband's petition undoubtedly would have the same effect as to the operation of the order in futuro and as to arrears. In every case the wife should preserve her claim to unpaid accrued installments under the interlocutory order by an express reservation in the decree of dismissal. If the final decree is one for divorce or for nullity of marriage, or a final decree for separate maintenance, the wife's claim to arrears under an interlocutory order should be safeguarded by a reservation and, if the suit is for absolute divorce or for nullity of marriage, the reservation should be incorporated in the decree nisi 23 [Form 75].

Generally, the allowance is less than the amount awarded as permanent alimony, being somewhat strictly limited to the actual needs of the wife according to the station in life of the parties. In exercising its discretion the court will consider the faculties of the husband, unpaid debts contracted by the wife against her husband for her support,' whether the wife has property or income independent of her husband, and her age, condition of health, and ability to earn support. If there are minor children in the wife's custody, an added allowance for them will be made.10 In addition, the court may allow a sum for suit money, including counsel fee.¹¹ 

The amount stipulated in an agreement of separation may be a guide in fixing alimony pendente lite, but it is not binding on the court.12 

§ 362. Revision of Order.13 The court may revise prospec tively orders for alimony pendente lite on proof of changed conditions,¹ but today it is not often that such an application should be made because of the dispatch with which, under the present practice, final hearing may be reached. However, in case of change in financial circumstances of the parties and unusual delay in reaching final hearing, it is sometimes proper to make such an application. The proofs must show that the circumstances existing at the time of the order have changed, so that the court may increase or decrease the amount of the allowance depending upon whether the application is made by the wife or by the husband.

In one respect the authority of the court to vacate orders for alimony pendente lite differs from its jurisdiction to vacate orders for permanent alimony. Where the interlocutory order is made under the court's original jurisdiction in a suit for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision the modification of the order may be retrospective as well as prospective where equitable considerations dictate such a course.10 However, as the law stands at the present writing arrearages due under an order for alimony pendente lite entered in a suit for divorce have been held to be vested.¹ At any rate, an order for alimony pendente lite may be vacated retroactively for fraud of the wife in the procurement of the order.18 An unperfected appeal does not impair the jurisdiction of the court to modify the order.18" -Procedure. The order for alimony pendente lite may be revised on petition and order to show cause or by notice [Forms 203 et. seq]. The practice is essentially the same as that existing on applications for the original order.19 Ordinarily, applications for revision should be made to the Advisory Master who advised the original order. § 363. 

Enforcement. Orders for alimony and maintenance pendente lite are enforced substantially in the same manner as are orders for permanent alimony. Farther on the various methods employed will be discussed,20 making it unnecessary to treat here of the enforcement of pendente lite orders, except to note that, if the husband is in contempt for failure to obey such an order, his defense may not for that reason be suppressed.21 However, if he is petitioner he cannot move his case without purging himself and, if defendant, the petitioner can move the case against him, if he is in court, or is properly represented by counsel.22

 § 364. Appeal.23 Because of the discretion lodged in the court in awarding alimony pendente lite 24 and because of the dispatch with which final hearing is reached under the present practice, it is usually inadvisable to take an appeal from a pendente lite order for alimony in suits for divorce or in suits for separate maintenance. The cause at final hearing is not prejudged by a temporary allowance. However, if special circumstances arise warranting an appeal [Forms 461, 462], it must be taken within 30 days.25 The appeal will act as a stay without a special order under Rule 161.26 

§ 365. Alimony Pending Appeal. Where the husband ap peals from a decree carrying a provision for permanent alimony or maintenance, the appeal has the effect of staying the operation of the order. Such provision cannot be enforced pending the appeal because it would impair the subject matter of the appeal.27 

But the Court of Chancery and the Court of Errors and Appeals are open for application by the wife for the allowance of alimony, pending the appeal, by a provisional order of the same nature as an order for alimony pendente lite in suits pending in the Court of Chancery.28 Apparently, the jurisdiction of the Court of Errors and Appeals is inherent, arising ex necessitate. 

An application for alimony or maintenance pending appeal should be made to the Court of Errors and Appeals [Forms 213219], unless some special cause exists, such as where that court is on vacation or where, after application made to the Court of Errors and Appeals, there is a direction by that court to apply to the Court of Chancery, or leave to make such application.

§ 366. Jurisdiction of Chancery. In connection with the permanent award, the reader should refer as well to a previous chapter where, for convenience, a number of matters have been treated.¹ Until 1857 the ecclesiastical courts in England had jurisdiction to award permanent alimony as an incident to a decree of divorce a mensa et thoro. It is extremely doubtful that these courts ever decreed permanent alimony in suits for the restitution of conjugal rights as a means of compelling the husband to take back his wife and to treat her with conjugal kindness.2 No original jurisdiction was exercised by the English Chancellor in matters of permanent alimony or permanent maintenance. The jurisdiction of the Chancellor which was exercised during the Commonwealth was not original, but was derived from commissions and the acts were confirmed by statute after the Restoration. The Chancellor did, however, assist the spiritual courts in enforcing decrees for alimony by issuing the writ of ne exeat against the husband.' 9

With us no court, not even the Court of Chancery, has succeeded to the jurisdiction of the church courts to decree a divorce,Ⓡ or to award temporary or permanent alimony. There being no original jurisdiction in the Court of Chancery in England to award alimony, our Court of Chancery inherited no such jurisdiction. While the jurisdiction of our Court of Chancery to order maintenance pendente lite in suits for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision (formerly section 26 of the Di vorce Act of 1907) is inherent, its authority to award permanent alimony and maintenance is derived solely from sections 2:50-37 and 2:50-39 of the Revision (formerly sections 25 and 26 of the

Divorce Act of 1907). The jurisdiction of the court does not extend beyond the terms of these two sections.10 And it may be noticed that the jurisdiction of the court specifically to enforce agreements between husband and wife for maintenance has now been curtailed, if not completely denied.11 Nevertheless, without the aid of statute the Court of Chancery may decree that a husband repay money to a third person advanced to the wife for necessaries.12

With us it has been stated that the permanent award under sec tion 2:50-37 of the Revision (formerly section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907) 17 and under section 2:50-39 of the Revision (for merly section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907) 18 is discretionary depending upon the means of the wife and the wealth of the husband. In one reported case a successful wife, of marriageable age, was refused permanent alimony in a suit for divorce because "no special reason is shown which calls for a decree allowing petmanent alimony." 19 In Dietrick v. Dietrick the denial of permanent alimony by the master was held erroneous in the circumstances of the case. "The wife," observed Justice Trenchard, "with or after a decree of divorce in her favor, is entitled to such an allowance of alimony as the circumstances of the parties and the nature of the case renders fit, reasonable and just." This seems to be the gist of another case.21 While the purpose of sections 2:50-37 and 2:50-39 is to liquidate as of a particular time the common law obligation of the husband to support his wife under the conditions specified, the enforcement of such obligation is discretionary with the Chancellor. "It shall be lawful for the 

Court of Chancery" is the grant of the necessary jurisdiction, but there is nothing in the statutes which makes the enforcement of the common law duty mandatory in these proceedings. A wife with independent means far exceeding those of her husband may be refused permanent alimony despite the continuing common law obligation of the husband, but the exact line can be drawn only in the particular case. § 368. 

The jurisdiction of the court being statutory,22 the award of permanent alimony may be made only in those suits mentioned in sections 2:50-37 and 2:50-39 of the Revision, namely, in suits by the wife for divorce or for separate maintenance. No permanent allowance may be ordered in suits for nullity of marriage although the marriage was voidable only and notwithstanding that the suit was at the instance of the wife.23 Where the husband has been guilty of fraud, the wife may have an action for fraud and deceit.24 Until recently, however, the Court of Chancery had unquestioned inherent jurisdiction specifically to enforce agreements between husband and wife for maintenance.25 

§ 369. Distinct Cause of Action from Divorce. In domestic suits for divorce the permanent allowance is made only in cases where the wife succeeds in obtaining a decree of divorce. It is incidental to a decree of divorce from bed and board or from the bond of matrimony.28 Nevertheless, in some respects the wife's right to permanent alimony is a separate and distinct cause of action,27 so much so that the wife has been permitted to sue for alimony independently after she has obtained a foreign decree of absolute divorce,28 

§ 370. Alimony When Husband Successful. The jurisdic tion of the court to allow permanent alimony being statutory,29 in suits for divorce no allowance may be made under section 

2:50-37 of the Revision except at the time of or after "decree of divorce." No award may be made where the wife's petition for divorce is dismissed, unless the petition may be sustained as a bill for separate maintenance.¹

Alimony in Decree Nisi. This subject applies to suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony and then only where the permanent award to the wife is made as an adjunct to the principal litigation. So far as concerns the marital status the decree nisi is conditional. The parties are husband and wife until the entry of the final decree.¹ The order for permanent alimony is placed in the decree nisi as is illustrated in Form 75, but nothing in the decree is nisi except that part which adjudges that the marriage is dissolved. The order for permanent alimony is final and is merged into the final decree of divorce without further express inclusion. Of course, if the husband appeals from the decree nisi and obtains a reversal and a dismissal of the petition, the order for permanent alimony falls with it and in this respect the alimony order is not final. 

If the provision for permanent alimony has not been included in the decree nisi, it cannot be placed in the final decree, but possibly the decree nisi may be amended to include the provision if the issue has been tried and an award had actually been made." At any rate, application for permanent alimony may be made after the entry of the final decree." § 372. Vested Right. der is made in pursuance of section 2:50-37 or section 2:50-39 of the Revision. Section 2:50-37 expressly provides that "orders so made may be revised and altered by the court from time to time as circumstances may require." Under section 2:50-39 the court has the authority to "from time to time, make further orders touching the same as shall be just and equitable." " 

As to arrears of permanent alimony awarded under section 

2:50-37 the wife acquires a vested right to them as fast as they accrue, which right survives the death of either of the parties.10 

Undoubtedly, accruals of permanent maintenance under a final decree for separate maintenance are also vested property rights. 11 § 373. Alimony in Gross. In the ecclesiastical courts permanent alimony as an incident to a decree a mensa was allotted to the wife for her maintenance from year to year,¹¹ so that ordinarily the court would not enforce arrears of alimony extending beyond a year.12 With us the award of permanent alimony as incidental to a suit for divorce from bed and board or from the bond of matrimony or the award of permanent maintenance in suits under section 2:50-39 of the Revision is a means of liquidating and enforcing as of a particular time the common law obligation of the husband to support his wife. The marriage creates this obligation; the decree liquidates it as of a particular time without altering its nature. The nature of this duty is a continuing one to supply the wife with her needs from day to day. 

At an early date it was decided in Calame v. Calame that the court was without jurisdiction under section 9 (now section 2:50-37 of the Revision) to decree alimony in a gross sum or in a portion of the husband's real estate. But the court enforced as a part of the divorce decree an agreement between the parties for a sum in gross and a portion of the husband's realty. The award was not alimony but the enforcement of an agreement for maintenance. "My deduction from these principles and decisions is," observed Chief Justice Beasley, "that it was within the competency of equity to enforce, as a part of the decree of divorce, the agreement made, in lieu of alimony, between the complainant and defendant.” 13

§ 373 

Since the decision in the Calame case the court has made awards in a lump sum with the consent of the parties.¹ In practice every variety of property settlement has been incorporated in such agreements for the payment of a gross sum in lieu of alimony which may consist of money or property or both. There have been trust arrangements by which property is to be turned over to a trustee for the wife's benefit in full or in part; they may concern life insurance policies and interests therein. Such awards are not alimony, but are in lieu of alimony. It may have been at one time, as in the Calame case, that the agreement of the parties, if suitable to the wife, could be enforced specifically as against the husband as part of the divorce decree, and not by way of alimony, but it may be wondered what effect the recent cases in the Court of Errors and Appeals have had which deny to Chancery the right specifically to enforce agreements for maintenance.15 -Procedure. The practice upon applications for settlement of alimony in gross is to place the parties on the stand at or after final hearing and to inquire from them as to all of the circumstances surrounding the agreement. The inquiry includes the ascertainment of the income, property and future prospects of the husband, and of the present and prospective situation, financial and otherwise, of the wife. Before approving the agreement the court must be satisfied that it is to the real interest of the wife to receive a lump sum in lieu of alimony, and to this end will inquire how the fund is proposed to be used. If the wife proposes to purchase with it an interest in some business of which she has had little or no experience the application will usually be denied. 

The test is whether or not it is reasonably probable that the wife will be able, by use of the fund, to render herself permanently independent of financial assistance from her husband. The court will exercise its independent judgment as to the probability of the

§ 374. -Effect of Award in Gross on Subsequent Appli cation. In suits for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision an agreement between the parties for maintenance,16 payable periodically, or in a lump sum, is not necessarily a bar to an award, or to an award for a larger sum than has been stipulated. Such an agreement, or a settlement or release, between husband and wife is in equity sub modo,¹ and will not be a bar to the wife's subsequent application for alimony or adopted as to amount, if it is not fair or equitable.18 Nevertheless, the income from a lump sum settlement, although made without the approval of the court, may be suitable and adequate so that it may be said that the husband does not "refuse or neglect to maintain and provide for her" suitably 19 within the meaning of section 2:50-39 of the Revision.20 But the income thus derived must be suitable and, if it is not, an additional award may be made. 21 However, a settlement grossly unfair to the wife, particularly where made to satisfy a prior order for separate maintenance under which the wife would have received a much larger amount, is no bar to a further award.22 Nor in a suit for separate maintenance will a prior lump sum settlement approved by the court in a former proceeding preclude a further award if the wife is in need. A recital in the order that the wife "expressed her complete willingness to accept the sum-in lieu of her right to any present and future alimony" is not an adjudication that the award is suitable and adequate for her support. When the court has found that the provisions for the wife are suitable and adequate, it has been held that the wife thereafter is concluded. "An order of chancery approving a settlement between the parties to a divorce suit, for alimony in gross, concludes the wife as well as the husband, when the order is based on a finding by the court that the settlement is for her benefit." "3 In this case the settlement had been made and approved some five years after the entry of the final decree of absolute divorce at the suit of the wife. Perhaps the result was influenced by the fact that the husband had re-married and had adopted a child. But does not the decision overlook the fact that the husband's common law obligation to support his wife continues beyond the dissolution of the marriage at the suit of the wife by reason of the express provisions of section 2:50-37 of the Revision (formerly section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907) and that by the provisions of the same section it is contemplated that the subject of alimony shall be dealt with continuously by the court as the circumstances change? The issue of alimony cannot be finally adjudicated. The doctrine of res judicata has no application under our statute as respects a change of circumstances of the parties in the future. The court being without jurisdiction to conclude the wife on the issue of alimony, its adjudication is not binding on a subsequent application. Of course the wife should carry a greater burden on the renewal of her application and, if an award is made, the amount already recieved should be taken into consideration.

 § 375. Amount of Permanent Allowance. The amount of the permanent award under sections 2:50-37 of the Revision in suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony and from bed and board and under section 2:50-39 in suits for separate maintenance will be considered together, but the differences between these two sections should not be ignored. As to the amount, section 2:50-37 provides that it shall be lawful for the court to make orders "as the circumstances of the parties and the nature of the case shall render fit, reasonable and just," etc. Section 2:50-39 specifies that it shall be lawful for the court to decree and order "suitable support and maintenance-for such time as the nature of the case and circumstances of the parties render suitable and proper in the opinion of the court. from time to time, make further orders touching the same as shall be just and equitable," etc. These statutory grants are comprehensive and leave much to the discretion of the Chancellor as to the amount to be awarded, for it would be quite impossible for the legislature to anticipate, and prescribe for, the varying circumstances which are bound to arise. 

It is difficult, if not undesirable, to attempt to state general rules. 

No two cases are exactly alike. What would be just in one case might be unjust in another. "I have looked carefully into the books," observed Chancellor Pennington in an early case, "to see if there was any fixed, general rule for allowances of this character, and had I found one, would cheerfully have followed it. I can find no such rule, none has been furnished me, and indeed it would be impossible to frame one which would work justly in all cases. Certain rules have, indeed, been laid down from time to time, so as to form some guide; still, every case must depend very much on its own peculiar circumstances." The factors which do enter into and serve as a basis for the determination of the amount must be proved by legal evidence and the burden of proof is on the wife.10 In admeasuring the amount of the permanent alimony it is usual to fix a sum larger than that ordered pendente lite.¹¹ It has been customary to allot to the wife roughly one-third of the husband's income in cases in which the wife is not charged with the custody

13. The rule announced in Dietrick v. Dietrick," and quoted with approval in Schaeffer v. Schaeffer,18 each of which was a suit for divorce, summarizes most of the factors already enumerated, but for convenience the rule may be repeated: "No rigid standard can be set up whereby to measure in every case the amount of permanent alimony for the support of the wife, but it is usually about one-third of the husband's income. The amount is not fixed solely with regard, on the one hand, to the actual needs of the wife, nor, on the other, to the husband's actual means. 

There should be taken into account the physical condition and social position of the parties, the husband's property and income (including what he could derive from personal attention to business), and also the separate property and income of the wife.

With us sections 2:50-37 and 2:50-39 of the Revision do not expressly fix the time at which the permanent award is to commence. Here again the matter should rest in the sound discretion of the court. If the decree 22 is one for separate maintenance or for a divorce from bed and board, the permanent award, as an adjunct to the principal suit, should ordinarily be computed from the date of the final decree.23 This was the usual practice in connection with decrees of divorce from the bond of matrimony prior to the adoption of the provision for decrees nisi. Any payments made after the final decree on account of the temporary order were credited on the permanent allowance.24 Yet in the discretion of the court the award may run from the filing of the bill or petition in the main suit,25 particularly where there has been no order for temporary support.20 

In suits by the wife for divorce from the bond of matrimony the provision for permanent alimony is inserted in the decree nisi when the award is made as an adjunct to the main suit. Ordinarily, then, the permanent award will commence as of the date of the decree nisi, although, in the discretion of the court, the award may be ordered as of an earlier date, especially where no alimony pendente lite has been allowed. The permanent award may be computed from the date of filing of the petition for divorce, but a deduction for amounts paid under an order for alimony pendente lite will be allowed.27 § 377.

Formerly, the re-marriage of the wife after a final decree of absolute divorce did not have the effect of terminating the award, and the burden was on the husband to establish that his former wife was no longer in need of alimony. However, in the year 1933 section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907 was amended. This amendment became section 

2:50-38 in the Revision and provides: 

2:50-38. If after the decree of divorce the wife shall remarry, the court of chancery shall not make any order touching the alimony of such wife except that the court of chancery, upon application of the former husband, on notice and upon proof of the marriage of the former wife after the decree of divorce, must modify any order or decree touching the alimony of the former wife by vacating and annulling any and all provisions in any such order or decree, or both, directing the payment of money for the support of the former wife.

As to arrears of alimony, the statute seems to indicate that irrespective of the husband's application for cancellation the court is without jurisdiction to make any order touching the wife's alimony after her re-marriage. This would seem to forbid on the application of the former wife the attachment of her husband for contempt for failure to pay alimony whether the arrears had accumulated prior or subsequent to the wife's re-marriage. The only authority of the count under the section would seem to be that upon the application of the former husband on notice and upon proof of the re-marriage it must (mandatory) vacate and annul the order or decree so far as it pertains to the wife's alimony, and that such cancellation is to operate retrospectively as well as prospectively.Ⓡ -Procedure. 

Under section 2:50-38 the husband should file a petition in the cause, duly verified, and take an order to show cause, serving copies of all papers in the usual manner upon the wife. On the return of the order to show cause, if there is any dispute as to the facts, that is, if the wife's re-marriage or the date of it are in dispute, the matter must be set down for hearing. 

Since it is in the nature of a final determination it may not properly be determined upon affidavits if there are disputed facts. 

An oral hearing is also required where an order sought to be vacated makes provision not only for the wife but for children in her custody without separation of the two, so that it is necessary for the court to adjust the award by omitting that portion of it which may equitably be adjudged to be allocated to the wife's subsistence. Upon the hearing of that question the Court will take evidence with respect to the needs of the children and the faculties of the husband. The result will not necessarily be a reduction in the amount originally fixed, for it may appear that the circum-

§ 380. Effect of Death. 

The permanent award, whether made in a suit for divorce or for separate maintenance, terminates prospectively upon the death of either of the parties.15 The arrears, vested as they are,16 are collectible by the wife, or in the case of her death, by her representative.17 § 381.

The application for a reduction or an increase of the permanent allowance, whether the original order has been made in a suit for divorce or in a suit for separate maintenance, is by petition in the cause, duly verified, and order to show cause or by notice [Form 205 et. seq.], rather than by independent bill.11 Although in suits by the wife for absolute divorce the order for permanent alimony is inserted in the decree nisi,12 the order really is a separate and distinct order. The application for a modification is made to an Advisory Master although the original order had been advised by a Vice Chancellor under the former system.¹7 § 382. Alimony After Decree of Divorce. Under former statutes there was some doubt as to the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery to order permanent alimony after the entry of a domestic final decree of divorce in which no order or reservation had been made.18 All doubts, however, were resolved by the express provision in the Divorce Act of 1902 and in the present act (section 2:50-37 of the Revision) that the court may make an order touching the alimony of the wife, etc., "after decree of divorce." The statute includes applications for alimony after a final decree of divorce from bed and board as well as after the rendition of a decree of divorce from the bond of matrimony. 

The effect of the statute is to reserve to a successful wife in a suit for divorce the right to apply for alimony subsequent to decree nisi or final decree although the petition for divorce and the decree nisi are silent as to alimony. The divorce cause is kept open after final decree for original applications for alimony as well as for the modification of orders already made.19

3. OTHER LAWFUL WAYS AND MEANS. These may include the appointment of a receiver,23 as where the husband is a non-resident and fails to pay the taxes and interest on encumbrances.24 Upon proper application expenses for repairs to the property may be allowed to the receiver.25 The court may enjoin the husband from conveying away or disposing of his property 26 and may set aside a fraudulent conveyance made by the husband.27 Elsewhere is discussed the question of liability of the surety on a ne exeat bond.28 

Contempt. The award of alimony being the liquidation of the husband's obligation to support his wife and not a debt,29 the order may be enforced by process of contempt without violating the constitutional prohibition. The procedure is outlined farther on. It is discretionary with the court whether or not a husband who has failed to comply with an order for alimony, pendente lite or permanent, shall be adjudged in contempt. Thus such process was refused where the wife had an unexhausted levy on lands, subject only to a judgment alleged to have been fraudulently obtained, and where the wife delayed her application for nearly a year after the entry of a decree of dismissal. Pending appeal from the order requiring the husband to pay alimony, pendente lite or permanent, the order may not be enforced by contempt."

Execution. The enforcement of alimony orders "by such other lawful ways and means" includes enforcement by execution. An order for alimony, although a pendente lite order in a suit for divorce, may be enforced by execution under section 2:29-57 of the Revision (formerly section 44 of the Chancery Act) and the provision in the Execution Act relative to installment executions applies to orders of the Court of Chancery. The income from a spendthrift trust would seem to be subject to execution. Lien on Husband's Property. As another of the "lawful ways and means" the wife may file an abstract of the decree in the office of the Clerk of the Supreme Court in pursuance of the provisions of section 2:29-58 of the Revision. Although the order or decree adjudges a lien, no lien attaches as against a stranger unless an abstract is filed in the office of the Clerk of the Supreme Court.10 Alimony to accrue in futuro does not resemble a judgment at law within the meaning of the section, but accrued alimony does, and, if the decree is properly docketed in the office of the Clerk of the Supreme Court, it becomes a lien on the realty of the husband as fast as it accrues.11 Nevertheless, it is now necessary that the abstract show that the Court of Chancery has definitely fixed and established the amount of arrearages.12 For this purpose an order in Chancery must be entered, on notice, fixing such arrearages [Form 296].

Alimony After Foreign Decree of Absolute Divorce.

The jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery to award alimony to the wife and maintenance to the children in an independent proceeding under section 2:50-37 of the Revision (formerly section 25 of the 

Divorce Act of 1907) after the wife has obtained a valid final decree of absolute divorce in another state or country has been established in a case in the Court of Chancery. However, if the court of the foreign state or country retains jurisdiction over the matter of alimony, our court's jurisdiction is concurrent and special circumstances are required to invoke it. 

We have not yet had a case in which under the law of the jurisdiction where the divorce decree was granted the wife's right to alimony has been lost because of failure to include it in the final decree or where there has been an adjudication against the wife as to alimony. In such cases it may be urged that the matter of her alimony is res judicata. But not necessarily. If the law of the foreign jurisdiction be such as to require alimony to be included in the decree it is analagous to the statute of limitation. It does not affect the right, at least it does not affect our notion of the right to alimony which in civilized countries follows the husband wherever he goes. "State boundaries do not make court barriers."

It is matter for plea in abatement rather than for plea in bar. 

The right is there although it cannot be enforced. It is a matter of procedure rather than of substance. Where there has been an adjudication against the wife with respect to alimony in a foreign jurisdiction it may of course have been based upon the lack of any need for alimony at the time. A later application based upon the continuing or inchoate obligation, if need thereafter should arise, is not to be defeated by the application of the doctrine of

§ 386. Introductory. Jurisdiction was first conferred upon the Court of Chancery to decree divorces, and alimony as an incident thereto, in 1794,¹ but not until the year 1818 was the court empowered to order separate maintenance to the wife without a divorce. The enabling act was first enacted on February 4, 1818, and authorized the wife in an independent proceeding to sue her husband for support in case of his abandonment and refusal or neglect to support her. Without the aid of statute the Court of 

Chancery is without jurisdiction to award permanent maintenance to the wife, although it may be noted that decrees for mainte-

The original act conferring jurisdiction has been amended to some extent since it was first adopted. The history of these changes may be found by referring to a recent case. Presently, sections 2:50-39 and 

2:50-40 of the Revision make provision for the wife's separate maintenance. These sections were formerly section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907. The Revision makes no substantial changes. 

Sections 2:50-39 and 2:50-40 provide: 

2:50-39. If a husband, without justifiable cause, shall abandon his wife or separate himself from her and refuse or neglect to maintain and provide for her, the court of chancery may decree and order suitable support and maintenance to be paid and provided by the husband for the wife and her children, or any of them, by their marriage, or to be made out of his property and for such time as the nature of the case and circumstances of the parties render suitable and proper in the opinion of the court. The court may compel the defendant to give reasonable security for such maintenance and allowance and may, from time to time, make further orders touching the same as shall be just and equitable and enforce such decree and orders in the manner mentioned in section 

2:50-37 of this title. During the time such maintenance shall be allowed, the husband shall not be chargeable with the debts of the wife. 

2:50-40. When a husband cannot be found within this state to be served with process, his estate, property and effects within this state and the rents and profits thereof may be sequestered to compel his appearance and performance of any decree or order which may be made in the suit. Such process of sequestration shall be issued only upon special order therefor, to be made upon proof of the claim alleged in the bill and that the defendant cannot be found within the state for the service of process. в 

In some respects sections 2:50-39 and 2:50-40 of the Revision have been duplicated in the statute relating to the settlement and relief of the poor." The purpose of sections 2:50-39 and 2:50-40

is to enable the wife to secure support from the husband in a direct proceeding where he abandons or separates himself from her without justifiable cause and refuses or neglects suitably to support her, and thus to remove the necessity of her resorting to the uncertain, circuitous and unsatisfactory remedy provided by the common law. The obligation of the husband to support his wife is created by the marriage. The decree for maintenance merely liquidates or admeasures the obligation as of the time of its entry, whether it is based upon evidence or entered by consent." 

The view has been repeatedly expressed that section 26 (now section 2:50-39 of the Revision) should be construed to give the wife a right of action against her husband whenever she separates from him under such circumstances as will enable a third person to maintain an action against him for necessaries furnished to her.10 The express exemption contained in the statute, protecting the husband from liability for the wife's debts during the time maintenance is allowed by the decree, or order of the court, supports this construction. However, as will be noted below, section 

2:50-39 (section 26 of the 1907 Divorce Act) has been construed as not permitting the wife to bring a direct proceeding in every case in which, under the common law, she may pledge his credit.11-12

Although the order is entered by consent, the award is not a debt within the constitutional prohibition against imprisonment.183

§ 388. 

Residence. Under earlier statutes conferring jurisdiction upon the Court of Chancery to award separate maintenance certain residential requirements were prescribed. As late as the 

Divorce Act of 1902 a residential requirement was made a condition for the exercise of the jurisdiction of the court in separate maintenance cases.2 27

The Divorce Act of 1902 was expressly repealed in the schedule to the Divorce Act of 1907,28 and while in suits for divorce and nullity of marriage the Divorce Act of 1907 expressly provided for certain domiciliary requirements which have already been discussed,2° it omitted to provide any residential requirements in suits for separate maintenance under section 

26 of the Divorce Act of 1907. Section 2:50-39 of the Revision does not differ in this respect from section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907. Nevertheless, we are without a definite determination as to whether the wife or the husband must be domiciled in this state at the commencement of the suit for separate maintenance. 

We do have conflicting dicta on the one hand to the effect that domicile is not necessary,¹ and on the other hand to the effect that the domicile of at least one of the parties is essential. The suit for separate maintenance is unlike the suit for divorce and nullity of marriage. Essentially it is a transitory action looking towards a money decree, not wholly dissimilar to the ordinary money decree in equity. prerequisite to relief under the separate maintenance statute.' The statute is in the disjunctive "refuse or neglect," and if the husband is guilty of a refusal or a neglect to support his wife and has abandoned her, relief will be decreed. To establish a refusal, a demand before the institution of the suit may be essential. The husband may not urge that he is under an order of another court to support his wife if, in fact, he has failed or refused to comply with such order. Nor may the husband offer a prior settlement in bar if the wife actually is in need of maintenance. Nevertheless, the income of the wife derived from a gross sum settlement may amount to suitable support in particular cases.10 A husband who almost immediately following the separation of the parties and before the filing of the bill offers to make a reasonable allowance to the wife and who constantly is ready to pay the money and frequently attempts to persuade his wife to accept a suitable allowance is not guilty of a refusal or neglect to maintain his wife. Yet an offer by the husband, pending suit, of rooms to live in with him has been held not to be sufficient to prevent a preliminary award of maintenance.12 The support contemplated by the statute is a suitable and proper support according to the nature of the case and the circumstances of the parties. The court may determine whether the support afforded, or offered to, a wife is suitable and proper, and, if it is not and the other conditions exist, it may enter a decree in favor of the wife for the proper amount.13 In conformity with this notion, the husband who abandons his wife cannot dictate the manner in which the money which he contributes to the support of his family shall be spent and the stores at which his wife is to make purchases by extending credit in such stores only, but he must pay her in cash the

§ 392. -Abandonment or Separation. An abandonment or separation by the husband of his wife is an essential element to be proved by the wife in a suit for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision. As yet our courts have not clearly distinguished between the words "abandon" and "separate," as used in the statute.15 In many instances an abandonment under section 2:50-39 has been regarded, except for the two years' requirement, as synonymous with a desertion in suits for divorce. 

However, the differences between a desertion and an abandonment should not be ignored, especially in cases where a maintenance decree is sought to be utilized in a subsequent suit by the wife for divorce to prove the original desertion.16 These differences are several. The intent (the willfulness) of the husband to abandon his wife has been recognized in the cases,17 but there has been a tendency to adjudge the husband guilty of an abandonment although the wife actively consents to his actual separation from her.18 In addition, it may be noticed that the commission of adultery by the husband outside of the home justifies the wife in leaving and claiming an abandonment,19 although in suits for divorce for a constructive desertion based upon the husband's adultery, the offense must have been committed within the home.20 

Furthermore, a foreign decree of divorce from bed and board may prevent or arrest the running of a desertion period, but will not preclude a charge of abandonment if the husband fails to pay support in compliance with the order.21 Then again, the possible different consequences which attach where the parties are separated by mutual consent should be noticed.22

§ 393. Departure by Wife; Constructive Abandonment. 

In the absence of the commission of a matrimonial offense by the husband and in the absence of the husband's consent to a separation, it is the duty of the wife to live with her husband at his home and to give to him her services and society.10 The wife may not abandon her husband and obtain support under the separate maintenance statute where, without justifiable cause, she actually leaves him or drives him away.11 Nevertheless, if the wife leaves without cause, repents, and offers in good faith to return, and has not been guilty of a matrimonial offense, she is entitled to relief if the husband refuses to take her back and neglects or refuses suitably to maintain her.12 If the wife leaves without justifiable cause, and especially where she has remained away a considerable length of time in consequence of which the husband had broken up housekeeping, he should be allowed a reasonable time in which to provide a new home and should be given assurances that she will return to him before he can properly be charged

§ 394. -Non-support as Abandonment.

§ 396. Justifiable Cause. Justifiable cause for the husband's abandonment in a suit for separate maintenance is the commission by the wife of a matrimonial offense. As in suits for divorce for desertion,22 nothing short of the commission of an offense by the wife, cognizable as a cause for divorce, will excuse the husband's abandonment.23 If desertion by the wife is urged by the husband as justification, it must be a desertion continuously obstinate as well as willful 24 for the term of two years.25 If the husband seeks to justify his separation on the ground of extreme cruelty, the alleged extreme cruelty of the wife must be proved to have been of the same degree as is necessary to warrant a decree of divorce for extreme cruelty. § 398. Effect of Consent to Separation. The inquiry here is as to the effect of the consent of either of the parties to the separation, whether the consent is oral or in writing, on the question of abandonment or separation without justifiable cause. suits for divorce for desertion it has already been observed that ordinarily a desertion cannot exist or persist as against the husband if the parties have separated by mutual consent, whether such consent is oral or is evidenced by articles of separation, unless and until the wife elects to terminate the separation by demanding a resumption of marital relations.15 Undoubtedly, the wife may terminate the separation by requesting a re-union,16 and in the absence of the commission of a matrimonial offense by her a refusal on the part of the husband to accede to the wife's demand would constitute an abandonment or separation without justifiable cause in a suit for separate maintenance. 

A separation agreement has been held not to constitute a bar to the suit for separate maintenance where the wife has subsequently sought a resumption of matrimonial relations.17 The wife has

"His failure to support her," observed the Vice Chancellor, "is an abandonment within the purview of our statute, in the absence of evidence that her original departure from his home or her continued absence has been under circumstances and of a nature to relieve him of the obligation of seeking her return. In short, all that is decided at this time is that when a wife resides away from her husband with his consent the husband's obligation to support her continues.' "26 At common law the husband is responsible for the wife's support during a separation with his consent, and she may pledge his credit for necessaries." The separate maintenance statute was enacted for the purpose of furnishing a direct remedy against the husband in lieu of the circuitous and unsatisfactory remedy provided for by the common law where the parties have separated, so that the enforcement of the husband's obligation in this direct proceeding where the parties have separated by consent would seem to be within the legislative intent. Such construction of the statute seems as reasonable as the interpretation which permits a wife to sue for separate maintenance where the parties have been forbidden to cohabit by the terms of a foreign decree of divorce from bed and board.28 Nevertheless, the cases cannot be reconciled without difficulty. In several instances the court has declined to award separate maintenance despite the dismissal of the husband's counterclaim for divorce for desertion on the ground that he had failed to make just advances, or, in other words, that the separation was with his consent. § 399. 

Effect of Decree A Mensa. In suits for divorce for desertion a foreign decree of divorce from bed and board, which restrains cohabitation until vacated by the court, will prevent or arrest the running of a period of willful and obstinate desertion whether the decree has been obtained at the suit of the wife or of the husband. But under the separate maintenance statute a husband may be guilty of an abandonment or separation without justifiable cause despite the order of the foreign court forbidding the cohabitation of the parties, at least where he has failed to contribute any support to his wife under the order of the court. [See Form 228.] In Freund v. Freund the parties were divorced from bed and board by the decree of a New York court which also ordered the husband to support his wife. The decree adjudged that the husband had abandoned his wife. The husband had failed to comply with the order, removed from the jurisdiction, concealed his residence and was finally discovered in New Jersey living in adultery. The demurrer (the practice then existing) was overruled on the ground that "abandonment" under section

The Freund case was followed by Tehsman v. Tehsman, and by Reik v. Reik. In the Tehsman case the court excluded evidence as to the husband's request for the resumption of marital relations. "Assuming that it (a letter) was written in good faith," observed the Chief Justice, "and showed an honest repentance on the part of the husband for his cruel treatment of the complainant, his repentance came too late to be of any avail to him so far as his legal responsibility to support his wife in a state of separation was concerned. The decree of the New York court established her right to live apart from him for the rest of her life if she wished to do so, notwithstanding any effort on his part to bring her back, and his tardy repentance not existing until after that decree was entered cannot operate to deprive her of the right thereby conferred upon her." 

The objection that the suit for separate maintenance is vexatious and unnecessary so long as the foreign decree a mensa is operative seems to have gained much less recognition than it has where the foreign decree was for a divorce from the bond of matrimony.Ⓡ 

At any rate, a husband should not be obligated to furnish support under two different decrees. If separate maintenance is to be awarded to a wife who has already obtained a foreign decree for support which is still in force, the decree should be conditioned on the vacation of the former order, and the court should not enforce the decree if the wife is collecting under the foreign decree."

§ 401.  By reason of section 9 of the 

Divorce Act of 1907 the process and procedure in suits for separate maintenance was essentially the general practice in the Court of Chancery.¹¹ Section 9 became section 2:50-19 in the Revision of 1937 and for some reason the section was restricted to suits for divorce and nullity of marriage instead of "in all such causes" as it was in section 9 of the Divorce Act of 1907. However, this omission was cured by legislation in 1938.12 It is not intended to treat of the general chancery practice here, but the reader may refer to several of the local textbooks 13 and to the sections hereinbefore relating to process and procedure in divorce and nullity suits wherein some of the general practice has been discussed.¹4 -Pleading. Since the Divorce Act of 1907 was silent as to whether the suit for separate maintenance was to be commenced by bill or petition, the general chancery practice 15 was applicable by reason of section 9 of the 1907 Act.16 Section 9 became section 2:50-19 of the Revision. No provision was made in that section for procedure in separate maintenance suits, but the 1938 Legislature has provided that the procedure shall be the same in such suits as in other cases in Chancery unless the Chancellor shall promulgate a rule otherwise.17 Until a rule is promulgated providing for the commencement of such suits by petition and order to show cause or citation (which at this writing has not been done), the suit is by bill and subpoena. The suit for separate maintenance may proceed in personam or quasi in rem. When the suit is in personam, the defendant is served with the usual process in suits in chancery, the subpoena ad respondendum, rather than with the citation which is the process issued in divorce and nullity suits. The defendant must be served within the state before the court may enter a personal decree against him, unless the defendant appears generally in the cause. Under the new Rule (290) a true copy of the bill must be annexed to and served with the subpoena. If a writ of ne exeat is served, the service of a subpoena is not necessary in the ordinary case. 10 But in view of Rule 290 requiring that a true copy of the bill be annexed to and served with the subpoena, it would seem to be the better practice in separate maintenance suits that the subpoena and true copy of the bill, or at least a true copy of the bill, be served when the sheriff executes the writ of ne exeat.

SEPARATE MAINTENANCE -Reference, etc. When the cause for separate maintenance is at issue, the procedure does not differ essentially from that already outlined in the chapter on process and procedure in divorce and nullity suits.13 [See Forms 236-240.] The cause is referred to an Advisory Master in the vicinage for final hearing. Rules 284, 285 as to fees for reference also apply. For failure of the complainant to prosecute, the bill is dismissed under Rule 203 rather than under Rule 286 which applies only to divorce and nullity suits.14 

Where the bill is dismissed after hearing, the decree should state the ground of the dismissal to the extent of showing whether the petitioner failed to show an abandonment or failed to show a neglect or refusal to maintain and provide for the wife to the end that, in a subsequent suit between the parties in which the decree is set up in bar, it will not be necessary for the court to examine the prior record or testimony [Form 240].

 § 405. Amount of Allowance. The amount of the allow ance, pendente lite and permanent, has, for convenience, been considered in connection with the awards in suits for divorce.28 

§ 406. Termination of Order. A decree for separate mainte nance in a suit under section 2:50-39 of the Revision goes no further than to adjudge that the husband without justifiable cause abandons and separates himself from his wife and refuses or neglects suitably to maintain her. Through its decree the court orders suitable support for the wife and children, but it does not order a separation of the parties for a limited time or permanently as is the case under a decree of divorce from bed and board. 

The maintenance decree in effect is nothing more than a money decree which liquidates as of a particular time the husband's obligation to support his wife while they are living in a state of separation. The way is open under the maintenance decree to an immediate restoration of the conjugal relation if each of the parties so desires. Where the maintenance decree has been premised upon a simple abandonment by the husband, as distinguished from a constructive abandonment, the husband may offer to resume cohabitation and upon making advances he is entitled to a vacation of the decree.29 These advances must be bona fide,¹ and must be made within the two years' period following the entry of the decree or else a cause of action for divorce for desertion may vest in favor of the wife.2 

If the maintenance decree was based upon a constructive abandonment by reason of the husband's adultery, the wife is not compelled to accept the husband's advances. The law will not compel her to condone such offense. Nor will the law compel the wife to sue for an absolute divorce for the husband's adultery. Although the maintenance decree was based upon a simple abandonment, the commission of adultery by the husband subse-

If the maintenance decree was based upon a constructive abandonment by reason of the husband's extreme cruelty, it is not to be supposed that the wife is bound to accept advances or to condone the offense in view of the vested character of the offense of extreme cruelty." This question has been noticed previously in connection with suits by the wife for divorce for constructive desertion." If a wife who obtains a maintenance decree based upon the husband's adultery or extreme cruelty refuses to sue for divorce on the ground of adultery or extreme cruelty or for constructive desertion at the end of two years, the decree for maintenance at the option of the wife becomes in effect a decree of divorce from bed and board. If the wife remains chaste, she may enforce the separation indefinitely at her choice and there is no method whereby the husband may alter the status and escape payment of support under the decree. 

If the parties become reconciled after the entry of a decree for separate maintenance, it will be cause for vacating the decree." 

At least a reconciliation in good faith would terminate the order as to payments which would have become due but for the reconciliation and to this extent at least the order may be vacated.⁹ 

But as to arrears of maintenance due under the final decree up to the time of reconciliation there may be some uncertainty.10 Such arrears vest as they become due, but perhaps it may be contended that the court should not enforce payment of arrears on the ground that such enforcement may impede the continued restoration of the conjugal relation.¹¹ However, as respects creditors, by the express terms of section 2:50-39 the husband is not chargeable with the wife's debts during the time such maintenance is allowed.

§ 411. Nature of Allowance. Not infrequently the word "alimony" has been used to include as well the allowance of suit money, including counsel fee.¹ Alimony is the allowance for the support of the wife, while suit money is the allowance made to the wife to prosecute or defend the suit, including counsel fee.2 In the matter of suit money in a suit for divorce the wife is more favored than when she seeks alimony. The matter is sui generis, resting in the discretion of the court.* 3 The allowance of a counsel fee does not establish a debt within the constitutional prohibition against imprisonment. Unless the court has secured jurisdiction of the person of the defendant, no order, operative in personam, may be made for alimony or for suit money, including counsel fee. It has been customary to regard the allowance of counsel fee as an allowance to the wife for the benefit of the solicitor and not as a direct allowance to the solicitor. The claim of the wife to counsel fee has been considered as a purely personal right so that, if the wife dies before the claim has been liquidated by an order of the court, the claim may not be pressed by her personal representative. Nevertheless, it has been held that the reconciliation

§ 412. Suits in Which Allowed. Ordinarily, an award of suit money, including counsel fee, is made to the wife in suits for divorce and for separate maintenance.11 In suits for nullity of marriage where the decree of nullity is in favor of the husband it was thought formerly that an allowance for counsel fee would be improper,¹² but recently the court has been of the opinion that in a proper case counsel fee may be awarded to the wife under the statute although the decree for nullity is in favor of the husband.18 

However, in this case, in which the wife sued for divorce and the husband succeeded on his counterclaim for nullity for impotence, the court adjudged that under the circumstances an additional allowance after decree would be improper and denied the application.14 Upon a decree of nullity of marriage in favor of the wife counsel fee has been allowed.15

§ 415. 

Enforcement. The enforcement of the order, as well as the award itself, is not dependent upon the statute. However, the methods employed to enforce alimony 20 are usually available for the enforcement of suit money. The method of enforcement is largely within the discretion of the Chancellor. If the husband is petitioner, his suit may be stayed until he complies with the order pendente lite.21 Counsel fee allowed pendente lite may be enforced by process of contempt although the order for payment is embodied in the final decree of dismissal.22 Execution is available, including an installment execution.28

As respects agreements between the solicitor and wife, alimony is available, if so ordered, for the payment of counsel fee.24 

§ 416. § 418. 

Source of Right to Sue. Any person, however poor, being otherwise competent, has the same right as another to sue in the Court of Chancery. If in fact such person be indigent and have a probable cause of action he or she may be permitted in the discretion of the court to sue in forma pauperis.¹ In matrimonial suits section 2:50-18 of the Revision makes express provision for the prosecution of suits in forma pauperis. The section provides: 

2:50-18. Whenever any poor person shall have cause of suit under this chapter, and shall make an affidavit that he is not worth one hundred dollars clear estate, the chancellor may, at his discretion, assign to such person a solicitor and counsel learned in the law, to prosecute the cause, who, together with all other officers, shall perform their respective duties therein without fee or reward.2

In England the Court of Chancery followed without statutory authority the practice of the law courts, based upon the statute 

11 Henry 7, c. 12. In New Jersey a general act was passed January 28, 1799,³ later substantially incorporated in the Practice Act. 

The Act of 1799 related to equity and law actions, but seems to

There is ample inherent jurisdiction in the court to make orders in forma pauperis at any stage of the suit up to final decree." § 419. 

Matrimonial Suits in Which Allowed; Appeal. -Divorce. Applications for leave to prosecute suits for divorce are expressly included in section 2:50-18 of the Revision. -Nullity of Marriage. Applications for leave to prosecute suits to annul marriages on statutory grounds are also expressly included in section 2:50-18. It would seem that the power of the court to grant leave to sue in forma pauperis is not confined to cases arising under the statute," although there appears to be no reported case in New Jersey on the point. Where the application is for leave to bring suit in forma pauperis to annul a void marriage, the court is not deterred by considerations of public policy which often influence it in dealing with applications for leave to sue in forma pauperis for divorce." -Separate Maintenance. While applications for leave to bring suits for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the 

Revision in forma pauperis are within section 2:50-18, there appears to be no reported case in New Jersey in which such an application has been granted. No leave to sue in forma pauperis should ordinarily be granted in this class of actions, because if the husband be indigent the suit cannot benefit the wife, and if he have financial means he should be ordered to pay suit, money. 

However, if it appear that the wife cannot raise the $25.00 deposit required upon the filing of the bill and that the husband has financial means, the court may permit the suit to be instituted in forma pauperis on condition that application for allowance of suit moneys as against the husband be made promptly

§ 425. Matters Governing Disposition of Application. In granting or denying applications for leave to sue in forma pauperis the court will be governed by a sound discretion. The matter is purely discretionary, and before granting such leave the court must be convinced that substantial justice requires that it be granted." If a previous application has been denied, that fact will preclude the granting of leave upon a subsequent petition, unless the circumstances have substantially changed. The investigation of every application should include inquiry as to whether an earlier application has been made. 

It must appear from the inquiry that the applicant probably has a good cause of action,28 that the domiciliary requirements of jurisdiction 29 are present,¹ that the application is made in the utmost good faith,² and that the applicant is a person of deserving character.8

Ordinarily, where it appears that petitioner's parents, children or other members of her family are financially able to provide funds for the prosecution of the suit, her application will be denied.*

If the petitioner's object in securing a divorce is to marry again and such new marriage has been arranged, the situation may be such that her application to proceed in forma pauperis ought to be denied on the ground that the man who intends to marry her should be required to advance the necessary funds. Where no such re-marriage has been arranged, but it is probable that petitioner may be able to re-marry advantageously with the result that she and her children will be the less likely to become public charges, her application may be granted.5 

The petitioner's motive in seeking a divorce is always an important subject of inquiry. The wife's application may properly be granted where she seeks a divorce in order to secure protection against molestation by a husband afflicted with a loathsome venereal disease contracted through adulterous acts, or where the husband's degenerate tendencies have so affected the petitioner as to cause her to attempt suicide on several occasions," or where defendant split open petitioner's head with an axe, resulting in affecting her mentality and her rehabilitation was retarded by the continuation of the marital status, or where petitioner's parents, residing in another state, engage to provide employment for petitioner and her child on condition that she secure a divorce, thus relieving this state of the burden." The relief or probable relief of the state from the burden of support is often a controlling consideration. Thus leave was denied where it appeared that, if granted, the petitioner would in all probability ultimately become a burden on the state, so that the preservation of the matrimonial status was in the interest of the state by keeping the husband criminally chargeable with his wife's support and maintenance.10 

Where the petitioner is in receipt of income barely sufficient to provide the necessaries of life, her receipt thereof will not preclude the granting of her application where the other circumstances are such as to move the court to grant such leave.¹¹ But where it appears that her husband's failure to provide over a long period of time has been due largely to her acquiescence and her failure to pursue her remedies to enforce support, her application may be denied.12 In a case where petitioner was receiving

§ 426. Filing Papers and Order.
