Disbursements and Compensation. After an order has been made granting leave to sue in forma pauperis Rule 289 is applicable. It provides:

Except as provided by any order of the court no solicitor or counsel, or other person, shall take or agree to take, or seek to obtain, payment of any fee, profit or reward for the conduct of such proceedings, for office or other expenses; and no solicitor or counsel shall be required to expend any of his own money in the prosecution of cause in forma pauperis. 

All disbursements required to be made in connection with the suit, such as the cost of postage, advertising, and witnesses' fees, must be found by the applicant,14 but all services of officers of the court are gratuitous.15 The applicant is not to be placed under any disability with respect to his suit because of his inability to pay for services rendered to him.10

This rule seems to have been departed from in England in the cases cited by Biddle and with good reason, for if any such costs are recovered they should go for the benefit of the "Counsel and Clerks," whose "Labour" would unjustly enrich the pauper if he were permitted to retain them.

17. Biddle, N. J. Divorce (2nd Ed.) p. 176. 

Rule 288 provides 

18. Scatchmer v. Foulkard, 1 Eq. Rep. 125, 21 Eng. Rep. 931. There is a dictum to the same effect in Rice v. Brown, 1 Bos. & Pul. 39, 126 Eng.

§ 551 

The court may at any time, upon good cause being shown or appearing therefor, discharge the order for leave to sue as a poor person; and may order such dispauperized person to pay costs.

The statute impliedly authorizes the court to revoke orders to sue in forma pauperis previously made, in the exercise of its discretion.10 Upon revocation of such order the court may order the person so dispaupered to pay costs.20 

The court is careful to make no orders except in cases clearly calling for it and it is correspondingly alert to revoke an order when it is shown that it should not have been made or that, since it was made, the circumstances of the case have changed. At least until final decree the court possesses the power to make an order at any stage of the suit dispaupering the applicant. 

The phrase "at any time" appears to have been limited in practice to any time prior to the final decree. There seems to be no reported case in which after final decree the party has been dispaupered and ordered to pay costs. In principle, however, there seems to be no reason why this cannot be done in a proper case. 

There are cases which arise in practice in which the pauper is proved to be able to pay a small amount, not sufficient to cover costs if they were taxed. It is within the discretion of the court to allow such smaller amount to be accepted by the solicitor and applied either entirely to his own fees or distributed between the solicitor, sheriff and the officers of the court. There is nothing inconsistent in accepting a sum from the pauper less than sufficient to pay costs, if taxed, without dispaupering such person. An order to dispauper will not be made, however, until the full amount sufficient to pay the taxed costs and a reasonable sum for counsel fee has been paid. 

In a suit prosecuted by a wife in forma pauperis she may apply for alimony or maintenance pendente lite. If the situation disclosed upon the motion be such as to indicate that the defendant is able to pay suit moneys, the court will make an appropriate order to that effect, which when obeyed will be followed by an order dispaupering the petitioner on motion of petitioner's solicitor or on the court's own motion. In such case it is the duty of the wife's solicitor to advise the court that such payment has been made. [See Forms 245A, 247, 247A].

430. STATUS OF THE FOREIGN DECREE 431. JURISDICTION OF FOREIGN COURT 432. NECESSITY OF FINAL DECREE 433. SUIT IN CHANCERY OR AT LAW § 430. Status of the Foreign Decree. Section 2:50-35 of the Revision applies to foreign decrees of divorce and nullity of marriage,¹ but has no application to the enforcement of foreign decrees for alimony except as the alimony phase of the decree may stand or fall with the decree of divorce of which in most jurisdictions it is an incident. As

Unlike a valid foreign decree of divorce or of nullity of marriage, a decree or judgment of a foreign court for alimony or maintenance is not self-executing in this state. The foreign decree for alimony has no efficacy in this state as a judgment. in the case of ordinary foreign judgments for money, it must be reduced to a domestic judgment or decree to have any vitality for the purpose of enforcement, and then it may be enforced only in the mode and manner in which judgments of the court are customarily executed. Equity will decline specifically to enforce the mandate of a foreign court that the husband execute a mortgage to the wife as security for the alimony decreed notwithstanding that the situs of the property is in New Jersey.³ 2

§ 432. Necessity of Final Decree. Under the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution a suit need not be allowed on a money decree of a sister state unless the decree is a final decree. Such a decree is final if by the law of the state in which the decree is rendered the alimony becomes vested as accrued. 

The principles underlying this phase of the enforcement of foreign decrees of alimony as to alimony accrued and alimony to accrue in the future have been elaborately discussed in our own cases as well as in cases in the United States Supreme Court.

REVISION OF ORDERS TERMINATION OF AWARD ENFORCEMENT 446. CHILDREN OF PARENTS DIVORCED IN FOREIGN JURISDICTION 447. CHILDREN OF PARENTS LIVING SEPARATELY § 434. Liability at Common Law. The duty of a husband at common law to support his wife and his responsibility at law to third persons who supply her with necessaries are quite clear.¹ 

By the natural law the father, and the mother as well, are under a duty to provide for and maintain their children." But the 

Supreme Court, following the English precedents, has declined to translate this natural duty into a legal duty in such wise as to hold the father liable to third persons for necessaries furnished to his child. In the law courts the duty of the father is no more than a moral duty and, in order to hold the father responsible to third persons, his authorization, express or implied, must be shown. The English case relied upon by the Supreme Court postdated the revolution and hence was not binding as part of our common law. This rule of ours, based, as it is, on the de- 4

Court of Errors and Appeals has not as yet passed upon the point.

No duty rested upon a brother or sister at common law to support an indigent brother or sister. A number of statutes have imposed the responsibility of support for a minor child on the father and mother and on other persons. In England the statute of 43 Eliz. c. 2 charged the father and mother, grandfather and grandmother of poor, impotent persons with the responsibility of maintenance. This statute is the prototype of our own act for the settlement and relief of the poor.10 -Illegitimate Children. The mother is the natural guardian of her illegitimate offspring and, while it has been stated that the law from an early day has imposed upon her the duty of its maintenance,¹¹ yet there is authority that at common law there was no obligation on the mother to maintain her bastard child.12 Nor was the putative father liable at common law.13 However, statutory enactments provide that the father and mother are responsible.14

§ 440. Upon Decree for Separate Maintenance. Section 2:50-39 of the Revision (formerly section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907) expressly authorizes an allowance for the children of the marriage in case the decree goes for the wife. In the absence of an assumption by the husband of the obligation, children of the wife by a former marriage are not included. However, on the basis of estoppel and the specific performance of contract the court has ordered a husband to support an illegitimate child of the wife.⁹

It has not been the uniform practice in matrimonial causes to fix a sum for the children in the decree separate from that awarded to the wife as alimony, but this practice has been suggested.¹ The allotment of a separate sum for the maintenance of the children may assist the court should the matter subsequently come before it. It has been held that alimony awarded in a decree nisi to the wife and children in a lump sum may not subsequently be apportioned with retroactive effect.15 If the amount awarded to the mother for the maintenance of the children prove insufficient, the proper course is to apply to the Court of Chancery for an increase rather than to appeal from the order.16

The extent of the allowance for the child has not been, and naturally cannot be, determined with absolute precision. With respect to the enforcement of the allowance for the child made in suit for divorce or for separate maintenance, the methods available are the same as those already noticed for the enforcement of orders for the support of the wife.20 Usually the sum allotted to the wife for her support is lumped with that allowed for the child and the one order is enforced. The award for the child would seem to be no more a debt within the constitutional prohibition against imprisonment than is the allowance for the wife, so that process of contempt is equally proper.¹ 

§ 446. Children of Parents Divorced in Foreign Jurisdic tion.2

Section 9:2-1 of the Revision concerning minors pro vides that after a divorce decreed in a foreign jurisdiction, if minor children of the marriage are inhabitants of this state, the Court of Chancery on the petition of either parent, or of a next friend in behalf of the children, such notice being given to parents as the court shall direct, may make such decree concerning their care, custody, education and maintenance as if the divorce had been obtained in this state, etc. This section was enacted in 1871 as a part of the Divorce Act, but since the year 1902 the statute was included as part of the Minors' Act. The section was amended in 1936 and became section 9:2-1 of the Revision.

Under this section the child must be an inhabitant of the state, but, if he is not, the court, nevertheless, may take jurisdiction in an independent proceeding under section 2:50-37 of the Revision. The power of the court to "make" orders for the child's support and custody includes also the authority to revise such orders although no reservation is made in the original order.Ⓡ 

Likewise, the power to "make" orders as if the divorce had been obtained in this state would seem to permit enforcement of such orders in the same manner as orders are enforced when made incidentally to a suit for divorce in this state. It is likely that the court will allow maintenance pendente lite for the child in a proceeding under section 9:2-1 of the Revision or in an independent proceeding under section 2:50-37, although neither of these sections expressly so provide.10 

Section 9:2-1 was first enacted at a time when "divorce" included "nullity" 11 and, consequently, it is probable that the intention of the legislature was to provide, as well, for children of parents whose marriage has been annulled in a foreign jurisdiction. The word "divorce" comprehends divorces from bed and board as well as divorces from the bond of matrimony. -Procedure. As directed by the statute, the suit is commenced by the filing of a petition [Form 333] and by "such notice being given to parents as the court shall direct" [Form 334]. If a personal decree for the support of the child is sought, process must be served upon the defendant within the state,12 but, if the defendant is a non-resident and has property within the state, the court may issue the writ of sequestration as original process and decree support to the extent of the property sequestered.13

General Jurisdiction of Chancery. Prior to the 

Revolution the Court of Chancery in England exercised a general jurisdiction over infants. "This court ," observed Lord Hardwicke, "has a general right delegated by the Crown as pater patriae, so (sic) interfere in particular cases, for the benefit of such who are incapable to protect themselves. And it is no objection, that the father of such persons be living; for infants, in the life of their father, sue in this Court by prochein amy, and 567 1

§ 448 

defend by guardian." 1 With us the general jurisdiction of the 

Chancellor by virtue of his high office to establish the permanent control and custody over infants has been recognized. "The existence of a general equity jurisdiction over the custody of the persons of infants has been finally settled in this state This jurisdiction is placed upon the exercise by the chancellor as parens patriae of a portion of the powers which in this capacity originally vested in the chancellor of England, as the representative of the king, to whom, as sovereign, in the character of parens patriae, the duty of protecting infants was attributed." " 

The general jurisdiction of the Chancellor over the custody of infants, which may be contrasted with the want of inherent jurisdiction with respect to compelling a parent to support his child,* exists in pari passu with, and is not dependent upon, statutory grants. The exact limits of the general jurisdiction have never been defined. This jurisdiction is much more extensive than the grants conferred upon the court by the statutes." Nor is the general jurisdiction of the Chancellor restricted by the use of the writ of habeas corpus as process to bring the infant before him.'

Other courts have exercised a jurisdiction over the custody of minor children. In England the Court of King's Bench exercised a jurisdiction on habeas corpus, but there seems to have been some confusion as to whether the court might, in addition to liberating the infant, also dispose of its permanent custody. This same uncertainty seems to have prevailed in the cases coming before our Supreme Court on habeas corpus. The Act of

§ 449. 

Jurisdiction in Matrimonial Causes. By "matri monial causes" is meant suits for nullity of marriage, whether instituted under the statute pertaining to divorce or under the general equity jurisdiction of the court, suits for divorce from the bond of matrimony and from bed and board, and suits by the wife for separate maintenance.

In England until 1857 the ecclesiastical courts, as already observed, took cognizance of causes matrimonial.22 The jurisdiction was restricted to the granting of decrees of nullity and decrees of separation. As incidental to a decree for separation the court awarded alimony to the wife. However, the spiritual courts declined to make any orders affecting the custody of the children. "It is no part of my duty," observed Dr. Lushington, "to consider, and I have not a shadow of authority to determine, whether the wife is or is not to have the custody of the children: the whole matter as to the care and custody of children belongs to another jurisdiction." 28 Recourse was usually had to the Court of Chancery.24

With us the jurisdiction to dissolve marriages has been lodged with the Court of Chancery. The jurisdiction is statutory, except in suits for nullity of marriage based upon fraud, duress and possibly certain types of mistake.25 Together with the grant of jurisdiction to decree divorces the legislature in section 2:50-37 

of the Revision (formerly section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907) 

has conferred upon the Court of Chancery in certain cases the authority to award alimony to the wife and to make orders "touching the care, custody, education and maintenance of the

The procedure on application for an order of custody pendente lite does not differ essentially from the practice on application for allowances pendente lite. If the wife is the moving party, the order as to the custody may be incorporated in the same order allowing her alimony and suit money pendente lite.10 " 11 In disposing of the custody of infants pendente lite the court ordinarily will not look into the merits of the case to determine the truth or falsity of the charge. "The duty of the Court was to look at all the actual circumstances of the present application: the age of children, the position in which they find themselves in relation to other members of the family, the fact that a suit is pending between the parents, in which such and such charges are made on both sides, but not to attempt to ascertain the truth or falsehood of the charges." So a wife charged with adultery who petitioned for custody of her children pendente lite was awarded their custody where in answer to her petition no charge against her character was made. 12 Nevertheless, in a suit for divorce for adultery against the wife wherein the husband petitioned for the custody of a child seven years of age, alleging that the mother was unfit and supporting such allegations by affidavits, the court gave the child to the grandmother because of the wife's failure to deny the charge by answer or by affidavit.13

§ 457. -Enforcement. Under section 2:50-37 of the Re vision orders relating to the custody of children made in divorce and nullity suits may be enforced substantially in the same manner as are orders for alimony.26 The court may require security to insure obedience to an order for access 27 and may enforce its order by process of contempt.28 Furthermore, the court may issue the writ of ne exeat to keep a parent within the state to answer the exigencies of an order for access to a minor child by the other parent.29 In addition, if a parent refuses to produce a child in pursuance of an order of the court relating to its custody, the court may issue a writ of habeas corpus commanding the production of the child [Form 348]. Disobedience of the command of the writ constitutes a contempt.¹ However, the taking of the infant under a warrant of arrest would seem preferable to the use of the writ of habeas corpus.2

An appeal by one of the parents from an order of custody should not stay the operation of the order. The child is no part of the contest between the parents. Pending the appeal it is essential that the child be lodged in the custody of some competent person and, unless the Court of Errors and Appeals supersedes the order of Chancery, the order should stand and be enforceable pending the appeal. § 458. 3 -Habeas Corpus. It is unusual to resort to the use of the writ in matrimonial causes. The jurisdiction of the court to adjudicate the question of custody is not, at any rate, dependent upon the presence of the child in court by force of the writ

Several reported cases may be observed in which the writ has been issued in a matrimonial cause. Application may be made to an Advisory Master in the vicinage under Rule 128e. Usually, however, if it is deemed necessary or advisable to bring the child before the court, it may be done by arresting the child on a bench warrant, eliminating the use of the complicated machinery of habeas corpus. If the order for custody is disobeyed, process of contempt is available to compel production of the child without resorting to the writ of habeas corpus. 

Jurisdiction of Chancery in Non-matrimonial § 459.

Causes. In addition to the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery over the custody of infants in matrimonial causes, the court exercises a jurisdiction in causes in which the parents seek no relief from the court affecting the marriage relation. The term "non-matrimonial causes" is intended to embrace proceedings for the custody of infants other than those ancillary to a suit for divorce, nullity of marriage, or for separate maintenance in this state. In the statute relating to minors the legislature has conferred certain jurisdiction on the court in non-matrimonial causes, but such statutory grants of authority cannot be said to restrict the general jurisdiction of the court over the custody of infants. Under its general jurisdiction the court may dispose of the custody of a child who is actually residing here although domiciled in another state.10

§ 463. Habeas Corpus. The origin of the writ of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum is not definitely known. In England originally it was issued as a means of relief from arrest or from forcible imprisonment under color of law. Later on and before the American Revolution the writ was employed in cases affecting children who were not under restraint by warrant of law. 

With us the jurisdiction of the Chancellor to issue the writ of habeas corpus is inherent 17 and in non-matrimonial cases involving the custody of infants the writ has been used frequently in the past. The office of the writ in cases involving infants is twofold. The writ may serve the function of a strict common law writ of habeas corpus to lift a restraint imposed unlawfully upon an infant. In such cases no provision is made by the Chancellor for the permanent custody of the infant.18 

The use of the writ, however, does not restrict the Chancellor to the exact limits of the writ in removing an unlawful restraint if the pleadings and proofs are addressed to the court to provide for the permanent custody of infants. "The jurisdiction of the court of chancery to settle and dispose of the care and custody of infants, through a procedure like this, is established. The parties, in their litigation, have, by their pleadings and proofs, presented issues within the cognizance of that court, under its general juris- 13. 1 R. S. (1937) 9:2-9 to 9:2-11.

subordinate the strict legal right of the father to considerations affecting the welfare of the child whether the legal right is asserted in a controversy between the father and mother,16 or between the father and a third person.17 "A child cannot be lawfully regarded as a mere inanimate chattel which must be restored to the lawful owner in all circumstances. Like the parent, the child has rights, and the strict legal rights of a father, as such, can only be enforced in this court with proper regard to the best interests of the child. A father cannot be denied the custody of his child merely because another person desires the custody and is better able to provide for the present or future interests of the child; but when it is entirely clear that a father cannot properly provide for his child, the silent but overpowering appeal of the best interests of the child must be respected. In such case custody is not refused the parent because another has the legal right of custody, but because the best interests of the child deny to this court the right 'to substitute a worse for a better custodian.' "18 

§ 465. Rights as Between Natural Parents. At common law the father has the legal right to the control and custody of his legitimate minor children.19 As between the father and mother, however, the strict right of the father has been subordinated in equity to the welfare of the child irrespective of statutory modifications presently to be noticed.20 

The common law right of the father to the custody of his legitimate minor children is subject to the control and regulation of the state and in controversies between the father and mother his common law right has been qualified by statutory enactments. 

The first statute enacted seems to be that of 1860, which directed that where the parents were separated, without being divorced, and the child was brought before the court on habeas corpus, the child, if within the age of seven years, was to be delivered to the mother.21 The restriction had no application, however, when the application was made by petition to the Chancellor under the

Act of 1871.22 This oddity on the statute books 23 was, however, discarded by subsequent legislation.24 

The Act of 1871 further curtailed the common law right of the father to the custody of his children. This legislation was originally contained in the Divorce Act 25 and provided that in a controversy between the parents they were, in the absence of misconduct, equally entitled to the custody of the children. It has since been transposed to the statute relating to minors with some modifications.20 This statute, giving each parent the equal right to custody in the absence of misconduct has been held to be declaratory of the rule existing in the Court of Chancery prior to its passage.27 The act has been held to be applicable when the proceeding for custody is before the Chancellor on habeas corpus under section 9:2-7 of the Revision 28 and applicable, as well, where the award is made under section 2:50-37 of the Revision as an adjunct to a decree of divorce.29 The statute does not forbid an award of custody to the party guilty of misconduct if the welfare of the child demands it. "The provision as to misconduct of either party was intended to give a preference to the innocent party, and to impose upon the party charged with or found guilty of misconduct under the statute the burden of overcoming this preference, and showing that, notwithstanding the misconduct and the inequality of rights, still the welfare of the children requires an award of the custody to the party guilty." "Misconduct," as used in the statute, means such conduct as to deprive the spouse of a moral right to the custody of his or her children.2

The legal rights of each parent have little vitality in determining, as between them, to whom the custody of the child shall be awarded. 

In a large measure the determination is within the discretion of the court. Each case must be determined on its own peculiar facts. In determining to which parent the child shall be delivered the court will consider the personal safety, morals, health and happiness of the child." The Court of Chancery will not convert a proceeding between parents for the custody of a child into a proceeding for the restitution of conjugal rights, of which it has no jurisdiction, by ordering the child into the joint custody of the parents at the father's house. Some cases illustrating the manner in which the court has exercised its discretion may be noted. For instance, in the absence of misconduct by the mother, it is customary to award to her the custody of a child of tender years, 10 particularly where in a suit for divorce the father has been adjudged guilty of adultery.11 Even where the mother has been adjudged guilty of adultery, the court may deem it best to give her a child of tender years. § 466. 

-Death of Parent Having Custody. Section 9:2-5 

of the Revision provides for the disposition of minor children in case the parent, in whose custody the child has been placed by the Court of Chancery, dies, or in case of the death of the parent in whose custody the children actually are when the parents have been living separately and no custody award has been made. This section was enacted in 1871 as a part of the Divorce Act, 18 but in 1902 was transplanted to the act concerning minors.19 The purpose of the statute evidently was to change what appears to have been the rule that upon the death of one parent the right to custody devolves upon the surviving parent.20 It seems to be conceded that the legislature may change the law with respect to whom the custody of the child may be awarded upon the death of one of the parents.21 [See Forms 342, 343].

In most instances the parent has been the moving party seeking to regain the custody of the child. disposing of the child's custody in such controversies in the Court of Chancery the strict legal right of the parents, especially of the father,24 must be considered, and such legal right will control the judgment of the court unless circumstances of weight and importance connected with the welfare of the child exist to overbear such legal right.25 The determination of the court has not been controlled by any statute when the proceeding is under the general jurisdiction of the court. 26 Section 9:2-4 of the Re vision 27 relates to controversies between the parents and has no application in contests between parents and third persons.28 

What are the "circumstances of weight and importance connected with the welfare of the child" which will overbear the strict legal right of the parents? Certainly the court will not, under the guise of the child's welfare, take, or keep, a minor from its parents because another person is in a more fortunate position to give the child greater advantages. "The millionaire cannot steal the child of the humble laborer and maintain its custody because the court finds that the interests of the child would be promoted by disregarding the parental right." 29 The court is anxious to maintain the natural relationship between parent and child whenever it can, and before it will subordinate the legal right of the parents, the circumstances must be such that, if the child is retained by, or returned to, its parents, the personal safety, morals, health or happiness of the child will be imperiled. § 468. -Rights as Between Persons Other Than Parents. 

As against strangers persons standing in loco parentis have the same right of custody to an infant as have the parents.22 This right is a strict legal right and "will control the judgment of the court, unless circumstances of weight and importance connected with the welfare of the child exist to overbear such strict legal right. If in addition to this strict legal right, the welfare of the infant is best served by awarding its custody to the persons standing in loco parentis, there is little hesitancy on the part of the court in doing so. Thus where the child's future might have been jeopardized by an adoption, the court awarded an infant to an orphanage, standing in loco parentis, as against one who conducted a private charity.24 Yet in a contest between the petitioning maternal grandparents of an orphaned infant and its paternal grandparents to whom the deceased father had delegated the care, custody and nurture of the infant, the court awarded the infant to its maternal grandparents for two months of each year where it appeared that each set of grandparents was fit and able properly to care for the child. The court deemed it to be for the best welfare of the child to make such award and in so doing declined to be bound by the father's selection of a guardian.25 In connection with contests between persons other than the parents of the infant reference should be made to certain provisions of the statute concerning minors.20

§ 469. -Illegitimate Children. The mother of an illegitimate child is its natural guardian and, in the absence of special circumstances, it may be said that she is entitled to the custody of the child.27 She has a superior natural right to the child's custody as against the putative father 28 and as against a stranger.20 Even as against the mother the court may allow the putative father reasonable access to the child if it is for the best interests of the child.¹ However, as in the case of legitimate offspring, the best interest of the illegitimate child is the controlling consideration in the Court of Chancery in determining to whom the custody shall be awarded. The peculiar facts of each case must be noticed. In one case the court upheld the right of the mother as against a stranger who took the child for adoption without the mother's consent. In another case the court permitted the State 

Board of Children's Guardians to place the child in the custody of its mother under its observation and direction. In a contest between the mother and putative father, the Court of Chancery, in a habeas corpus proceeding by the mother, has given effect to a voluntary agreement whereby the mother transferred the custody to the father by declining to award the custody to the mother in the absence of proof that the child's interests would thereby be best served.5

The statute relative to the custody of illegitimate children was originally enacted in the year 1913 and was intended to be declaratory of the law then existing." § 470. -Adopted Children. A step-parent as such has no right to the custody of a step-child, particularly as against the parent or a person standing in loco parentis to the child. Section 9:2-4 of the Revision, which provides that in controversies between parents the rights of both parents, in the absence of misconduct, shall be held to be equal, has no application in a controversy between a step-parent and parent or between a step-parent and a stranger.10 Nevertheless, if the step-parent stands in loco parentis to the child, he or she has the right of custody as against strangers, unless the step-parent is unfit and the welfare of the child requires a different custodian.11 In this connection certain provisions of the statute relative to minors should be considered.12 

§ 472. 

-Preference of Infant. In determining to whom the custody of a minor child shall be awarded it has been the practice for the court to examine the child, if of sufficient age and discretion, in order to ascertain his wishes in the matter. Such an examination may be conducted irrespective of whether the contest is between the parents, or between the parents and a third person, or between persons other than the child's parents. The examination of the child is not restricted to a strict common law writ of habeas corpus wherein the only purpose of the writ is to relieve an unlawful restraint, but it is proper to examine the child whether the proceeding for custody is under the general jurisdiction of the court aided by the writ of habeas corpus, or by petition to the Chancellor under the general jurisdiction of the court, or auxiliary to a suit for divorce.13

The predilection of the child is some evidence of what will best subserve the welfare of the child and is a circumstance which the court has taken into consideration in disposing of the child's custody. But by no means is the court conclusively bound by the 7. 1 R. S. (1937) 9:3-9.

Where the parent has transferred the custody of the child to another from the time of infancy and the child's welfare will be subserved best by leaving it with those who have cared for and nurtured it, the preference of the child is important. "In resolving the general question of what will best subserve the interest and happiness of the child, its own wish and choice may be consulted and given weight, if it be of an age and capacity to form a rational judgment. There is no fixed age which capacitates such choice. It depends upon the extent of its mental development. 17 "The wishes of children of sufficient capacity to form them are given especial consideration, where the parents have for a length of time voluntarily allowed their children to live in the family of others, and thus form home associations and ties of affection for those having their care and nurture, and when it would mar the happiness of the children to sever such ties." 18 Yet in the absence of an abandonment by the parent, or unfitness, the child's choice is of less significance, particularly where his preference is a result of influence by those claiming his custody.19

§ 474. 

Religion as Affecting Award. Religion has been a factor considered in awarding the custody of a child, but it has not always been a controlling element. It may be that the court will decline to award the custody to a person of the same religious beliefs as that of the child if other circumstances indicate that the best welfare of the child would be sacrificed. The natural right of the parents, the age of the child, the fitness of the persons seeking custody and the welfare of the child must also be considered. But few reported cases have touched upon religious considerations as affecting custody. In one case in a contest between the father and mother in a suit for divorce a promise made by the mother to a clergyman to rear the children in the religion of the father did not prevent the award to the mother who was of a different religious belief.29 In the Flynn v. Flynn case Vice Chancellor Stevenson dealt with the religious factor quite at length. 

In a contest between the child's step-mother and aunt, the father being dead, he awarded the custody of a six year old boy to the step-mother, notwithstanding that she was of a religious faith different from that of the child's deceased father. The Vice Chancellor declined to decide whether, if the step-mother failed to educate the child in the religion of his deceased father, the Court of Chancery would order in what denomination the child should be educated. The English authorities on the question were, however, discussed.¹ The subject of religion has also been discussed in custody cases wherein the parents have sought to regain possession from a denominational aid society, and where an adoptive mother has attempted to recover the custody of her child from a stranger.³

§ 475. -Access and Visitation. The right of access to an infant child is, in a measure, separate and distinct from the right to its custody, yet it has been held that such relief is properly a mere incident to a decree fixing the custody of an infant and that a bill for that purpose only will not lie in the Court of Chancery where the child is not before the court. The court was of the opinion that upon a petition, or bill, bringing the infant into court, or upon a habeas corpus under section 12 of the Minors' Act of 1902 (now section 9:2-7 of the Revision) it could make provision for access if it then concluded that the child should be committed to its present custodian, the mother." This was done in a subsequent case brought before the court on habeas corpus under section 12 (now section 9:2-7) where the father's prayer for custody was denied although his petition for custody omitted to pray for access in the event of his failure to obtain custody." 

Nevertheless, we are not without authority that the presence of the child before the court by force of the writ of habeas corpus, or otherwise, is not essential to the Chancellor's jurisdiction to award custody," and in one case observed, heard on petition, answer and replication, the court awarded a putative father access to illegitimate children after counsel on the argument declined to press his claim for custody, although it does not appear that the court by order confirmed the mother's right of custody or that the children were before the court.8

At any rate, in controversies involving the custody of a child it has been customary to make provision for access and visitation whether the contest is between the parents, or between the parents and a third person, or between persons other than the parents, if such provision is for the welfare of the child. The jurisdiction of the court to make such provision in divorce decrees in connection with an award of custody may be rested upon section 2:50-37 of the Revision providing that the court may make orders touching the "care, custody,-of the children,-as the circumstances of the parties and the nature of the case shall render fit, reasonable and just, " Other statutes expressly provide for the right of access and visitation in conjunction with custody awards, 10 but in the 4. 1 R. Cha 250 absence of statute the Court of Chancery under its general jurisdiction over the custody of infants 11 may make provision for access and visitation in connection with custody awards if it is for the welfare of the child. 

As to whether in a particular case the Court of Chancery will give a person the right of access and visitation to an infant depends largely on the circumstances. The question of access, like the question of custody, is one that must be considered in equity from the viewpoint of the best interests of the child.12 In controversies between parents, if it is for the welfare of the child, the father may be given access to the child although the mother is awarded its custody,13 or the court may deny the father the right of visitation.¹ If the father is awarded the custody of the child, the court may grant the mother the right of visitation, although in a suit for divorce she has been adjudged guilty of adultery.15 

When the child is committed to a person other than one of the parents the court may grant the right of visitation to the parents.10 

Thus where the court, at the mother's suggestion, awarded an infant's custody to a maternal aunt, the right of visitation was reserved to the father and to the paternal grandmother.17 In another instance, in a controversy between the father and the maternal grandfather who had the custody of the children, the custody of the infants was awarded to the grandfather subject to reasonable visitation by the father.18 Where a parent is awarded the custody of a child in the possession of grandparents, the court may provide for visitation by the grandparents if it is conducive to the best interests of the child.19 In a contest between maternal and paternal grandparents of an orphaned infant the maternal grand-

Section 9:2-2 of § 476. Removal of Children from State. 

the Revision provides that when the Court of Chancery has jurisdiction over the custody and maintenance of minor children 22 of parents divorced, separated or living separate, and such children are natives of the state, or have resided five years within its limits, they shall not be removed out of its jurisdiction against their own consent, if of suitable age 23 to signify the same, nor while under that age without the consent of both parents, unless the court, upon cause shown, shall otherwise order, and the court, upon application of any person in behalf of such minors, may require such security and issue such writs and processes as shall be deemed proper. This provision was enacted in 1871 as part of the Divorce Act,24 but in the year 1902 was transferred to the act concerning minors.25 [See Forms 337-341].

Section 9:2-2 is an express prohibition against the removal of the children specified "out of its jurisdiction" when "the court of chancery has jurisdiction" unless the conditions enumerated arise. 

Section 9:2-2 is unlike section 9:2-4 26 in that the prohibition against removal is not directed to the Court of Chancery. The power of the court to order a removal is recognized in the words "unless the court, upon cause shown, shall otherwise order." 27

Arrest of Minor. In recent years the practice of arresting a minor under a warrant has largely superseded the use of the writ of habeas corpus, where the circumstances justify precaution against the threatened removal, or abuse of the minor, or whenever the immediate production of the child before the court is deemed necessary and there is good cause to apprehend that an order to show cause may not be obeyed. Vincent v. Vincent.¹¹

§ 478. Foreign Decrees. The recognition of decrees or orders of foreign courts relating to the custody of children is governed by the rules of comity and, in the case of decrees or orders of sister states, is regulated, as well, by the full faith and credit clause of the Federal Constitution.12 Section 2:50-35 of the Revision 13 re lates to the extraterritorial effect of foreign decrees of divorce and of nullity of marriage and has no application to foreign decrees or orders affecting the custody of children except perhaps insofar as the validity of a custody order in a divorce or nullity suit may be dependent upon the validity of the decree of divorce or of nullity.

A foreign decree or order is given extraterritorial recognition if the foreign court had jurisdiction of the parties at the time of the adjudication. Such adjudication is conclusive of the status of the child and its parents as of the time the order was rendered, but it is not res judicata as to facts and circumstances affecting the child which have since arisen.14

ENFORCING THE AGREEMENT IN CHANCERY AND AT LAW 

§ 479. Enforcing the Separation. The law favors not only marriage, but, as well, the continued and normal cohabitation of the parties as man and wife. A separation agreement between husband and wife, insofar as it provides for a separation, is therefore much in disfavor and will not be enforced in equity or at law.2 

Either of the parties may terminate the separation by requesting a resumption of marital relations. Nevertheless, a separation of husband and wife by mutual consent is tolerated by the law. No legal machinery is available to compel them to live together if they wish to live apart, and not even is the suit for the restitution of conjugal rights available to the spouse who tires of separation. -Effect of Divorce or Pendency of Suit.¹ 

absence of a contrary provision in the agreement for maintenance, it is not terminated by the institution of a suit for divorce by the wife, or by the husband, or by the commencement of a suit by the wife for separate maintenance. But if the wife is awarded alimony pendente lite in the divorce or maintenance suit the agreement will not be enforced during the time the order is operative and complied with, although the award is less than the periodical payment stipulated in the agreement. 

In the absence of a provision in the agreement for maintenance to the contrary, an agreement executed during the marriage is not terminated by a decree of absolute divorce obtained in this state by the wife so as to preclude recovery of payments due after the decree. Yet, if the wife elects to apply for and is awarded permanent alimony, this would seem to render the agreement inoperative, whether the alimony award is greater or less than the sum stipulated in the agreement, at least while the order for alimony is being obeyed by the husband.10 Similarly, a decree for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision 11 would probably suspend the operation of the maintenance agreement. Without a qualifying clause in the agreement for maintenance, it is not abrogated by a subsequent decree of divorce obtained by the wife in another state, particularly where the agreement was executed pending the divorce proceeding in the other state.12 Nevertheless, if the wife obtains an award of alimony in this state after the entry of the foreign decree of absolute divorce at her suit,13 such award should suspend the operation of the maintenance agreement while the husband complies.

§ 487. -Enforcing the Agreement in Chancery and at Law. 

Agreements executed between husband and wife during the marriage without the interposition of a third person are void at law. 

In equity, however, such agreements are sub modo and to the extent that they are fair and equitable they have been enforced against the wife. If the husband comes into equity seeking to enforce an agreement with his wife, the burden is placed upon him to show the fairness of the agreement and the equities which call for its enforcement. Similarly, where the wife is party plaintiff, the husband, if he thinks the agreement unfair, must prove such fact in order to defeat recovery.20

Articles of separation, insofar as they provide for a separation, are unenforceable at law or in equity.27 Unenforceable also at law and in equity is the accessorial part of the articles relating to the wife's separate maintenance in the event of a future separation.28 Likewise condemned are agreements for maintenance, or in lieu of alimony, which have for their purpose the promotion of divorce.29 Until recently, however, the inherent jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery to enforce payments due under a noncollusive agreement in lieu of alimony, or payments accruing for the wife's separate maintenance under a provision contained in articles of separation operative in praesenti, was unquestioned.

The jurisdiction was inherited from the English Court of Chancery. Not only was the jurisdiction unquestioned, but it would seem to be constitutionally unquestionable, by virtue of Article X, Section 1, of the Constitution of 1844. Since the Court of Errors and Appeals is itself the Court of Chancery when it sits upon appeals from Chancery, we have the unusual situation of a court denying its own constitutional jurisdiction. 

No doubt the Court of Errors and Appeals was influenced by cases of unusual hardship caused by the financial depression then, and still, prevailing. It has always been a serious defect in the administration of this remedy that no flexibility was afforded. No allowance was made for changing circumstances of the parties. 

While the remedy might have been granted to the wife on condition that she took a decree for a smaller sum than her contract provided, the court was without authority to increase the sum contracted to be paid where the circumstances called for it. It was therefore considered that equity required strict adherence to the terms of the contract. It was for this reason that the court declined to allow defenses based upon the husband's change of financial circumstances. The resulting inflexibility was unfortunate, but was necessarily implicit in the form and theory of the remedy. The early English cases recognized this defect, and before the jurisdiction was finally settled there was much debate as to whether the remedy of specific performance ought to be extended to agreements between husband and wife, which ordinarily by their nature are not contracts in the true sense of the word because they do not give rise to the husband's obligation to support his wife, but are intended merely to liquidate or admeasure the quantum of that obligation under the circumstances prevailing at the time when they are made. Out of this early controversy the principle was finally settled in favor of such extension, for the practical reason that the only other remedy of the wife then available was the cumbersome, circuitous and unsatisfactory action at law by the creditor to whom the wife had pledged her husband's credit for necessaries.

Later on Chancery was given statutory jurisdiction to decree alimony and separate maintenance for the wife. This statutory jurisdiction as it has been developed and enlarged, is a much more flexible and equitable remedy than that of specific performance, and is to be preferred for that reason whenever it is ap-

§ 613 

SEPARATION AGREEMENTS 

plicable. But it does not apply in those cases where the husband's obligation arises from his contract rather than from his common law duty to support, as, for example, where the husband secures a decree of divorce from the bond of matrimony for the wife's matrimonial misconduct, and is therefore absolved from his common law duty to support. If he still remains under such obligation it must arise from his contract. If the wife cannot sue upon the contract she is without a remedy, unless it can be said that the contract amounts to a waiver by the husband of his defense that the decree of divorce terminates his liability to pay alimony. And it would seem that an agreement for the wife's support entered into in another state by the law of which state the contract is absolutely binding upon the husband may be entitled to the protection of the 14th Amendment of the Federal Constitution if sued on here. Similarly, such an agreement made in a foreign country whose law recognizes it as a binding and absolute contract, may be entitled to our recognition of it as such by virtue of treaty provisions. 

It would have been less confusing had the Court of Errors and Appeals based its recent decisions upon the ground that since the statutory remedy was available in those cases the Court of Chancery should have applied it in preference to the remedy of specific performance, upon the principle that as long as the husband's common law duty of support persists the parties are incompetent to make more than a sub modo contract with respect thereto. 

And this may be all that the Court of Errors and Appeals intended to hold in those cases. We must await a further exposition of its views before this subject can be clarified. 

The Court of Chancery in the State of Delaware, meanwhile, continues to exercise unquestioned jurisdiction to enforce by way of specific performance agreements for maintenance executed during the marriage, except in cases where there is an adequate remedy at law, as where a trustee is a party to the agreement." -At Law. Ne Exeat. In England the writ of ne exeat regno was a prerogative writ which originally was issued only for the purpose of the State, but which later was used in aid of the subjects 615

§ 489. —Application for Writ. 

It is not intended to treat of the application for the writ of ne exeat except in matrimonial causes, and in non-matrimonial causes heard before Advisory Masters. Application for the writ is made usually by the wife to secure the payment of alimony, and principally in suits by the wife for separate maintenance under section 2:50-39 of the Revision. § 490. Order for Writ. If from an examination of the pleadings and affidavits the court is satisfied that the writ should issue, an order for the writ is advised [Forms 358-360]. In recent years it has been the practice in some cases for the Advisory Masters to advise the order for the writ on the condition that the defendant may apply without notice to any Advisory Master in the vicinage wherein he may be apprehended and that a written notice shall be served with the writ advising the defendant of his right to make such application and listing the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of the Advisory Masters in the vicinage. 

Such an order tempers the severity of this type of equitable process. The order for the writ may be drafted by the solicitor and presented to the court when application is made. 

The court exercises a sound discretion in ordering the writ.19

Forms of writs without special provisions are ordinarily obtainable at the several Chancery Chambers, already signed by the Clerk, so that the writ may issue as soon as the order is advised. § 493. -Privilege from Arrest. As a general rule a non resident party to a civil suit, or a witness, including a prosecuting witness, is exempt from service of process, or civil arrest, including apprehension under a writ of ne exeat, while necessarily going to, staying at, or returning from the court." Residence in this connection means domiciles and the burden of proof is on the party or witness alleging non-residence as a basis for setting aside the service." -Liability of Sureties on Bond. The liability of the sureties. 

on a ne exeat bond, as on other bonds, is contractual. In some respects the obligations are the same as bail at common law." 

The extent of the liability of the sureties depends upon the form of the bond. The bond may be in common form or in form prescribed by Rule 227, but the sureties are nevertheless liable under a bond at variance with the terms prescribed by the rule when it is voluntarily entered into by them and accepted by the court. 

The condition of the bond in common form is that the defendant shall not depart or leave the state without the permission of the court [Form 370]. This condition is breached if the defendant leaves the state at any time without leave of the court. A single departure from the state without leave breaches the condition. If the defendant returns, the court may, however, remit the forfeiture.¹ 10

The condition of the Rule bond is that the defendant shall cause his appearance to be entered in the main suit and continue such appearance by a solicitor of the court, residing here, and that he shall at all times render himself amenable to the orders and processes of the court [Form 371]. The condition of the 

Rule bond is less rigorous than that of the bond in common form.¹¹ 

The condition is not breached by the departure of the defendant from the state without leave so long as he renders himself amenable to the orders and processes of the court. The condition of the Rule bond is not broken by defendant's failure or refusal to 11

The obligation of the sureties being contractual, they are discharged by the substitution of a different cause of action. Thus where the wife in her petition alleged extreme cruelty and prayed for a divorce from bed and board, the sureties were discharged by the substitution of a cause of action for separate maintenance.19 The death of the principal, although self-inflicted, entitles the surety to a discharge.20 The entry of the final decree in the cause does not, of itself, absolve the sureties, whether the bond is in common form,21 or executed in pursuance of Rule 227.22 Nor are the sureties released from their obligation under a Rule bond by reason of the execution of a subsequent bond to secure the payment of alimony ordered in the final decree, 23

The mere fact that the defendant has furnished security to secure his release from custody does not bar him from applying thereafter for a discharge of the writ.28 However, if he enters into an agreement with the complainant or petitioner by which the amount of bail is reduced, or the order for the writ is substantially modified, it would seem that under the doctrine of estoppel he is precluded by his agreement from asking for the discharge of the writ. But there is no objection to defendant's application for a discharge of the writ and, in the alternative, for a reduction of bail. 

The writ may be discharged and the bond given as security cancelled, whenever it appears that the writ was improvidently granted and should not have issued.29 The writ may be discharged and the bond ordered to be cancelled where the bill or petition does not state a cause of action in equity, or where the main proceeding was instituted in bad faith,2 or on the ground that service of the writ was void because it was executed on Sunday, or because the defendant at the time of service was privileged from arrest. The court may discharge the writ when it is satisfied from the affidavits of the defendant that he does not intend to depart from the state, or where the suit is by the wife for separate maintenance, that she abandoned her husband by unjustifiably refusing to go with him to another state. However, the court is not obliged to discharge the writ on the defendant's denial under oath that he intends quickly to depart from the state. The court will not discharge a writ obtained upon affidavits substantiating declarations and acts of the defendant as evidence of his intention to leave the state upon an answering affidavit by the defendant denying the intention.10 -Procedure. Application to discharge the writ of ne exeat is made in the main cause. It is not necessary to file a petition to discharge the writ, unless short notice is sought. Generally, the better practice is to proceed by affidavits and notice, when notice is necessary. The notice, when necessary, must set out the grounds relied upon for the vacation of the writ.11 The affidavits in support of the application for a discharge of the writ must be full and explicit and should show particularly and circumstantially that the defendant does not intend quickly to depart from the state if such is the fact.

Under Rule 168 five days' notice of the motion for the discharge of the writ must be given, unless the court otherwise orders. As explained above,12 the court may otherwise order by inserting in the order for the writ the condition that the defendant shall have the right immediately to apply ex parte to modify or vacate the writ and that written notice be given to the defendant advising him of such right and containing a list of the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of the Advisory Masters in the vicinage in which he is apprehended. Delay in moving the application may prompt the court to deny relief. In one instance an application, not made until the cause was noticed for final hearing, was refused.13 The application may be moved by the defendant although he has not answered the main cause.14

It has been held in the ordinary case that the defendant on this application is entitled to the benefit of his sworn answer, 15 but in suits for divorce the statute provides that the answer shall not be sworn to.16

The application for the discharge of the writ in matrimonial causes should ordinarily be made to the Advisory Master who advised the order for the writ, but, if he is unavailable, application may be made to any other Advisory Master in the vicinage, or elsewhere. If the court is satisfied that the writ should be vacated and the bond, if given, cancelled, an order will be made accordingly [Forms 374-380]. If the writ is discharged, the court may nevertheless direct the defendant to give security to abide the decree.¹7 

Although the writ is retained, the court may in its discretion permit the substitution of a bond to answer the decree, if the restraint of the writ interferes with the freedom of defendant's movement in business engagements outside of the state." 18 

§ 496. Civil Contempt. Contempts are classified as civil and criminal. In a civil contempt the proceeding is remedial; it is a step in the cause the object of which is to coerce one party for the benefit of the other to do or to refrain from doing some act specified in the order of the court. Hence, if imprisonment be ordered, it is remedial in purpose and coercive in character, and to that end must relate to something to be done by the defendant by the doing of which he may discharge himself. As quaintly expressed, the imprisoned man "carries the keys to his prison in his own pocket." Criminal contempts are offenses against organized society which, although they may arise in the course of private litigation, are not a part thereof, but, like other criminal offenses, raise an issue between the public and the accused. Hence, 13. Miller v. Miller, 1 N. J. Eq. 386, 388 (1831).

It is no defense that the order of the court is founded on error of law or of fact. The method of correcting such error is by appeal, and not by disobedience. Advice of counsel is not an excuse, although it may be considered in mitigation of punishment.10 Ignorance of the law is no defense.¹¹ 

However, it may be shown that the Court of Chancery was without jurisdiction to make the order alleged to have been contemned.12 Any facts existing which would support a motion to discharge from custody 13 may be shown on the application to hold the party in contempt.14

In civil contempts the purpose is to compel the party in default to comply with the order or decree of the court for the benefit of the other party. The proceeding is essentially remedial, not punitive. -Procedure by Writ of Attachment. 

may be employed to bring an alleged contemnor before the court is by petition for a writ of attachment. This is a body attach- 

But as Vice Chancellor Howell pointed out, the procedure in recent years has been by way of order to show cause rather than by way of attachment or committal. In injunction cases the statute recognizes the procedure by body attachment." In pursuance of the writ the sheriff apprehends the party. The writ of attachment is returnable at such time and place as the court shall direct (Rules 222, 229). Imprisonment is proper in alimony cases, but such confinement is not for a fixed period but only until the contemnor complies with the order of the court or shows his inability.18 Imprisonment until the further order of the court is improper.19 If the court undertakes to fix a punishment, its order must be final and entire for the particular contempt and may not be broken up into portions.20

The warrant for commitment [Form 392] is directed to the sheriff of the county in which defendant may be apprehended. In alimony cases the amounts due must be specified in the warrant of commitment.25 

After apprehending the defendant, the sheriff makes his return that he has him in custody, or has discharged him upon payment of the amounts specified [Forms 393, 394]. A husband adjudged guilty of contempt for failure to comply with an order for alimony may be discharged on condition. Thus the discharge may be conditioned upon the transfer of rents to a receiver to be applied towards the payment of alimony. Although the husband's previous conduct has been contemptuous, if it appears that he cannot pay all of the amount required, he is sometimes released upon payment of whatever he can pay. The court is mindful that his destitute wife and children may suffer from his prolonged incarceration more than he will. This consideration is apt to weigh heavily with the court where it appears that the defendant has a position or may secure one upon his release, particularly if the defendant is willing to execute an equitable assignment of a portion of his wages to his wife and children and the employer is willing to honor it. If the husband is discharged upon certain conditions and he accepts the benefit of the order, he may not by appeal attack one or more of the conditions imposed." 

A husband adjudged guilty of contempt for failure to pay alimony is entitled to a discharge where the order adjudging him in contempt, or the warrant of commitment, does not specify the amount to be paid. Application for a discharge may be made by petition in the cause, duly verified, and should be made on notice (Rule 168) to the Advisory Master who advised the order adjudging the defendant in contempt. A form of order discharging defendant is included hereinafter [Form 396] which may be varied to suit the particular case.

of Chancery.10 This rule applies where the order allowed is to show cause why the husband should not be adjudged in contempt for his failure or refusal to pay alimony.¹¹

An appeal lies from an order adjudging a party in civil contempt. The statute now expressly allows an appeal "for acts done or omitted elsewhere than in the presence of the court." 12 

This act was originally passed in the year 1909 for the purpose of allowing appeals from criminal contempts not committed in facie curiae.18 It applies to civil contempts as well, but the right of appeal from orders adjudging a person in civil contempt had been recognized for some years before the enactment of the statute.¹4 

The appeal must be taken within three months.15

An appeal from an order allowing alimony pendente lite in a suit for divorce stays the operation of the order without a special direction of the court under Rule 161, so that the order may not be enforced 10 against the husband by process of contempt.17

Similarly, an appeal by the husband from a final decree for separate maintenance automatically stays the operation of the decree so that there may not be an adjudication for contempt.18

On appeal from an order adjudging a party in civil contempt, the appellate court may reverse the conviction on the ground that the Court of Chancery was without jurisdiction to make the order alleged to have been contemned.19 Thus on appeal from an order adjudging the husband in contempt for failure or refusal to comply with a personal order for alimony the appellate court may reverse the conviction on the ground that the court was without personal jurisdiction of the husband to award alimony.20 The

Criminal Contempt. Criminal contempts are offenses against organized society which, although they may arise in the course of private litigation, are not a part thereof, but, like other criminal offenses, raise an issue between the public and the accused. If imprisonment is adjudged, it is punitive in purpose and definite in character.23 Criminal contempts are of two kinds: (1) direct, (2) constructive or consequential. Direct contempts are those committed in facie curiae, although it is not essential that they be committed before a judge in open court.24 Consequential or indirect contempts are those committed at a distance from the court which plainly tend to create a disregard of the authority of the court.25 The statute with respect to what may constitute a contempt has been held to be unconstitutional so far as it may be claimed to apply to the Court of Chancery.20 27 Examples of criminal contempts which may arise in the course of matrimonial litigation are the making of false affidavits, as a false affidavit by the wife on an application for allowances

§ 506. 

-Defenses. While a disavowal of any intention to commit a contempt may be reason for inflicting less or no punishment,18 it is not a defense, 19 especially where the acts constituting the contempt are admitted, or where a contempt is clearly apparent from the circumstances surrounding the commission of the act.20 Ignorance of the law,21 or acting upon the advice of counsel, is no excuse for the commission of a contempt.22 Nor is carelessness or forgetfulness.28 § 507. -Application. In matrimonial causes, if the contempt occurs in facie curiae, the Advisory Master may direct the Sergeant-at-Arms to hold the respondent in his custody until an order and warrant may be prepared and signed, and may adjudge him guilty of contempt and impose a penalty without further formality or delay. Criminal contempts are entitled "In Chancery of New Jersey. In the matter of (naming the respondent) charged with contempt of court." 24

If the contempt is not committed in facie curiae, the accused must be given ample notice and a full opportunity to defend.25 

It is not essential that the proceeding be initiated by the court on its own motion.26 It may be brought to the attention of the court by a solicitor in the cause. In the case of perjury, prosecution for criminal contempt should be instituted within two years from

The rules governing the hearing in other criminal contempts ordinarily govern. Generally, the respondent is entitled to the substantial rights of a person accused of crime. He is entitled to the right of an accused that the facts by which his guilt is determined shall be established by the oaths of witnesses subject to cross-examination, unless he has either expressly or by implication waived the right thus intended for his protection. But the respondent may waive the right of an accused to have his guilt established by the oaths of witnesses subject to cross-examination and impeachment in cases where he has been served with due and proper notice of the proceeding against him and fails to appear in person or by counsel. -Extent of Punishment. The statute providing for punishment for disobedience of orders of the court does not apply to criminal contempts. The extent of punishment is discretionary with the court, and in the absence of abuse will not be disturbed on appeal. The punishment may consist of a fine, imprisonment, or both, or even to the confiscation of the estate of the contemnor. 

But the Court of Chancery, being a court of conscience, tempers justice with mercy, and in passing sentence does not seek revenge or enrichment at the expense of the offender, but acts to protect its own honor and dignity as a branch of government and to compel respect for its orders and decrees. The statute limiting fines to fifty dollars does not apply to criminal contempts.10 If imprisonment is ordered, it is for a fixed period of time and not until the contemnor complies with an order of the court. The court may sentence the contemnor to the state prison, even at hard labor if it sees fit.11

§ 510. -Costs and Counsel Fees. In criminal contempts costs, and a counsel fee for the petitioner, may be assessed against a respondent adjudged guilty.18 Conversely, costs, including a reasonable allowance for counsel fee may be awarded the successful defendant against the petitioner.19 § 511. -Appeal.20 Formerly, there was no appeal from an order of the Court of Chancery adjudging a person guilty of criminal contempt except for lack of jurisdiction.21 Beginning in the year 1909 the statute has allowed appeals from orders adjudging a person in contempt of the Court of Chancery "for acts. done or omitted elsewhere than in the presence of the court." 22
