§ 512. Sequestration; Statutory Provisions. The statutes provide for the issuance of the writ of sequestration as original process in the case of absent defendants and as final process in execution of an order,or decree rendered in personam. -Original Process. There are two different statutes providing for the issuance of the writ of sequestration as original process. 

In suits by the wife for separate maintenance the writ may issue as original process under section 2:50-40 of the Revision (formerly contained in section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907). 

2:50-40. When a husband cannot be found within this state to be served with process, his estate, property and effects within this state and the rents and profits thereof may be sequestered to compel his appearance and performance of any decree or order which may be made in the suit. Such process of sequestration shall be issued only upon special order therefor, to be made upon proof of the claim alleged in the bill and that the defendant cannot be found within the state for the service of process.

Upon process of sequestration a bond, as provided in cases of ne exeat, may be given in discharge of the writ and the sum in which the party shall give bond, with sufficient surety, shall be indorsed upon the writ in words at length. Where the proceedings are by process of sequestration and the defendant does not appear, the decree shall be enforceable only out of and against the estate sequestered. 

Moreover, a general statute relative to the issuance of the writ exists. This statute was originally enacted in the year 1919 as part of the Chancery Act and now constitutes sections 2:29-88 to 

2:29-109 of the Revision. 

25. In re Hendricks, 113 N. J. Eq. 93, 98, 166 Atl. 211 (E. & A. 1933). 26. 1 R. S. (1937) 2:15-12.

§ 

651 

SEQUESTRATION LIBERAL CONSTRUCTION OF STATUTE. 

2:29-88. This article is remedial, provides additional remedies, and shall be liberally construed to effect its purpose, which is to subject the property of nonresidents to the satisfaction of claims cognizable in a court of equity in analogy to attachment proceedings at law; nor shall it be so construed as to circumscribe or impair any power or jurisdiction and (sic) possessed by the court of chancery. 

A corporation shall be deemed nonresident when it is not incorporated under the laws of this state and has no license to transact business in this state, or when it has no agent in this state upon whom process may be served. 

WHEN WRIT Issues. 

2:29-89. In any proceeding commenced in the court of chancery in which a money decree is prayed against a defendant, and it shall be made to appear, by affidavit, that the defendant is a nonresident and has property, real or personal, moneys, effects, rights or credits within this state, the court may, upon the filing of the bill or petition or at any time. thereafter, issue its writ or writs of sequestration directed to the sheriff of any county in which such property may be situate, or to any master of the court, commanding such sheriff or sheriffs or master to take into his or their possession such property, and hold the same subject to the orders and decrees of the court.

ISSUANCE AGAINST DECEDENT'S ESTATE. 

2:29-90. The writ of sequestration may also issue against an executor, administrator, trustee, heir or devisee in all cases in which it might have been issued against a decedent immediately prior to his decease; and all real estate descended from or devised by such decedent to the heir or devisee may be taken under the writ in the same manner as personal estate in the hands of the executor, administrator, trustee or other person may be so taken. The executor, administrator, trustee, heir, devisee and such other persons, or any or all of them, may be joined as defendants in the same proceeding.

8512 

 ISSUANCE WHERE AMOUNT CERTAIN OR UNCERTAIN. 

2:29-91. The writ of sequestration may issue in any case where the amount demanded is uncertain, as well as in cases where it is certain. If certain, the writ shall command the officer to sequester the property to answer the demand of the complainant or petitioner for the amount demanded; if uncertain, to answer the demand of the complainant or petitioner according to the prayer of the bill or petition, reciting sufficient of the prayer as to indicate the nature of the relief prayed.

PROPERTY TO BE TAKEN UNDER WRIT; RELEASE; ERROR IN STATING AMOUNT DUE. 

2:29-92. Upon the issuance of a writ of sequestration the court may, by order, direct what property and of what amount in value shall be taken, and may, at any time in the course of the proceedings, issue alias writs to take additional property, and may release property from the operation of the writ or writs. No error in stating the amount demanded shall invalidate the writ or proceedings thereunder, but the writ and proceedings shall remain effective to secure the amount finally found due from defendant to complainant or petitioner.

EVALUATION OF PROPERTY. 

2:29-93. When it shall be necessary to determine the value of property, the court may proceed either by reference to a master or in such other way as it shall deem proper. 

MANNER OF EXECUTING WRIT. 

2:29-94. The writ of sequestration may be executed by the officer to whom directed, by taking possession of the property of defendant and may be executed in the same manner provided by law for the execution of writs of attachment at law; and such officer shall have the same powers and authority to reduce the property of defendant to his possession, to discover property of a defendant, to avoid alleged liens or charges, as a sheriff or auditor has or may have under a writ of attachment at law.

§ 653 

SEQUESTRATION WHEN WRIT BINDS DEFENDANT'S PROPERTY. 

2:29-95. A writ of sequestration shall bind the personal property, including moneys and effects and rights and credits of a defendant from the time of its execution, and the real estate of a defendant in the state, from the time it is recorded in the office of the clerk of the supreme court, or in any county, from the time it is recorded in the office of the county clerk thereof.

RECORDING Of Writ by Supreme CourT AND COUNTY Clerk. 

2:29-96. The clerk of the supreme court and the clerks of the various counties shall record writs of sequestration, upon the lodgment with them of certified copies thereof, in the same manner, in the same books and for the same fees as writs of attachment are directed to be recorded. 

PROCEDURE AFTER ISSUANCE; NOTICE. 

2:29-97. In a proceeding in which a writ of sequestration issues as herein provided, the cause shall proceed against the nonresident defendant as in other cases in which the court is authorized to proceed against nonresidents. 

The notice served or published shall contain a statement that a writ of sequestration has issued and that the property of the defendant taken thereunder within the state will be taken to satisfy such order or decree as the chancellor may make in the cause.

NOTICE TO DEFENDANT; ALIAS NOTICE IF FURTHER PROPERTY 

SEIZED. 

2:29-98. Within twenty days after the actual execution of a writ or alias writ, notice shall be given to the defendant, as in case of absent defendants, of the property taken under such writ or alias writ, and the defendant shall have until the time stated in such notice, which time shall be fixed by the court as in case of absent defendants, to appear specially or generally. Such notice may be contained in the notice given in pursuance of section 2:29-97 of this title. If, after the giving of such notice, other property be taken under such writ or alias writ, a similar notice must be again given, and

8512 

no property not seized under the writ prior to final order or decree, and of the seizure of which notice shall have been given as heretofore provided, shall be taken to satisfy the order or decree.

GENERAL OR SPECIAL APPEArance; ReleASE OF PROPERTY; 

BOND. 

2:29-99. The defendant may appear generally or specially in the cause. If he appears generally, the property seized under the writ may be released by the court, upon his giving bond with sufficient surety in such sum, not exceeding the value of the property, as the court may direct, conditioned to pay the sum mentioned in the bond as the court of chancery in the cause, shall, by order or decree, direct; or the property may be released without bond, if the court so order. 

If he appears specially, the property seized may be released upon his giving bond with sufficient surety, either in an amount equal to the value of the property seized, conditioned that the obligors will pay the sum mentioned in the bond as the court of chancery shall, by order or decree made in the cause, direct, or in an amount to be fixed by the court, conditioned to pay and satisfy any order or decree the court may make in the cause.

SPECIAL APPEARANCE; EFFECT OF ORDER OR DECREE. 

2:29-100. If the defendant appears specially, the order or decree made in the cause shall be effective only as against property seized prior to the entry of the final order or decree, unless the court have jurisdiction, not depending in anywise upon any provisions of this article, to make an order or decree generally effective.

QUASHING OF WRIT. 

2:29-101. A motion to quash the writ of sequestration may be made under special appearance on five days' notice, or such other time as the court may direct, to complainant or petitioner, on which motion affidavits or other proof, taken as the court may direct, may be considered, and the court shall determine whether the writ shall stand upon the proofs as they appear on such hearing.

§ 655 

SEQUESTRATION ADVERSE CLAIMANTS OF PROPERTY. 

2:29-102. Adverse claimants of any property taken by virtue of the writ of sequestration may apply, by petition in the cause, to the court of chancery for the release of any property taken, and that court may, upon such application, upon such notice to such persons as it may, by order, direct, determine the rights of adverse claimants in such property, provided that such remedy shall not deprive adverse claimants of any right which they would have at law or in equity as in cases of property taken under execution out of the court of chancery. If adverse claimants shall, however, apply to the court of chancery for a determination of their rights, they shall be held to have waived any other remedy.

DISPOSITION OF PROPERTY TO SATISFY DECREE. 

2:29-103. The property taken under the writ of sequestration may be sold or disposed of by the officer to whom the writ is directed or by any officer appointed by the court, to satisfy the final decree in the same manner as property may be sold or disposed of under a writ of execution out of the court of chancery. It shall not be necessary, after final order or decree, to issue a writ of execution; but the court may direct the officer to proceed under the writ of sequestration to dispose of the property to satisfy the order or decree. 

CONVERSION OF PROPERTY LIABLE TO DEPRECIATION. 

2:29-104. The court of chancery may, at any time during the course of the proceedings, if it appear that the property seized is liable to depreciate in value, direct its conversion into cash, upon such notice to such persons as the court may, by order, direct.

APPOINTMENT AND POWERS OF RECEIVER. 

2:29-105. The court of chancery may, at any time during the course of the sequestration proceeding, appoint a receiver, with all the powers of the sheriff or master and with such other powers, including that of continuing a business, that the court may give a receiver of property in its custody.

§ 512 

 SEIZURE OF FURTHER PROPERTY AFTER FINAL ORDER 

or Decree. 

2:29-106. If, after final order or decree in the cause, it appears that defendant has property within the state not seized, the court may reopen the proceedings and direct the seizure of such property, and then proceed to final order or decree and the satisfaction thereof, in the manner herein provided.

DEATH OF DEFENDANT DOES NOT ABATE. 

2:29-107. If a defendant dies after issuance of a writ of sequestration as herein provided, the proceedings thereunder shall not be thereby abated or discontinued, but shall be carried on to final determination as if the death had not intervened, upon the suggestion of the death upon the record and the revival of the suit as in other cases; and all proceedings and deeds had and made in such case shall be valid and effectual in law as if had and made in the lifetime of the defendant.

ERRORS OF FORM OR SUBSTANCE; AMENDMENT. 

2:29-108. Errors of form or substance which do no substantial damage shall not vitiate the sequestration proceeding, and the court may, at any stage of the proceedings, permit amendments of the pleadings, affidavits and process, or the submission of additional affidavits.

POWER OF CHANCELLOR TO MAKE RULES, ETC. 

2:29-109. The chancellor may make such rules or special orders as he deems necessary for the effectual carrying out of the purpose of this article, and may prescribe the form of writs, notices and process. 

-Final Process. Section 2:50-37 of the Revision (formerly section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907) provides for the issuance of the writ in execution of an order or decree for alimony, etc. rendered in personam. For convenience the statute, as amended in 1938, is here set out. The provisions relating to sequestration are placed in italics.

SEQUESTRATION 

2:50-37. Pending a suit for divorce or nullity, brought in this State or elsewhere, or after decree of divorce, whether obtained in this State or elsewhere, the Court of Chancery may make such order touching the alimony of the wife, and also touching the care, custody, education and maintenance of the children, or any of them, as the circumstances of the parties and the nature of the case shall render fit, reasonable and just, and require reasonable security for the due observance of such orders, and upon neglect or refusal to give such reasonable security, as shall be required, or upon default in complying with the order, may award and issue process for the immediate sequestration of the personal estate, and the rents and profits of the real estate of the party so charged, and appoint a receiver thereof, and cause such personal estate and the rents and profits of such real estate, or so much thereof as shall be necessary, to be applied toward such alimony and maintenance as to the said court shall from time to time seem reasonable and just, or enforce the performance of the said orders by such other lawful ways and means as is usual, and according to the source and practice of the Court of Chancery; orders so made may be revised and altered by the court from time to time as circumstances may require.

The general statute pertaining to the issuance of the writ of sequestration as final process is section 2:29-63 of the Revision. 

2:29-63. When a complainant obtains a decree in the court of chancery the court may: a.

Issue process for the immediate sequestration of the real and personal estate of the defendant, or so much thereof as may be sufficient to satisfy the demand of the complainant in the decree specified, with costs, and the court shall order the decree to be satisfied out of the sequestered property, according to the true intent and meaning of the decree. 

§ 513. Sequestration as Original Process. The writ of se questration issues out of the Court of Chancery as original and as final process. In England the writ as original process was issued by the Court of Chancery under its inherent jurisdiction at least to compel the appearance of a defendant.27 But in New Jersey there appears to be some doubt whether the Court of Chancery 

27. See cases cited in Maloney v. Maloney, 12 N. J. Misc. 397, 405, 174

Atl. 28 (1934); 24 R. C. L. p. 785 §§ 3, 4.

§ 513 

has inherent power to issue the writ as original process in cases where a money decree is sought, 28 although there appears to be an inherent jurisdiction in the court to issue the writ to compel an appearance or to enforce an order of the court. At any rate, the court has been given statutory authority to issue the writ as original process in suits for a money decree. In the year 1919 a statute was enacted allowing the issuance of the writ as original process against property of a nonresident in any proceeding in which a money decree is prayed for. This statute became section 

2:29-89 of the Revision. It conforms to the requirement of "due process." 20 The statute is remedial and is to be construed liberally to effect its purpose which is to subject the property of nonresidents to the satisfaction of claims cognizable in a court of equity in analogy to attachment proceedings at law.¹ 

Section 2:29-89 applies to any proceeding commenced in the 

Court of Chancery in which a money decree is prayed for against a nonresident defendant. The suit must be one in which a money decree is sought.2 The writ may issue in any case where the amount demanded is uncertain, as well as in cases where it is certain, and may issue in favor of a nonresident as well as a resident, on a claim arising within or without the state.* In matrimonial litigation the writ issues out of the Court of Chancery as original process principally to insure the payment of alimony or maintenance to be awarded to the wife and children, where it is impossible for the court to obtain personal jurisdiction of the husband for the purpose of rendering a decree in personam." 

In suits for separate maintenance against a husband who cannot be found within the state the writ as original process issues in pursuance of section 2:50-40 of the Revision, although the general statute regulating the issue of the writ where a money decree is prayed for [1 R. The provision for sequestration in separate maintenance suits was originally enacted in the year 1902, and became a part of section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907. The statute is constitutional. A subsequent conveyance of real estate by a husband is subordinate to the lien created by the execution of a writ of sequestration as original process in a suit by a wife for separate maintenance under section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907 [now section 2:50-40 of the Revision]. The effect of the execution of the writ of sequestration as original process in separate maintenance suits is to place a lien on the husband's property from the time of the levy, which lien persists for the benefit of the wife until it has been discharged by the order of the court or by the husband's performance of the decree. The lien created by a writ of sequestration issued in a suit by the wife for separate maintenance is superior to judgments obtained after the writ is issued and executed. Moreover, a writ of sequestration issued in a separate maintenance suit has been held to be prior to an earlier undisclosed assignment of part of the husband's interest in an estate, and prior to an earlier judgment on which no execution was issued or levy made." In a suit for divorce where the writ issued as final process in execution of an order for alimony, it has been held that the execution of the writ of sequestration, and possession by a receiver, can reach only the rents and profits of the real estate and that the fee continues to be liable to execution on a judgment at law.

§ 522. -Adverse Claimants. When the writ issues as original process under the general statute, section 2:29-102 of the Revision provides that adverse claimants of any property taken may apply by petition in the cause [Form 421] for the release of the property and the court may upon such notice to such persons as it may by order direct, determine the rights of the adverse claimants. The notice is ordinarily by an order to show cause directed to the sheriff, or master, and the complainant in the main cause [Form 422]. Upon determination of the rights of adverse claimants an order is entered [Form 423]. The statute does not deprive adverse claimants of any right which they would have at law or in equity as in cases of property taken under execution out of the Court of Chancery, but if the adverse claimants do apply in the cause, they are held to have waived any other remedy. 

This statute (section 2:29-102) applies where sequestration is allowed as original process in proceedings for alimony pending a suit for divorce or subsequent to decree of divorce, because in such cases the proceeding for the writ is under the general statute. Moreover, section 2:29-102 would seem to apply in cases where the writ issues as original process in a separate maintenance suit under section 2:50-40.8 

§ 523. -Sale and Conversion of Property; Receiver. Un der the general statute regulating the issuance of the writ of sequestration as original process section 2:29-103 provides that the property taken may be sold or disposed of by the officer to whom the writ is directed or by any official appointed by the court, to satisfy the final decree in the same manner as property is sold or disposed of under a writ of execution [Form 428]. It is not necessary to take out a writ of execution to satisfy the final order or decree. A sale of the property under the writ of sequestration dispenses with the need of a writ of execution. Under the general statute [1 R. S. (1937) 2:29-104] the property seized under a writ of sequestration as original process may be converted into cash if it is liable to depreciate in value [Form 437]. Notice must be given to such persons as the court may by order direct. Furthermore, under section 2:29-105 the court may appoint a receiver with all the powers of a sheriff or master and with other powers, including that of continuing the business [Forms 429, 438-441].

Sequestration as Final Process. As final process in execution of a decree or order of the court rendered in personam, the writ is resorted to infrequently. As final process the writ may issue under section 2:29-63 of the Revision which is a statute of general application in the Court of Chancery.12 But in matrimonial causes the writ as final process issues under section 2:50-37 of the Revision 13 (formerly section 25 of the Divorce Act of 1907) as a means of enforcing orders for alimony, etc., in suits for divorce and nullity of marriage, and under section 2:50-39 of the 

Revision (formerly section 26 of the Divorce Act of 1907) for the purpose of enforcing orders and decrees made in suits for separate maintenance. Sequestration in such cases is for the purpose of enforcing a decree or order rendered in personam. In McGuinness v. McGuinness it was held that the court must have had personal jurisdiction of the husband to enter a personal order or decree against him before the writ of sequestration as final process will be effective.14 The allowance of the writ as original process by section 2:50-40 of the Revision does not validate a writ of sequestration issued as final process in execution of an order or decree

Under section 2:50-37 of the Revision which governs the issuance of the writ as final process in alimony cases, only the personal estate and the rents and profits of the real estate of the husband may be applied towards the payment of alimony and maintenance.15 The statute does not provide for the sale of the husband's real estate, and it would seem that the general statute relative to the issuance of the writ as final process [1 R. S. (1937) 

2:29-63] does not apply. Nor does the general statute relating to the issuance of the writ as original process and providing for the sale of the property of the defendant apply [1 R. S. (1937) 2:29103].

As final process in execution of an order or decree in personam for alimony, etc., a petition [Form 413] is filed, ordinarily with the Advisory Master who advised the order or decree. The order for the writ may be drafted as in Form 414.
